**The phase rule: `not supported yet`.** While Sea v1 is built phase by phase (§8), a program that
uses a construct the current compiler does not implement yet stops with the compile error `not
supported yet: %s` (code 259, `NOT_SUPPORTED`; driver status 1), reported by pass 2a (by `seaname` at
an item or in a signature, by `seacheck` elsewhere: "Which program reports it" below; pass 1
parses the whole grammar of LANGUAGE.md Appendix A from phase 1 on, so syntax errors are always
the real ones). It takes part in pass 2a's plain source order with every other pass-2 error: the
first error in source order is reported, whichever kind it is. Its position is the AST node that
the table's row names, and of several such nodes the first in source order: for a `str` local
its declaring `pname` (or `for` node), for a `str` parameter its `param` node, for a `str` result
the result's `type` node, for a default argument the `param` node, for a named argument the
`narg` node, for a library function the `call`, for a `for` over anything but a range the
`for` node, for `+` or a comparison on `str` operands the operator node. The format literal of
`printf` is not a `strings` construct, and neither is a string literal argument of `printf`: a
misplaced one is reported by the format checks (`format "%d" expects an integer or f64, found
str`). The `%s` is one of the words below. It is
not a rule of the language: LANGUAGE.md describes v1 complete, and a phase's compiler is a
conforming v1 compiler for the programs it accepts. When v1 is complete (phase 10) no construct is
reported any more; the message is retired and its code stays reserved, never reused. In phase 1
(the scalar core, §8) these constructs are reported, with these words:

| Construct (phase 1) | `%s` |
|---------------------|------|
| an array type, array literal, indexing, `$`, a range used as a value, a `for` over anything but a range, a view | `arrays` |
| a `struct` item, a struct type, a struct literal, a field access or projection | `structs` |
| a record literal or record type | `records` |
| a `match` statement | `match` |
| a `str` other than a string literal that is the argument of a `%s` conversion of `printf`: the `str` type, a `str` local, parameter or result, `+`, comparisons or `str(x)` on strings, a string literal anywhere else | `strings` |
| an `elemental fn` | `elemental functions` |
| a named argument | `named arguments` |
| a parameter default (reported at the `param` node) | `default arguments` |
| `%` with an `f64` operand (it needs the exact `fmod` of LANGUAGE.md §6.6) | `f64 %` |
| a handle type | `handle types` |
| a call of a library function other than `printf`, `now`, `f64`, `i64` and `idiv` (LANGUAGE.md §10–§13), and from phase 3 `log`, `exp`, `sin`, `cos`, `pow` and `hypot` (§4.10.5) | its name, e.g. `sqrt` |

Included in phase 1, so not reported: `const` items, the constants `pi inf nan eps`, `i64`, `f64`
and `bool` scalars, every scalar operator except those above, `if`/`while`/`for` over ranges,
`break`/`continue`, functions with scalar parameters and results, `ref` parameters of scalar
locals, multiple results, and `printf` with `%d %i %f %F %e %E %g %G %s`. Each later phase of §8
removes the rows it implements from this table, together with its tests. Because named
arguments, struct literals and fixed-size arrays are reported first, the errors 204–208,
216–222, 224 and 225 cannot occur in phase 1.

**The phase rule in phase 4** (sub-phases 4d–4h, §8). Each sub-phase removes from the table
above exactly the constructs it implements, in the same change as its tests; until then a
construct keeps its row and its words. The `arrays` row is removed in two steps and the library
row loses names in every sub-phase:

| Sub-phase | No longer reported (implemented) | Still reported, with these words |
|-----------|----------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| 4d | dynamic array types `T[]`, `T[,]` of `f64`, `i64`, `bool` (locals, parameters, results, `ref` parameters, annotations); indexing by scalar indices (read, `=` and `op=` of one element); `$` in a scalar index; a `for` over a vector; the library functions `zeros`, `ones`, `filled` (with an `f64`, `i64` or `bool` value), `len`, `rows`, `cols`, `numel`, and on scalars `abs`, `sign`, `sqrt`, `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc`, `round`, `isnan`, `min`, `max`, `where`, `ind2sub`, `sub2ind` (Decision 23) | `arrays` for: an array literal, a range used as a value, an index that is a range, `:`, an index vector or a mask (at the index's node), a view (`.T`, `.flat`, `.col`, `.row`, at the `dot` node, whose position is the start of its operand, §3.3), a fixed-size array type (at its `type` node, §3.4.2), an element-wise operator or comparison with an array operand (at the operator node), an array argument of an elemental library function (at the `call`), `dyn`, `fix` and an array conversion `f64(a)`/`i64(a)` (at the `call`/`cvt` node); `strings` for `str[]` and every other `str` use of the phase-1 row; `structs` for a struct element type; the name `max` or `min` for a call of `max` or `min` with one argument (the reduction of LANGUAGE.md §10.5, 4f), at the `call`, while an array argument of the two-argument form is `arrays` |
| 4e | every remaining `arrays` construct: array literals and concatenation (Decision 20; of `f64`, `i64`, `bool` elements), range values (also as the vector of a `for`), ranges, `:`, steps, index vectors and masks in reads, `=` and `op=`, views, fixed-size arrays of `f64`, `i64` and `bool` (types, locals, parameters, `ref` parameters, results and tuple components: Decision 32), `dyn`, `fix`, element-wise operators, comparisons and logic with broadcasting, array conversions, `where` and the elemental library functions on arrays (`ind2sub` with a scalar first argument and an array second one included: Decision 33) | the `arrays` row is gone; a literal of `str` or struct elements is `strings` or `structs` (at the `arr` node); a fixed-size type of `str` or struct elements is `strings` or `structs` (at its `type` node); `max(v)` and `min(v)` of one argument stay their names until 4f; new row: `ind2sub` for a call of `ind2sub` whose first argument is an array (at the `call`; until phase 6, Decision 33) |
| 4f | the library functions `sum`, `mean`, `variance`, `std`, `max` and `min` of one vector, `argmax`, `argmin`, `nnz`, `any`, `all` (with `dim:`), `sort`, `argsort` (with `desc:`), `find`, `find_first`, `find_last`; the named arguments `dim:` (of `sum mean variance std max min any all nnz`) and `desc:` (of `sort`, `argsort`) of these calls (Decision 21), with their errors 225, 237, 262 and 243 ("Readings fixed by 4f" below); `sort` and `argsort` of a `str` vector stay `strings` until 4g (the `str[]` type is reported where it comes from) | `named arguments` for every other named argument (of a user `fn`, or a name the library function does not take in v1, which is the compile error `unknown parameter` of LANGUAGE.md §8.1 once named arguments are complete) |
| 4g-1 | the `match` row and the `strings` row except fixed-size types (Decision 47): `match` (a resolved region, §3.4.2), every `str` construct (`str` in signatures, locals, parameters, `ref` parameters, results and tuple components; the dynamic `str[]` and `str[,]`; string literals anywhere; `+`, `+=` and the six comparisons on `str`, also element-wise on `str` arrays, Decision 45; `str` constants, lead decisions L-f and L-g; `len` of a `str`; `filled` with a `str` value; `printf` `%s` of any `str`; `sort` and `argsort` of a `str` vector, Decision 40); the library functions `str`, `lower` (Decision 46), `error`, `args`; with their errors 207, 208, 240 and 243 ("Readings fixed by 4g" below) | `strings` for a fixed-size type of `str` elements (`str[3]`, at its `type` node, as from 4e); `structs` for a struct item, a struct type, a struct literal, a field access or a projection, and `records` for a record literal or record type, with the positions of the phase-1 rows |
| 4g-2 | the `structs` and `records` rows and the rest of `strings`: struct items, types, literals, fields (read, written, `ref` paths), projection, struct arrays and their literals, `filled` with a struct value, records (Decision 48), fixed-size arrays of `str`, struct and record elements (types, locals, parameters, `ref` parameters, results, tuple components, `dyn`/`fix`, element-wise `str` operations on them); with their errors 201 (a record type where another type is expected), 204–206, 221, 222, 229 at a literal, 235 (two fields of one name), 238, 239, 240 (`p == q`), 249 and 256 | — |
| 4h | the library functions `linspace`, `bincount`, `meshgrid`, `setdiff` (the prelude, §2.5) | — |

**Readings fixed by 4d** (`seacheck`). An index of an element access: an `f64`, `str` or `bool` scalar index, or an `f64` or `str`
array index, is `index must be i64` (203) at the index (a `str` literal is first `strings`
by the phase rule); an index of type `i64[]`, `bool[]` or `bool[,]`, a range or `:` is `arrays`
until 4e. The bounds of a range are checked as `i64` wherever the range stands, not only in a
`for`: `v[0.5..2]` is `type mismatch: expected i64, found f64` (201) at the bound, which ties in
position with the range's `arrays` and is found first. A library call with an operand error:
it keeps a result type only where that type does not depend on the arguments (as the phase-1
functions do); `abs`, `sign`, `min`, `max`, `where` and `filled` then have the type 0 (which
raises no further error), while a call that has no overload for well-typed arguments keeps its
fixed result type. `filled(v, …)` with a `str` v adds no error at the call (the `str` is
reported where it comes from, a literal or a local's declaration) and has the type 0. For an
element-wise operator, elemental function, conversion or compound assignment with an array
operand the overload on the element types is checked first, so a v1 error (240, 241, 243) wins
over `arrays`; a vector with a matrix operand is 202.

**Readings fixed by 4f** (`seacheck`; LANGUAGE.md §8.1, §10.5, §10.6; Decisions 21, 39, 41 and the
lead decisions of 4f, §0). The overloads are judged on the types of the positional arguments, after
the named options:

* `sum`, `mean`, `variance`, `std`, `max`, `min`, `argmax`, `argmin` with one positional argument: an
  `f64` or `i64` vector (dynamic or fixed-size); the result is the element type for `sum`, `max` and
  `min`, `f64` for `mean`, `variance` and `std`, `i64` for `argmax` and `argmin`. `nnz` (`i64`), `any`
  and `all` (`bool`): one `bool` vector. With `dim:` (the nine functions above other than `argmax` and
  `argmin`): one matrix of those element types; the result is a vector of the same result element
  type, dynamic for a dynamic matrix, and for a fixed-size `T[r,c]` the fixed-size vector of c
  elements (`dim: 0`) or r elements (`dim: 1`) (Decision 39); the HIR is `lib name.dim` (§3.5.5).
* `sort(v)`, `argsort(v)`: an `f64` or `i64` vector (a `str` vector: the call has the type 0 and adds
  no error of its own, the `str[]` being reported as `strings` where it comes from, until 4g); the result is the dynamic vector
  of v's element type (`argsort`: `i64[]`), also for a fixed-size v (Decision 39). `find(m)`: a `bool`
  vector, result `i64[]`; `find_first`, `find_last`: a `bool` vector, result `i64`.
* `max` and `min` with two positional arguments are the elemental functions of LANGUAGE.md §10.4.
  Every other combination (a matrix without `dim:`, `dim:` with a vector, a
  `bool` vector for `sum`, a numeric one for `nnz`, a second positional argument, no argument) is
  `no overload of '%s' accepts (%s)` (243) at the `call`, its types spelled with the named
  arguments as `name: T` (above).
* **Named options.** A `narg` named `dim` in a call of one of the nine reductions, or `desc` in a call
  of `sort` or `argsort`, is checked here and not reported by the phase rule; every other `narg`
  (of a user function, of any other library function, or another name) is `not supported yet: named
  arguments` at the `narg`, as before. A name that a call gives twice is `parameter given twice`
  (225) at the second `narg` (a repeated name that the function does not take is reported by the
  phase rule, at its first `narg`). The arguments are checked in source order (each value, then its
  `narg`), then the call. A `narg` is checked only after its value, and only a value without an
  error reaches the duplicate check: a value with an error (one of its own, such as `undeclared
  name`, or 201, 237, 262, 260 or 261 of the option) leaves the `narg` and the call the type 0, so the
  call reports neither 225 nor 243 (`sum(A, dim: 0, dim: qq)` is `undeclared name 'qq'` at `qq`, not
  225 at the second `dim`; test `err_red_dim_twice_value_first`). `argmax` and `argmin` take no `dim:`: a `dim:` of theirs is a name
  the function does not take, so `not supported yet: named arguments` at its `narg` (in v1 `unknown
  parameter`, 224), never 243. A `dim:` value must have type `i64` (else 201, `type mismatch: expected
  i64, found T`, at the value), be a constant expression (else `not a constant expression`, 237, at
  the value), and have the value 0 or 1 (else `dim must be 0 or 1`, 262, at the value), checked in
  that order. The value is evaluated exactly, as a constant is (§3.5.2): an `i64` overflow or division
  by zero in it is 260 or 261 at the operator node of the value whose evaluation fails first (the
  `expr` rule of 260 and 261), in place of 262. A `desc:` value is any `bool` expression (else 201, `expected bool`, at the value).
  Pass 2a writes the options as §3.5.5 says: `name.dim` with the `ci` 0 or 1, `sort`/`argsort` with
  the value of `desc:` or the inserted `cb 0`.
* A positional argument after a named one never reaches pass 2: pass 1 reports it (115, Decision 41).
* A call with an argument error keeps a result type only where it does not depend on the arguments
  (the 4d reading): `argmax argmin nnz find_first find_last` `i64`, `any all` `bool`, `mean variance
  std` of no `dim:` `f64`, `argsort` and `find` `i64[]`; `sum max min sort` and every `dim:` form
  then have the type 0.

**Readings fixed by 4g** (`seacheck` unless said; LANGUAGE.md §4.6, §4.7, §6.2–§6.4, §7.6, §10.9,
§10.10; Decisions 45, 46, 48 and the lead decisions of 4g, §0). From 4g-1:

* **`match`** (L-a). The scrutinee must be a `str` (else `type mismatch: expected str, found T`,
  201, at the scrutinee). `match is not exhaustive` (207) is reported at the `match` exactly when
  its last arm is not a `_` arm, a `match` with no arm included. `unreachable pattern` (208) is
  reported at every arm that follows a `_` arm (a second `_` arm included) and at every arm one of
  whose patterns equals, byte for byte, an earlier pattern of the same `match` (in the same arm or
  an earlier one); an arm is reported once, whichever reasons it has. These take part in plain
  source order with every other error: 207 stands at the `match` keyword, before the scrutinee and
  the arms, so it is reported before any error inside the `match` (`_` followed by a string arm
  reports 207, not the arm's 208). The patterns are string literals (Appendix A) and add no other
  error.
* **`str` operators** (Decision 45). `+` of two `str` is `bin cat` (§3.5.5), type `str`; the six
  comparisons of two `str` are `bool`. With an array operand they are element-wise, judged by the
  overload rule of 4d (element types first, then the shapes): a `str` array with a `str` or
  another `str` array gives, for `+`, the `str` array of the broadcast shape (dynamic; from 4g-2 a
  fixed-size shape as for numeric operands) and, for a comparison, the `bool` array; a vector with
  a matrix is 202. Every other operator with a `str` operand (`- * / ^ % @ & |`, unary `-` and `!`),
  and `+` or a comparison of a `str` operand with a non-`str` one (`"a" + 1`, `names == 1.0`), is 240
  or 241 at the operator, with the operand types (`operator '-' cannot be applied to str[] and
  str`). `x += e` of a `str` local, `ref` parameter, element or field is `+` as above (a `str[]`
  local with a `str` e is element-wise, rule 15 (i)).
* **`str(x)` and `lower(s)`** (Decision 46). `str` takes one argument of type `i64`, `f64`, `bool`
  or `str` (an untyped integer literal is `i64`, as for `f64(…)`), result `str`; for a `str`
  argument pass 2a writes the argument itself and no `lib` node (§3.5.5). `lower` takes one `str`,
  result `str`. Any other argument type (an array of any element type, another type) is 243 at the
  `call`, as is any other number of arguments of `lower`. `str` is a conversion, `conv_type "("
  expr ")"` (LANGUAGE.md Appendix A), so `str()` is the syntax error `unexpected token ')'` and
  `str(1, 2)` `unexpected token ','` (pass 1), never 243. Both keep the result type `str` after an
  argument error.
* **`error`, `args`** (L-d). `error(fmt, …)` is checked as a formatting call ("Within one formatting
  call" below: 233, 234, 211, 210), type `void`. `args()` takes no argument, result `str[]`; any
  argument is 243 (`args(1)` reports `no overload of 'args' accepts (i64)`, as `now(1)` does), and
  so is every wrong number of arguments of `lower` (of `str` a syntax error, above).
* **Strings elsewhere.** `len` of a `str` is `i64` (L3). `filled(v, …)` with a `str` v is `str[]` or
  `str[,]` (the 4d reading that gave it the type 0 no longer applies). `sort` and `argsort` accept a
  dynamic `str` vector, result `str[]` (`argsort`: `i64[]`): the clause of "Readings fixed by 4f"
  that gave such a call the type 0 no longer applies; a fixed-size `str[n]` argument (from 4g-2)
  gets pass 2a's `dyn` as a numeric one does (Decision 39).

From 4g-2:

* **Fields, projections and views of structs and records** (Decision 48, L-c). A `dot` on a struct or
  record value names one of its fields (else `no field '%s' in %s`, 249, at the `dot`, the type
  written as the field `text` above says: a struct's name, a record as `{name: T, …}`). On a vector of
  structs or records (`S[]`, `S[n]`) it is a view name of LANGUAGE.md §5.6 or a projection of a field
  of scalar or `str` type (a field of any other type is `cannot project field '%s' of type %s`, 256;
  a name that is no field 249). On a matrix of structs or records (`S[,]`, `S[r,c]`) it is a view
  name or 249 with the matrix's type (`no field 'nom' in Dim[,]`, L-c).
* **Record literals** (L-b). A name given twice is `duplicate field` (205) at the second `init`, and
  a name `T`, `flat`, `col` or `row` is `field name reserved for views` (222, at word `fieldname`) at
  its `init`, both found by `seacheck` in source order with the initializers' own errors (the
  struct declaration's 222 stays `seaname`'s); 204 and 206 cannot occur in a record literal.
* **Record types** (Decision 48). A record type is identified structurally (§3.5.1): a record value is
  accepted wherever the same record type is expected (a `var` record assigned, an `if` arm, an
  element of an array literal, the value of `filled`, a field of a record) and is 201 wherever
  another type is (`type mismatch: expected P, found {a: i64}`). Structs and records never compare
  (`==` of two is 240). A record passed to a struct parameter is 201 even when its field names and
  types are the struct's (`type mismatch: expected P, found {x: f64, y: f64}`): records and structs
  are distinct types, Decision 48. A field or element assigned through a `let` struct, record or
  array is 238 at the target, its `%s` the root variable of the path (`cannot assign to immutable
  'a'` for `a[0].y = …` and for `s.lim.lo = …` with `let s`); a projection anywhere in a target
  (`dims.nom = v`, `dims.nom[0] = 1.0`) is 239.
* **Fixed-size `str`, struct and record arrays.** A dynamic value returned as a fixed-size `str[n]`
  or `S[n]` result, or as such a tuple component of a `return`, gets the same run-time `fix` check
  as a binding (`shape mismatch: expected n, got m`, LANGUAGE.md §4.5), at the same position. An
  array literal whose elements are structs or records is always dynamic, whatever its length
  (`S[]`, LANGUAGE.md §4.5, §6.9, Decision 20); a fixed-size one exists only by annotation.
* **Targets and `ref` arguments.** In an assignment target a selection (a range, `:`, an index
  vector or a mask) is allowed only in the outermost `idx` of the path, and `.flat` only as that
  `idx`'s base (`a[0..2].x = …` and `a[0..2].v[0] = …` are 239; LANGUAGE.md §7.3 lists `x[…]`,
  `s.f[…]` and `A.flat[…]`); a `ref` argument is a name, element or field path with no selection
  and no view (`ref argument must be a mutable variable, element or field`, LANGUAGE.md §8.3); a
  `$` in an index of the path is the extent of that level's array (LANGUAGE.md §5.3), for an `idx`
  under a field of an element read only after the checks before it (LANGUAGE.md §5.5, §3.5.9
  L17).

**Readings fixed by 4h** (lead decisions L-s, L-t, L-z; `seaname` and `seacheck`):

* **Prelude names** (L-s). The items of file 0 of a stream with more than one `#file` record (the
  prelude, §3.2) are exempt from 212, as LANGUAGE.md §3.3 says (its first rule applies to the
  user's file only); 213 applies to the prelude's locals as to the program's. The four prelude
  names `linspace`, `meshgrid`, `setdiff` and `bincount` resolve only as entered items: with the
  prelude they name its `fn` items (`rname fn`), and with `--no-prelude` they resolve as `none`,
  so a use is `undeclared name '%s'` (200) at the name, as §2.2 says. A program item with such a
  name is still 212 and a local 213 (LANGUAGE.md Appendix C still lists them).
* **Prelude calls** (L-t). A call of a prelude function is checked as a call of a user function
  (§3.5.5, "Library calls of phase 4"): `missing argument` (226) and `too many arguments` (242) at
  the `call`; `type mismatch` (201) at an argument that does not convert to its parameter's type
  (`linspace(0.0, 1.0, 2.5)` is `type mismatch: expected i64, found f64`, `bincount([1.0], 2)`
  `expected i64[], found f64[1]`, the literal being fixed-size, LANGUAGE.md §4.5; an `i64[]` argument of `meshgrid` converts, LANGUAGE.md §4.2);
  `'%s' is not a ref parameter` (255) naming the parameter as LANGUAGE.md §10 names it
  (`bincount(ref v, 2)` is `'idx' is not a ref parameter`); a named argument is `not supported yet:
  named arguments` until phase 6. A prelude call is never `no overload` (243).
* **Errors inside prelude code** (L-y): "Uses of an existing message" below.
* **The close-out** (L-z). 4h removes the last row of the phase-4 table above (its four library
  names), so from 4h the table in force is exactly the after-phase-4 table below; the phase-1
  table and the phase-4 table above stay as the record of how it shrank. No test names one of the
  four removed words, so none is retired; 4h adds one test for each after-phase-4 row that has
  none (`@` of two matrices, a call of `format`, of `solve` and of `figure`, §6.2).

**After phase 4** the table is exactly this, and from 4h it is the table in force (positions as
above: the node the row names, of several the first in source order); 4h removes every other row
and the tests of the removed words, and phase 6 and later remove these:

| Construct (after phase 4) | `%s` | Removed in |
|---------------------------|------|------------|
| the matrix product `@` of two numeric array operands that are not both vectors (at its operator node) | `@` | phase 8 |
| an `elemental fn` (at the item) | `elemental functions` | phase 6 |
| a named argument other than `dim:` and `desc:` of the library calls of 4f (at the `narg` node) | `named arguments` | phase 6 |
| a parameter default (at the `param` node) | `default arguments` | phase 6 |
| `%` with an `f64` operand (Decision 23) | `f64 %` | phase 6 |
| a handle type (`Figure`, `Axes`, `Lu`, `Chol`, at its `type` node) | `handle types` | phases 8 and 9 |
| a call of `format`, `write_json`, `print` or `make_dir` | its name | phase 6 |
| a call of `ind2sub` whose first argument is an array (from 4e, Decision 33) | `ind2sub` | phase 6 |
| a call of `solve`, `lu`, `chol`, `rcond` or `eig_sym` | its name | phase 8 |
| a call of `figure`, `panel`, `twin_y`, `plot`, `bar`, `barh`, `contour`, `image`, `xline`, `legend`, `title`, `xlabel`, `ylabel`, `xlim`, `ylim`, `x_ticks`, `y_ticks`, `grid`, `axis_equal`, `y_reverse` or `save_svg` | its name | phase 9 |

Phase 6 removes its rows in the steps of §2.11.2 (6b, 6c, 6d; agreed 2026-10-26), whose "Readings fixed by
phase 6" fix the front end's reading of named and default arguments, elemental functions and the
library calls of phase 6.
Every other predeclared function of LANGUAGE.md Appendix C is implemented after phase 4. The
operand errors of `@` (LANGUAGE.md §6.2) are reported as in v1 from 4d on, before the `@` row
is considered: a scalar operand or a `bool` array operand is `operator '@' cannot be applied to %s and %s`
(240), and `vector @ vector` is 230, both at the operator node; only the remaining operand pairs
(numeric matrix @ matrix, matrix @ vector, vector @ matrix) are `@` until phase 8. Because `print` is reported at its `call`, a
program prints a `str` through `printf("%s", s)` until phase 6. Errors that the removed rows made
impossible (§2.6.2, the paragraph above: 204–208, 216–222, 224, 225) become reachable in the
sub-phase that removes their row, except 216 (`fixed-size array too large`), which is reachable
from 4d: `seaname` resolves the extents of every type node before the phase rule (§3.4.2), so
`f64[300]` is 216 in 4d, and `f64[3]` is `arrays` until 4e; then 217–220, 252 at an untyped `[]` (Decision 36), 257 (`VIEW_RANK`) and 239 (a `.T`, `.col` or
`.row` assignment target) in 4e, 225 at a repeated `dim:` or `desc:` of a library call in 4f,
207, 208 at a `match` in 4g-1, 204–206, 221, 222 and 229 at a literal (and 249, 256 at a `dot` of a
struct or record) in 4g-2, and 224, 225 of a user
function and 236 (named and default arguments of user functions) in phase 6. (*Erratum, 4f
specification:* this sentence read "207, 208, 224 and 225 (named and default arguments) in phase
6"; 207 and 208 are the `match` errors of 4g, 236 was missing, and 225 is reachable from 4f.)
Error 115 (`positional argument after a named argument`, Decision 41) is new in 4f; it is pass 1's,
so it is reported before every pass-2 error, the `named arguments` row included.

**Which program reports it** (phase 4a on, Decision 17: pass 2a is `seaname` and then
`seacheck`, §2.1, §3.4.1). `seaname` reports the errors of the declaration checks, which a
single pass-2a program finds before all others:

* of the items, in stream order: `redefinition of predeclared name` (212; from 4h none for an item
  of the prelude, L-s), `redefinition of
  '%s'` (235) of two items, and `not supported yet` (259) at an item (`elemental functions`,
  `structs`);
* then of the signatures of the entered functions (§3.4.1), in item order, each function's
  parameters in order and then its result types: `redefinition of '%s'` (235) of two parameters,
  `local name shadows a predeclared name` (213) at a parameter, `not supported yet` (259) for a
  parameter default (`default arguments`), for a `str` parameter or result type (`strings`, until
  4g-1; from 4g-1 only a fixed-size `str` type, at its `type` node, until 4g-2) and
  for a type of a signature (`arrays`, `structs`, `handle types`), and `unknown struct type`
  (229) in a signature;
* the capacity limits (400) `symbols` (§3.4.1), `types` for the types it creates, and, while
  it reads `sea.ast`, `nodes`, `strings` and `constants` for the literals (§2.7).
* from phase 4 (§3.4.2), within those steps: the errors of resolving type nodes (229, and 200,
  201, 237 at a dim, 263, 216, 258, and 259 at a type node), of the annotations of the entered
  constants before the constants are evaluated, of the struct fields (and the struct
  declaration checks 235, 222 and 221, 4g) before the signatures, and of every other type node
  after the signatures, in file order. A type node outside items and signatures (a `let`/`var`
  annotation) lies in a body, so its error competes in source order with `seacheck`'s errors
  through the `rerr` record like any other (below); no `seacheck` error can stand at a `type`
  node, so the order at one position is unchanged.
* from phase 6 (§2.11.2, L-bw, L-cq): in the signature step, a parameter without a default after
  one with a default (236, at its `param`), a `ref` parameter's default (227, at the default), a
  `ref` parameter of an elemental function (228, at its `param`) and an elemental function's result
  type (253, at the `fn` item); and, after the bodies are resolved, the errors of the call pre-pass
  at body positions: 228 at the first `call` of a function with effects inside an elemental
  function's body and 232 at the first `call` between two functions of an elemental function's
  strongly connected component of the call graph (L-di), handed on through `rerr` like a type
  node's error in a body.

`seacheck` reports every other pass-2a error (from phase 6 also the value checks of a parameter
default, Decision 91): every code of 200–262 at every other place
(phase 4 adds 204–206 and 249 at struct literals and fields, 229 at an `rslit` with `sid` 0 and
262 at a `dim:` argument; 263 is `seaname`'s alone, at a type node; a negative extent of
`zeros`, `ones` or `filled` is the run-time `ARRAY_SIZE` even when it is a constant),
among them `undeclared name` (at an `rname none`), `local name shadows a predeclared name` at a
local or loop variable, `not a constant expression` (also at the name that closes a cycle), all
errors of `const` items (it checks every constant, §3.4.1; 260 and 261 from an `rcne` outcome),
those of the type annotations of `const` items and of `let`/`var`, `missing return`, the
`types` limit for the types it adds and the `constants` limit for the values of constants. The
limits `nesting`, `parameters`, `results` and `fields` are pass 1's alone (§2.7): neither
program of pass 2a reports them, and both size their stacks and records from them (a tree
nested at most `SEA_LIM_NESTING` deep, at most `SEA_LIM_PARAMS` parameters and
`SEA_LIM_RESULTS` results).

**Order across the two programs.** The rule is that of one program: the first error in source
order (file, line, column), of two at one position the first found, and a capacity error before
every other. `seaname` hands its first error to `seacheck` in the `rerr` record (§3.4.1), and
`seacheck` starts its search with that error as the first one found. Because `seaname`'s errors
are exactly those a single program finds first (items and signatures come before constants and
bodies; from phase 6 the call pre-pass's 228 and 232 stand at `call` nodes in bodies, where they are
the first check a single program makes at a `call` node, before any `seacheck` error at the same
node, and compete with every other body error by source order through `rerr`), and an `rcne`
outcome is reported by `seacheck` where a single program evaluated the constant, the error reported
is the one a single program reports. A capacity error of `seaname`
is reported by `seaname` at once (status 10), before `seacheck` runs; a capacity error of
`seacheck` wins over every other error, the `rerr` one included. The two differences from a
single program, both only for a compilation over two capacity limits at once: one that exceeds
a limit `seaname` enforces and the `types` limit in `seacheck` reports `seaname`'s, and one that
exceeds a limit `seaname` enforces and the `constants` limit through the values of constants
(counted by `seacheck`, §3.4.1) reports `seaname`'s, wherever the two lie. A later phase may move an error into
`seaname` only if a single program finds it before every error that stays in `seacheck` at the
same position (or no other error can occur at its position), so that this rule keeps holding.

**Within one formatting call** (`printf`, `format`, `error`) pass 2a first parses the format
literal (`format must be a string literal`, `invalid format conversion`), then compares the
number of arguments with the number of conversions (`format "%s" expects %d arguments, found
%d`), then checks each argument against its conversion in order (`format "%s" expects %s, found
%s`); an argument's own errors come before all three, in source order.

Uses of an existing message, so no further text is needed: `&&`/`||` with an array
operand, a `match` scrutinee that is not `str`, and a `return` value of the wrong type are `type
mismatch`; an out-of-range `bincount` value v (prelude code) is `INDEX_OOB` with v, dimension 0
and extent n, at the site of the program's call (§3.6.4, "Sites"); `sub2ind(r, i, j)` checks only
i against r (LANGUAGE.md §10.7) and reports `INDEX_OOB` with i, dimension 0 and extent r
(dimensions count from 0, LANGUAGE.md §5.4). From 4h (lead decision L-y) every other error of
prelude code is an existing message too, each at the site of the program's call: `bincount` with
n < 0 or n above 2³¹ − 1 and `linspace` with n above 2³¹ − 1 are `ARRAY_SIZE` with n (`invalid
array size %d`, from the allocation of the result, made before any other check of the body that
can fail, §2.5; `linspace` with n < 1 allocates its empty result without an error), and a
`meshgrid` result that cannot be allocated is `OUT_OF_MEMORY`.

**Exit statuses** (LANGUAGE.md §9.4; §2.2):

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_EXIT_RUN_OK` | 0 | compiled program: normal end |
| `SEA_EXIT_RUN_ERROR` | 1 | compiled program: run-time error, including `error` and a failed write |
| `SEA_EXIT_PASS_OK` | 0 | pass: success, the output ends with `#end` |
| `SEA_EXIT_PASS_BAYSICK` | 1 | pass: a Baysick run-time error inside the pass |
| `SEA_EXIT_PASS_COMPILE` | 10 | pass: a Sea compile error (`STOP 10`) |
| `SEA_EXIT_PASS_INTERNAL` | 11 | pass: a phase `P` check failed (`STOP 11`) |
| `SEA_EXIT_OK` | 0 | driver: success |
| `SEA_EXIT_COMPILE` | 1 | driver: Sea compile error |
| `SEA_EXIT_USAGE` | 2 | driver: usage or file error |
| `SEA_EXIT_TOOLCHAIN` | 3 | driver: `as`/`ld`/`xcrun` missing or failing |
| `SEA_EXIT_INTERNAL` | 4 | driver: pass status 1 or 11, a missing `#end`, out of memory |

**Runtime tables.** `SEA_EMIT_ERRMSG_TABLE name` emits, in the current section (Mach-O
`__DATA,__const`, ELF `.data.rel.ro`), an 8-byte aligned table of `SEA_E_RT_END` records indexed
by run-time code (record 0 is zero) and then the strings; `SEA_EMIT_ERRNO_TABLE name, host`
(`host` `darwin` or `linux`) emits `SEA_ERRNO_COUNT` records indexed by id, holding that host's
errno values, and then the texts. Their labels other than `name` are `sea_errmsg_<code>`,
`sea_errargs_<code>` and `sea_errno_text_<id>`, so each macro is instantiated at most once per
object file (by each runtime's `_sea_err`).

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_E_RT_END` | 22 | one past the last run-time code: records 0 … 21 |
| `SEA_ERRNO_COUNT` | 23 | number of errno records (ids 0 … 22) |
| `SEA_ERRTAB_MSG` | 0 | ptr: NUL-terminated message text |
| `SEA_ERRTAB_ARGS` | 8 | ptr: NUL-terminated `args` letters (empty for `-`) |
| `SEA_ERRTAB_SIZE` | 16 | record size; record k at table + 16·k |
| `SEA_ERRNO_HOST` | 0 | i64: host errno value (−1 in record 0) |
| `SEA_ERRNO_TEXT` | 8 | ptr: NUL-terminated text |
| `SEA_ERRNO_SIZE` | 16 | record size; record id at table + 16·id |

**Line shapes for the `DATA` generator.** Baysick programs read `errors.inc` with `LINPUT`, so its
records have fixed shapes (they are also valid assembler):

* an **error record** is a line between `.macro SEA_ERROR_LIST m` and the next `.endm` of the
  form: four spaces, `\m`, one space, then `code, NAME, phase, at, args, "text"`;
* an **errno record** is a line between `.macro SEA_ERRNO_LIST m` and the next `.endm` of the
  form: four spaces, `\m`, one space, then `id, NAME, darwin, linux, "text"`;
* an **exit status** is a line `.equiv SEA_EXIT_<NAME>, <decimal>`, optionally followed by spaces
  and a `/* … */` comment;
* fields are separated by a comma and one space; `code`, `id`, `darwin`, `linux` are decimal
  (with a leading `-` only for −1); inside `"text"`, `\"` stands for `"` and `\\` for `\`, and no
  other escape occurs; `code`, `id`, `darwin`, `linux` are canonical decimal numbers of at most 9
  digits (no leading zeros, no `+`); in an `.equiv` line the comma may be followed by one or more
  blanks. A line between a `SEA_*_LIST` macro and its `.endm` that is neither a record of the
  shape above nor a comment (`//`) is an error of the generator; every other line outside those
  lists is ignored.

**The generated `DATA` lines.** A Baysick string constant cannot contain `"` (Baysick
LANGUAGE.md §4.3), and texts 19, 20, 210, 211 and 234 do. So every string the generator writes into
a `DATA` statement is a quoted Baysick string holding the **`DATA` escaping** of its bytes: the
escaping of §3.1 in which `"` is written `%22` as well (so a `DATA` string holds only `%`-escapes
and bytes `0x21`–`0x7E` other than `%` and `"`; the empty string is `%`). A pass decodes it with
the decoding of §3.1, which reads `%22` as `"`. The generator writes one `DATA` line per record:

* error record: `<line> DATA <code>,"<NAME>","<phase>","<at>","<args>","<text>"`, e.g.
  `DATA 19,"LINE_STYLE","R","-","s","invalid%20line%20style%20%22%25s%22"`;
* errno record: `<line> DATA <id>,"<NAME>",<darwin>,<linux>,"<text>"`;
* exit status: `<line> DATA <value>,"<NAME>"`;

numbers in decimal, and each table followed by its sentinel (§2.2): the line `<line> DATA -1`,
read where the next record's first number would be.

#### 2.6.3 The `DATA` generator and how a pass is built

**Input line shapes of `limits.inc`, `rt.inc` and `passes.txt`** (those of `errors.inc` are in
§2.6.2; every other line is ignored by the generator):

* a **constant** is a line of `limits.inc` or `rt.inc` of the form `.equiv SEA_<NAME>, <value>`,
  optionally followed by spaces and a `/* … */` comment, where `<value>` is decimal (with a
  leading `-` for a negative value) or `0x` and upper-case hexadecimal digits; the include guards
  `SEA_*_INC` are not constants;
* an **entry record** is a line between `.macro SEA_ENTRY_LIST m` and the next `.endm` of
  `rt.inc`: four spaces, `\m`, one space, then `id, NAME, symbol, site, args, results` (§4.8);
* a **`passes.txt` line** is an `enum`, `head` or `rec` line of §3.9.

**The generator's protocol** (`tools/gendata.bas`). It runs with `include/` as working
directory and opens the contract files under their fixed names (Baysick `FILES`): 1
`limits.inc`, 2 `errors.inc`, 3 `rt.inc`, 4 `passes.txt`, 5 `math_tables.inc`. Its standard
input is the selection: one block name per line, each at most once, in the order `errors errno
exits consts entries records mtab`. It writes the `DATA` lines of the selected blocks to standard output, numbered
consecutively from 89 000 across the blocks, each table followed by its sentinel. `errors` and
`errno` are the lists of `errors.inc`, `exits` its `SEA_EXIT_*` constants (NAME = the text after
`SEA_EXIT_`), `consts` the constants of `limits.inc` and then those of `rt.inc` in one table (NAME
= the text after `SEA_`; the other constants of `errors.inc` are not emitted), `entries` the
entry list of `rt.inc`, `records` the lines of `passes.txt`, `mtab` the `pow` tables of
`math_tables.inc` (below). A malformed record, a line over 255
bytes, a bad selection or a missing file is reported on standard error as `gendata: <file>:<line>:
<message> (record <id>)` (or without the parts that do not apply), and the generator stops with
status 1.

**Generated `DATA` lines** (in addition to those of §2.6.2), one per record, numbers in decimal,
strings quoted in the `DATA` escaping of §2.6.2:

* constant: `<line> DATA "<NAME>",<l3>,<l2>,<l1>,<l0>`, the value's 64-bit two's-complement
  pattern as four 16-bit limbs, most significant first (each 0 … 65 535), so a value of more
  than 9 digits (`2147483647`), a hexadecimal one (`0x10FFFF`) or a negative one (`-1`) arrives
  exactly (§2.8); the table ends with the sentinel `<line> DATA "-"`;
* entry record: `<line> DATA <id>,"<NAME>","<symbol>","<site>","<args>","<results>"`, ending with
  `<line> DATA -1`;
* `passes.txt` line: `<line> DATA "<kind>",<n>,"<f1>",…,"<fn>"`, where kind is `enum`, `head` or
  `rec` and f1 … fn are the line's other fields in order (for `rec`: set, code, opcode, pops, then
  the field specifications); ending with `<line> DATA "end",0`;
* `mtab` (the words `FEPOW` needs, §4.10.5): first `<line> DATA 32,128,128` (the counts of the
  `sea_mt_const` words, `sea_mt_exp` records and `sea_mt_log` records), then the 672 words of
  `sea_mt_const` (32), `sea_mt_exp` (128 × 2) and `sea_mt_log` (128 × 3) in file order, each as
  its four 16-bit limbs `<l3>,<l2>,<l1>,<l0>` (most significant first, each 0 … 65 535), **eight
  words (32 numbers) per line**, so 84 lines (4, 32 and 48 per table: no line mixes two
  tables), then the sentinel `<line> DATA -1`: 86 lines, each at most 11 + 32·5 + 31 = 202
  bytes. The `sea_mt_trig` and `sea_mt_tpi` tables are not emitted (no constant expression
  needs them). Input line shapes of `math_tables.inc` (§4.10.3): a label line is exactly
  `sea_mt_<name>:` from column 1; a word line is four spaces, `.quad 0x` and 16 upper-case
  hexadecimal digits; every other line is ignored; a table with a word count other than
  §4.10.3's is reported like a malformed record.

Every generated line, line number included, is at most 255 bytes (Baysick's physical line
limit); the generator stops with status 1 and a message naming the record if one would be longer.

**How a pass is built.** Each pass program `build/gen/<pass>.bas` is the concatenation, in this
order, of: the pass's own files `passes/<pass>/*.bas` (in name order); the shared modules of
`passes/lib/` it uses, in the order `io diag tables lirrw limb f64emu fltlit layout ralloc`
(`layout` from sub-step 4g-2, below; `ralloc` from sub-phase 5b, §4.9.2, L-ax; `lirrw` from
sub-phase 5c-2, a shared main-program part, below, L-bd, L-bi); the generated `DATA`
blocks it uses, among `errors`, `errno`, `exits`,
`consts`, `entries`, `records` and `mtab`, always in this order; and the line `99999 END`. The file
`passes/<pass>/build.list` names the modules and blocks: lines `lib <module>…` (among `io diag
tables lirrw limb f64emu fltlit layout ralloc`; a list naming `lirrw` together with `limb` or
`f64emu` is a build error, since their line ranges overlap, L-bi) and `data <block>…` (among `errors errno exits consts entries records
mtab`; only `seaname` lists `mtab`, §4.10.5), comment lines starting with `#`; the parts are
concatenated in the order above whatever the order of the list, and a name outside the two sets
is a build error. `tools/seaval.bas` is built the same way from `tools/seaval.build.list`. The
build regenerates `build/gen/` every time and compiles each result with `baysick`; nothing in
`build/` is committed. The modules' interfaces are internal to the compiler (not contract
files): `passes/lib/API.md` documents the `SUB`s of `io`, `diag` and `tables`, and
`passes/lib/API-arith.md` those of `limb`, `f64emu` and `fltlit` (each module's prerequisites
included); the `.bas` files carry one summary line per `SUB`.

**The module `layout`** (from sub-step 4g-2, lead decision L-k: built and linked only from 4g-2, since `str` needs no layout; `passes/lib/layout.bas`, documented
in `passes/lib/API.md`, tested by `tests/lib_check.sh`). The struct layout rule of §4.8 computed
once for both programs of pass 3a, so that `sealoop`'s addresses (§3.5.9 R18, R19, R24, L15, L17)
and `sealower`'s (rules 18, 19, 27, 29, 31, the `slay` records of rule 38) cannot disagree: from
the type table `T` of the pass (the `sea.hir` type records, §3.5.1: `tstruct`, `trec` and their
`fd` records, `tfvec`, `tfmat` and the predefined types), the size and alignment of a type, the
offset of a field of a struct or record type (of a nested field, the sum along the path), and the
ascending list of the byte offsets of the reference values a struct, record or fixed-size array
type holds (`str`, dynamic arrays and handles, those inside nested structs and fixed-size arrays
included): rule 15 (g)'s and rule 38's list. An empty struct has size 0 and alignment 1 (lead
decision L-h; its home is still an 8-byte slot, rule 27 (a)). The module uses only the tables it
is passed and needs no array letter of its own.

**The shared main-program part `lirrw`** (from sub-phase 5c-2, lead decisions L-bd, L-bi;
`passes/lib/lirrw.bas`, documented in `passes/lib/API.md`). The LIR reader, validator and writer
of pass 3b (§3.6.5: the whole validation list, the capacity limits, the header records, the
renumbering writer) and T10 of §5.8 (clean-up and renumbering), moved out of `seaopt` unchanged so
that `seaopt` and `sealopt` read, check, clean and write LIR identically. They are main-program code
reached by `GOSUB` over about 25 arrays and dozens of scalars of the pass, which Baysick `SUB`s
cannot take (a `SUB` shares no variable and has at most 16 parameters, Baysick LANGUAGE.md §7.27),
so `lirrw` is not a module of `SUB`s but a **main-program part**: lines of the main program that the
build concatenates exactly as it concatenates a module (in the canonical order, after `tables`;
the generator needs no change, since Baysick lets main-program lines follow `SUB` blocks and passes
control around those blocks, §7.27). Its contract, written at its head and in `API.md`: the names
and bounds of every array and the names of the scalars it reads or writes, which each pass that
loads it `DIM`s and sets identically (so a pass loading `lirrw` gives up those letters; L-bp). The
reserved names, measured on the lines of `seaopt` that move (its reader, validator and writer, the
opcode codes, categories and field roles, T10 with its compaction, block table, dead-record marking
and renumbering): the numeric arrays `A B C D E F G H I J K L M N O P Q R T U W X Y Z` (24, with
`seaopt`'s bounds; `W` is scratch that the write entry overwrites, and of `R` the reader owns column
1 and T10 column 2), the string arrays `A$ D$ E$ F$ G$ H$ J$ N$ Q$ S$ U$ V$ W$ Y$` (14), and 173
scalars (172 measured, and `V8` added by L-bu), 149 numeric (`V8` and `A0 A1 A2 A3 A4 A5 A6 A8
A9 B0 B1 B2 B3 B4 B5 B7 B9 C0 C1 C3 C4 C5 C6 C7 C8 C9 D7 D8 E0 E2 E3 E4 E5 E6 E7 E8 E9 F1 F6 F7 F8 F9 G2 G3 G4 G5 G6 G7 G8 H1 H2 H5 H8 H9 I0 I1 I2 I3 I9
J0 J1 J2 J8 J9 K0 K1 K4 K5 K6 K7 K8 K9 L0 L1 M6 M7 M8 M9 N0 N1 N2 N3 N5 N6 N7 N8 N9 O1 O2 O9 P0 P1
P2 P3 P4 Q0 Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Q6 Q9 R0 R2 R8 R9 S6 S8 S9 T T0 T1 T2 U9 V V0 V1 V9 W0 W1 W2 W3 W4 W5
W6 W7 W8 W9 X0 X1 X2 X3 X4 X6 X9 Y0 Y2 Y3 Y4 Y5 Y6 Y7 Y8 Y9 Z6 Z7 Z8`) and 24 string (`B$ C0$ C1$
C2$ C3$ C4$ C5$ D$ E1$ G1$ K1$ K2$ K3$ L$ M$ P$ R1$ R2$ R3$ S1$ T$ Y1$ Y2$ Z$`). Every reserved
scalar may be changed by any entry; those that carry state between the pass and the part (the
limits, the counts of the current function, the pass name `P$`, the target `T$`, the file state)
are named as such in `API.md`. WP-LIRRW writes the final list into `API.md` and records here any
name that differs. A pass loading `lirrw` therefore has the numeric array letters `S V` free (2),
and string arrays and scalars outside these lists; it may also use the columns of `R` other than 1
and 2, and `W` between entries, as `seaopt`'s transformations do. The part contains its own operand
visitor with T10's two modes and never jumps to a line of the pass (a pass's visitor, with its own
modes, stays in the pass); its entry
lines (read a function into the tables, write the current function, T10, the header copy, the end
of input), each a `GOSUB` target ending in `RETURN`; and its first line, a guard that ends the pass
with the internal error of `dg_bug` if control ever falls into it. It has no `DATA`, no `END` and
no `SUB`, and reaches the `SUB`s of `io`, `diag` and `tables` by `CALL`. Its lines 69 000 – 81 999
overlap those of `limb` and `f64emu` (not `fltlit`, at 82 000 – 85 999), which no LIR pass loads
(`seaopt` computes its magic numbers without `limb`, L-am).

**The build lists** (each `passes/<pass>/build.list`; the parts in the order above):

| Program | `lib` | `data` |
|---------|-------|--------|
| `seaparse` | `io diag tables limb fltlit` | `errors exits consts records` |
| `seaname` | `io diag tables limb f64emu` | `errors exits consts records mtab` |
| `seacheck` | `io diag tables` | `errors exits consts records` |
| `seaexpand` | `io diag tables limb f64emu` | `errors exits consts records` |
| `sealoop` (from sub-phase 4e-0) | `io diag tables`; from 4g-2 `io diag tables layout` | `errors exits consts records` |
| `sealower` | `io diag tables`; from 4g-2 `io diag tables layout` | `errors exits consts entries records` |
| `seaopt` | `io diag tables`; from 5c-2 `io diag tables lirrw` | `errors exits consts entries records` |
| `sealopt` (from 5c-2) | `io diag tables lirrw` | `errors exits consts entries records` |
| `seagen_a64`, `seagen_x64` | `io diag tables`; from 5b `io diag tables ralloc` | `errors exits consts entries records` |
| `tools/seaval.bas` (`tools/seaval.build.list`) | `io diag tables` | `errors consts records` |

So from phase 4a on the exact arithmetic of constants (`limb`, `f64emu`, `FEPOW` and `mtab`, §2.8,
§4.10.5) lives in `seaname`, and `seacheck` holds none: it takes every value it writes from its
input (literals as written, the `f64` bits of integer literals from `rint`, the values of
constants from the `rcn…` records, §3.4.1). The line numbers keep the parts apart:

| Part | Line numbers |
|------|--------------|
| the pass's own files | 1 – 59 999 |
| `passes/lib/io.bas`, `diag.bas`, `tables.bas` | 60 000 – 62 999, 63 000 – 65 999, 66 000 – 68 999 |
| `passes/lib/limb.bas`, `f64emu.bas`, `fltlit.bas` | 69 000 – 74 999, 75 000 – 81 999, 82 000 – 85 999 (82 000 – 88 999 before 4g-2) |
| `passes/lib/lirrw.bas` (from 5c-2, a main-program part; never in a program with `limb` or `f64emu`, L-bi) | 69 000 – 81 999 |
| `passes/lib/layout.bas` (from 4g-2) | 86 000 – 86 999 (86 000 – 88 999 before 5b) |
| `passes/lib/ralloc.bas` (from 5b, L-ax) | 87 000 – 88 999 |
| generated `DATA`, numbered consecutively | 89 000 – 99 998 |
| `END` | 99 999 |

The pass's own files and the modules contain no `END`, and the modules contain no `DATA`; a pass
reads its own `DATA` (keyword tables and the like) before the generated blocks, which follow in
line order (Baysick reads `DATA` in line order). All parts together count against Baysick's
10 000 lines per program (§2.7; `make lines` reports each pass's count).

### 2.7 Living within Baysick's limits, and the size of the compiler

**Baysick facts that shape the compiler** (Baysick LANGUAGE.md):

| Baysick rule or limit | Consequence |
|-----------------------|-------------|
| 10 000 stored lines per program; one statement per line; `REM` lines count | the compiler is several programs (§2.1); comments are kept short and dense |
| `IF … THEN` only jumps to a line number | every conditional action costs a jump and a line; control flow is the main line cost (measured below) |
| scalar names are a letter plus at most one digit (286 per unit); 26 array letters per unit; no global variables | each pass keeps its state in a few 2-D tables, passed to every `SUB`; scalars are local to each `SUB` |
| at most 16 parameters per `SUB`/`CALL` | at most 8 tables per pass are passed everywhere (below), leaving 8 parameters for scalars; related arrays are packed into one 2-D table |
| arrays: ≤ 10⁶ elements, bounds inclusive (`DIM N(99999,8)` is 100 000 × 9 = 900 000 elements), `DIM` bounds constant | the capacity limits below |
| numeric constants: at most 9 mantissa digits (`2147483647` is `ILLEGAL CONSTANT`) | larger constants are built by arithmetic (`214748364 * 10 + 7`) or carried as hex limbs |
| string constants outside `DATA`: ≤ 65 536 bytes in the whole program (`TOO MANY LABELS`) | error texts, instruction templates and keyword tables are `DATA` strings (which do not count); string constants are kept to short delimiters |
| string `=` ignores trailing blanks, and `SEG$` past the end returns `""`, which then equals `" "` | the passes never compare a possibly blank-terminated string with `=`: they compare lengths first, or work on character codes from `CHANGE` (as the calibration lexer does) |
| `OUT OF DATA` and the end of input on a plain `INPUT`/`LINPUT` end the program with status 0 | the end-of-input discipline of §2.2 |
| `FILES`: ≤ 8 names, fixed at compile time | each pass uses ≤ 2: its input file (pass 1 reads standard input as file 0) and its output |
| 1024 active `CALL`s, 2 097 152 words of activations | recursion only in the parser, bounded by the nesting limit 64; later passes iterate over post-order records |
| 1000 `FOR` statements per program | counted in each pass by a build check; a pass near it is split |

**Table layout and the capacity limits derived from it.** The largest pass (2a) needs these
tables (from phase 4a both its programs, `seaname` and `seacheck`, keep this layout and read the
same tree into `N`, §3.4.1); every other pass uses a subset of the same layout:

| Table | `DIM` | Elements | Rows | Fields |
|-------|-------|---------:|-----:|--------|
| `N` nodes | `N(99999,8)` | 900 000 | 99 999 | kind, operator, first child, next sibling, type, file and line (F·10⁹ + L), column, symbol, flags |
| `Y` symbols | `Y(49999,9)` | 500 000 | 49 999 | name string, kind, type, scope, declaring node, flags, offset, … |
| `T` types | `T(19999,7)` | 160 000 | 19 999 | kind, element type, rank, extent 1, extent 2, struct id, field list, flags |
| `W` work stack | `W(199999)` | 200 000 | — | scope stack, worklists |
| `C` constants | `C(19999,4)` | 100 000 | 19 999 | four 16-bit limbs of an `f64`/`i64` bit pattern |
| `S$` strings | `S$(199999)` | 200 000 | 199 999 | identifiers, string literals, file names (interned) |

Six tables, passed to every `SUB` (6 of 16 parameters). Hence the **capacity limits**
(compile errors `program too large: %s`): at most 99 999 AST nodes, 49 999 symbols, 19 999
types (types, not rows of `T`: the continuation rows of a tuple or struct type do not count),
19 999 distinct numeric constant values (a literal counts once per kind as written, `ci` or `cf`,
and value, however often it occurs; each `const` item's value is one value) and 199 999 distinct
strings per compilation (prelude included); every pass compares with the `SEA_LIM_*` values it
reads from the generated consts table (§2.6.3), never with a written number;
nesting depth ≤ 64, ≤ 64 parameters and ≤ 64 results per function, ≤ 64 fields per struct.
Pass 1 enforces the nesting, parameter, result and field limits as it parses (and the node and
string limits as it builds the tree; the `prog` root is not counted as a node, and the `#file`
paths count as strings); pass 2a the symbol, type and constant limits (`seaname` the symbol limit,
the constant limit for literals and the types it creates, `seacheck` the types it adds and the
constant limit for the values of constants, §2.6.2); passes 3a,
3b and 4 the LIR limits, and from sub-phase 4e-0 `sealoop` also the node, symbol and type limits
for `sea.hirl` as a whole (its nodes, its locals and its types, the `tptr` types included,
§3.5.9), as pass 2b does for its `write_json` expansion. **Nesting depth** counts the constructs that make pass 1 recurse: a
block `{ … }` (of any statement or function), a parenthesized expression, the argument list of a
call, an index list, an array literal, a struct or record literal, an `if` expression, a unary
operator and the right operand of `^`; the top level is depth 0, and each such construct
contained in another adds 1. The `{ … }` of a `match` (its arm list) does not count (the arms'
blocks do); a parenthesized expression counts also after `return`; a conversion `f64(x)` counts
once (its parentheses are its argument list); the `if` after `else` in an `if` statement adds
nothing (its blocks are at the depth of the first `if`'s), while in an `if` expression it is a
nested `if` expression and adds 1. A construct at depth 65 is `program too large: nesting`, reported
at its opening token (`{`, `(`, `[`, `if`, the unary operator, or the `^`). For the LIR limits,
the operand fields of an instruction are all its fields after the opcode except its `site`
(§3.6.4), also when the site is `-` (an `rcall` of an entry that cannot fail); the fields of `func`, `slot` and data records are not operands. The distinct sites are
the distinct `F:L` among the instructions' `site` fields and the `pos` of every `func` record
(§4.9), counted over the compilation. No record of any format has more than 300 fields (the
longest are `func` and `call` with 64 parameters, hidden result addresses and 64 results), and
passes 3a and 4 split a LIR record into at most 300 fields (a longer one is `BAD_RECORD`).
(A node's position needs its file, §3.1: the sixth field of `N` holds the file index and the line
as F·10⁹ + L, exact in a Baysick number.)

**Tables of the LIR passes.** Pass 3a (from sub-phase 4e-0 its program `sealower`, which reads
`sea.hirl`; `sealoop` holds the HIR of the whole program in the same six tables and writes it
out again, §3.5.9) keeps the HIR of the whole program in the
six tables above and, in two more, the current function's LIR and the data items it collects
(it writes each function when the function is lowered, because its `slot` records come first,
and the data records at the end of the file, §3.6). Passes 3b, 3c and 4 hold one LIR function at a
time, plus the per-compilation tables:

| Table | `DIM` | Elements | Rows | Fields | Pass |
|-------|-------|---------:|-----:|--------|------|
| `L$` LIR records | `L$(199999)` | 200 000 | 199 999 | one record of the current function, as text | 3a |
| `D` data items | `D(49999,3)` | 200 000 | 49 999 | kind, source HIR node, count | 3a |
| `I` instructions | `I(199999,4)` | 1 000 000 | 199 999 | opcode, first operand in `O`, operand count, site in `X` | 3b, 4 |
| `O` operands | `O(799999)` | 800 000 | — | the operand fields: register, immediate in `C`, label, slot, block or string number | 3b, 4 |
| `R` registers | `R(99999,7)`; in `seaopt` from phase 5 `R(99999,9)` (L-ad) | 800 000; 1 000 000 | 99 999 | class, first definition, last use; the remaining columns (four, six in `seaopt`) hold `seaopt`'s facts of §5.8 from phase 5 and are unused in pass 4, whose allocator keeps its per-register state in its own widened `D` (§4.9.2, L-ac) | 3b, 4 |
| `K` blocks and slots | `K(19999,4)` | 100 000 | 19 999 | rows 1–9 999 blocks: kind, opening, `else`, closing instruction; rows 10 000–19 999 slots: size, alignment, frame offset | 3b, 4 |
| `C` immediates | `C(199999,4)` | 1 000 000 | 199 999 | four 16-bit limbs of an `li`/`lf` value | 3b, 4 |
| `X` sites | `X(49999,1)` | 100 000 | 49 999 | file index, line (`_sea_sites`, §4.8) | 4 |
| `S$` strings | `S$(199999)` | 200 000 | 199 999 | names, entry points, file paths (interned) | 3a, 3b, 4 |

Pass 3a passes 8 tables (`N Y T W C S$`, with the `C` of §2.7 above, and `L$`, `D`), pass 3b 6
(`I O R K C S$`) and pass 4 7 (`I O R K X C S$`) to every `SUB`, leaving at least 8 parameters for
scalars. Hence the
limits `SEA_LIM_LIR_*` of §2.6.1: per function 199 999 instructions (or buffered records),
799 999 operand fields, 99 999 registers, 9 999 blocks, 9 999 slots and 199 999 immediates; per
compilation 49 999 data labels and 49 999 distinct sites. Pass 4 copies the data records from its
input to `sea.s` as it reads them, so it stores none of their elements. At an estimated
6–10 nodes per source line, about 10 000–16 000 source lines fit. The workloads are 300–440 lines
of MATLAB each and the prelude an estimated 100–200 lines.

**Size calibration (item measured, not guessed).** Two representative pieces were written in
Baysick and run (scratch programs, not part of the repository):

* **Lexer core** (`lex.bas`, 188 lines, 12 of them `REM`): reads the `|`-tagged stream with
  `IF END #0`/`LINPUT #0`, works on `CHANGE` codes, recognises identifiers, keywords (table in
  `DATA`), integer and float literals with `_` and exponents, strings with five escapes, all
  operators with longest match, `//` comments, and the newline rules 1 and 2 of LANGUAGE.md §3.7; writes one
  token per line; reports errors with `PRINT #-1` and `STOP 10`. It lexed the 442 lines of Sea in
  the agreed design's examples (now LANGUAGE.md; 4 304 tokens), and the same repeated 20 times (8 840 lines, 86 000
  tokens) in 0.02 s on the
  development Mac. Missing for a complete LANGUAGE.md §3 lexer: block comments, hex literals, `\x`/`\u`/`\r`
  escapes, literal validity rules, column numbers, rule 3 (`else`), token records with
  positions. Judged to be about 60 % of the lexer.
* **Expression parser** (`expr.bas`, 145 lines): precedence climbing over the 8 binary levels
  of LANGUAGE.md §6.1 with non-associative comparisons, unary `-`/`!`, right-associative `^` with a signed
  right operand, parentheses, calls, indexing with argument counts, field access, error
  messages; recursive `SUB`s sharing 4 arrays and a cursor; writes postfix. Missing: ranges,
  `:` and `$`, named and `ref` arguments, array/struct/record literals, `if` expressions, AST
  records with positions. Judged to be about 25 % of the expression parser.

From these: the full lexer ≈ 300–350 lines, the expression parser ≈ 550–700, statements, items,
types and patterns ≈ 700–1 000, the header protocol, error handling and record output ≈ 200–300;
**pass 1 ≈ 1 800–2 400 lines**. The measured density is about 1.5–2 Baysick lines for each line
an equivalent C implementation would have (jump-only `IF`, one statement per line), which is the
factor applied to the later passes, sized by the rules they implement (LANGUAGE.md and this document):

| Pass | Estimate (Baysick lines) | Basis |
|------|-------------------------:|-------|
| 1 `seaparse` | 1 800–2 400 | measured pieces above |
| 2a `seacheck` | 6 000–9 000 | LANGUAGE.md §4–§9 and LANGUAGE.md §11.1 rules: scopes, types, ranks, conversions, overloads of ~80 library functions, format checking |
| 2b `seaexpand` | 2 500–4 000 | elemental instantiation, `write_json` expansion, folding with exact arithmetic (§2.8), reachability |
| 3a `sealower` | 5 000–8 000 | inlining, fusion, views, checks, COW, temporaries |
| 3b `seaopt` | 3 000–5 000 | the §5.2 optimizations, scalar replacement, vectorization |
| 4 `seagen_a64`, `seagen_x64` | 4 000–7 000 each | instruction selection (templates in `DATA`), linear-scan allocation, frames, error-site tables |
| **total** | **≈ 26 000–42 000** | eight programs (original estimate of phase 0; recalibrated below) |

The uncertainty was large (±50 % on the later passes); the estimate above is the original one of
phase 0, kept for comparison, and is recalibrated below from the real phase-1 passes (§8).
Runtime assembly per target, by analogy with
Baysick's runtimes (9 000 and 11 000 lines): core runtime 8 000–12 000 lines, plotting and JSON
2 500–4 000, Sea's own kernels (GEMV, LU/Cholesky panels, triangular solves, eigenvalues, sort,
elementary functions in scalar and vector forms) 6 000–10 000 — all estimates.

**Recalibration from the phase-1 passes (measured with phase 1 complete, on the tree of the
round-3 fixes that follow sea commit 3f07e31).** `make lines
check-limits` counts the stored lines of each built program `build/gen/<pass>.bas` (§2.6.3: the
pass's own files, the shared modules of its `build.list`, the generated `DATA`, and `99999
END`); the split comes from the line-number ranges of §2.6.3. FORs and string bytes are the
counts Baysick's limits apply to (§2.7 table above).

| Pass | Own | Lib modules | `DATA` | Total | FORs | String bytes | Original estimate (whole v1 pass) |
|------|----:|------------:|-------:|------:|-----:|-------------:|-----------------------------------|
| 1 `seaparse` | 1 528 | 1 845 (io diag tables limb fltlit) | 501 | 3 875 | 74 | 2 511 | 1 800–2 400 |
| 2a `seacheck` | 2 778 | 2 123 (io diag tables limb f64emu) | 501 | 5 403 | 127 | 4 276 | 6 000–9 000 |
| 2b `seaexpand` | 852 | 2 123 (io diag tables limb f64emu) | 501 | 3 477 | 90 | 3 512 | 2 500–4 000 |
| 3a `sealower` | 1 649 | 892 (io diag tables) | 504 | 3 046 | 67 | 2 351 | 5 000–8 000 |
| 3b `seaopt` | 952 | 892 (io diag tables) | 504 | 2 349 | 55 | 4 172 | 3 000–5 000 |
| 4 `seagen_a64` | 1 935 | 892 (io diag tables) | 504 | 3 332 | 88 | 3 104 | 4 000–7 000 |

(Totals include the `END` line. Limits: 10 000 lines, 1000 `FOR`s, 65 536 string bytes.)

**How far off the original estimate was.** Pass 1 parses the whole grammar from phase 1 on
(§2.6.2), so it is the one pass that can be compared whole: its own code (1 528 lines) is 15 %
below the low end of the estimate, so the density factor of 1.5–2 Baysick lines per C line held
for the code itself. The estimate missed the shared part: the modules and the generated `DATA`
that every pass carries add 1 396 (passes 3a, 3b, 4) to 2 624 (passes 2a, 2b) lines to each
pass, so pass 1's total is 1.6–2.2 times its estimate. The other passes are incomplete in
phase 1, so their totals are compared with the estimate only through the re-estimate below.

**Re-estimate for v1** (an estimate, not a measurement). Method: each pass's v1 size is its
measured phase-1 size plus, for each later phase of §8, an increment for the features that phase
adds to that pass, sized by comparing the work it adds with the measured phase-1 own lines of
the same pass and the share of that pass's v1 features phase 1 already covers (pass 1 nearly all;
passes 2a, 4 about a third; pass 3a about a quarter; pass 2b and 3b mostly their input
validation); the modules and `DATA` stay as measured, except `DATA` growing to about 600–700 lines
in the passes that load the runtime entries (3a, 3b, 4) as phases add entries. Own-line
increments per phase:

| Pass | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | v1 total (with modules and `DATA`) |
|------|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|------------------------------------|
| 1 `seaparse` | — | — | 0–100 | — | 0–100 | — | — | 0–100 | 3 900–4 200 |
| 2a `seacheck` | — | 100–300 | 2 500–3 500 | — | 800–1 200 | — | 150–250 | 300–600 | **9 300–11 300** |
| 2b `seaexpand` | — | — | 200–400 | — | 700–1 200 | — | — | — | 4 400–5 100 |
| 3a `sealower` | — | 100–200 | 2 500–3 500 | — | 1 000–1 500 | 800–1 500 | 200–400 | 200–300 | **7 900–10 600** |
| 3b `seaopt` | — | — | 200–300 | 1 500–2 500 | — | 1 000–2 000 | — | — | 5 200–7 300 |
| 4 `seagen_a64` | — | 50–100 | 800–1 200 | 600–1 000 | — | 600–1 000 | 100–200 | — | 5 600–7 000 |
| 4 `seagen_x64` | 1 900–2 300 (new pass, as `seagen_a64` in phase 1) | 50–100 | 800–1 200 | 600–1 000 | — | 600–1 000 | 100–200 | — | 5 600–7 400 |
| **all passes** | | | | | | | | | **≈ 42 000–53 000** |

The increments are judged, not measured: ±30 % on each, which the ranges carry. FORs grow with
the code at the phase-1 ratio (one per 25–45 lines), so no pass approaches 1000; string bytes
stay small because text lives in `DATA`.

**Passes at risk of the 10 000-line limit.** Pass 2a: about 8 000–9 200 lines after phase 4 and
8 800–10 400 after phase 6, so it is the first pass likely to reach the limit, in phase 6 (and
above 9 000 already after phase 4 at the high end). Pass 3a: about 5 700–6 900 after phase 4, 6 700–8 400 after
phase 6 and 7 500–9 900 after phase 7, reaching the limit only at the high end, in phases 8–9. No
other pass comes near it. **Phase 3 adds to pass 2a** (Decision 16 (a), §4.10.5): `FEPOW` and its
cores in `f64emu.bas`, an estimated 400–600 lines (counted in pass 2b too, which loads `f64emu`
but never calls `FEPOW`; 2b stays far below the limit), and the 86 `mtab` `DATA` lines, so pass
2a's v1 estimate becomes about 9 800–12 000 lines and the split described next is expected
during phase 4 rather than phase 6. The
response is the one §7.3 orders first and Decision 2 in §9 pre-agrees: **split the pass into two
programs with an intermediate file** (pass 2a, for example, into name resolution and typing of
statements and expressions, then the library-call and format checks; pass 3a into the lowering of
statements and calls, then fusion and inlining), done when `make check-limits` first reports a
pass above 9 000 lines, so that the split is made before a phase's work is blocked; Baysick is
grown only if a pass cannot be split cleanly (§7.3, step 2).

**The split of pass 2a (phase 4a, Decision 17).** Phase 4 adds an estimated 3 000–4 300 own lines
to pass 2a (struct and record items and literals, array types and their extents, indexing and
`$`, array literals, broadcasting, views and projections, `ref` paths, `dyn`/`fix`, `str`,
`match`, about 40 library overloads with their options, and their emission), which would take the
one program from about 5 900 lines to 8 900–10 200, across the 9 000-line trigger. So phase 4
starts by splitting it (sub-phase 4a, before any phase-4 code goes in): `seaname` (`sea.ast` →
`sea.res`) resolves names and scopes, checks items and signatures and owns the exact arithmetic
(constant values, constant exponents, the `f64` bits of integer literals, `limb`, `f64emu`,
`FEPOW` and `mtab`); `seacheck` (`sea.res` → `sea.hir1`) keeps typing, every other check and the
emission, and no arithmetic module (§2.6.3, §3.4.1). Estimates (judged from the phase-1 files;
±30 % on own lines; modules and `DATA` as built):

| Program | Own lines | Modules | `DATA` | After 4a | After phase 4 | v1 |
|---------|----------:|--------:|-------:|---------:|--------------:|---:|
| `seaname` | 1 850–2 200 (reading, items and signatures, scopes and the resolution walk, the constant order, the typing of constant expressions on their well-typed path, the evaluator moved from `seacheck`, writing `sea.res`) | 2 452 (io diag tables limb f64emu) | about 600 (with `mtab`) | **4 900–5 250** | 5 700–6 200 (struct declarations, extents of type nodes, literal field sets, syntactic checks of paths: 750–900) | 5 900–6 600 |
| `seacheck` | 2 300–2 600 (the phase-1 code without items, signatures, scopes and the evaluator; reading `sea.res`, the constant outcomes) | 892 (io diag tables) | about 515 | **3 700–4 000** | 5 950–7 400 (the typing side of phase 4: 2 250–3 400) | 7 000–9 250 (phases 6, 8 and 9: 1 050–1 850) |

Both stay below 9 000 after phase 4 with a margin of at least 1 600 lines; `seacheck` reaches
the trigger at v1 only at the high end of every range, so the measurement after phase 4 (§8,
phase 4h) decides whether its library-overload checks move to a third program then. 4a is done
when `make check-limits` reports the two programs and their measured sizes replace these
estimates here. **Measured after 4a** (`make lines`): `seaname` 4 776 lines (1 720 own), below
the estimate; `seacheck` 4 268, about 270 above it. Projected from these (same increments):
`seaname` 5 530–5 680 after phase 4 and 5 730–6 080 at v1; `seacheck` 6 520–7 670 after phase 4
and 7 570–9 520 at v1, so the measurement after phase 4 decides whether its library-overload
checks move to a third program.

**`sealower` in phase 4, and its seam.** Phase 4 adds an estimated 3 000–4 500 own lines to pass 3a
(allocation and addressing, five index kinds read and written, `$`, bounds checks, element-wise
loops with broadcasting, reductions, literals, fixed arrays, structs and hidden results,
projections, reference counts on every exit, copy on write, strings, `match`, `error`, `args`,
`fore`, and the inlining of prelude calls, Decision 18), more than the 2 500–3 500 above, which
counted neither the prelude inlining nor reference counts on every exit: about 6 100–7 600 lines
after phase 4, below the trigger, and 7 900–10 600 after phases 6 and 7. It is not split in
phase 4. Sub-phase 4a cuts its one file `sealower.bas` into files by area without changing any
line or line number (§2.6.3 builds a pass from its files in name order, so the files are named in
line order): `sl0main.bas`, its lines 100–3125 (the header, the tables, reading `sea.hir`, writing functions
and data, the frame machine), and `sl1scal.bas`, its lines 3130–8745 (the nodes and their
rules, §3.6.6); the files later phases add take line ranges after 8745 (or free ranges between,
keeping name order equal to line order). When it reaches
9 000 (expected in phase 7, possibly 6) the planned seam is a pass **`sealoop`** (`sea.hir` →
`sea.hir`: every array expression made explicit as scalar loops over element accesses, its
checks, temporaries and reference-count and copy-on-write points as new HIR statements, and the
fusion grouping of phase 7) before **`sealower`** (that HIR → LIR: the scalar rules plus the
explicit points); it needs new HIR records, so it is specified with the phase that needs it.

**Re-assessed with the phase-4 specification (4b review, 2026-10-22).** Measured before phase 4:
`sealower` 3 145 built lines with 4 free array letters (Baysick names arrays by one letter,
and every table of the pass takes one), `seacheck` 4 291. The rules of §3.6.6 that phase 4
adds (15–38 with the deferred `ref` arguments and the ownership cases of rule 15 (f)–(j)) are
larger than the estimate above assumed, and the four letters, not the lines, are the nearer
limit: phase 4 needs tables for slots and homes, the hidden locals of `fore` and `match`, the
bound locals per block for releases on every exit, struct layouts and the `slay` labels, the
deferred `ref` arguments and the inlined prelude bodies, which four letters hold only by packing
several into one array. A split before 4d would move nothing (the code it would move, the array
expressions, comes in 4e–4f) and needs HIR records 4b does not define, so it is not made then.
Instead a **size gate** closes sub-phase 4d (§8): `make lines` and a count of the free array
letters of `sealower` and `seacheck`. If `sealower` exceeds 5 000 built lines, or has fewer
than 2 free letters, or its projected size passes 8 000 lines — the *projected size* is its
built size after 4d plus 3 × its 4d increment (the built size after 4d minus the built size
before 4d; 3 is the share of rules 20–29, 32–33 and 37 in §3.6.6 against 4d's rules), never the
size before 4d plus that product — the split into `sealoop` and `sealower` runs as
sub-phase 4e-0 before 4e, with its own specification step (the new HIR records, agreed like 4b)
and no change of behaviour, so that 4e's and 4f's array-expression code is written once, in
`sealoop`; otherwise 4e proceeds and the gate is repeated after 4f with the same thresholds
(the projected size then being the built size after 4f plus 1.5 × the increment of 4e and 4f
together). `seacheck` (4 291) gains the typing side of phase 4 (2 250–3 400 lines
estimated, §2.7 above: 6 550–7 700 after phase 4), below the trigger with the same margin as
estimated; the gate after 4d records its size and free letters too, and only if it passes 7 000
lines or has fewer than 2 free letters is its library-overload and format checking moved into a
third program (`sealib`, `sea.hir1` → `sea.hir1`, before pass 2b) before 4f, which brings most of
the library overloads; otherwise the decision stays with the measurement after phase 4 (4h).

literals), 29 and the element loops of rule 30 over `str` and struct elements (with 4g), rule 33 (`match` can be a pure

| `sealoop` | 4 400 | 4 550–4 690 | 4 835–5 200 | 7 935–8 300 | yes | 4 (`B C J X`); 4g needs 0–1 |
| `sealower` | 6 087 | 6 327–6 497 | **6 887–7 447** | 7 987–8 547 | **at risk** | 4 (`C O S X`); 4g needs 0–1 (struct types in `T`, the `slay` labels in `D`) |
| `seacheck` | 5 830 | 6 130–6 330 | 6 480–6 930 | about 7 030 to the end of phase 4 | yes (margin ≥ 70) | 14 |
| `seaname` | 5 063 | 5 143–5 213 | 5 343–5 563 | — | yes | — |
| `seaexpand` | 4 070 | 4 090–4 110 | 4 130–4 190 | — | yes | — |

**The risk.** `sealower` crosses 7 000 built lines in the upper half of its 4g range: the 800 lines
that §2.7's tables allowed it for 4g and 4h together are about what the struct half alone needs
(560–950, comparable to 4d's array ownership), and its v1 projection keeps as little as 450 lines
of margin under 9 000. `seacheck` comes close too (6 930 at the upper end). Moving `match` (L16),
projection (L15) and every reference and aggregate store (L17) into `sealoop` is already counted
in these numbers; without L16 and L17 `sealower` would gain a further 200–350 lines (Decision 44).
Hence Decision 47: 4g-1 first, which measures the shared ownership machinery (R17, R20, R22, R25,
rules 15 and 16 for `str`) before the struct half commits to its design, then a gate.

**The size gate after 4g-1** (Decision 47). After 4g-1, `make lines`, `make check-limits` and the
free numeric array letters of the main programs of `sealoop`, `sealower` and `seacheck` (counted as
at the gate after 4d). Let S be `sealower`'s built size after 4g-1 and m its 4g-1 increment (S
minus 6 087). Its 4g-2 increment is re-projected from the measured one: the upper end of its
estimate, 950 (860 and 90 for `layout`), scaled by m / 410 (410 being the upper end of the 4g-1
estimate), so P = S + 950 · m / 410. `sealower` passes when P ≤ 7 000, P + 1 100 ≤ 9 000 and it has
at least 2 free letters. If it fails, a relief is specified and agreed with the user before any
4g-2 code, chosen among: (1) further struct work as `sealoop` rewrites (rule 18's field reads of
elements as `xblk`s of an R24 `eld`, the `slit` of a `bind` written into its home by `sealoop`);
(2) a compaction of `sealower` with no change of behaviour (its constant and entry loading takes
about three lines per name for some thirty names; a table-driven loop saves an estimated 60–80
lines; the dumps prove the neutrality); (3) a split of `sealower`, specified and agreed like 4e-0.
The same re-projection is applied to `seacheck` (its 4g-2 upper end 600, scaled by its measured
4g-1 increment over 500, the upper end of its 4g-1 estimate) and `sealoop` (its 4g-2 upper end
510, 420 plus 90 for `layout`, which is built only from 4g-2, scaled by its measured 4g-1 increment
over 290), and recorded with `sealower`'s. `sealoop` fails when its projection after 4g-2 passes
7 000 built lines, that projection plus 3 100 (4h, phases 6 and 7) passes 9 000, or it has fewer
than 2 free letters; `seacheck` fails when its projection after 4g-2 passes 7 000 built lines or
it has fewer than 2 free letters (its v1 size is the question of the measurement after phase 4).
A program that fails is brought to the user with a relief of the same kinds before 4g-2 (`seacheck`'s
being the `sealib` split of the gate after 4f). The measurements, the projections and the outcome
are recorded here. After 4g-2 the sizes are measured and recorded again.

return inside it (values owned, releases down to the block's scope mark, `mov`s, `exit`) 40–80,
the rule-12 and evaluation-order hooks of a statement-bearing expression 10–30, fixes found by W5
and the prelude tests 0–30. Phases 5–10 bring 1 100 at the recorded upper end (per phase: 5 none, 6
