**The `sealower` relief** (Decisions 49–52). Sub-step 4h-0 (§8) compacts `sealower` with no change
of behaviour, by these patterns (counted on the 4g-2 code; the savings are estimates):

| # | Pattern | Change | Saves (est.) |
|---|---------|--------|-------------:|
| C1 | two-line shapes `LET v = e` / `GOSUB`·`GOTO t` repeated at many sites, and `GOSUB t` / `RETURN` tail pairs (as 4g-1's 7532) | an entry line in front of the target that sets v and falls into it; `GOTO` for a tail call; the dead store after 7970 dropped | 180–230 |
| C2 | 502 `REM` lines, many short | a comment merged into the `REM` before it within 250 bytes, every comment's text kept | 120–135 |
| C3 | constant and entry lookups (`LET Q1$ = "…"` / `GOSUB 1850` / `LET G = Q1`, the lookups of 9580 and 8705) | one multi-line numeric `DEF` per table (the consts table, the entries row) with a string parameter, its body the lookup loop | 55–65 |
| C4 | the `V1`…`V5` register-name protocol of the emit helpers (7500, 7532, 7540, 7575, 7640, 7650, 11410, 11530, 32950) | a multi-line string `DEF` giving `" "` and the register's text, numbered at first use as 7500 numbers it; on overflow the function itself sets `A$(1) = "registers"` and calls `dg_compile` (as built in 4h-0: the same error at the same node and point as the old 7500 and 2390); an instruction becomes one `LET L1$ = "op" & FN…$(a) & FN…$(b)` and one emit, Baysick evaluating `&` left to right, each operand to its value (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §4.6 (c)), so the numbering order is unchanged | 250–350 |
| C5 | recurring validation tests before `THEN 2360` | 3–4 predicate subroutines, as 30900 and 30920 are | 30–60 |
| C6 | 8 copies of "evaluate the children onto U, resume at S" | one shared loop with the resume point as a parameter | 30–50 |
| | all, less 70–100 that C4 absorbs from C1 | | 600–770 |

The functions of C3 and C4 are Baysick multi-line `DEF`s of `sealower`'s main program (Baysick
LANGUAGE.md §7.10, §7.10.1): three distinct letters (a letter names one function, numeric or
string), called only from `sealower`'s own lines (the modules of `passes/lib` are `SUB`s), their
bodies without `GOSUB`, `RETURN`, jumps out of the body or recursion, reading and writing the
global tables; none is used in any pass before 4h-0, so WP-0 prototypes them first (§8). Expected,
at the conservative −600: after 4h-0 about 6 394, after 4h about 6 694, at v1 7 794 (recorded upper
ends), 7 944 (per phase) and 8 344 (stress). C4 also lowers the lines per emitted instruction from
about 6–8 to 2–3, which phases 6–9, mostly instruction emission, inherit. If WP-0 fails, C3 and
C4 become C1-style entry lines and the expected saving is 415–540.

**Reserves**, applied in this order when a gate below fails, each specified and agreed with the
user before the next code: (V) `sealower`'s semantic validation of `sea.hirl` beyond `passes.txt`
and the tree (§3.5.9 "What the passes validate") moved into `tools/seaval.bas` (format `hirl`),
`tests/run.sh` then running `seaval hirl` on the `sea.hirl` of every program test, frees 300–400
(Decision 51); rule 36's composite sequences (`f64` `sign`, `i64` `abs`, `sign`, `min`, `max`) and
`ind2sub`, `sub2ind` as `sealoop` rewrites into existing records with exactly §3.6.6's LIR, frees
150–170 at a `sealoop` cost of 60–100; a middle HIR→HIR pass between `sealoop` and `sealower`
taking rules 18, 19 and 36 and the field reads of structs as rewrites into the same `sea.hirl`
format, frees 440–520, a step the size of 4e-0 (driver, `Makefile`, test scripts, a dump kind).

**The gates of `sealower` from 4h-0** (Decision 50). The cap stays 7 000 built lines through 4h.
At each gate `make check-limits` and the free numeric array letters of the main program (counted
as above) are measured and recorded here, with the projection to v1 by the remaining upper ends
and the stress projection (the remaining phase-level part × 1.5):

  300 + 1 100 ≤ 9 000, S + 300 + 1 650 ≤ 9 000 and it has at least 2 free letters. If it fails

* **after 4h:** built ≤ 7 000, built + 1 100 ≤ 9 000 and built + 1 650 ≤ 9 000;
* **after phase 6:** built + the upper ends of phases 7–9 (100 + 150 + 120, table-driven, Decision
  52) ≤ 9 000, and built + 1.5 × 370 ≤ 9 000;
* **after phase 8:** built + 120 (phase 9) ≤ 9 000, and built + 180 ≤ 9 000.

A gate that fails applies the next reserve (V, then rule 36 into `sealoop`, then the middle pass),
specified and agreed with the user before the next phase's code. `sealoop`'s own v1 margin (467)
is weighed with its fusion seam at the gate after phase 6, where the same C1 and C4 compaction is
a candidate.

*Readings of the 4h-0 build.* WP-0's prototype confirmed the multi-line string `DEF` as Baysick
LANGUAGE.md §7.10 specifies it: the globals are shared with the body, `&` evaluates left to right,
a `CALL` inside a body works, and `GOSUB`, jumps out of the body and recursion are rejected; the
function form ran slightly faster than the `GOSUB` protocol it replaces. On register overflow
`FNR$` sets `A$(1) = "registers"` and calls `dg_compile` itself, no flag being needed (C4 above).
The neutrality proof (L-p) held: `--emit lir1` byte-identical before and after for 387 programs
(every `tests/programs` program, every run-phase `tests/errors` program, `tests/accept/w4_sor.sea`),
identical standard error for the 297 test programs that stop at an earlier error, every stage pair,
`make test` and `make cross`. The independent review also compared the old and new binaries on
the error and capacity paths (register-overflow sweeps, type limits, `BAD_RECORD` fields, 3 200
random mutants): all identical.

*Readings of the 4h build* (where the specification was silent):

* `sealoop`'s L18 rebuilds the record stream with the prelude calls inlined and then reads it
  again through its existing reader; a file with no prelude function is processed exactly as
  before.
* Capacity: the nodes counted are the copies, the `tmp`s, the `iblk` and the `xblk`, and the
  replaced `call` stops counting; the prelude functions' own nodes and locals are not counted
  (they are dropped). Both limits are checked as each node or local is added and reported at the
  position P of the outermost inlined call. Each inline call copies the whole body, so about 188
  calls of `setdiff` in one program reach `program too large: nodes`, which LANGUAGE.md §3.1's
  capacity bound allows.
* The no-cycle check of the prelude's call graph runs along the inline stack.
* The `.i` loop variables are numbered at their `forr` (post-order), literally as §3.5.4 says: in
  `meshgrid`, `xj` is `.i5`, `i` is `.i6` and `j` is `.i7`.
* Under a `bind`, the release of an owned argument `tmp` comes after `mov D R1`; under an `eval`
  of an owned result, the argument `tmp` is released first, then R1.
* Several `iret`s of one `iblk` share R1 … Rk, numbered at the first `iret`'s `mov`.
* An empty `_` arm under L16 still writes its `else B`.
* Every site in inlined code carries the call's line, the sites of `chkb`, `rcount`, `iaddc` and
  `rcall` included.
* `sealower`: R1 … Rk are new registers that the `iblk` pushes on its value stack; after `enddo`,
  a destination D > 0 gets `mov D R1`, except when the frame is an `asg` whose x1 equals D (rule
  15 (d)'s V, or the `asg set` of a scalar `ref` parameter), where R1 replaces V with no `mov`.
  Under a `tbind`, `mov L Ri` comes before T2's releases; a scalar-local `tasg` component is
  handed to rule 2 (d)'s step. An `iret` releases the scope entries down to the scope height
  recorded at the `iblk`'s entry. The rule-12 pre-pass does not visit `iblk` bodies. R30's parent
  inline `xblk` is found as "last sibling + 1".

### 2.8 Numbers inside the compiler

The passes run as Baysick programs, whose numbers are doubles, which cannot represent ∞ or NaN,
and whose arithmetic stops the program with `OVERFLOW` or `DIVISION BY ZERO` before any check of
the result could run (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §5.4); `SQR` takes `sqrt(|x|)`. Therefore:

* **Float literals** (LANGUAGE.md §3.4) are converted to their exact IEEE bit pattern by pass 1 with exact
  big-integer arithmetic (decimal digits × 10^e as a big integer or rational in arrays of 16-bit
  limbs, then rounding to 53 bits, ties to even), and carried as hex in every later file. The
  assembler only ever sees `.quad 0x…` patterns. Test vectors for the converter come from the
  IEEE definition (hard-rounding cases included), §6.2.
* **Constant folding** (pass 2b, §3.5.7) and the evaluation of constants and constant exponents
  (pass 2a, §3.5.5) compute every `f64` operation with the exact IEEE emulation of
  `passes/lib/f64emu.bas` (`FEADD`, `FESUB`, `FEMUL`, `FEDIV`, `FESQR` on bit patterns held in
  16-bit limbs), never with Baysick's doubles. The emulation is integer arithmetic on limbs, so it
  cannot overflow or divide by zero in Baysick, and it gives the IEEE binary64 result
  (round to nearest, ties to even) for every operand, finite or not: overflow to ±∞, underflow
  to subnormals or ±0, `x ÷ 0` → ±∞ (or NaN for `0 ÷ 0`), every operation on ±∞ or NaN, −0 kept
  (`-0.0 * 1.0` folds to −0.0, `sqrt(-0.0)` to −0.0, as at run time). So no operation is
  guarded: a foldable operation (§3.5.7) folds whatever its operands' values, and every `f64`
  constant expression built from foldable operations folds to one `cf` (constant substitution
  therefore never makes the tree larger than one literal per constant use). No guard is needed
  for exactness either: the emulation is exact by construction, and the only rounding is the
  one IEEE prescribes. (Until phase 1's review the folding was guarded by exponent checks
  because Baysick's doubles could not hold the results; with the emulation those checks are
  gone.) Folding folds only subtrees that are constant on their own (`2 * pi * rpm / 60` folds
  `2 * pi` only, LANGUAGE.md §6.8).
* **NaN bits.** A folded NaN has the bits arm64 produces for the same operation (FPCR.DN = 0,
  the macOS default): if an operand is a NaN, the result is that operand with its quiet bit
  (bit 51) set, the first NaN operand in operand order (a, then b) when both are; otherwise (an
  invalid operation: ∞ − ∞, 0 × ∞, 0 ÷ 0, ∞ ÷ ∞, `sqrt` of a negative number) the default NaN
  `#7FF8000000000000`. Sea's `nan` is `#7FF8000000000000` (§3.5.5), and unary `-` flips the sign
  bit exactly, so the NaNs that occur in folding are `#7FF8000000000000` and
  `#FFF8000000000000`, and every compile-time NaN is quiet. x86_64 (SSE2/AVX2) produces the
  default NaN `#FFF8000000000000` for an invalid operation (and propagates the first NaN
  operand), so run-time NaN bits can differ between the targets and from the folded ones. This is
  never visible: a NaN prints as `NaN`, never signed (LANGUAGE.md §11.1), `write_json` writes
  `null`, comparisons and `isnan` ignore sign and payload, and no Sea operation exposes a value's
  bits (LANGUAGE.md §6.5).
* **`i64` arithmetic** beyond 2⁵³ (literals, overflow checks of folded constants, the magic
  numbers for division by a constant) uses multi-limb integer routines in the pass that needs it.
* **Constant exponents and extents** (pass 2a, §3.5.5) are evaluated with the same emulation
  (and exact `i64`), never with Baysick's floating-point operations; pass 2a writes no folded
  value, only the decision `powk k` (or the extent of a type). A NaN or ∞ exponent is not
  integral, so it is no `powk`.

### 2.9 Self-hosting is not a goal

The Sea compiler stays a Baysick program. Sea is a numerical language: it has no recursive data
structures, no maps, no pointer types — the things a compiler is made of — and adding them for
the compiler's sake would work against the language's purpose. Writing the compiler in Baysick
is also the point of the Baysick project.

| Path | Contents |

| `include/` | the contract files (§2.6) |

| `build/` | the build output and installation directory: the pass executables, `sea`, `std.sea`, `errors.inc`, `limits.inc`, `libsea.a` and `libbaysickrt.a` (one of each, for the build's target), and the generated `build/gen/`; never committed |

`make` builds `build/`; `make test` runs the tests of §6.2; `make test-rt`, `make test-stage`,
`make test-math` and `make check-data` run single groups of them (§6.2); `make test-math` builds
`tests/math/math_check.c` with `xcrun cc -O1 -ffp-contract=off` against `build/libsea.a` and
compares all six elementary functions bit for bit over `tests/math/*.vec` (§4.10.6);
`make math-tables` is a developer check that is not part of `make test`: `timeout 120 uv run
--with mpmath python tools/math_tables.py --check`, which verifies the committed
`include/math_tables.inc` against its definitions (§4.10.6); `make lines` reports each built pass's
line count against Baysick's 10 000 lines, and `make check-limits` checks each built pass against
Baysick's other per-program limits of §2.7 (1000 `FOR` statements, 65 536 bytes of string
constants outside `DATA`, 255-byte lines); `make check-includes` and `make check-contracts`
check the contract files (§2.6).

### 2.11 Phase 6: functions and output (sub-phase 6a)

**Status: agreed 2026-10-26.** This section is the specification of phase 6 of §8 (row 6,
"Functions and output"), written as sub-phase 6a in the way 5a specified phase 5 and revised after
two independent reviews. Its questions are **Decisions 80–93** of §9, each decided by the user as
option (a) (2026-10-26). Its smaller readings are the lead decisions **L-bw – L-cx** (§9, "Lead
decisions of phase 6"), agreed with the text. No code, test or contract file changes with 6a: the
contract changes this section needs are listed in "Contract changes" below and are made by the work
package WP-CONTRACT of sub-phase 6b, each with its document table in the same change (the contract
rule of §2.6); WP-CONTRACT is done: `rt.inc`, `passes.txt` and the tables of §3.4.1, §3.5.4 and §4.8
hold them.

#### 2.11.1 Scope

Phase 6 implements, on both targets, everything row 6 of §8 names and its "done when" needs:

* **named and default arguments** of user and prelude functions (LANGUAGE.md §8.1), with the
  errors 224, 225, 226, 236 of user functions (§2.6.2);
* the **inlining rule of LANGUAGE.md §8.6** for the program's own functions: every call of an
  elemental function, of a function called from exactly one call site, and of a non-recursive
  function without a loop of at most `SEA_LIM_INLINE_STMTS` statements is inlined (Decisions 81,
  83);
* **elemental functions** (LANGUAGE.md §8.5): the item, its checks (228, 232, 253), calls with
  scalars (ordinary calls, inlined) and with arrays (broadcast element by element, Decision 84);
  and `ind2sub` with an array first argument (Decision 33's phase-6 part, L-cl);

#### 2.11.2 The phase rule in phase 6

Each sub-phase removes from the after-phase-4 table of §2.6.2 exactly the rows it implements, no
more and no fewer (the `write_json` row is part of the library-names row until 6d: `format`,
`print` and `make_dir` leave it in 6b, `write_json` in 6d), in the same change as its tests (the
phase-4 practice); each row still in force keeps one `err_ns_*` test until its sub-phase (6b adds
`err_ns_lib_write_json`, retired in 6d):

| Sub-phase | No longer reported (implemented) | Still reported |
|-----------|----------------------------------|----------------|
| 6b | `named arguments` (every named argument: of user functions, of prelude functions, and names a library function does not take, which are now 224, L-by), `default arguments`, `f64 %`, and the library names `format`, `print`, `make_dir` | `elemental functions`, `ind2sub` (array first argument), `write_json` |
| 6c | `elemental functions` (at the item) and `ind2sub` (at the `call`) | `write_json` |
| 6d | `write_json` | — |

After phase 6 the table in force has exactly the rows of phases 8 and 9 (`@`, `handle types`,
`solve` `lu` `chol` `rcond` `eig_sym`, and the plotting names with `save_svg`). The errors the
removed rows made unreachable become reachable in the sub-phase that removes the row: 224, 225 and
226 of user and prelude functions, 236, 227 or 254 at a default or a named argument (L-bw), 237,
201, 260 and 261 at a default (Decision 91), and 243 for `format`, `print` and `make_dir` with
wrong arguments in 6b; 228, 232, 253, and 202, 217 and 201 at an elemental call in 6c; 243 of `write_json` with a
handle type in 6d (no handle type can be written before phase 8, so its test uses a handle-typed
parameter's type in a signature only from phase 8; until then the `handle types` row reports first,
and the 243 case is tested when phase 8 removes that row). The tests of the removed words are
retired with their rows (`err_ns_lib_format` and the other `err_ns_*` goldens of the removed rows,
§6.2), and no new test names a removed word.

**Readings fixed by phase 6** (front end; lead decisions L-bw, L-bx, L-by, L-cq):

* **Defaults** (L-bx; Decision 91). `seaname` resolves a default's names (§3.4.1, as amended) and
  makes the structural checks, in the signature step of
  "Which program reports it" (§2.6.2), each function's parameters in order: after a parameter with
  a default, a parameter without one is `parameter needs a default value` (236) at its `param`
  node; a `ref` parameter with a default is `ref argument must be a mutable variable, element or
  field` (227) at the default expression (L-bw); the names in a default are resolved like those of
  a `const` item's value. The value checks are `seacheck`'s (Decision 91), made where it checks the
  `const` items (§3.4.1: before the bodies), in item order, each default exactly as the value of a
  `const` item annotated with the parameter's type (LANGUAGE.md §7.2): `not a constant expression`
  (237), `type mismatch` (201), and an evaluation that overflows or divides by zero 260 or 261, each
  at the node the `const` rules name. `sea.res` carries no outcome for a default, so `seacheck`
  evaluates a default's `i64` operations exactly itself, as it does for a `dim:` value (§2.6.2,
  "Readings fixed by 4f"), and detects 260 and 261 there; a default that names a constant uses that constant's outcome
  (Decision 25: a constant without a value, or of the error type, is not evaluated, so the default
  reports nothing more). Every error competes in source order with every other (§2.6.2, "Order
  across the two programs": a default's error on line 50 loses to a constant's on line 1). A default
  without an error is copied into every call that omits it as §3.5.4 says (the expression, with its
  own positions); its value is not written.
* **Named arguments** (L-by, L-bw). A named argument of a user or prelude function names one of its
  parameters (else `unknown parameter`, 224, at the `narg`); a name given twice is 225 at the second
  `narg`; a parameter given neither positionally nor by name and without a default is `missing
  argument` (226) at the `call`, except in a call that reports 224, where 226 is not reported (the
  unknown name may be the missing parameter, L-cy). A library function other than a prelude function takes no named
  argument other than its options (LANGUAGE.md §10, "Options"): any other name is 224 at the `narg`
  (the reading "Readings fixed by 4f" promised). A named argument whose parameter is a `ref`
  parameter is `argument for ref parameter '%s' must be marked ref` (254) at its value, since
  `name: ref x` does not parse (Appendix A's `arg`): a `ref` parameter is given positionally only,
  and LANGUAGE.md §8.1 says so (Decision 93). The arguments are checked in source order (each
  value, then its `narg`), then the call, as in 4f. Pass 2a writes the arguments in parameter order
  with the temporaries of "Evaluation order" (§3.5.5) when that order differs from the source's
  (L-cp).
* **Elemental functions and effects** (L-cq; Decision 81). `seaname` checks an `elemental fn`'s
  signature in the signature step: a `ref` parameter is `effects in elemental function` (228) at its
  `param` node, and a result type other than `f64`, `i64` or `bool` (or a tuple of those) is 253 at
  the `fn` item, after its parameters and result types, and not when a result type is the error
  type (L-dk); an elemental function without results is accepted (Decision 92). After resolving
  every body, `seaname` makes one whole-program pass over the
  resolved bodies (the *call pre-pass*) that computes, for every `fn` item, whether it has effects
  (LANGUAGE.md §8.1: it calls `printf`, `print`, `write_json`, `make_dir`, `save_svg` or a plotting
  function of §12, has a `ref` parameter, or calls a function with effects; `error` is not an
  effect; a fixpoint over the call graph), the cycles of the call graph, and the §8.6 class
  (§2.11.3). Every part of the pre-pass is iterative (a worklist for the fixpoint, an explicit stack
  for the cycle search, both in arrays sized by `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` and `SEA_LIM_NODES`), never
  recursive `CALL`s, so Baysick's limit of 1 024 active `CALL`s does not bound the call graph's
  depth. It reports, as body errors through the `rerr` record (§3.4.1, "Order across the two
  programs"), `effects in elemental function` (228) at every `call` inside an elemental function's
  body that calls a function with effects (a library function with effects, or a user function with
  effects; the first in source order is the one reported), and `elemental function cannot be
  recursive` (232) at the first `call`, in source order, between two functions of an elemental
  function E's strongly connected component of the call graph (E reaches the caller and the callee
  reaches E; L-di). Whether 232 is reported agrees with "a cycle through E", but the call named may
  differ: with `b` calling `a` first, `a` calling `b` and `e`, and the elemental `e` calling `a`, 232
  stands at `b`'s call of `a`, on no simple cycle through `e` (finding the first call on such a cycle
  is the directed two-disjoint-paths problem). At one `call` 228 is found before 232 (L-dk); the
  library functions with effects are those of LANGUAGE.md §8.1, every plotting function of §12
  and `save_svg` (L-dj). The pre-pass is the first check a single program makes at a `call` node, so a 228 or
  232 is found before any `seacheck` error at the same position (§2.6.2's condition for moving an
  error into `seaname`); errors earlier in source order still win.
* **Elemental calls** (`seacheck`, LANGUAGE.md §8.5, §6.3). Arguments convert to their parameters'
  types as for any call, element by element for an array argument of an elemental parameter (an
  `i64[]` to an `f64` parameter gets a `cvt`; an array of another element type is 201 at the
  argument with the parameter's type expected, `type mismatch: expected f64, found bool[2]`, L-dm).
  A call whose elemental arguments are all scalars is an ordinary `call`. Otherwise its elemental
  arguments are combined, in parameter order (the order of L19's run-time checks; the arguments are
  still checked in source order) and after the 226 check, by the shape rules of LANGUAGE.md §6.3
  with the static checks of §3.5.5 ("Static shapes"): a vector with a matrix is 202 and a mismatch
  of two compile-time extents 217, both at the `call` (an argument of the error type at an
  elemental parameter makes the call's type the error type, L-dm); its type is the result type (one
  result) or the tuple of result types (several) as arrays of the broadcast shape, fixed-size
  exactly when every array argument of an elemental parameter is fixed-size; uniform parameters
  (`str`, structs, records, arrays) take their arguments unchanged. Pass 2a writes it as a `call`
  (§3.5.6: only `sea.hir1` has a `call` of an elemental function with array arguments).
* **Library calls of phase 6.** `format(fmt, …)`: a formatting call ("Within one formatting
  call", §2.6.2), type `str`. `print(s)`: one `str`, type `void`. `make_dir(path)`: one `str`, type
  `void`. `write_json(path, value)`: `path` a `str`, `value` of any type that is not and does not
  contain a handle type (else 243 at the `call`, LANGUAGE.md §11.4), type `void`. Each with another
  number or type of arguments is 243 at the `call` (a `print` of an `i64` is `no overload of 'print'
  accepts (i64)`); a `ref` argument of `print`, `make_dir` or `write_json` is 255 naming the function (`'write_json' is
  not a ref parameter`, L-dy). `%` with an `f64` operand is `bin mod` of `f64` operands (an `i64` operand
  converted, LANGUAGE.md §6.5), element by element for arrays. `ind2sub(r, k)` with an array `r`:
  `r` and `k` are elemental (`i64` or `i64` arrays), combined as an elemental call's arguments.

#### 2.11.3 Front end and pass 2b

**`seaname`** (Decision 81). Besides the readings above: the `elemental` item is accepted (no
phase-rule error at the item), and the call pre-pass computes the **§8.6 class** of every ordinary
`fn` item of the program's file (the prelude's functions are always inlined by rule 37 and are not
classed), which `seaname` writes in its `rfn` record's `el` (2 for a function that LANGUAGE.md §8.6
(b) or (c) covers; 1 for an elemental function, which §8.6 (a) covers; 0 otherwise). On the source as
written (lead decisions L-ch, L-ci, L-cj):

* (b) **one call site**: exactly one `call` node of the whole stream names the function, counting
  calls in every function of the program's file whether or not `.main` reaches it, calls in the
  function's own body; each `call` node counts once, however often it runs (one inside a loop or in
  an elemental function's body applied to an array) (L-ch; LANGUAGE.md
  §8.6 as amended by 6a);
* (c) **not recursive** (the function lies on no cycle of the call graph of every `call` node of
  the stream, L-cj), **no loop** (its body holds no `while` and no `for` node), and **at most
  `SEA_LIM_INLINE_STMTS` statements**, counted as LANGUAGE.md §8.6 (as amended by 6a) counts them,
  one per Appendix A `statement`: every node of the kinds `let`, `var`, `asg`, `tasg`, `cstmt`,
  `while`, `for`, `match`, `break`, `continue` and `return` counts 1; an `if` counts 1 except an
  `if` that is the `else` child of an `if` (an `else if` of the same `if_stmt` chain), which counts
  0; a `block` counts 1 when it is a statement (a child of a `block`) and 0 as the body of a
  function, loop, `if` branch or `arm`; the statements inside every block count (L-ci).

**`seacheck`** checks named and default arguments, elemental calls and the library calls of phase 6
as the readings say, and writes each function's `fn` record with kind `elem` (an elemental
function), `inl` (an `rfn` with `el` 2) or `fn` (§3.5.4, contract change 2).

**`seaexpand`** implements steps 3 and 4 of §3.5.7 as written (step 4 as amended by 6a: `str` values
and `str` arrays are JSON scalars and vectors, a fixed-size array of JSON scalars is written as
`jvec (dyn e)` or `jmat (dyn e)` so the emitter's entries receive heap arrays only, L-ce, `sealoop`'s
L10 materializing the `dyn`, and a matrix of structs or records with no element is guarded to `[]`);
step 5 keeps the functions that
the kept `emap` instances name (as §3.5.7 says); its G12 validation (§3.5.7) gains, with 6c, an
`inst` record's argument count and types against its function's parameters (an elemental parameter
an array of the parameter's element type or the scalar itself, a uniform one exactly the
parameter's type) and an `emap`'s n and children against its instance, and keeps the `fn` kinds
`inl` and `elem` unchanged. Step 3 as built (L-dl): it runs at `#end` over every function in file
order, before reachability; a `call` becomes an `emap` when an argument of an elemental (`f64`,
`i64`, `bool`) parameter is an array; instances are numbered in order of first reference by an
`emap` across all functions, and step 5 renumbers the kept ones densely in that order, their types
numbered (§3.5.1) before those of the functions; the call's type must be `void` for no result and
else each result as an array of the rank of the array arguments (and two applications with one
instance must have one type), else `BAD_RECORD`; more than `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` instances is `program
too large: symbols` at the call. Step 4's capacity as built (L-eb): its new records count against
`SEA_LIM_NODES` (`nodes`), its `.j` locals, counted program-wide, against `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS`
(`symbols`; a guard for its internal table, not a count of all the symbols, §3.5.9), and the
dynamic types it adds for a `dyn` and the `i64[]` of a matrix's ranges against `SEA_LIM_TYPES`
(`types`), each reported at the last position read, the `eval`'s P.

#### 2.11.4 Pass 3a: `sealoop` (L19, L20)

`sealoop`'s reader accepts, from 6c, the `inst` and `emap` records and the `fn` kind `elem`, from 6b
the kind `inl`, and from 6d the `j*` records of §3.5.5 (it rejects each of them as `BAD_RECORD`
before its sub-phase). Two rewrites are added, and L18 is generalized; none adds a record or field
to `sea.hirl` (only the HIR records `iblk` and `iret` of 4h are used).

* **L20** (LANGUAGE.md §8.6; Decision 83) `call P ty fid n` whose callee F has kind `elem` or
  `inl`: as L18, with these differences. (1) The copied nodes keep their own positions (§3.6.4
  "Sites": code inlined from the program's own functions keeps its own sites); the `xblk`, its
  `tmp`s and the `iblk` take P, and so do the `loc` records of the new `.i` locals (L-cf). (2) A
  `ref` parameter's argument is the `rarg` as written, bound by `tmp Ai = rarg …`; Ai is then a
  *ref local* of the inline block (R31). (3) A `tret C` in the copy becomes `tbind` of k new `.i`
  locals (the function's k result types) of C, followed by `iret P′ k` of their `lv`s (P′ the
  `tret`'s own position). (4) F's result type may be any type: scalars, `str`, dynamic arrays, structs,
  records, fixed-size arrays and tuples of those (an aggregate result: R32). (5) A `call` in the copy
  whose callee has kind `elem` or `inl` is rewritten by L20 again, and one of a prelude function by
  L18, so inlining is recursive; it terminates, because no elemental function lies on a cycle (232),
  an `inl` function of class (c) is not recursive, and a cycle of the reachable program always holds
  a function with two call sites (one from the cycle, one from outside it), which has class 0. When
  every call is rewritten, `sealoop` drops the prelude, `elem` and `inl` functions (their records
  from `fn` to `end`) and renumbers the remaining functions densely in their order, rewriting every
  `fid` field (L-v extended, L-cg); no `inst` or `emap` record is written to `sea.hirl` (L19 has
  replaced every `emap`), so `sealower` never sees the kinds `elem` and `inl`, `inst` or `emap`.
* **L19** (LANGUAGE.md §8.5; Decision 84) `emap P T iid n` with children a1 … an, instance I of
  function F (parameters p1 … pn, k results; an *array argument* is an argument of an elemental
  (`f64`, `i64` or `bool`) parameter whose type in I's list is an array; an argument of a uniform
  parameter, an array parameter included, is passed as `lv Ai` like a scalar one, L-dn): (1) `tmp Ai
  = ai` for every argument in order, so every argument is evaluated once, in full, before any
  element is computed (L-ck); (2) the broadcast extents of the array arguments and their run-time
  `shape mismatch` checks, exactly as rule 22 forms and checks them for an elemental `lib` with
  array operands (the same records, sites and order; the static mismatches were pass 2a's); (3) for
  each result j that the enclosing statement does not discard, a new array `tmp Rj = anew P Tj 0 r`
  of the broadcast extents (Tj the j-th result type of T; for a fixed-size Tj its home, rule 27
  (a)); a result is discarded when its component of the `tbind` or `tasg` holding the `emap` is `-`
  or `skip` (Decision 84; under an
  `eval` every result is discarded; when every result is discarded, k = 1 included, the body of
  step (4) is the inline call as a statement, `eval`, exactly as for k = 0, and nothing is stored);
  (4) rule 22's loop nest over the broadcast extents (column-major:
  the row index innermost, so the element positions run in increasing linear order), whose body reads
  each array argument's element at the position (index 0 in a dimension of extent 1, as rule 22 reads
  a broadcast operand), and calls F (`call P ty1 fid n`, ty1 F's result type) with the element
  values in the elemental positions and `lv Ai` in the uniform ones; L20 inlines that call, every
  site in it the callee's own (an error raised in the body therefore stops the program at the first
  failing element in increasing linear order, with the callee's line, LANGUAGE.md §8.5); for k = 1
  the value is stored by `est` into R1's element at the position; for k ≥ 2 the body is a `block`
  whose first statement is a `tbind` of new `.l` locals E1 … Ek (`-` for a discarded result) of the
  inline call (R8's L12 form) followed by the `est` of every kept Ej; for k = 0 (an elemental
  function without results, Decision 92) no result is allocated and the body is the inline call as
  a statement (`eval`), run for its errors only; (5) the `emap`'s value: for k
  = 1 `lv R1` (owned: T2 moves it out); for k ≥ 2, in place of the `tbind`, `tasg`, `tret` or `eval`
  that holds the `emap`, the statement forms L11 writes for `ind2sub` with k components in place of
  two (the `tbind`'s locals bound from the Rj, a `tasg`'s targets stored by rule 15 (j) with their
  `cv`, `ret k` for a `tret`, nothing kept for an `eval`). An empty broadcast shape gives empty results
  and runs no element (rule 22's guard). L19 then rewrites its output like any code (L4, L7, L10, L12,
  L20). As built (L-do): every kept result's home is allocated first, and a fixed-size broadcast's
  extents (a vector's one, a matrix's rows and columns) are then read from the first kept home; with
  no kept result they are `tmp`s of `ci` of the static extents; an `emap` under an `eval` (any k)
  becomes a new statement `block P n` in place of the `eval`, with no `xblk` of type 1; when the
  holding statement's value is a `seq` whose value is the `emap`, the `seq`'s `bind`s become
  statements of the rewrite and the `seq` is dropped.
* **`ind2sub` with an array `r`** (L-cl): a two-result elemental application of rule 36's scalar
  sequence (`imodf`, `idivf` at P) by L19's steps (1)–(5), with P's site for every check; L11 keeps
  the case of a scalar `r`. The element body (L-dp) is a `block`: `tmp d` = r's element, `tmp g` =
  k's element, `tmp f = bin mod g d`, `tmp h = lib idiv g d`, both always computed (so a discarded
  result's errors are still raised), every node at the `lib`'s position P, then one `est` per kept
  result; as a call statement (`eval`) every result is discarded and both are still computed.
* **`f64 %`**: an element-wise `bin mod` with an `f64` array operand is rewritten by L7 as every other
  element-wise operator; its scalar `bin mod` per element is lowered by rule 39 (`FMOD`, L-cm).
* **`write_json`** (6d): the `j*` records are statements `sealoop` keeps, rewriting their children
  like any expression (`jvec (dyn e)` by L10; a `jopen`'s path and a `jval`'s value as operands);
  the `fore` and `forr` loops of pass 2b's expansion are rewritten by L4 and by the scalar `forr`
  path as any loop. Validation: a `j*` record only where pass 2b writes it (the block of §3.5.7 step
  4: `jopen` first, `jclose` last, `jobj`/`jarr` balanced by `jend` within the block, a `jkey` only
  inside an object, a `jval` child of type `f64`, `i64`, `bool` or `str`, a `jvec` or `jmat` child of
  a dynamic vector or matrix type of those four element types); any violation is `BAD_RECORD`. As
  built (L-dw): a `j*` record only as a statement (a child) of a `block`, and only between a `jopen`
  and its `jclose` in file order, with no `jopen` inside that span; balance is checked per block
  (every `jobj`/`jarr` of a block closed by a `jend` of the same block, a `jkey`'s innermost open
  object opened in the same block, a block's `jclose` its last statement after its `jopen`); between
  a `jopen` and its `jclose` the statements `bind`, `tbind`, `eval`, `asg`, `tasg`, `while`,
  `break`, `cont`, `ret`, `tret`, `match` and `arm` are rejected (only `block`, `if`, `forr`, `fore`
  and the `j*` records remain, as pass 2b writes them); a `jopen`'s child is a `str`; the order of
  keys and values inside an object or array (the value grammar) is not checked.
* **Capacity**: as L18 (§3.5.9 "Capacity"): the nodes L19 and L20 add count against
  `SEA_LIM_NODES` and their `.l` and `.i` locals against `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS`, a limit reported at the
  position of the `emap` or `call` being rewritten. A program whose inlining multiplies its size
  (an `inl` function calling another `inl` function twice, nested deeply) can reach `program too
  large: nodes`, which LANGUAGE.md §3.1's capacity bound allows.

#### 2.11.5 Pass 3a: `sealower` (rule 39, R31, R32)

* **Rule 39, library calls through the entry table** (Decision 52, specified here; §3.6.6). A node
  of the mapping table below is lowered generically from its entry's record in the `entries` block
  (`rt.inc`'s `SEA_ENTRY_LIST`, §4.8): (1) its operands left to right by rule 1, each already of the
  class the entry's Args letter names (pass 2a typed them); for the formatting entry the `fmt` record
  and the argument slot exactly as rule 8 builds them (`sa S`, the stores, `la F`); (2) `rcall
  <symbol> <site> nr <results> na <arguments>`, the site the node's line when the entry's Site is `S`
  and `-` otherwise, each result into a new register (the last one the destination of rule 2); (3) a
  `p` result is owned (rule 15 (k)), and the owned temporaries among the operands are released right
  after the `rcall` (rule 15 (b)). The rules already written for `printf`, `now`, the elementary
  functions, `error`, `args` and sorting (8, 9, 14, 24, 34, 35) stay as they are, so no earlier golden
  changes (L-cr). `sealower`'s dispatch over node kinds is an `ON … GOTO` line already 215 bytes
  long, so the new kinds (the nine `j*` records) take a second `ON` line rather than lengthening it
  (§2.7's 255-byte limit). Mapping:

  | Node | Entry | Operands |
  |------|-------|----------|
  | `lib format` (its `fmt`) | `FORMAT` | F, S as rule 8 |
  | `lib print(s)` | `PRINT` | s |
  | `lib make_dir(path)` | `MAKE_DIR` | path |
  | `bin mod` of two `f64` | `FMOD` | left, right (no site: the entry cannot fail) |
  | `jopen` / `jclose` | `JSON_OPEN` / `JSON_CLOSE` | the path / none |
  | `jobj` / `jarr` / `jend` | `JSON_OBJ` / `JSON_ARR` / `JSON_END` | none |
  | `jkey v` | `JSON_KEY` | a new `str` data record of v for each `jkey` node (rule 7's `la`; repeated keys share none, L-dv) |
  | `jval` of an `f64` / `i64` / `bool` / `str` | `JSON_F64` / `JSON_I64` / `JSON_BOOL` / `JSON_STR` | the value |
  | `jvec` / `jmat` | `JSON_VEC` / `JSON_MAT` | the array (borrowed) |

* **R31, `ref` arguments of an inline call** (Decision 83). An inline `xblk` (R26) one of whose
  `tmp`s binds a `rarg` is a call for rules 12 and 31 in every respect: the `rarg` is lowered at its
  place in the argument order exactly as for a `call` (a scalar local's slot `sa A` and its store, a
  reference local's `stp`, a struct or fixed-size local's home address, an element or field path's
  checks, cows and address, the deferred case of rule 31 included), and the `tmp`'s local Ai (a *ref
  local*) is then the `p` register holding that address; inside the `iblk` a read of `lv Ai` is the
  callee's read of a `ref` parameter (`ldi`/`ldf`/`ldp` from `Ai - 0 0`, rule 12, 31), an assignment
  to it the callee's store, and its element stores use the cow of the memory location (Ai, 0) (rule
  19); the roots of the inline `xblk` (rule 12) are those of its `rarg`s, so the reads before it are
  protected as before a call (R30 extended); the reloads of rule 12 follow `enddo B`, before R27's
  destination `mov` (as they follow a `call` before `mov x R`). T1's alias does not apply to a ref
  local.
* **R32, aggregate results of an inline call** (Decision 83). An `iblk` whose type is a struct, a
  record or a fixed-size array (or a tuple with such components) gets, before `do B`, a new home H
  of each such result type (rule 27 (a)), as a call's hidden result address is a home the caller
  provides (§3.6.3); an `iret` stores each such value into its H as rule 27 (d) stores into a home
  (the reference fields of a borrowed value retained, an owned value moved), then `exit B`; the
  `iblk`'s value for that component is H, owned as a call's aggregate result is (rule 15 (g)), and a
  destination receives it as rule 27 receives a call's result home. Refined by L-da: H is always a
  new home, allocated before `do B` after the `tmp`s and the R32 homes before the deferred rule-31
  stores; under a `bind` H is moved into the local, under a `tbind`, `tasg`, `tret` or `eval` it is
  copied into the home the parent provides, in R27's place of the `mov`; a struct-literal value goes
  into its own home V, then `li N size; mcopy H V N`, per rule 27 (d).
* **Validation** (in addition to §3.5.9): an `iblk`'s type may be any result type (R32); a ref local
  only as a `tmp` of an inline `xblk` whose child is a `rarg`; a `j*` record's child of the type the
  mapping table requires; no `fn` of kind `elem` or `inl`, no `inst`, no `emap` (L-cg). Any violation
  is `BAD_RECORD`. As built (L-ea): where a `j*` record stands is `sealoop`'s validation (§2.11.4),
  not `sealower`'s; `sealower` checks a `j*` record's child type by the table above and its operand
  count and classes against the entry's Args; no JSON entry has a result; a borrowed operand (an
  `lv`, a field loaded by `ldp`/`ldf`/`ldi`/`ldb`) is neither retained nor released, an owned one
  (L10's `xblk` under a `jvec`, a `str` temporary) is released right after the `rcall`; each `jkey`
  node gets its own new `str` data record (L-dv).

#### 2.11.6 Runtime entries of phase 6

The sixteen entries of phase 6 (Decision 85), ids 23–38, entered `rt.inc`'s `SEA_ENTRY_LIST` and
§4.8's Id-first entry table with WP-CONTRACT (§2.11.1); the table there, with its Contract column,
is their specification (§2.6's contract rule), and this section gives the rules they share. Each
`S` entry takes the site as its last integer argument (§4.8); every returned object is owned,
every argument borrowed; a failing entry calls `_sea_err` and never returns.

Every emitter entry other than `JSON_OPEN` writes into the buffer and flushes it when full. On a
failed flush (or a failed final write or `close` in `JSON_CLOSE`) the entry itself closes the
descriptor if it is still open (ignoring that `close`'s result), sets the descriptor field to −1,
keeps the state and its retained path, and calls `_sea_err` with `CANNOT_WRITE`, the path and the
saved errno; `_sea_err` then finds no open file and does not flush or close again; the path stays
valid until the process exits (`_sea_err` does not return), so the message can use it.
`_sea_err` (§4.5, §4.8), on any run-time error while a JSON file is open (the emitter's state exists
and its descriptor field is not −1), flushes that file's buffer and closes it, ignoring a failure of
that flush (LANGUAGE.md §9.2 step 3; the error it reports is the original one), so `rt_err.s` changes
on both targets (L-ca); an error raised inside `JSON_OPEN` before the descriptor is stored finds no
open file. **Layout** (LANGUAGE.md §11.4; L-bz):
a value at depth d (the top value at 0) is written as follows: a scalar as above; a non-empty object
as `{`, LF, each member on its own line indented 2(d + 1) spaces as `"key": ` and its value at depth
d + 1, every member but the last followed by `,`, then LF, 2d spaces and `}`; a non-empty array
likewise with `[`, its elements and `]`; an empty object `{}`, an empty array `[]`; a matrix of r ≥ 1
rows and c ≥ 1 columns as an array of r arrays of c elements, element (i, j) at position j of row i;
then, after the top value, one LF. A key is written as a string. The emitter keeps one state per
open container (its kind and whether it has an element yet) in a stack on the heap, grown as needed
and freed by `JSON_CLOSE` (L-co: no depth limit, `OUT_OF_MEMORY` if it cannot grow); it trusts the
nesting pass 2b writes, as `sea_printf` trusts its format. The live-object count of `SEA_HEAP_CHECK`
is unchanged by a completed `write_json`.

Where they live (both targets, written alike): `FORMAT` in `rt_fmt.s` (beside `sea_printf` and
`sea_error`, whose formatting and sink it shares) and `PRINT` in `rt_out.s` (beside the
standard-output buffer it writes into); `MAKE_DIR` and the JSON emitter in a new
`rt_file.s`; `FMOD` in `rt_math.s`; the runtime object lists of `Makefile` and `Makefile.linux` gain
`rt_file.s`.

#### 2.11.7 Passes 3b, 3c and 4

No transformation, template or rule changes. `seaopt` and `sealopt` (through `lirrw`) validate the
new `rcall` entry names against the `entries` block as before (their capacity, 399, suffices), and
pass 4 calls the new entries by the calling convention of §4.8 (its capacity raised by
WP-CONTRACT). Phase 5's shapes (§5.2) and the `make test-shape` lines must still hold: the W5 and W4
hot loops are in functions §8.6 does not inline (`lcg_fill` has four call sites and a loop; W4's
loop is in `.main`), while `stack_gap` (one call site in `w5_stats.sea`) is now inlined, which no
shape line names.

#### 2.11.8 The ports and their acceptance

`sea/ports/` is a new directory of the sea repository. `w5_tolerance_mc.sea` is LANGUAGE.md Appendix
D without its figures section and without the `--figures` branch of its option loop (Decision 80);
`w1_shaft_design.sea` is a new port of `w1_shaft_design.m`, written statement by statement as
Appendix D is (operation order kept, LANGUAGE.md §6.8; 1-based indices in its JSON; faithfulness notes
in its header comment), with `shaft_safety` an `elemental fn` called with scalars (`bisect_diameter`),
the 2001-element sweep vector and the 90 × 120 grids (LANGUAGE.md §2.1), and no figure code. Each
accepts only `--export-reference` (any other argument is its `unknown option` error, as Appendix D's
`_` arm). The token maps `sea/ports/<name>.tokens` are written from the MATLAB scripts' `fprintf`
formats and `compare.py`'s `RULES`, never from Sea output (§6.4). `tests/accept.sh` (§6.3, Decision
86) runs them.

## 3. Intermediate files

The passes of §2.1 communicate through seven text files in the temporary directory (six before
sub-phase 4e-0, which adds `sea.hirl`). This section
fixes their exact formats; `sea/include/passes.txt` (§3.9) is the same information in a form the
passes' generated `DATA` blocks are made from (§2.6), and the two change only together.

| File | Written by | Read by | Content |
|------|-----------|---------|---------|
| `sea.ast` | 1 `seaparse` | 2a `seaname` | the syntax tree as parsed, untyped (§3.4) |
| `sea.res` | 2a `seaname` | 2a `seacheck` | the same tree with names resolved, declarations checked and constants evaluated (§3.4.1) |
| `sea.hir1` | 2a `seacheck` | 2b | the resolved, typed tree (§3.5) |
| `sea.hir` | 2b `seaexpand` | 3a `sealoop` | the same after constant substitution and folding, elemental instantiation, `write_json` expansion and reachability (§3.5) |
| `sea.hirl` | 3a `sealoop` | 3a `sealower` | the same with the array constructs made explicit as scalar loops over element accesses (§3.5.9; from sub-phase 4e-0) |
| `sea.lir1` | 3a `sealower` | 3b | loop-level code over virtual registers (§3.6) |
| `sea.lir2` | 3b `seaopt` | 3c `sealopt` | the same after T1–T4 and T10 of §5.8 (§3.6; from sub-phase 5c-2, Decision 74; before it `seaopt` wrote `sea.lir`) |
| `sea.lir` | 3c `sealopt` | 4 | the same after T5–T10 of §5.8 and, from phase 7, scalar replacement and vectorization (§3.6); from phase 7 those two run in a pass 3d of their own after `sealopt` instead, whose file names (and which file pass 4 reads) phase 7's specification settles (Decision 78) |

The pass-1 input stream (§2.2) uses the header records of §3.2; pass 4 writes `sea.s`, which is
assembly text and has no records. `sea build --emit X` copies `sea.X` unchanged (§2.2), so a
dump is the file itself; §3.8 says how dumps are tested.

### 3.1 Lines, fields and field encodings

* A file is a sequence of **records**, one per line, each line ended by LF. Every byte of a file
  is LF or in `0x20`–`0x7E`: strings are escaped (below), so no other byte occurs.
* A record is a sequence of **fields** separated by exactly one space, with no leading or
  trailing space and no empty field. The first field is the record's **opcode** (lower-case
  letters and digits, or `#` + a name for a header record, §3.2); the fields after it are fixed
  by the opcode, in the order of the tables below and of `passes.txt`.
* A line is at most 65 536 bytes (`SEA_LIM_RECORD_BYTES`), Baysick's input-line limit
  (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §12, §15.2), so every record is read with one `LINPUT #k`. Every record
  stays far below it:
  * a record holds at most one string field, and a string field is at most 12 288 bytes: a
    string literal lies on one source line of at most 4096 bytes (LANGUAGE.md §3.1, §3.5), its
    value has at most as many bytes as its source text, and escaping writes each byte as at most
    3 bytes; a `#file` path is at most 4096 bytes (the operating systems' path limit); names and
    keys are identifiers of at most 63 bytes. No record carries a variable number of strings
    (the patterns of an `arm` are child `str`/`cs` nodes, §3.4, §3.5.5), except `rerr` of
    `sea.res` (§3.4.1): at most three substitutions of one error, each at most 4 096 bytes;
  * the records with a variable number of fields (`rtup`, `rfn`, `ttuple`, `inst`, `tbind`,
    `func`, `call`, `rcall`, `ret`, `chk`) repeat numbers or registers, each at most 7 bytes with its separator,
    and their counts are bounded by the limits of §2.6.1: at most `SEA_LIM_PARAMS` parameters
    and `SEA_LIM_RESULTS` results per function, plus one hidden address per result (§3.6.3),
    and the fixed arities of the runtime entry points and error codes (§4.8, §2.6.2); so such a
    record has fewer than 200 fields and 1 400 bytes.
* The last record of every file is `#end` (§2.2, end-of-input discipline).

**Field types.** Each field has one of these types (the names are those of `passes.txt`):

| Type | Written as | Read by a Baysick pass with |
|------|-----------|-----------------------------|
| `u` | an unsigned integer 0 … 999 999 999 in decimal, no sign, no leading zeros (`0` for zero) | `VAL` (at most 9 digits, Baysick LANGUAGE.md §6.1) |
| `i` | an `i64` value: if −10⁹ < v < 10⁹, an optional `-` and decimal digits as for `u` (zero is `0`, never `-0`); otherwise `#` and the 16 upper-case hexadecimal digits of its two's-complement 64-bit pattern (`#FFFFFFFFC4653600` is −1 000 000 000) | `VAL`, or four 16-bit limbs of 4 hex digits |
| `f` | always `#` and the 16 upper-case hexadecimal digits of the IEEE-754 binary64 pattern, sign bit first (`#3FB999999999999A` is 0.1, `#8000000000000000` is −0.0) | four 16-bit limbs (§2.7, table `C`) |
| `s` | a byte string, escaped (below) | `CHANGE` to codes, then decoding |
| `pos` | a source position `F:L:C`: `F` the index of the `#file` record (0 for the first, in header order), `L` the line in that file (from 1), `C` the column (from 1, counting bytes), each a `u` | `POS` of `:`, `VAL` |
| `site` | a run-time error site `F:L`: file index and line as in `pos` | as `pos` |
| an enumeration | one of the words `passes.txt` lists for it (`add`, `f64`, `arm64-macos`, …) | comparison with `DATA` words |
| a reference | a `u` number naming a table entry of the same file: `ty` a type (§3.5), `lid` a local, `fid` a function, `cid` a constant, `iid` an elemental instance, `blk` a structured LIR construct; or a prefixed token: `d`*n* a LIR data label, `s`*n* a stack slot, and the LIR registers `i`*n*, `f`*n*, `p`*n*, `x`*n*, `y`*n*, `m`*n* (§3.6) | `SEG$`, `VAL` |
| `fl` | `printf` flags: `-` for none, else the letters `l` (flag `-`), `p` (`+`), `s` (space), `z` (`0`), `a` (`#`), each at most once, in this order | codes |

A field is written `name:type`, then optionally `?`, then optionally `*` and a count. With `?`
(`u?`, `lid?`) the field may instead be the single character `-`, meaning "absent". With
`*count` (`ty*n`) the field is repeated as many times as the value of the earlier `u` field
`count`, each repetition a field of its own; both may be combined (`lid:lid?*n`: n fields, each a
local or `-`). In the tables of this section a bare reference type (`ty`, `lid`, `fid`, `cid`,
`iid`, `lab`, `slot`, `blk`), possibly with `?` or `*count`, stands for the field of that name and
type (`lid?*n` is `lid:lid?*n`); `passes.txt` writes every field as `name:type`.

**String escaping.** A string field holds the bytes of the string, each byte `b` written as the
character `b` itself if `0x21 ≤ b ≤ 0x7E` and `b ≠ 0x25` (`%`), and otherwise as `%` followed by
two upper-case hexadecimal digits: space is `%20`, `%` is `%25`, LF is `%0A`, the UTF-8 bytes of
`é` are `%C3%A9`. The **empty string** is the field `%` alone (a `%` not followed by two
hexadecimal digits occurs nowhere else). `#` and `-` in a string are ordinary characters: a field's
type is known from its position, and only the first field of a record can be a header opcode.

**Why these encodings.** Numbers are exact for Baysick: `VAL` reads at most 9 digits and doubles
cannot carry an `f64` pattern or an `i64` beyond 2⁵³, so everything else travels as hexadecimal
limbs (§2.8). A field never contains a blank and is never empty, so records split with `POS` on
`" "` and `SEG$`, Baysick's `PRINT #` writes every field unchanged (its lazy spaces never drop a
trailing blank, because there is none: Baysick LANGUAGE.md §8), and `=` compares two whole fields
exactly: the trailing-blank rule of §2.7 cannot apply to strings that contain no blank. A decoded
string value (which may contain blanks, or be empty) is never compared with `=`; passes compare
its codes or its length first (§2.7).

### 3.2 Header records

| Record | Fields | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| `#sea` | `ver:u` | the format version; `1` for the formats of this section |
| `#target` | `t:target` | the compilation target (enumeration `target`: `arm64-macos`, `x86_64-linux`) (`--target`, §2.2) |
| `#file` | `path:s` | one source file, in stream order: `std.sea` first (absent with `--no-prelude`, §2.2), then the program, its path as given to `sea`. File index `F` of positions counts these records from 0 |
| `#end` | — | the last record of the stream or file |

* **Pass-1 input stream** (written by the driver, §2.2): `#sea 1`, `#target`, then for each file
  its `#file` record followed by its source lines, then `#end`. A source line is written as `|`
  and its bytes, unescaped, then LF; a last line without LF is written the same way. Baysick's
  `LINPUT` removes one CR before the LF (Baysick LANGUAGE.md §15.2), which is the CR rule of
  LANGUAGE.md §3.1.
* **Intermediate files**: `#sea 1`, `#target`, all `#file` records in stream order, then the body
  records, then `#end`. Pass 1 writes this header (it writes its output after reading its whole
  input); every later pass copies the header records of its input unchanged.
* A pass stops with status 11 (§2.2) if its input lacks a header record, has them out of order,
  has a version other than 1 or an unknown target, or has a body record before the header ends.

### 3.3 Trees in post-order

`sea.ast` and `sea.hir*` hold trees. A tree is written in **post-order**: every node is one
record, written after the records of all its children, the children in source order (left to
right). Each node record **pops** a number of nodes, fixed by its opcode or given by one of its
fields (the "pops" column below and in `passes.txt`): those nodes are its children, the
earliest-written first. A reader therefore needs one stack: for each node record it pops that
many entries, builds the node with them as children in order, and pushes the node. Records never
refer to other nodes by number; the structure is given by the order alone. The header records,
the declaration records of §3.4.1 (`rerr`, `rtup`) and those of §3.5 (`t…` type records: `tvec tmat tfvec tfmat tstruct trec ttuple` and
`tptr` of §3.5.9; `fd`, `inst`, `fn`, `par`, `loc`) are not nodes and do not touch the stack; this list, not `passes.txt`, says which records are not nodes, and tools
take it from here. The records that end a section (`prog`, `cn`, `end`) pop their nodes and
push nothing, and the stack must then be empty; anything else is an internal error (status 11).

**Positions.** Every node of `sea.ast` and `sea.hir*` carries a `pos`: the position of the first
token of its source text. Parentheses are not nodes and are not part of the text of the node they
enclose, but they are part of the text of an enclosing node that starts with them: in
`(a + b) * c` the `+` node is at `a` and the `*` node at `(`. A node that a later pass creates
takes the position its rule names. Diagnostics (LANGUAGE.md §9.1, §9.2) report the position or
line of a node; which node each message reports is part of the error table (§2.6).

**Why post-order.** A pass reads its whole input into its tables (§2.7) and builds every tree
with one stack, without forward references; the stack never holds more entries than there are
nodes. The parser's recursion (bounded by the nesting limit 64, §2.7) produces post-order
naturally, and later passes iterate over post-order records (§2.7).

### 3.4 `sea.ast`

The syntax tree of the whole compilation unit, prelude first, exactly as parsed by the grammar of
LANGUAGE.md Appendix A: no names are resolved and nothing is typed. The body is the post-order of
each top-level item and statement in stream order, followed by `prog n`, the last record before
`#end`, which pops all n of them and is the one record without a position.

**Records** (every record except `prog` has `pos` as its first field after the opcode; the
"Pops" column is the number of child nodes as `passes.txt` writes it, §3.9, and "Children" names
them in order):

| Record | Fields after `pos` | Pops | Children (in order) | Source |
|--------|--------------------|------|---------------------|--------|
| `prog` | `n:u` (no `pos`) | `n` | n items and statements | the compilation unit |
| `const` | `name:s t:u` | `1+t` | [type if t = 1], expr | `const name [: type] = expr` |
| `struct` | `name:s n:u` | `n` | n `field` | `struct name { … }` |
| `field` | `name:s` | `1` | type | `name: type` in a struct |
| `fn` | `name:s el:u np:u nr:u` | `np+nr+1` | np `param`, nr types, block | `[elemental] fn name(…) [-> result] { … }`; el = 1 for `elemental`; nr = 0 (no result), 1 (`-> T`) or the number of types of a tuple result |
| `param` | `name:s rf:u d:u` | `1+d` | type, [default expr if d = 1] | `[ref] name: type [= expr]`; rf = 1 for `ref` |
| `type` | `base:s shape:shape nd:u` | `nd` | nd dims (each an `int` or `name`) | `base` is `f64`, `i64`, `bool`, `str` or an identifier; shape `s` (no brackets, nd 0), `v` `[]` (0), `m` `[,]` (0), `fv` `[d]` (1), `fm` `[d, d]` (2) |
| `let`, `var` | `t:u` | `2+t` | pattern, [type if t = 1], expr | `let`/`var pattern [: type] = expr` |
| `pname` | `name:s` | `0` | — | a name in a pattern |
| `pskip` | — | `0` | — | `_` in a pattern or as a tuple-assignment target |
| `ptuple` | `n:u` | `n` | n `pname`/`pskip` | `(p1, p2, …)` |
| `asg` | `op:asgop` | `2` | target, expr | `target op expr`; op `set add sub mul div` for `= += -= *= /=` |
| `tasg` | `n:u` | `n+1` | n targets (expressions or `pskip`), expr | `(t1, …, tn) = expr` |
| `cstmt` | — | `1` | a `call` | a call statement |
| `if` | `e:u` | `2+e` | cond, block, [else if e = 1: a `block`, or an `if` for `else if`] | `if` statement |
| `while` | — | `2` | cond, block | |
| `for` | `name:s npos:pos` | `2` | iterable (a `range` for a range loop, else an expression), block | `for name in … { … }`; `pos` is that of `for`, `npos` that of `name` (the loop variable); fields in this order |
| `match` | `n:u` | `n+1` | scrutinee, n `arm` | |
| `arm` | `k:u` | `k+1` | k `str` patterns, block | `"a" \| "b" => { … }`; k = 0 for `_` |
| `break`, `continue` | — | `0` | — | |
| `return` | `k:u` | `k` | k expressions | k = 0 `return`, 1 `return e`, ≥ 2 `return (e1, …, ek)` |
| `block` | `n:u` | `n` | n statements | `{ … }`, at the `{` |
| `int` | `v:i` | `0` | — | an integer literal's value (unsigned, ≤ 2⁶³; 2⁶³ is `#8000000000000000` and occurs only as the operand of `neg`) |
| `float` | `v:f` | `0` | — | a float literal, converted by pass 1 (§2.8) |
| `str` | `v:s` | `0` | — | a string literal's bytes after escape processing (LANGUAGE.md §3.5) |
| `true`, `false` | — | `0` | — | |
| `name` | `name:s` | `0` | — | an identifier |
| `dollar` | — | `0` | — | `$` |
| `neg`, `not` | — | `1` | operand | unary `-`, `!` |
| `bin` | `op:binop` | `2` | left, right | op `add sub mul div mod pow matmul eq ne lt le gt ge band bor and or` for `+ - * / % ^ @ == != < <= > >= & \| && \|\|` |
| `call` | `n:u` | `n+1` | callee, n arguments | `callee(a1, …, an)` |
| `narg` | `name:s` | `1` | expr | a named argument `name: expr` |
| `ref` | — | `1` | target | a `ref target` argument |
| `conv` | `t:cvtype` | `1` | expr | `f64(e)`, `i64(e)`, `str(e)` (there is no `bool(e)`: LANGUAGE.md Appendix A) |
| `index` | `n:u` | `n+1` | base, n indices (each an expression, `all` or `range`) | `base[i]`, `base[i, j]` |
| `all` | — | `0` | — | `:` as an index |
| `range` | `incl:u st:u` | `2+st` | lo, hi, [step if st = 1] | `lo..hi` (incl 0), `lo..=hi` (incl 1), `step` |
| `rangev` | — | `1` | a `range` | `( range )`, a range used as a value |
| `dot` | `name:s` | `1` | operand | `x.name`: field, projection or view, decided in pass 2a |
| `array` | `r:u` | `r` | r `row` | `[ … ]`, at the `[`; r = 0 for `[]` |
| `row` | `n:u` | `n` | n expressions | one row of an array literal |
| `slit` | `name:s n:u` | `n` | n `init` | `Name { … }` |
| `rlit` | `n:u` | `n` | n `init` | `{ … }` |
| `init` | `name:s` | `1` | expr | `name: expr` in a struct or record literal |
| `ifx` | — | `3` | cond, then-expr, else-expr (an `ifx` for `else if`) | `if` expression |

**What pass 1 has checked.** Every error of LANGUAGE.md §3 and every violation of the grammar of
LANGUAGE.md Appendix A and its disambiguation rules is reported by pass 1, so a written `sea.ast` is
syntactically valid: the child of `cstmt` is a `call` (otherwise `expression statement has no
effect`), `dollar` occurs only inside the index list of an `index` node (array-literal brackets
do not count, LANGUAGE.md §5.3), the operand `#8000000000000000` of `int` occurs only directly
under `neg` (parentheses produce no node, so `-(9223372036854775808)` is accepted too),
and
`a < b < c` has been rejected (comparisons are non-associative; a parenthesized comparison is an
ordinary operand). Everything that depends on names or types is reported by pass 2a.

**Example** (`ex.sea`, compiled with `--no-prelude`, so the program is file 0):

```sea
struct P {
    x: f64
    n: i64
}
fn scale(p: P, k: f64 = 2.0) -> f64 {
    return p.x * k ^ 2 * (0.5 * 3)
}
let p = P { n: 3, x: 1.5 }
var t = 0
for i in 0..p.n {
    t += scale(p, k: i)
}
t += scale(p)
printf("%.3f\n", t)
```

`sea build --emit ast --no-prelude ex.sea`:

```

#file ex.sea
```

`k ^ 2` binds tighter than `*` and `*` is left-associative (LANGUAGE.md §6.1), so the
`return` expression is `(p.x * (k ^ 2)) * (0.5 * 3)`; both outer `*` nodes start at `p`
(column 12), the parenthesized product at `0.5` (column 27). The float literals are 2.0
(`#4000000000000000`), 0.5 (`#3FE0000000000000`) and 1.5 (`#3FF8000000000000`); the format
string's bytes are `%.3f` and LF.

#### 3.4.1 `sea.res`

The syntax tree of `sea.ast` with its names resolved and its declarations checked: the output of
`seaname` and the input of `seacheck`, the two programs of pass 2a (§2.1, Decision 17). Nothing
in it is typed except what the declarations fix. Its records are those of `sea.ast` (§3.4) and
the records of this section (codes 50–63 of set `A` in `passes.txt`, §3.9), which occur only in
`sea.res`.

**Body**, in this order: at most one `rerr`; the `rtup` records, in id order; then the tree: the
records of the body of `sea.ast`, in the same order, each copied unchanged except the
replacements below. A replacement record is a node at the same position with the same children
(the same pops); its fields are those of the record it replaces, in the same order, followed by
its new fields (`rpowk` drops the operator field, always `pow`). So both programs build the same
tree and number its nodes alike, and every position, child count and error position of `sea.ast`
is unchanged in `sea.res`.

**Entered items and resolved regions.** An *entered* item is a top-level item that becomes a
symbol: every `fn`, `const` and `struct` item except one whose name an earlier item already has
(the later one is `redefinition of '%s'` and is not entered; an item with a predeclared name is
entered, after its `redefinition of predeclared name`, which from 4h an item of the prelude, in
file 0 of a stream with more than one `#file` record, does not get, lead decision L-s). The *resolved regions* are the body block
of every entered `fn`, the top-level statements of the program's file (the body of `.main`),
and the expression (not the type annotation) of every entered `const`, without the *skipped
regions*: every `match` statement and every `for` whose iterable is not a `range` (each whole
statement, the iterable and the body included), which the single program never walks while the
phase rule reports them (`not supported yet: match`, and `not supported yet: arrays` at the
`for`; until phase 4 implements them, which then removes them from this list). Then:

* every entered `fn`, `struct` and `const` item record is replaced by `rfn`, `rst`, or one of
  `rcni rcnf rcnb rcne rcn` respectively; a not-entered item is copied unchanged;
* every `int` record of the file becomes `rint`;
* in the resolved regions, every `name` becomes `rname` (the subtree of a `type` node is not
  part of a resolved region: its `int` and `name` dims stay as they are, apart from `rint`), every `pname` `rpname`, every `for`
  `rfor`, and every `bin` with operator `pow` that is a `powk` by the rule below becomes `rpowk`;
* from phase 6 (Decision 91, L-bx) a parameter default is a resolved region too: its `name`
  records become `rname` (resolved like those of a `const` item's value) and its `bin pow` records
  `rpowk` by the rule below; `seaname` writes no outcome for it (no `rcn…` record), and `seacheck`
  evaluates and checks it (§2.11.2);
* nothing else changes: `type` records (also those of signatures), struct fields (and, until phase
  6, parameter defaults), and everything outside the resolved regions (the bodies of not-entered
  functions among it) are copied unchanged apart from their `int` records.

**Declaration records** (not nodes, §3.3):

| Record | Fields | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| `rerr` | `pos:pos code:u k:u a:s*k` | the first error `seaname` found ("Errors" below): its position, its code (§2.6.2) and its k substitutions in text order, spelled as §2.6.2 says (k ≤ 3, the most `args` letters an error has; each a name, a word or a type, at most 4 096 bytes); the one record with more than one string field (§3.1) |
| `rtup` | `id:u n:u t:ty*n` | a tuple type (§3.5.1 `ttuple`): the results of a function with n ≥ 2 results; ids from 10, dense, in order of creation (the signatures of the entered functions in item order, a tuple already created reused) |

A `ty` field of `sea.res` is 0 (a type that has an error, already reported), 1–9 (the predefined
types of §3.5.1) or the id of an `rtup` of the same file. `seacheck` adds the types it infers and
numbers all types again when it writes `sea.hir1` (§3.5.1).

**Replacement records:**

| Record | Fields after `pos` | Pops | Replaces | Meaning |
|--------|--------------------|------|----------|---------|
| `rfn` | `name:s el:u np:u nr:u fid:u rty:ty t:ty*np` | `np+nr+1` | `fn` | an entered function: `el` 0 for an ordinary function, 1 for an elemental one and 2 for an ordinary function that LANGUAGE.md §8.6 (b) or (c) requires inlined (§2.11.1, §2.11.3); its `fid` (§3.5.4: `.main` is 1, the entered `fn` items follow from 2 in stream order), its result type `rty` (1 for none, the type of one result, the `rtup` of several; 0 when a result type has an error) and its parameters' types `t` in order (0 for a parameter whose type has an error, among them a `str` parameter while strings are `not supported yet`, §2.6.2) |
| `rst` | `name:s n:u sid:u` | `n` | `struct` | an entered struct: its number `sid`, from 1 in stream order among the entered structs |
| `rcni` | `name:s t:u cid:u v:i` | `1+t` | `const` | an entered constant (`cid` from 1 in stream order among the entered constants, as `cn`, §3.5.2) whose value is the `i64` v |
| `rcnf` | `name:s t:u cid:u v:f` | `1+t` | `const` | … whose value is the `f64` v |
| `rcnb` | `name:s t:u cid:u v:u` | `1+t` | `const` | … whose value is the `bool` v (0 or 1) |
| `rcne` | `name:s t:u cid:u e:cerr epos:pos` | `1+t` | `const` | … whose evaluation fails: e `ovf` (`integer overflow`, code 260) or `div0` (`integer division by zero`, 261) at the operator node at `epos` |
| `rcn` | `name:s t:u cid:u` | `1+t` | `const` | … for which `seaname` has no value ("Constants" below) |
| `rpname` | `name:s lid:lid` | `0` | `pname` | the local the name declares |
| `rfor` | `name:s npos:pos lid:lid` | `2` | `for` | the local of the loop variable |
| `rint` | `v:i fv:f?` | `0` | `int` | `fv`: the bits of the literal's value as an `f64` when that value is exact in `f64`, else `-`; for the literal 2⁶³ (only the operand of a `neg`, §3.4) the bits of −2⁶³, `#C3E0000000000000`, because the two are written as one constant (§3.5.5) |
| `rname` | `name:s k:nkind ref:u` | `0` | `name` | what the name denotes where it stands: k `loc` a local or parameter of the current function (ref its lid), `cst` an entered constant (its cid), `fn` an entered function (its fid), `st` an entered struct (its sid), `pd` a predeclared name (LANGUAGE.md Appendix C; ref 0; from 4h every name of Appendix C except `linspace`, `meshgrid`, `setdiff` and `bincount`, which only an entered item names, lead decision L-s), `none` nothing (ref 0) |
| `rpowk` | `k:i` | `2` | `bin` (`pow`) | a `^` whose exponent is a constant integer k with \|k\| ≤ `SEA_LIM_POWK` (below); both children are kept |

**Names.** Each name is looked up by the scope rules of LANGUAGE.md §3.3, §7.2 and §7.7: the
locals and parameters of the current function that are in scope (innermost first), then the
entered items, then the predeclared names (from 4h without the four prelude names `linspace`,
`meshgrid`, `setdiff` and `bincount`, which only an entered item names: with `--no-prelude` they
resolve as `none`, lead decision L-s). In the body of a prelude function (file 0 of a stream with
more than one `#file` record) the entered items are only those of the prelude: an item of the
program, even one that redefines a predeclared name (212), is never found there, so a program item
cannot capture a call inside the prelude (lead decision L-s). Locals are numbered as §3.5.4 says (the parameters
1 … np, then the declared names in source order; a shadowing declaration is a new local), and
the lids of `rpname`, `rfor` and `rname loc` are those numbers, so they are the lids of the
`loc` records `seacheck` writes. The expression of a constant sees no locals. A skipped
region keeps its `sea.ast` records: it declares no local, so its `pname`s and its `for` carry no
lid and take no number, and the locals after it are numbered as if it were absent (as the single
program numbered them). `seacheck` takes every lid from `sea.res`; it never derives a lid from a
counter of its own and never compares such a counter with the lids of `sea.res` (it checks only
what "What `seacheck` validates" lists).

**The `symbols` limit** is `seaname`'s. It counts cumulatively, as the single program entered its
symbols: 1 for `.main`, then each entered item in stream order, then for each entered function
in fid order its parameters and then the locals of its body, then the locals of `.main`, each
function's locals in the order of their lids; skipped regions count nothing. The declaration
that would make the count exceed `SEA_LIM_SYMBOLS` is reported (`program too large: symbols`,
at the position §2.6.2 gives for it).

**Reading `sea.res` in `seacheck`.** Its reader is that of the single program with these
requirements: a record has up to 72 fields with its opcode (`rfn` with 64 parameters: 71 after
the opcode; `rtup` with 64 components: 66), and every `u`, reference and enumerated field of a
record is kept (up to 69 for `rfn`, 66 for `rtup`), not only the first three, so the splitting
of a record into at most 12 fields and the three `u` slots of a node row must change; `rerr` and
`rtup` are not nodes and are never pushed on the tree stack; the strings of `rerr` are not
interned (they count against no limit); an `fv` creates no row of the constants table (a
literal's row comes from its `v`, as for `sea.ast`); and the count of types for the `types`
limit starts at the number of `rtup` records.

**Constants.** Both programs take the entered constants in one *constant order*: for each
entered constant in stream order that is not yet visited, it is visited: marked *waiting*, then
the nodes of its expression are scanned in file order, and each `rname cst` among them that
names a constant not yet visited is visited first, recursively (an explicit stack, no Baysick
recursion); when a constant's scan ends it is *checked* (`seacheck`) or *evaluated*
(`seaname`) and marked done. In `seacheck`, a name of a waiting constant met during a check
closes a cycle: it is `not a constant expression` (code 237) at that name.

`seaname` evaluates each entered constant, in the constant order, on the well-typed path only:
it types the expression by the rules of LANGUAGE.md §4.2 and §6 (untyped integer constants,
the conversion to an annotated `f64`, `i64` → `f64` where an operator converts), decides the
`powk` of every `^` in it (below), and evaluates it as §3.5.2 says (`FEPOW` for the other `^`
and for `pow`). It reports no error and checks no rule: where it cannot type or evaluate the
expression (a node other than a literal, `true`, `false`, `neg`, `not`, `bin`, `rpowk`, a name
of a constant or of `pi inf nan eps`, or a call whose callee is an `rname pd` naming `pow` or
`sqrt`, with positional arguments only (a call of a function item named `pow` or `sqrt`,
entered after its `redefinition of predeclared name`, is none of these); operand types the rules
do not accept; an annotation it cannot use; a name of a waiting
constant), and wherever the rule of LANGUAGE.md §7.2 leaves a constant unevaluated (it names a
constant without a value, Decision 25), it writes `rcn`. Its outcome is written in the item's
record: `rcni`, `rcnf`, `rcnb` a value; `rcne` an evaluation that fails (the first failing
operation in evaluation order); `rcn` none of these (no value). A constant with an `rcne` or
`rcn` outcome has no value for the constants after it.

`seacheck` checks every entered constant itself, in the constant order, as the single program
does, reports its errors, and then decides its value (§3.5.2, Decision 25):

1. if the check found an error, the constant has no value, and the outcome is ignored;
2. otherwise, if its expression names a constant without a value, or its type is the error type
   (0), or a node of its expression has the error type, or its expression holds a node `seaname`
   does not evaluate (one outside the list above: in a constant without an error of its own this
   is a call of a function item named `pow` or `sqrt`, or a node below an error-typed one), it has
   no value and no error, and the outcome is ignored (Decision 25 as refined: "a part of the
   expression whose type is in error");
3. otherwise the outcome must be a value of the kind of its derived type (`rcni` for `i64`,
   `rcnf` for `f64` (a constant `f64` `%`, `5.5 % 2.0`, is evaluated, L-dd), `rcnb` for `bool`), which becomes its value, or an `rcne` whose `epos` is
   the position of a `bin` or `neg` node of that constant's expression, `ovf` only at an `add`,
   `sub`, `mul` or `neg` and `div0` only at a `mod`: `seacheck` then reports `integer overflow`
   or `integer division by zero` at `epos` at that moment, so it takes its place in its find
   order, and the constant has no value. Any other outcome (`rcn` among them) is `BAD_RECORD`
   (status 11).

So a program without errors has a value for every constant, and `seacheck` reports
`BAD_RECORD` if it would write `sea.hir1` with a constant that has none. `seacheck` adds each
value to its constants table (`C` rows, §2.7) and enforces the `constants` limit for the
values of constants, at the constant's item (§2.6.2); `seaname` does not count them. A constant
without a value is read as a poisoned value (§3.5.2): it makes no `powk` and no further error.

**Constant exponents.** A `^` in a resolved region becomes `rpowk k` when, were it well typed,
§3.5.5's rule ("Constant exponents") would make it `powk k`: the exponent typed by the rules of
LANGUAGE.md §4.2 and §6 as `seacheck` types it (an untyped exponent taken as `f64`, an `i64` one
converted), its names resolved as above, and evaluated exactly; an exponent that names a
constant without a value is not constant. `seacheck` writes `powk k` for an `rpowk` whose `^` it
finds well typed, exactly where the phase-1 rule did (§3.5.5), and checks and writes nothing of
the exponent's value itself.

**Errors.** `seaname` reports the errors of the declaration checks only: those of the items (in
stream order) and then those of the signatures of the entered functions (in item order), the
codes §2.6.2 assigns to it ("Which program reports it"). It keeps the first of them in source
order (of two at one position, the first found), writes it as the `rerr` record, and still
writes the whole file and ends with status 0, so that `seacheck` checks the rest; with no such
error there is no `rerr`. A capacity limit `seaname` enforces (§2.7) is reported by `seaname`
itself at once, status 10 (the driver then uses no output). `seacheck` starts its own search
with the `rerr` error as the first error found, so of two errors at one position `seaname`'s is
reported (it was found first, by the order of §2.6.2).

**Protocol** (§2.2 steps 5–7). `seaname` reads `sea.ast` (Baysick file 1) and writes `sea.res`
(file 2); `seacheck` reads `sea.res` (file 1) and writes `sea.hir1` (file 2). Each copies the
header records of its input (§3.2), reads its input only with `LINPUT #1` after `IF END #1`,
requires the final `#end` (else `<program>: internal error: truncated input`, status 11, where
`<program>` is `seaname` or `seacheck`), writes `#end` last, and writes nothing to standard output.
The driver runs `seacheck` only on a `sea.res` that ends with `#end` (§2.2 step 6), and also when
it holds an `rerr`. `seaname` validates `sea.ast` as the single program did (a record of codes
50–63 in `sea.ast` is `BAD_RECORD`), and reports its errors and capacity errors as §2.6.2 says.

**What `seacheck` validates** (before checking anything; any violation is `BAD_RECORD`, status
11): every record against `passes.txt` (every enumerated field one of its words, every `pos`
well formed, only bytes 0x20–0x7E); `rerr` and `rtup` only before the tree, at most one `rerr`,
its `code` a code of phase `C2` with k equal to the number of its `args` letters; `rtup` ids
dense from 10 and every `ty` field 0, 1–9 or a defined id; no record of codes 50–63 outside the
places listed above, and none of `fn`, `const`, `struct`, `name`, `pname`, `for` or `int` where a
