| `rcount` | `d:ri e:ri lo:ri hi:ri st:ri incl:u site:site` | for the range `lo..hi step st` (incl 0) or `lo..=hi step st` (incl 1), LANGUAGE.md §5.1, whose exact number of elements n is 0 … 2⁶⁴: `e` = 1 if n > 0, else 0; `d` = (n − 1) mod 2⁶⁴ as an unsigned 64-bit value when n > 0 (the `last` of a `loop` over the range; a full-range loop such as `-2^63..=2^63-1` has n = 2⁶⁴ and `d` = 2⁶⁴ − 1), and `d` = 0 when n = 0 (the empty range); `st` = 0 is `range step is zero`, checked before anything is written |
| `fadd fsub fmul fdiv` | `d:rf a:rf b:rf` | one IEEE binary64 operation, round to nearest even (LANGUAGE.md §6.8) |
| `fneg fabs` | `d:rf a:rf` | flip / clear the sign bit |
| `fsqrt` | `d:rf a:rf` | correctly rounded square root |
| `fmin fmax` | `d:rf a:rf b:rf` | LANGUAGE.md §10.4: if one operand is NaN the other; of equal operands the first (`fmin(-0, +0)` is −0) |
| `ffloor fceil ftrunc fround` | `d:rf a:rf` | LANGUAGE.md §6.7; `fround` ties away from zero |
| `fcmp` | `cc:cc d:ri a:rf b:rf` | IEEE comparison: with a NaN operand only `ne` gives 1 |
| `fnan` | `d:ri a:rf` | 1 if the operand is NaN |
| `itof` | `d:rf a:ri` | `i64` → `f64`, round to nearest even |
| `ftoi` | `d:ri a:rf site:site` | `f64` → `i64` if integral and in range, else `conversion to i64` (LANGUAGE.md §4.2) |
| `padd` | `d:rp a:rp b:ri` | address plus a byte offset |
| `ldi ldb` | `d:ri base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | load from base + idx·scale + off (idx `-`: 0): 8-byte `i64`; 1 byte zero-extended |
| `ldf` | `d:rf base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | load an `f64` |
| `ldp` | `d:rp base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | load an address |
| `ldx` | `d:rx base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | 2 consecutive `f64`, lane 0 at the lowest address |
| `ldy` | `d:ry base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | 4 consecutive `f64` |
| `ldm2 ldm4` | `d:rm base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | 2 or 4 consecutive `bool` bytes as mask lanes |
| `sti stb` | `s:ri base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | store 8 bytes; store the low byte |
| `stf` | `s:rf base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | store an `f64` |
| `stp` | `s:rp base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | store an address |
| `stx` | `s:rx base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | store 2 lanes |
| `sty` | `s:ry base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | store 4 lanes |
| `stm2 stm4` | `s:rm base:rp idx:ri? scale:u off:i` | store mask lanes as bytes 0/1 |
| `mcopy` | `d:rp s:rp n:ri` | copy n bytes (n ≥ 0) from address s to address d; the two regions never overlap (phase 4: struct and fixed-size array copies, constant array data, contiguous runs of elements) |
| `xadd xsub xmul xdiv xmin xmax` | `d:rx a:rx b:rx` | lane by lane, each lane exactly the scalar instruction of the same name |
| `xneg xabs xsqrt xfloor xceil xtrunc xround` | `d:rx a:rx` | lane by lane |
| `xcmp` | `cc:cc d:rm a:rx b:rx` | lane by lane `fcmp` into a 2-lane mask |
| `xsel` | `d:rx m:rm a:rx b:rx` | per lane: the first vector where the mask lane is set, else the second |
| `xsplat` | `d:rx a:rf` | every lane = the scalar |
| `xlane` | `d:rf a:rx k:u` | lane k |
| `yadd ysub ymul ydiv ymin ymax` | `d:ry a:ry b:ry` | as the `x` forms, with 4 lanes |
| `yneg yabs ysqrt yfloor yceil ytrunc yround` | `d:ry a:ry` | as the `x` forms, with 4 lanes |
| `ycmp` | `cc:cc d:rm a:ry b:ry` | into a 4-lane mask |
| `ysel` | `d:ry m:rm a:ry b:ry` | as `xsel` |
| `ysplat` | `d:ry a:rf` | as `xsplat` |
| `ylane` | `d:rf a:ry k:u` | as `xlane` |
| `mand mor` | `d:rm a:rm b:rm` | lane-wise mask logic |
| `mnot` | `d:rm a:rm` | lane-wise negation |
| `vfeat` | `d:ri f:feat` | 1 if the selected kernel variant (§4.4) is `avx2` (feat `avx2`; `x86_64-linux` only) |
| `loop` | `b:blk ind:ri start:ri last:ri step:ri` | a counted loop that runs at least once: start, last and step are read once on entry; for k = 0 … last inclusive, k and last compared as unsigned 64-bit values (last + 1 iterations, up to 2⁶⁴), the body runs with `ind` = start + k·step computed modulo 2⁶⁴ (two's complement); the body never writes `ind`; an empty range is excluded by an enclosing `if` on `rcount`'s flag (§3.6.6 rule 4) |
| `endloop` | `b:blk` | the end of loop `b`: if k = last the loop ends, else k + 1 and the body runs again |
| `do` / `enddo` | `b:blk` | a loop left only by `exit`, and its end |
| `if` / `ifz` | `b:blk c:ri` | the first part runs if the register is not 0 (`if`) or is 0 (`ifz`), the `else` part otherwise |
| `else` / `endif` | `b:blk` | the start of the `else` part, the end of the construct |
| `exit` / `next` | `b:blk` | leave loop `b` / start its next iteration (`loop`: as at `endloop`, so `next` after k = last ends the loop; `do`: the top) |
| `ret` | `n:u v:reg*n` | return the results |
| `call` | `name:s nr:u d:reg*nr na:u a:reg*na` | call a Sea function; nr is the callee's result count, or 0 to discard its results |
| `rcall` | `entry:s site:site? nr:u d:reg*nr na:u a:reg*na` | call a runtime entry point, named as `rt.inc` lists it (§4.8); `site` for entries that can fail (allocation, I/O, the checks of library functions) |
| `chkb` | `idx:ri ext:ri dim:u site:site` | if idx < 0 or idx ≥ ext: `index … out of bounds for dimension … of extent …` (LANGUAGE.md §5.4) with idx, `dim` and ext; `dim` counts from 0 (LANGUAGE.md §5.4): 0 for the rows (or a vector's only dimension), 1 for the columns, printed as is |
| `chk` | `c:ri err:s site:site n:u a:reg*n` | if c ≠ 0, stop with the run-time error whose code name in `errors.inc` is `err`, the arguments substituted |
| `retain` / `release` | `a:rp` | count one more / one fewer reference to a runtime object; `release` frees it at zero (§4.2) |

After a `loop` ends normally (at `endloop` or a `next` with k = last), its `ind` holds start +
last · step (modulo 2⁶⁴), the value of the last iteration, as §4.9.2's closing sequence leaves it; a
read of `ind` after the loop sees that value (L-ay). After an `exit` it holds the value of the
iteration that left.

The `off` field of the loads and stores is any `i64` value (field kind `i`, §3.1); passes 3b and
4 hold it as four 16-bit limbs, not as an entry of the `C` table (which holds only the `li`/`lf`
constants that the immediates limit counts, §2.7), so no 2⁵³ bound applies to it.

Blocks (`loop`, `do`, `if`, `ifz`) are numbered per function from 1 in the order of their opening
records and nest properly; `exit`/`next` name an enclosing `loop` or `do`.

**Properties of `sea.lir1` that passes 3b and 4 rely on** (from phase 5, §5.8; L-ae). Pass
3a's rules guarantee them; no pass checks them. (1) No `sti`, `stb`, `stf`, `stp` or `mcopy` writes a
byte of an array's header or of a string's header: a header changes only inside runtime entries
and, for the count, by `retain` and `release`; an array's element kind, rank, rows, cols and data
address (`SEA_ARR_EK` … `SEA_ARR_DATA`, §4.8) never change after the entry that created it returns.
(2) Every register is written on every path before it is read (rules 1 and 2: every local has an
initializer, every temporary is computed before its use). (3) The memory a `ref` parameter's address
reaches is reached in the callee only through that parameter and the calls it is passed to: Sea has
no global variables (LANGUAGE.md §7.2), a `ref` argument shares no root with another argument of
its call (LANGUAGE.md §8.3), and the arrays on an element or field argument's path are made unique
before its address is taken (rule 31). (4) A slot of a function is reached only through the `sa`
registers of that slot and what those registers are passed to or copied into. The four
properties hold for `sea.lir2` and `sea.lir` too (L-bh): every transformation of §5.8 keeps them (a
moved or new instruction is placed where its operands are already written, T5's pre-load and T7's
`Q` are written before the loop, T6's and T9's copies carry their own writes, and none stores to a
header or reaches a slot or `ref` memory another way; T4's selection reads its own destination,
and T10, last in both passes, deletes it when that destination is dead, L-bn); §4.9.2's liveness
rule relies on property 2.

**Sites.** An instruction's site is the file index and line of the position of the
HIR node whose check or call it implements. **Code from the prelude** never reports a prelude
line: pass 3a inlines every call of a prelude function, at every call site and recursively (the
prelude has no recursion), in addition to the calls LANGUAGE.md §8.6 requires, so no prelude
function is a LIR function; and in code inlined from the prelude every site is the site of the
call in the program's file into which it was (transitively) inlined. A run-time error inside
`bincount`, for instance, reports the line of the program's `bincount(…)` call, as
LANGUAGE.md §9.2 requires (`<file>` is the program's file). Code inlined from the program's own functions
keeps its own sites.

**Reproducibility is in the instruction set** (LANGUAGE.md §6.8): there is no fused multiply-add
and no instruction that rounds twice or not at all; every `fadd fsub fmul fdiv fsqrt` and vector
lane is one correctly rounded IEEE operation; no pass reorders `f64` operations except by moving
whole instructions without changing which operands they read; pass 4 maps each such instruction
to exactly one machine instruction of the same operation (never contracting two into an FMA).

#### 3.6.5 `sea.lir1` and `sea.lir` compared

Both use the records above. `sea.lir1` (pass 3a) uses only the classes `i`, `f`, `p` and no
`ldx ldy ldm2 ldm4 stx sty stm2 stm4 x… y… m… vfeat`; it keeps every bounds check, COW check and
stack slot pass 3a emits. `sea.lir` (pass 3b) may in addition contain the vector classes and
instructions (vectorized loops, §5.1; on `x86_64-linux` each vectorized loop in an `if` on
`vfeat` with the 4-lane form first and the 2-lane form in the `else` part, §4.4), and it has
fewer checks (those §5.8's T1 proves; a check that stays is never moved), fewer copy-on-write
checks in the copy of a loop that runs when the counts are 1 (T6), fewer slots (scalar replacement)
and hoisted or strength-reduced instructions (§5.2, §5.3, §5.8).

**Pass 3b in phase 1** (§8). Pass 3b reads `sea.lir1` completely and validates it (the header
records and `#end`, every record against `passes.txt`, register classes and the numbering of
§3.6.1, block numbering and nesting, slots, data labels and their records) and writes it
unchanged as `sea.lir`; it transforms nothing. The validation also covers: the parameter
registers of each `func` record (numbered 1 … np in order, §3.6.1); every `ret` against its
`func` (n = the function's nr, each value of the result's class; `.main` returns 0); every
`call` (a `func` of that name exists, na = its np with each argument of its parameter's class,
nr = its nr or 0, each result register of the result's class); the `u` fields that encode a
choice (`incl` of `rcount` and `dim` of `chkb`: 0 or 1); each `chk` (n = the number of argument
slots that the `args` letters of the error `err` need, §2.6.2); no instruction inside a `loop`
writes its `ind`; exactly one `func` of kind `main`, named `.main`; each `fconv` (class `p`
exactly for `s`, `i` or `f` for the numeric conversions); every `la` names a data label the
file defines (labels are `d1`, `d2`, …: `d0` is never one); no two `func` records have the same
name. Any violation is `BAD_RECORD`. The transformations of §5.2–§5.3 and §5.1 arrive
in phases 5 and 7. So that the phase-1 `.lir` dump tests stay valid after them, they use only
programs on which the complete pass 3b changes nothing either: no loop-invariant instruction in a
loop, no array access or removable check, no slot that §5.3 could scalar-replace (the slots of
phase 1, rules 8 and 12 below, escape to a call), no address to strength-reduce and nothing to
vectorize.

**Pass 3b from phase 4** (sub-phase 4c, §8) still transforms nothing and validates, in addition:
`retain`, `release` and `mcopy` (their operands of class `p`, `p`, `p p i`); every `slay` record
(a label defined once, followed by exactly n `soff` records whose offsets are strictly
ascending multiples of 8, each at most its size − 8; a `soff` only inside such a group); every `rcall`
against the `entries` table (§2.6.3): the entry exists, its `site` field is present exactly when
the entry's site is `S`, nr is the entry's result count or 0, and the argument and result
registers have the entry's classes in order (a `la` of a `slay` label is valid like one of any
data label; no use of its register is tracked). Any violation is `BAD_RECORD`.

**Pass 3b from phase 5** (sub-phases 5c-1 and 5c-2, §8). Pass 3b validates each function
exactly as above, then applies T1–T4 and T10 of §5.8 in the order §5.8 gives, and writes the
result renumbered (from 5c-2 as `sea.lir2`, Decision 74) as §3.6.1 and §3.6.4 require (registers by first appearance, blocks by opening
record); slots, data labels and data records are unchanged, and it writes no record that `sea.lir1`
may not hold (no vector class before phase 7). Its output is a function of `sea.lir1` alone and the
same for both targets. A transformation whose result would exceed a LIR capacity limit of the
function (§2.6.1: instructions, operands, registers, blocks, immediates) is not applied (Decision
72), so optimization never makes a compilation fail. The same holds for the pass's own scratch
tables (`seaopt`'s and `sealopt`'s working tables of a transformation, such as `sealopt`'s in its
free arrays `S()` and `V()`, and the pass's columns of `R`, L-bv): every write into such a table is
bounded by the region (rows or columns) the pass gives that table, tested before the write; when a
table would exceed its region, the transformation that needs it is not applied to that loop (or,
for a function-wide analysis, to that function), with no crash, no write outside the region and no
overlap with another table, and the function's output is then exactly what it is without that
transformation there, still correct. One exception is accepted: when T9's `PLACE` tables overflow
after the split has been rebuilt, the split is kept and only the placement is dropped, so the output
equals T9's with nothing placed, which is correct (the placeable instructions stay before the outer
`if`, ahead of every copy); the same holds for the Decision 72 capacity failure in `PLACE`
(the paragraph "Readings fixed by the 5c-2 build", after the lead decisions). The phase-1 and phase-4 `.lir` goldens that
the transformations change are re-derived from §5.8 (L-ak), in the sub-phase that adds the
transformation changing them: those T1–T4 and T10 change in 5c-1, those T5–T9 change in 5c-2
(`gen_arith` is not one: it is a hand-written pass-4 test, `.lir` and `.out` only, which no
`seaopt` or `sealopt` run produces, L-bj); the rest are checked
against §5.8 by the same work package (§6.2).

**Pass 3c** (`sealopt`, from sub-phase 5c-2, Decision 74). Pass 3c reads `sea.lir2`, which has
the records and properties `sea.lir1` may have except the two `sea.lir1`-only label rules (§3.6.4; `passes.txt`'s set for `sea.lir1`:
no vector class before phase 7), and validates it with the same module (`lirrw`, §2.6.3; without
the two label rules that hold for `sea.lir1` only, §3.6.2, L-bu), then
applies T5, T6, T8, T7, T8 again, T9 and T10 of §5.8 and writes `sea.lir` renumbered, under the
same rules as pass 3b (a function of its input alone, the same for both targets, Decision 72's
capacity rule). Since T10 is idempotent on its own output, a function to which none of T5–T9
applies is written unchanged: its `sea.lir` equals its `sea.lir2`. Both outputs are canonical
(Decision 69): the `.lir2` goldens are derived from T1–T4 and T10, the `.lir` goldens from T5–T10
applied to them (§6.2).

#### 3.6.6 Canonical lowering of scalar code

So that LIR dumps are reproducible, pass 3a lowers the scalar subset (scalar `i64`, `f64` and
`bool` parameters, locals and results; constants, `lv`, `cvt`, `un`, `bin` on scalars, `ifx`,
`seq`, calls, `rarg` of a scalar local, `bind`, `tbind`, `eval` of a call, `asg` to a local, `if`,
`while`, `forr`, `break`, `cont`, `ret`, `tret`, `block`; the library calls `printf`, `now`, `f64`,
`i64` and `idiv` and string constants as `printf` arguments; from phase 3 the elementary functions
`log exp sin cos pow hypot` and `bin pow`, rule 14) exactly as follows; pass 3a inlines
exactly the calls LANGUAGE.md §8.6 requires and the calls of prelude functions (§3.6.4, "Sites"),
and no others.

**Inlining is deferred to phase 6** (§8), except for prelude calls. The phase-1 to phase-5 pass 3a
inlines no call of a program's own function (the performance guarantee of LANGUAGE.md §8.6 is not
observable in a program's output); from phase 4 it inlines every call of a prelude function, in
the canonical form of rule 37 (Decision 18). The dump tests of phases 1–5 were meant to use only
programs in which LANGUAGE.md §8.6 requires no inlining; the review of the phase-6 specification found
21 lowering dump tests whose function §8.6 (b) or (c) covers (listed in §6.2, "Phase-6 tests"), and
every `.res`, `.hir1` and `.hir` golden of a program with such a function changes with the `el` value 2
and the kind `inl`; phase 6 treats them by Decision 90. The prelude calls are tested by program tests, by `.hir`, `.hirl` and `.lir1` dump
tests built with the prelude (a `NAME.prelude` marker, §6.2, Decision 57), whose expected dumps
follow rule 37, and by stage goldens of hand-written two-file `sea.hir` (Decision 55).
From phase 6 (§2.11) pass 3a inlines exactly the calls LANGUAGE.md §8.6 requires (the
functions of kind `elem` and `inl`, §2.11.3) by `sealoop`'s rewrite L20 (§2.11.4) with
`sealower`'s refinements R31 and R32 (§2.11.5), the copied code keeping its own sites; the dumps of
the inlined forms are the `inl6_*` and `elem6_*` tests of §6.2, and a golden that inlining changes
is treated by Decision 90 and re-derived from these rules (L-ct). Phase 6 adds rule 39 (library calls through the entry table,
Decision 52), stated in §2.11.5.

Rules 1–14 are the scalar subset of phase 1–3; rules 15–38 are the arrays, structs, strings,
reference counts and copy on write of phase 4 (§8, sub-phases 4d–4h), each introduced by the
sub-phase that implements its construct; rule 39 is phase 6's (§2.11.5).

**Two programs from sub-phase 4e-0** (Decisions 26–29). The rules below say what `sea.lir1` holds
for a construct, whichever program of pass 3a does the work. From 4e-0 `sealoop` rewrites the array
constructs into the records of §3.5.9 and `sealower` lowers them by "Lowering of the `sea.hirl`
records" (after rule 38); a rule whose construct `sealoop` rewrites (17 and 30 from 4e-0; 20–22, 25,
26 for numeric literals, 27 (i), (j) and 28 from 4e, §3.5.9 L5–L11; 23 and 24 from 4f, §3.5.9 L13
and L14; from 4g 26 for `str` and struct literals (L9), 29 (L15), 30 for `str` and struct elements
(L4), 33 (L16), and the stores of reference and aggregate values and through field paths of rules
19, 27 (d), (f) and 15 (i) (L17), §3.5.9 "What `sealoop` rewrites in 4g") is met by that rewrite and that lowering together, with
the instructions, registers, blocks, slots, labels and sites the rule gives, unchanged. Rules 12,
15, 16 and 31 are applied by `sealower` to `sea.hirl` (Decision 27), and so is rule 27 (homes),
except its (i) and (j). Where a rule leaves an order or a register open, the rewrite of §3.5.9
fixes it (each extent loaded once per rewrite and reused; addresses computed in the innermost
body in post-order; the sites listed with each rewrite).

1. Each local and parameter has one register of its class. Expressions are lowered in post-order,
   left operand first, one instruction per node, except: `lv` emits nothing (its register is the
   operand); `ci`/`cb` emit `li` and `cf` emits `lf`, a new register for every occurrence; `cvt`
   is `itof`; `i64` `add sub mul` are `iaddc isubc imulc` and `un neg` is `inegc`, with the
   node's line as site; `f64` arithmetic and `un neg` are `fadd fsub fmul fdiv fneg`;
   comparisons are `icmp`/`fcmp`; `un not` is `bnot`; `bin band` and `bin bor` (`&`, `|` on
   `bool`) are `iand` and `ior`.
2. **Destinations.** An instruction's destination is a new register, except that when a value is
   stored into a local L (`bind`, `tbind`, `asg` to `lv L`), the instruction computing the root
   of the value writes L's register directly; a root that is `lv M` becomes `mov L M`. `asg op`
   with op ≠ `set` to `lv L` is the instruction for `L op value` with L's register as
   destination and first operand. A root that is an `ifx`, `and` or `or` is the exception: it is
   computed into its new register R (rule 3) and then copied with `mov L R`, so that L still
   holds its old value while the operands are evaluated. `tbind` and `tasg` give the call the
   registers of their target locals as result registers, and a new register for each `-` or
   `skip` (`_`). A read of a `ref` parameter P (rule 12) whose value is stored straight into a
   local L, or is an operand or arm with destination R (rule 3), is its `ldi`/`ldf` with L or R
   as destination. An `asg` with op `set` to a `ref` parameter P computes the value into a new
   register V by the same rule (a root that is `lv M` of a plain local becomes `mov V M`), then
   `sti`/`stf V P - 0 0`. **`tasg`** `(t1, …, tn) = call` is lowered exactly as: (a) the call's
   arguments left to right (rules 5 and 12); (b) `call` with one result register Ri per component
   i: the register of the target local L when ti is a local, its `cv` is 0 and the call does not
   pass L by `ref`, otherwise a new register of result i's class (for `skip`, for a target that
   is a `ref` parameter, for a component with `cv` 1 (an `i` register), and for a local the call
   passes by `ref`); (c) the reloads of rule 12, in argument order; (d) for each component i in
   order that got a new register, except `skip`: if its `cv` is 1, `itof F Ri` into a new
   register F and V = F, else V = Ri; then `mov L V` for a local L, or `sti`/`stf V P - 0 0` (by
   V's class) for a `ref` parameter P. So in `.main`, `var a = 0.0`, `var b = 0`, `(a, b) =
   two()` with `two` returning `(i64, i64)` is `lf f1 #0000000000000000`, `li i2 0`, `call two 2
   i3 i2 0`, `itof f4 i3`, `mov f1 f4`.
3. `a && b` and `a || b`: a new register R; a with destination R; then `if B R` (for `&&`) or
   `ifz B R` (for `||`), b with destination R, `endif B`. `ifx c a b`: c, then `if B c`, a with a
   new destination R, `else B`, b with destination R, `endif B`. "With destination R" follows
   rule 2: an operand or arm whose root is a constant is its `li`/`lf` into R directly, one that is
   `lv M` is `mov R M`, any other root's instruction writes R. An `&&`, `||` or `ifx` that itself
   has a destination which is not a local (it is an operand or arm with destination R′ of an
   enclosing `&&`, `||` or `ifx`) uses R′ as its R: no new register and no `mov`.
4. `if c then [else]`: c, `if B c`, then, [`else B`, else], `endif B`. `while c body`: `do B`,
   c, `ifz B2 c`, `exit B`, `endif B2`, body, `enddo B`. `forr L (rng lo hi [st])`: lo, hi, then
   st or (if absent) `li` 1, then `rcount C E lo hi st incl site` (C and E new registers, in that
   order; site the `for` line), `if B E`, `loop B2 L lo C st`, body, `endloop B2`, `endif B`, so
   the `if` is block B and the `loop` block B2 = B + 1. `break` is `exit` and `cont` is `next` of
   the innermost loop (B2 of its `forr`).
5. Calls: the arguments left to right, then `call` with the result registers (rule 2); `eval` of
   a call with results uses nr 0. `ret k` is `ret k` of the values' registers. `tret`: the call
   with a new register for each result, then `ret` of those registers in order. `seq`: its `bind`
   nodes in order (rule 2), then its value, which is lowered as if it stood in the `seq`'s place.
6. A function whose result type is `void` ends with `ret 0` unless its last statement is a
   `ret`; `.main` always ends with `ret 0`. A function with results gets nothing after its last
   statement (LANGUAGE.md §8.1 guarantees that every path returns): when that statement is an
   `if` with `else` whose branches all return, the body ends with its `endif` and the `endfunc`
   follows, and pass 4 emits no code after the construct. `block` emits nothing for scalar
   locals.
7. **String constants.** A `cs` (in phase 1 only as the argument of a `%s` conversion of
   `printf`, §8) is a `str` data record `str dN v` (a new label for every occurrence, §3.6.2) and
   `la P dN` into a new register P.
8. **`printf`.** `lib printf` with its `fmt` of n conversions: the arguments of the conversions,
   left to right, each by rule 1; then `sa S s` of a new slot s of 8·max(n, 1) bytes, alignment
   8; then for each argument j (from 0) its store into slot word j: `sti`, `stf` or `stp` (by the
   argument's class) `value S - 0 8j`; then `la F dM` of a `fmt dM k` data record, k the number
   of the format's pieces (`ftext` and `fconv` records, §3.6.2), whose records are those pieces in
   order (each `fconv` with the class of its
   argument: `i` for `i64` and `bool`, `f` for `f64`, `p` for `str`); then `rcall sea_printf
   site 0 2 F S`, with the `printf` call's line as site (§4.8: pass 4 adds the site index as the
   entry's last argument).
9. **`now`.** `lib now` is `rcall sea_now - 1 R 0` into a new register R (`f`).
10. **Conversions.** `lib f64(x)`: `itof` for an `i64` or `bool` x, `mov` for an `f64` x; `lib
    i64(x)`: `ftoi` with the call's line as site for an `f64` x, `mov` for an `i64` or `bool` x.
11. **Integer division.** `lib idiv(a, b)` is `idivf` and `bin mod` of two `i64` is `imodf`, each
    with the node's line as site.
12. **`ref` arguments.** A `rarg` of a local L of the caller that is not itself a `ref` parameter:
    when the argument is reached in the left-to-right order, `sa A s` of a new slot s of 8 bytes,
    alignment 8, and `sti`/`stf L A - 0 0` (L's current value); A is the argument; after the
    `call`, for each such argument in argument order, `ldi`/`ldf L A - 0 0` reloads L. A `rarg` of
    a local that is a `ref` parameter of the caller passes that parameter's `p` register
    unchanged (no slot, no store, no reload). In the callee a `ref` parameter's register is a `p`
    (§3.6.3): a use of it is `ldi`/`ldf` into a new register from `P - 0 0`, and a store into it
    (`asg`, rule 2) computes the value into a new register and writes it with `sti`/`stf V P - 0
    0`. For `asg op` the parameter's current value is loaded first (it is the left operand,
    LANGUAGE.md §6.8 rule 5), then the value is computed, then the operation into a new register,
    then the store.

    **Reads before a `ref` call.** Within one statement, a read of a local L that is evaluated
    (in the order of LANGUAGE.md §6.8 rule 5) before a `call` that passes L by `ref`, or passes
    a `ref` parameter that aliases L, is copied at its evaluation point into a new register T
    (`mov T L`; for a `ref` parameter, its `ldi`/`ldf` writes T), and the later use reads T.
    This covers `y = x + g(ref x)`, `f(x, g(ref x))` and `x += g(ref x)` (the read of x by `+=`
    precedes the call). A read evaluated after the call sees the updated value. In `x = g(ref
    x)` (an `asg`, `bind` or `tbind` whose value is a call that passes the target by `ref`) the
    call writes a new result register R, then the reloads above follow, then `mov x R`, so the
    assignment wins over the reload. The copy is made for every such read of the statement,
    whichever `&&`, `||` or `ifx` arm it is in and whichever arm holds the call.

    **Reference and struct values before a `ref` call** (phase 4). The *roots* of a `call` are
    the root variables (LANGUAGE.md §8.3) of its `ref` arguments; a read *has* a root when its
    path starts at that local or `ref` parameter. Names decide: inside a function two distinct
    parameters, or a parameter and a local, never share a root (LANGUAGE.md §8.3 rejects such
    calls), so no other aliasing exists. A value read before a call of the statement that has its
    root among the call's roots, and consumed after that call, is protected as follows (a value
    consumed before the call, `f(len(a), g(ref a))`, needs nothing):
    (a) a reference-type local L: the copy above is `mov T L` and then `retain T`; T is owned, a
    temporary released right after the node that consumes it (rule 15 (b)), so the callee's
    assignment to L, which releases L's old value, cannot free what T holds (`f(a, g(ref a))`);
    (b) a reference value loaded by `ldp` from an element or field of such a path (`f(v[0], g(ref
    v))` with `v` a `str[]`, `f(s.name, g(ref s))`, a `ref` parameter's `ldp V P - 0 0`): `retain`
    of its register right after the load; it is then owned and released after its consumer;
    (c) a struct or fixed-size value of such a path used as a whole (a local, an element or a
    field): copied at its evaluation point into a new temporary home by rule 27 (c), with the
    retains of a borrowed source; the home's reference fields are released after the consumer
    (rule 15 (g)), so the consumer sees the value as it was read.
    From 4g-2, (b) and (c) apply also to reads through elements of struct and record arrays
    (`f(dims[0].name, g(ref dims))`, `f(a[i].lim, h(ref a))`): the path's root is the array's
    root variable, whatever fields and elements follow.
    The base of an element read is such a read: in `d[growi(ref d)]` the base `d` is evaluated
    first (LANGUAGE.md §5.4), so it is copied and retained by (a), and the element is read from
    the old array, its checks against the old extents. The base of an element *assignment target*
    is not: for `=`, for `op=` (whose left operand, the element's old value, is a read and is
    protected as above) and for each element target of a tuple assignment, no copy is made; the
    target's checks, copy on write and store use the variable as it is after the value and the
    indices are evaluated (LANGUAGE.md §5.5: value, then indices, then the checks against the
    variable), so `d[0] = growi(ref d)` and `d[0] += growi(ref d)` store into the array that
    `growi` left in `d`.
    The `ref` arguments of the outer call itself are rule 31's "deferred" case.
    From 4e-0 `sealower` applies this rule to `sea.hirl`. `sealoop` moves no call and no `rarg`:
    it names each operand it uses later by a `tmp` at the operand's evaluation point (§3.5.9 T1),
    so a read this rule copies is copied there, and the `tmp` then names the copy (its register is
    the copy's T). The "one statement" of this rule in `sea.hirl`: the statements inside an `xblk`
    belong to the statement that holds the `xblk` (they are not statements of their own here); a
    `tmp` directly in a block (as in L4) is a statement, whose expression is its child; an `hloop`
    is a statement whose expression is its range only (its first three children), like a `forr`;
    the `bind` of L4 is a statement like any `bind` (its expression the vector, as the `fore` was).
    Inside an `iblk` the "one statement" is each statement of the inlined body (the callee's
    statements, L-w), and an `iret` is a statement just as a `ret` is (L-cz).
    From 4e the statements of an L6 or L12 `block` (§3.5.9), and the statements L11 writes (in place of a `tbind`,
    or as the `block` of a `tasg` or `tret`), together form one statement, the rewritten `asg` or `tasg` (or tuple statement): their `tmp`s and `bind`s are not
    statements of their own. A read of a local that this rule copies there (the value, an index, a
    mask, a fixed-size value, the left operand of a compound store) is copied at its evaluation point
    by `mov T L` and (a)–(c), and T1's alias exception does not apply to it: the `tmp` or `bind`
    names the copy (an owned copy is released at the block's end, R11, or with the held locals, rule
    21 (8)). The reads of the store into the target stay uncopied (its base `lv T` in IX 2–4 of
    the store, its extents, `cow` and data):
    they use the variable as it is after the value and the indices (LANGUAGE.md §5.5). So `v[0..g(ref
    k)] = k` stores the old `k`, `B[i, g(ref i)..3] = 0.0` uses the old `i`, and `A.flat[k] += g(ref k)`
    the old `k`.
13. **Constant exponents.** `powk k` lowers its base x first, then into a new destination d (or
    the destination of rule 2): k = 0 `lf d 1.0`; k = 1 `mov d x`; k = 2 `fmul d x x`; k = 3
    `fmul t x x`, `fmul d t x`; k = 4 `fmul t x x`, `fmul d t t` (t a new register). For k < 0,
    x^|k| is computed as above into a new register t (t is x itself when |k| = 1), then `lf o
    1.0` into a new register o and `fdiv d o t`.
14. **Elementary functions** (phase 3, §4.10.5). The arguments are lowered left to right by rule
    1, then one `rcall` into a new register d of class `f` (or the destination of rule 2), with no
    site: `lib log(x)` is `rcall sea_log - 1 d 1 x`, and `lib exp`, `lib sin`, `lib cos` the same
    with `sea_exp`, `sea_sin`, `sea_cos`; `lib pow(x, y)` and `bin pow x y` (a `^` that is not a
    `powk`) are `rcall sea_pow - 1 d 2 x y`; `lib hypot(x, y)` is `rcall sea_hypot - 1 d 2 x y`.

**Phase 4: arrays, structs, strings, reference counts and copy on write.** The rules below extend
rules 1–14 to every construct of phase 4 (§8). Their building blocks are named once and used by
name afterwards; every name stands for exactly the records it is defined as, with new registers
numbered in the order they appear (§3.6.1) and new blocks numbered in the order they open
(§3.6.4). The offsets are the `rt.inc` values of §4.8 (`SEA_ARR_RC` 0, `SEA_ARR_ROWS` 16,
`SEA_ARR_COLS` 24, `SEA_ARR_DATA` 40, `SEA_STR_LEN` 16), which pass 3a reads from its `consts`
table (§2.6.3); `site` is the line of the HIR node a rule lowers unless the rule says otherwise.
Each dump example is a fragment of one function: the registers, blocks, slots and labels of the
fragment are numbered as if the function's earlier records used those the fragment does not
show, and the comment after it names what the shown registers hold. Pass 3a does not cache a
loaded extent, data pointer or count across nodes: every node loads what it needs (phase 5
hoists, §5.2), so a dump shows every load.

15. **Reference values: owned and borrowed.** A reference value (a `str`, a dynamic array, a
    handle) is a `p` register. Every reference value pass 3a computes is **owned** — it carries
    one count its holder must give up: the result of a `call` or `rcall` that returns a reference,
    a fresh array (rule 17) or string, a value after `retain` — or **borrowed**: `lv` of a local or
    parameter, a static string (`la` of a `str` record, rule 7), an element or field loaded with
    `ldp`, the loop variable of an element loop (rule 30). Then:
    (a) a reference value stored into a place that holds a count (a local by `bind`, `tbind`,
    `asg`; an element or a field, rules 19, 21, 27; an element of a fresh array; a field of a
    struct literal; a hidden result, rule 27; a `ret`) must be owned: a borrowed value gets
    `retain R` right after its own instructions, an owned one is moved (no instruction);
    (b) an owned value that is not stored is a **temporary**: `release R` comes right after the
    instructions of the node that consumes it (for several temporaries of one node, in operand
    order), except after `sea_error` (rule 34), which does not return; an `ifx` of a reference
    type makes each arm owned in its destination (rule 3 with (a)), so its value is owned;
    (c) an ordinary parameter is borrowed for the whole call: the callee neither retains nor
    releases it unless (a) applies;
    (d) `asg set` to a local L of a reference type computes the value into a new register V
    (owned by (a)), then `release L`, then `mov L V` (rule 2's direct destination is used only by
    `bind` and `tbind`, which have no old value); a `tasg` component that is a reference-type
    local gets a new result register in rule 2 (b) and is stored the same way;
    (e) `retain`/`release` of a static object change nothing (§4.8), so a static string is a
    borrowed value like any other, and a register that is released is never null (§4.2);
    (f) a borrowed value *derived from a temporary* — an element or field loaded by `ldp` from an
    array or struct that is itself a temporary (`args()[0]`, `f().name`) — is made owned at once:
    `retain R` right after its load; a struct or fixed-size element or field of a temporary used
    as a whole is copied into a new temporary home by rule 27 (c) with the retains of a borrowed
    source. The base is then released as usual, right after the node that consumes it (the `idx`
    or `fld`), and the derived value is an owned value like any other: moved when stored
    (`let s = args()[0]`), released after its consumer otherwise (`printf("%s", args()[0])`:
    `rcall sea_args`, the load, `retain`, `release` of the `str[]`, the `printf`, `release` of the
    string; `match args()[0]` holds it as its owned scrutinee, rule 33);
    (g) *releasing a struct or fixed-size value* at a home H is, for each reference field or
    element in ascending offset order (nested structs and fixed-size arrays included), `ldp T H -
    0 off` and `release T`; it is what (b) does after the consumer for an owned struct or
    fixed-size temporary (a `slit`, a call's hidden result, a copy of rule 27 (c), a `fix`, a
    fixed-size element-wise result, an `ifx`, rule 27 (k)), in operand order with the other
    temporaries of the node; a home without reference fields needs nothing;
    (h) the value of an `eval` (an expression statement) that is owned — a call or `rcall`
    returning a reference, or a call with a struct or fixed-size result that holds counts — is
    released right after the statement (a reference by `release`, a hidden result home by (g)); a
    `_` component of a `tbind` or `tasg` whose type holds counts is a result register or hidden
    result home released the same way, right after the statement's stores;
    (i) *compound assignment of a reference value* `x op= e` (an array operand: element-wise,
    rule 22; a `str` `+=`: rule 32) to a local, a `ref` parameter, a field of a struct local or
    `ref` parameter, or an element by scalar indices: in the order of LANGUAGE.md §5.5 (C6) and
    §7.3: the target's indices (left to right), the read of x (borrowed, protected by rule 12
    when e passes its root by `ref`), e, the operation into a new owned register R (rule 22 or
    32, their checks with the node's line), then the store of R exactly as `asg set` stores an
    owned value: (d) for a local; `ldp O P - 0 0`, `stp R P - 0 0`, `release O` for a `ref`
    parameter (rule 31); rule 27 (f) for a field; rule 19 (3)–(5) for an element, its checks and
    cow done after e (e may have changed the array). A retained read and a temporary e are
    released right after the operation. A selection target is rule 21;
    (j) *tuple assignment to targets that are not locals* (LANGUAGE.md §7.3: the call first, then
    each target in order; in `sea.hirl` realized by L12, §3.5.9, for a selection, `.flat` or
    converting target): the call writes a new result register for every component (a new temporary home for
    a struct or fixed-size result, rule 27 (l)); then, in target order, each target is stored as
    an `asg set` of that owned value: a local by (d), an element by rule 19 (its indices evaluated
    now, after the call, then its checks and cow), a selection by rule 21 (indices, checks, shape
    check for an array value, cow, store; a scalar value is stored into every selected element), a field by rule 27 (f) or (d); `_` by (h). A run-time error in a later
    target leaves the earlier targets stored.
    (k) *the records of `sea.hirl`* (from 4e-0, §3.5.9): `anew` of a dynamic array type is owned (of a fixed-size type it is a home,
    rule 27, R1); an `xblk` is owned
    exactly when its value is owned (an owned node, or `lv` of an owned `tmp` of it, T2); a `tmp` is not a place that holds a
    count, so a borrowed value it binds is not retained, and an owned value it binds is a
    temporary of its `xblk`, released right after the `xblk`'s value, unless that value names it
    (moved out); `eld` of a reference element is borrowed, except that an `eld` whose address is
    `adat (lv T)` with T an owned `tmp` of the same `xblk` is derived from a temporary (f): `retain`
    right after its load, before the `xblk`'s releases, and its value owned; an `eld` of a
    reference type whose address comes from a root that a `ref` argument reaches, read before an
    `rarg` and consumed after it (a view element read such as `u.col[1, 0]`, L17's compound read
    T0), is protected by rule 12 (b); an `est` of a reference value is an
    initializing store, the value owned by (a); `ext`, `adat`, `eld` and `wbin` consume their
    operands like any node (an owned operand is released right after them). From 4g (§3.5.9
    R17–R25): an `est` of a reference value into an address that is not fresh is a replacing
    store (`ldp O`, `stp V`, `release O`, R17); an `est` directly in a `block` of the `lv` of an
    owned `tmp` of that block moves it, and that `tmp` is not released (R17 (b)); an `eld` of a
    struct, record or fixed-size element is its address, borrowed (R18); a struct or record
    `anew` is a home, released by (g) when it is an owned temporary (R21); an owned `tmp` written
    directly in a `block` is released also by the exits that leave the block, as a hidden local
    of rule 16 (f) (R22); an L12 store of `lv Li` with cv 0 into a target that L6 does not rewrite
    moves Li's value (R25).
    Example (`a`, `b` are `str` locals in `p1`, `p2`; line 4 `let s = a + b`, line 5 `let t = s`,
    line 6 `printf("%s\n", a + b)`):

    ```
    rcall sea_str_cat 0:4 1 p3 2 p1 p2
    mov p4 p3
    retain p4
    rcall sea_str_cat 0:6 1 p5 2 p1 p2
    sa p6 s1
    stp p5 p6 - 0 0
    la p7 d1
    rcall sea_printf 0:6 0 2 p7 p6
    release p5
    ```

    (`s` is `p3`, `t` is `p4`; the concatenation of line 6 is a temporary released after the
    `printf` that consumes it.)

16. **Scopes and exits.** A local *holds counts* when its type is a reference type, or a struct or
    fixed-size array type with reference fields or elements (rule 27). A local is *bound* at a
    point of its block when its declaring record (`bind`, `tbind`, the `forr`/`fore` of a loop
    variable) comes before that point in the block; which locals are bound is known statically.
    *Releasing a local* is `release L` for a reference local, and for a struct or fixed-size
    local at home address P, for each reference field or element in ascending offset order, `ldp
    T P - 0 off` and `release T`. Then:
    (a) at the end of a `block`, the bound locals declared directly in it that hold counts are
    released in reverse order of their declarations (before rule 6's final `ret 0` for a body
    block); no releases are written at the end of a block whose last statement is a `ret` or
    `tret`, nor at the end of the body block of a function whose result type is not `void` (its
    end is never reached: `missing return`, LANGUAGE.md §8.1), while a block whose last statement is a
    `break` or `cont` still gets them after its `exit` or `next` (dead code, never executed); (b) `break` and `cont` release, before their `exit`
    or `next`, the bound locals of every block they leave, from the innermost block out to the
    body block of the loop they name, each block's in reverse declaration order, and the hidden
    locals (below) of the statements they leave inside that loop, innermost first; (c) `ret`
    computes its values first (owned, rule 15 (a); a struct result into the hidden result
    memory, rule 27), then releases the bound locals of every enclosing block of the function,
    innermost first, and every enclosing hidden local, then returns; so `return a` of a local `a` in
    `p5` is `retain p5`, the releases (`release p5` among them) and `ret 1 p5`, the retain giving
    the caller its count; (d) parameters, loop
    variables of element loops (borrowed, rule 30) and range loop variables are never released;
    (e) the `.t` locals of a `seq` (§3.5.5) are released like temporaries, right after the node
    that consumes the `seq`'s value, in their declaration order, after the `seq`'s own value when
    that is an owned temporary (rule 15 (b)); (f) *hidden locals* are the
    vector an element loop holds (rule 30) and an owned `match` scrutinee (rule 33): each is
    released right after its statement and by (b) and (c) on the exits through it; the hidden
    vector of the loop that a `break` or `cont` names is not released by that `break` or `cont`
    (`break` leaves to the end of the loop construct, where rule 30 (3) releases it, and `cont`
    stays in the loop), while a `ret` inside the loop releases it with every other enclosing
    hidden local by (c). A run-time error releases nothing. From 4e-0, for (e), a `seq` whose
    value a `tmp` binds is consumed by the innermost `xblk` holding that `tmp`, its `.t` locals
    released right after that `xblk`'s own temporaries (§3.5.9 T2), and those of a `seq` that is
    the vector of L4's `bind` at the end of L4's block, right after H. From 4e-0 the vector an element loop
    holds is the local H that `sealoop` binds in the block it writes for the `fore` (§3.5.9 L4), so
    (a)–(c) release it exactly as (f) says; a `tmp` local is never a bound local of this rule. Example (line 1 `fn f(n: i64) -> i64 {`, then `var k = 0`, `while k
    < n {`, `let v = zeros(n)`, `if k == 3 { break }`, `k += 1`, `}`, `return k`, `}`):

    ```
    func f fn 0:1:1 1 i1 1 i
    li i2 0
    do 1
    icmp lt i3 i2 i1
    ifz 2 i3
    exit 1
    endif 2
    li i4 1
    li i5 1
    li i6 1
    rcall sea_arr_new 0:4 1 p7 4 i4 i5 i1 i6
    li i8 3
    icmp eq i9 i2 i8
    if 3 i9
    release p7
    exit 1
    endif 3
    li i10 1
    iaddc i2 i2 i10 0:6
    release p7
    enddo 1
    ret 1 i2
    endfunc
    ```

17. **Array headers and allocation.** *ext(A, d)* is `ldi E A - 0 16` for d = 0 and `ldi E A - 0
    24` for d = 1, and *data(A)* is `ldp D A - 0 40`, for a dynamic array A; for a fixed-size
    array the extents are `li` of its static extents and its data address is its home address
    (rule 27). `len(v)` is ext(v, 0) (a `str`: `ldi d S - 0 16`); `rows(A)` and `cols(A)` are
    ext(A, 0) and ext(A, 1); `numel(A)` is ext(A, 0), ext(A, 1), `imul d r c` (`numel(v)` of a
    vector is `len(v)`). *arrnew(ek, rank, R, C)* is `li K ek`, `li N rank`, for a vector `li C
    1`, then `rcall E site 1 P 4 K N R C`, with R (and for a matrix C) registers already computed
    and P the new array (owned), where E is `sea_arr_new_u` for ek 1–3 (the buffer is not cleared:
    every rule that uses arrnew writes every element of the new array before anything reads one,
    §4.8) and `sea_arr_new` for ek 4; for struct elements it is `la L dS` (the `slay` record of
    the struct type, rule 38) in place of `li K ek` and `rcall sea_arr_new_s site 1 P 4 L N R C`.
    *arrnewz* is arrnew with `sea_arr_new` for every ek (a cleared buffer); only `zeros` and `[]`
    use it. ek is `SEA_EK_F64` 1, `SEA_EK_I64` 2, `SEA_EK_BOOL` 3 or `SEA_EK_STR` 4. *loop(N; K)* is the
    counted loop over 0 … N − 1: `li Z 0`, `icmp gt E N Z`, `if B E`, `li O 1`, `isub L N O`,
    `loop B+1 K Z L O`, the body, `endloop B+1`, `endif B`. `zeros(n)` and `zeros(r, c)`: the
    arguments, then arrnewz (the buffer is zero-filled, §4.8: +0.0). `ones(…)` and `filled(v, …)`:
    the arguments, arrnew, the element count (a vector's n, a matrix's `imul N r c`), for `ones`
    `lf V #3FF0000000000000`, then data(P), then loop(N; K) storing V at element K (`stf V D K 8
    0`). `filled(v, …)` of a `str` or struct value makes each store an initializing store of a
    borrowed copy, whether V is owned or not: a `str` gets `retain V` before each `stp`, a struct
    is copied into each element by rule 27 (c) with the retains of a borrowed source (`li S size`,
    `imul T K S`, `padd E D T`, `li N size`, `mcopy E V N`, then `ldp`/`retain` per reference
    field); after the construct (`endif B`) an owned V is released once, a `str` by `release V`, a
    struct temporary by rule 15 (g), so with zero elements only that release happens.
    Example (`let u = ones(n)`, line 1, `n` in `i1`):

    ```
    li i2 1
    li i3 1
    li i4 1
    rcall sea_arr_new_u 0:1 1 p5 4 i2 i3 i1 i4
    lf f6 #3FF0000000000000
    ldp p7 p5 - 0 40
    li i8 0
    icmp gt i9 i1 i8
    if 1 i9
    li i10 1
    isub i11 i1 i10
    loop 2 i12 i8 i11 i10
    stf f6 p7 i12 8 0
    endloop 2
    endif 1
    ```

    (`u` is `p5`.)

    From 4e-0 `zeros`, `ones`, `filled`, `len`, `rows`, `cols` and `numel` reach `sealower` as the
    records `sealoop` writes for them (§3.5.9 L1–L3); the lowering of those records gives exactly
    the instructions above (the example's `ones` is L2's `xblk`, its value moved into `u` by T3).

18. **Element reads by scalar indices, and `$`.** An `idx` whose indices are all scalars: the
    base, the indices left to right (LANGUAGE.md §5.4: all evaluated before any check), then for
    each dimension d in order ext(B, d) and `chkb I E d site`, then data(B), then for a matrix
    the linear index `imul T I1 E0` and `iadd X I0 T` (E0 the rows loaded for the check; a vector
    uses I0), then the load at X: `ldf` (`f64`), `ldi` (`i64`), `ldb` scale 1 (`bool`), `ldp`
    (`str`, borrowed), all others scale 8. A struct element read through a field (`fld` of the
    `idx`, also nested `fld`s) is one load `ld? R D X size off` with scale the struct's size and
    off the field's offset; a struct element used as a whole is its address `li S size`, `imul T
    X S`, `padd R D T` (borrowed, rule 27). A `dol dim` is ext(B, dim) of the innermost enclosing
    `idx`'s base into a new register at its place (for a folded view, the view's extent, rule
    28). Examples (line 7 `T[j-1, i]` with `T` a `f64[,]` in `p1`, `i`, `j` in `i2`, `i3`; line 9
    `dims[d].nom` with `dims` a `Dim[]` in `p1` (size 48, `nom` at 8) and `d` in `i2`):

    ```
    li i4 1
    isubc i5 i3 i4 0:7
    ldi i6 p1 - 0 16
    chkb i5 i6 0 0:7
    ldi i7 p1 - 0 24
    chkb i2 i7 1 0:7
    ldp p8 p1 - 0 40
    imul i9 i2 i6
    iadd i10 i5 i9
    ldf f11 p8 i10 8 0
    ```

    ```
    ldi i3 p1 - 0 16
    chkb i2 i3 0 0:9
    ldp p4 p1 - 0 40
    ldf f5 p4 i2 48 8
    ```

19. **Element stores by scalar indices, and copy on write.** `asg set` to an `idx` with scalar
    indices: (1) the value (owned if a reference, rule 15); (2) the target's indices, left to right
    (an index of an array on the path, `a[i].v[k]`, in source order); (3) the bounds checks of rule
    18, outermost array first, against the variable as it is now (the base of a target is never a
    copy made before a `ref` call, rule 12); (4) *cow(L)* of every dynamic array on the path, outermost first;
    (5) data, the linear index, and the store (`stf`, `sti`, `stb`, `stp`); a reference element
    is replaced as `ldp O D X 8 0`, `stp V D X 8 0`, `release O`; a struct element by rule 27's
    assignment. An element of a fixed-size array or a field in a slot needs no copy on write.
    *cow(L)* for an array held in a register L (a local) is `ldi C L - 0 0`, `li O 1`, `icmp ne S C
    O`, `if B S`, `rcall sea_arr_unique site 1 N 1 L`, `mov L N`, `endif B`; for an array held in
    memory at P + off (a `ref` parameter: `P - 0 0`; an array field of a struct; an array field
    of an element of an array of structs, at the element's address) it is `ldp A P - 0 off`, then
    the same with A, the `mov A N` preceded by `stp N P - 0 off`; the array is then A. When the target's array is held in memory
    (a `ref` parameter P), the base for (3) is loaded by `ldp B P - 0 0` at the base's place, after
    the value and before the indices, and the memory form of cow in (4) loads it again; for a
    compound `asg op` the read loads it for its own checks, and the repeated checks of (3) load it
    once more (`ldp B P - 0 0` after the operation), since the value may have replaced it. A static
    array (count 0) always differs from 1, so it is copied; `sea_arr_unique` gives up the
    variable's count on the old array (§4.8). For a compound `asg op` (op ≠ `set`) to a scalar
    element: (2), the read by rule 18 (checks included) into T, the value, the operation into R
    (rule 1, checked `i64` operations with the node's site), then (3)–(5) storing R (the checks
    repeated: the value may have changed the array through a `ref` argument; §5.8's T1 deletes a
    repeated `chkb` only when its facts prove it, which they do not for a `ref` root). *Paths through several arrays* (`a[i].v[k] = x`, `a` a `var` array of structs
    whose field `v` is a dynamic array): (3) checks the outermost index against ext(a), then loads
    the next array through the path as it is (`ldp V E - 0 off`, E = data(a) + i·s by rule 18's
    address) and checks the next index against ext(V), and so on inward; (4) cows outermost first:
    cow(a), then E recomputed from the (possibly new) data(a), then the memory form of cow at (E,
    off), which loads V again and replaces it in the element when it is shared, and so on inward;
    (5) data of the innermost array (as (4) left it) and the store. The inner arrays are loaded
    again after each outer cow because a copy of the outer array retains them (shared, count ≥ 2),
    so the inner cow copies them in turn. Example (line 12 `T[j, i] = tn`, `T` a `var` `f64[,]` in `p1`, `j`, `i` in `i2`,
    `i3`, `tn` in `f4`):

    ```
    ldi i5 p1 - 0 16
    chkb i2 i5 0 0:12
    ldi i6 p1 - 0 24
    chkb i3 i6 1 0:12
    ldi i7 p1 - 0 0
    li i8 1
    icmp ne i9 i7 i8
    if 1 i9
    rcall sea_arr_unique 0:12 1 p10 1 p1
    mov p1 p10
    endif 1
    ldp p11 p1 - 0 40
    imul i12 i3 i5
    iadd i13 i2 i12
    stf f4 p11 i13 8 0
    ```

    From 4g the stores this rule gives for a reference element (`ldp O`, `stp V`, `release O`), a
    struct element (rule 27's assignment), a field of an element and a path through several arrays
    are `sealoop`'s L17 (§3.5.9: its steps are (1)–(5) above in this order, the inner arrays read
    again after each outer cow, the data of the innermost array as (4) left it by R23), lowered by
    R17, R19, R23 and R24, with one difference in order: (1) computes the value, and the `retain`
    that makes a borrowed value owned comes at the store in (5), after the checks and cows (R17
    (a)), and with a second when an `idx` under a field of an element has a `$` in an index: from
    that `idx` on, its indices are evaluated in (3) only after the checks of the arrays before it,
    the `$` being the extent of its own array (L17 steps 3–4, LANGUAGE.md §5.5); `sealower` lowers
    (1)–(5) itself only for a numeric element by scalar indices of an array local or `ref`
    parameter, as in 4d.

20. **Selections (reads).** An `idx` with a range, `:`, an index vector or a mask among its
    indices. (1) The base, then the indices left to right; a range index is its operands then
    `rcount L E lo hi st incl site` (st `li 1` when absent; site the `rng` node's line), so `range
    step is zero` is reported where the range is evaluated. (2) The checks, dimension by dimension
    in order: a scalar index ext and `chkb`; a range ext(B, d), then `if B E`, `chkb lo E d site`,
    the last position `imul T L st`, `iadd P lo T` (exact: it lies between lo and hi), `chkb P E d
    site`, `endif B` (LANGUAGE.md §5.4); `:` only its ext(B, d); an index vector w its length and
    data, then loop(n; K) with `ldi X Dw K 8 0` and `chkb X E d site`; a mask m of a dimension
    ext(B, d), `ldi M m - 0 16`, `icmp ne S E M`, `li V -1`, `chk S SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 E V M V`;
    a matrix mask `A[M]` the rows and cols of both, `icmp ne` of each pair, `ior`, `chk S
    SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 rA cA rM cM`. (3) The kept extents: a range's count (`li O 1`, `iadd T L
    O`, `li Z 0`, `isel N E T Z`), `:` its extent, an index vector its length, a mask the number of
    its true elements (`li N 0`, data, loop over the mask with `ldb b Dm K 1 0`, `iadd N N b`), a
    matrix mask the same over its rows·cols elements. (4) arrnew of the result (one kept
    dimension or a matrix mask: a vector; two: a matrix). (5) data of the result, data of the base,
    the data of each index vector and mask in dimension order, `li O 0`, `li One 1`. (6) The *loop
    nest*: dimension 1 outside, dimension 0 inside (a vector base has only dimension 0; a matrix
    mask is one flat loop over the linear positions): a scalar index is no loop (its position is
    the index); a range is `if B E`, `loop B+1 P lo L st`, …, `endloop`, `endif` (P the
    position); `:` is loop(ext; P); an index vector is loop(n; K) with `ldi P Dw K 8 0` first in
    its body; a mask is loop(ext; P) with `ldb b Dm P 1 0`, `if B b` around the rest of its body.
    The innermost body reads the base element at the linear position (rule 18's address, without
    checks), stores it at result element O (an initializing store: a `str` is retained, rule 15
    (a); a struct copied by rule 27), and adds One to O. Temporaries are released after the nest
    (rule 15). Example (line 30 `let u1 = u[0..$ step 2]`, `u` an `f64[]` in `p1`):

    ```
    li i2 0
    ldi i3 p1 - 0 16
    li i4 2
    rcount i5 i6 i2 i3 i4 0 0:30
    ldi i7 p1 - 0 16
    if 1 i6
    chkb i2 i7 0 0:30
    imul i8 i5 i4
    iadd i9 i2 i8
    chkb i9 i7 0 0:30
    endif 1
    li i10 1
    iadd i11 i5 i10
    li i12 0
    isel i13 i6 i11 i12
    li i14 1
    li i15 1
    li i16 1
    rcall sea_arr_new_u 0:30 1 p17 4 i14 i15 i13 i16
    ldp p18 p17 - 0 40
    ldp p19 p1 - 0 40
    li i20 0
    li i21 1
    if 2 i6
    loop 3 i22 i2 i5 i4
    ldf f23 p19 i22 8 0
    stf f23 p18 i20 8 0
    iadd i20 i20 i21
    endloop 3
    endif 2
    ```

    (`u1` is `p17`.)

    From 4e a selection reaches `sealower` as §3.5.9 L5 (Decision 31's refinements make E a `bool`
    and the counter O a `.l` local); L5 fixes what this rule leaves open: an index vector's check
    loads ext(B, d) before its length and data; every extent is loaded once, by its dimension's
    check, and reused by (3), (4) and the nest (`:` included); the data of each index vector and mask
    are loaded again in (5); the linear position of a matrix base is `imul T P1 X0`, `iadd X P0 T` in
    the innermost body, right before the load, X0 the rows extent of (2); every site is the `idx`'s
    line except `rcount`'s.

21. **Selection stores, masked and compound assignment.** `asg set` to an `idx` with a selection:
    (1) the value; an array value that is borrowed is retained (owned for the store), so that a
    value sharing the target's buffer makes the target's copy on write copy it (LANGUAGE.md §5.5,
    "Aliasing"), and on a fixed-size target (no copy on write) a value that is the target variable
    itself is copied into a new home slot first; (2) the target's indices left to right (ranges with `rcount`), a borrowed index vector
    of a target whose element type is `i64` retained like the value (owned), since it may share the
    target's buffer and the stores must not change the indices (Decision 34, LANGUAGE.md §5.5); for a
    fixed-size `i64` target (no copy on write) an index vector that is the target variable itself is
    copied into a new home slot first (`li N bytes`, `mcopy`); (3) the checks of
    rule 20 (2), in dimension order; (4) when the value is an array, the selection's extents (rule
    20 (3)) and the shape check: a vector selection `icmp ne S N Nv`, `li V -1`, `chk S
    SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 N V Nv V`, a matrix selection both extents (`ior`) and `chk S
    SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 R C Rv Cv`, the selection's shape first (LANGUAGE.md §5.5); (5) cow of
    the target (rule 19); (6) data of the target, data of the value (an array value), the data of
    each index vector and mask, and for an array value `li O 0`, `li One 1`; (7) rule 20's loop
    nest storing into the target at each position the value (a scalar) or the value's element O
    (then O += One): a reference element is replaced (`ldp`, `stp`, `release` of the old), a value
    element retained first; (8) the owned value and the owned or retained index vectors and masks released. The extents a loop of the nest uses are
    those loaded in (3) (a `:` dimension loads its extent there). A compound `asg op` to a
    selection is: (2); rule 20 (2)–(6) into a temporary G; the value; G op value by rule 22 into R
    (owned; the shape check of rule 22 with G first); then (3)–(8) storing R with the index
    registers of (2) (extents and checks reloaded); G and the value are released after the
    operation, R after the store. Example (line 5 `v[m] = 0.0`, `v` a `var` `f64[]` in `p1`, `m` a
    `bool[]` in `p2`):

    ```
    lf f3 #0000000000000000
    ldi i4 p1 - 0 16
    ldi i5 p2 - 0 16
    icmp ne i6 i4 i5
    li i7 -1
    chk i6 SHAPE_MISMATCH 0:5 4 i4 i7 i5 i7
    ldi i8 p1 - 0 0
    li i9 1
    icmp ne i10 i8 i9
    if 1 i10
    rcall sea_arr_unique 0:5 1 p11 1 p1
    mov p1 p11
    endif 1
    ldp p12 p1 - 0 40
    ldp p13 p2 - 0 40
    li i14 0
    icmp gt i15 i4 i14
    if 2 i15
    li i16 1
    isub i17 i4 i16
    loop 3 i18 i14 i17 i16
    ldb i19 p13 i18 1 0
    if 4 i19
    stf f3 p12 i18 8 0
    endif 4
    endloop 3
    endif 2
    ```

    From 4e an indexed assignment of this rule (and an assignment to `.flat`, rule 28) reaches
    `sealower` as the block of §3.5.9 L6: a dynamic array value (and each retained index vector) is a
    held `.l` local of the block (`mov`, `retain` when borrowed), the other index vectors and masks
    `tmp`s (an owned one released at the block's end, R11), a fixed-size value a `tmp` naming its home
    (copied when it is the target itself); the releases at the block's end are (8); a fixed-size
    target has no cow;
    every check, `chk` and `sea_arr_unique` takes the `asg`'s line; a `ref` parameter target is read
    afresh (`ldp`) for each extent, for its cow (the memory form of rule 19) and for its data after the
    cow.

22. **Element-wise operations and broadcasting.** A `bin`, `un`, `cvt` or elemental `lib`
    (LANGUAGE.md §10.1, §10.4, §10.7) with an array operand: (1) the operands left to right; (2)
    the shapes: ext of each array operand in operand order, then the checks of LANGUAGE.md §6.3,
    folded left to right over the array operands: for vectors, for each array operand k after the
    first, `icmp ne S N1 Nk`, `chk S SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 N1 V Nk V` (`li V -1` once, before
    the first check); for matrices with the combined shape (R, C) (initially the first operand's)
    and the operand's (r, c): `li O 1` (once), `icmp eq a R r`, `icmp eq b R O`, `icmp eq c r O`,
    `ior a a b`, `ior a a c` and the same for the cols into a second register, `iand a a a2`,
    `bnot S a`, `chk S SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 R C r c`, then `icmp eq q R O`, `isel R q r R` and the
    same for C (new registers each time); no check when every array operand is fixed-size (pass 2a
    checked it); (3) the result: arrnew (dynamic), or a new home slot (fixed, rule 27); (4) for
    matrices, per array operand X with extents (rX, cX), its strides `icmp ne SI rX O`, `icmp ne t
    cX O`, `imul SJ t rX`; (5) data of the result, then of each array operand in order; (6) the
    loop nest: a vector loop(N; I) (I indexes every operand and the result); a matrix loop(C; J)
    around loop(R; I), with per array operand `imul a I SI`, `imul b J SJ`, `iadd X a b`, and for
    the result `imul t J R`, `iadd Y I t`; (7) the body: each array operand's element loaded (rule
    18's load by element kind), the scalar operation of rules 1, 10, 11, 13, 14 or 36 with the
    node's line as site, and the store into the result element; `where` selects with
    `fsel`/`isel`; a `str` comparison is rule 32's sequence then `stb`; (8) owned operands released
    after the nest. Example (line 2 `let z = x * 2.0`, `x` an `f64[]` in `p1`):

    ```
    lf f2 #4000000000000000
    ldi i3 p1 - 0 16
    li i4 1
    li i5 1
    li i6 1
    rcall sea_arr_new_u 0:2 1 p7 4 i4 i5 i3 i6
    ldp p8 p7 - 0 40
    ldp p9 p1 - 0 40
    li i10 0
    icmp gt i11 i3 i10
    if 1 i11
    li i12 1
    isub i13 i3 i12
    loop 2 i14 i10 i13 i12
    ldf f15 p9 i14 8 0
    fmul f16 f15 f2
    stf f16 p8 i14 8 0
    endloop 2
    endif 1
    ```

    (`z` is `p7`.)

    From 4e this rule reaches `sealower` as §3.5.9 L7, which fixes: `li V -1` comes once, at the first
    check, after its `icmp` and before its `chk` (the order of rules 20, 21 and 27 (j); "before the
    first check" is before its `chk`), and only with two or more array operands; `li O 1` comes at its first use; the extents are loaded for every array
    operand when the result is dynamic, for the matrix operands only (their strides) when it is
    fixed-size, whose loop extents are then the `li` of its own static extents after its home slot;
    in a matrix body each array operand's index (`imul a I SI`, `imul b J SJ`, `iadd X a b`) comes
    right before its load, and the result's (`imul t J R`, `iadd Y I t`) after the operation, before
    the store. `ind2sub` with a scalar `r` and an array `k` is two such loops, `k % r` then `idiv(k, r)`,
    over held arguments (§3.5.9 L11, Decision 33; an array `r` is the phase-rule word `ind2sub` until
    phase 6).

23. **Reductions** (LANGUAGE.md §10.5), on a vector V with n = ext(V, 0) (or `li` for a
    fixed vector) and data D. *sum8(load)* is: `li Z 0`, `icmp gt E n Z`, `if B E`, `sa A s` (a new
    slot of 64 bytes, alignment 8), `lf M #8000000000000000`, `stf M A - 0 8k` for k = 0 … 7,
    data(V), `li Q 7`, `li O 1`, `isub L n O`, `loop B+1 K Z L O`, `iand W K Q`, `ldf a A W 8 0`,
    the element value x (load, plus the per-element operations), `fadd a a x`, `stf a A W 8 0`,
    `endloop B+1`, `ldf` of the eight words in order into new registers a0 … a7, `fadd` t1 = a0 +
    a1, t2 = a2 + a3, t3 = t1 + t2, t4 = a4 + a5, t5 = a6 + a7, t6 = t4 + t5, R = t3 + t6, `else B`,
    `lf R #0000000000000000`, `endif B` (R the destination of rule 2 or new). `sum` of `f64`:
    sum8 with x = `ldf x D K 8 0`; of `i64`: `li R 0`, data, loop(n; K) with `ldi x D K 8 0`,
    `iaddc R R x site`. `mean`: the sum, `itof F n` (an `i64` sum `itof` too), `fdiv R S F` (the
    empty case gives 0/0 = NaN). `variance`: `li Z 0`, `icmp eq E0 n Z`, `if B E0`, `lf R
    #7FF8000000000000`, `else B`, `li O 1`, `icmp eq E1 n O`, `if B+1 E1`, `lf R
    #0000000000000000`, `else B+1`, the mean m as above, sum8 with x = `ldf y D K 8 0`, `fsub d y
    m`, `fmul x d d` (an `i64` V: `ldi`, `itof` first), `isub N1 n O`, `itof F N1`, `fdiv R s F`,
    `endif B+1`, `endif B`. `std`: the variance, `fsqrt R v`. `max`/`min` (`argmax`/`argmin`):
    `li Z 0`, `icmp eq E n Z`, `la S dN` (the `str` record of the function's name), `chk E
    EMPTY_REDUCE site 1 S`, then `lf R #7FF8000000000000` (`i64`: `li R 0`), `li H 0`, `li X 0`
    (the index), data, loop(n; K): load x, for `f64` `fnan u x`, `bnot k u`, `fcmp gt g x R` (`lt`
    for min), `bnot h H`, `ior t h g`, `iand c k t`, for `i64` `icmp gt g x R` (`lt`), `bnot h
    H`, `ior c h g`; then `fsel R c x R` (`isel`), `isel X c K X`, `ior H H c`; the result is R
    (or X). `nnz`: `li R 0`, loop with `ldb b D K 1 0`, `iadd R R b`; `any`: `li R 0`, `ior R R
    b`; `all`: `li R 1`, `iand R R b`. `name.dim` (a matrix A, rows r, cols c): arrnew of the
    result (dim 0: a vector of c; dim 1: of r), data, then for dim 0 loop(c; J) around the vector
    rule over I in 0 … r − 1 with the element at `I + J·r`, the result stored at J; for dim 1
    loop(r; I) around the vector rule over J in 0 … c − 1 (`iand W J Q` for the lanes), the
    result stored at I; the 64-byte slot of one `sum8` is reused by every element of the result.
    Example (line 3 `let s = sum(x)`, `x` an `f64[]` in `p1`):

    ```
    ldi i2 p1 - 0 16
    li i3 0
    icmp gt i4 i2 i3
    if 1 i4
    sa p5 s1
    lf f6 #8000000000000000
    stf f6 p5 - 0 0
    stf f6 p5 - 0 8
    stf f6 p5 - 0 16
    stf f6 p5 - 0 24
    stf f6 p5 - 0 32
    stf f6 p5 - 0 40
    stf f6 p5 - 0 48
    stf f6 p5 - 0 56
    ldp p7 p1 - 0 40
    li i8 7
    li i9 1
    isub i10 i2 i9
    loop 2 i11 i3 i10 i9
    iand i12 i11 i8
    ldf f13 p5 i12 8 0
    ldf f14 p7 i11 8 0
    fadd f13 f13 f14
    stf f13 p5 i12 8 0
    endloop 2
    ldf f15 p5 - 0 0
    ldf f16 p5 - 0 8
    ldf f17 p5 - 0 16
    ldf f18 p5 - 0 24
    ldf f19 p5 - 0 32
    ldf f20 p5 - 0 40
    ldf f21 p5 - 0 48
    ldf f22 p5 - 0 56
    fadd f23 f15 f16
    fadd f24 f17 f18
    fadd f25 f23 f24
    fadd f26 f19 f20
    fadd f27 f21 f22
    fadd f28 f26 f27
    fadd f29 f25 f28
    else 1
    lf f29 #0000000000000000
    endif 1
    ```

    (`s` is `f29`; slot `s1` is `slot s1 64 8`.)

    From 4f this rule is met by `sealoop`'s L13 and `sealower`'s lowering (§3.5.9, with R12–R15 of
    Decision 38): the example is `bind s` of L13's `xblk` (`tmp V` = `lv x`, an alias of `p1`;
    `tmp N` the `ldi`; sum8's `tmp Z` the `li i3 0`; its `ifx` the `icmp`, `if 1`, the arm and
    `else 1`, `lf f29`, `endif 1`, with `s`'s register as its R by R12 (a), so `s` is the register
    the last `fadd` writes and no `mov` follows). Where the text above leaves an order open, L13
    fixes it (the data of a `dim:` form's matrix loaded once before the outer loop, the extent of
    isum and of `nnz any all` after their data, the `i64` mean's sum converted before n).

24. **Sorting and searching.** `sort(v, desc)`: v, desc, `rcall sea_sort site 1 R 2 V Dsc`;
    `argsort` the same with `sea_argsort` (§4.8). `find(m)`: m, n, the count of rule 20 (3) into
    N, arrnew of an `i64` vector of N, data of the result and of m, `li O 0`, `li One 1`, loop(n;
    K) with `ldb b Dm K 1 0`, `if B b`, `sti K DR O 8 0`, `iadd O O One`, `endif B`. `find_first(m)`:
    m, n, `li R -1`, `li U -1`, data, loop(n; K) with `ldb b Dm K 1 0`, `icmp eq u R U`, `iand c b
    u`, `isel R c K R`; `find_last(m)`: m, n, `li R -1`, data, loop(n; K) with `ldb`, `isel R b K
    R`. Example (line 8 `let r = argsort(c, desc: true)`, `c` in `p1`):

    ```
    li i2 1
    rcall sea_argsort 0:8 1 p3 2 p1 i2
    ```

    From 4f `sort` and `argsort` stay `lib` nodes in `sea.hirl` (§3.5.9 R16) and are lowered as
    above by `sealower`; a fixed-size v is first copied by the `dyn` that pass 2a writes (§3.5.5,
    Decision 39), and an owned v (a `dyn`, a materialized view or selection, an element-wise result)
    is released right after the `rcall` (rule 15 (b)). `find`, `find_first` and `find_last` are
    `sealoop`'s L14.

25. **Range values.** A `rng` that is neither an index nor the range of a `forr`: lo, hi, st (`li 1`
    when absent), `rcount L E lo hi st incl site` (site the `rng`'s line; from 4e §3.5.9 L8, also as
    the vector of an element loop, `for x in (0..n)`); the length `li O 1`, `iadd T L O`, `li Z 0`,
    `isel N E T Z`; the size check of LANGUAGE.md §5.1: `li X #000000007FFFFFFE` (2 147 483 646,
    `SEA_LIM_EXTENT` − 1, in the `i` field encoding of §3.1), `icmp gt g L X`, `icmp lt u L Z`, `ior b g
    u`, `iand b b E`, `li MX #7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` (2⁶³ − 1), `icmp eq e L MX`, `ior e e u`,
    `isel V e MX T`, `chk b ARRAY_SIZE site 1 V`; arrnew of an `i64` vector of N; data; `li Q 0`,
    `li One 1`; `if B E`, `loop B+1 P lo L st`, `sti P D Q 8 0`, `iadd Q Q One`, `endloop B+1`,
    `endif B`. Example (line 4 `(0..=nBin)` as a value, `nBin` in `i1`):

    ```
    li i2 0
    li i3 1
    rcount i4 i5 i2 i1 i3 1 0:4
    li i6 1
    iadd i7 i4 i6
    li i8 0
    isel i9 i5 i7 i8
    li i10 #000000007FFFFFFE
    icmp gt i11 i4 i10
    icmp lt i12 i4 i8
    ior i13 i11 i12
    iand i13 i13 i5
    li i14 #7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
    icmp eq i15 i4 i14
    ior i15 i15 i12
    isel i16 i15 i14 i7
    chk i13 ARRAY_SIZE 0:4 1 i16
    li i17 2
    li i18 1
    li i19 1
    rcall sea_arr_new_u 0:4 1 p20 4 i17 i18 i9 i19
    ldp p21 p20 - 0 40
    li i22 0
    li i23 1
    if 1 i5
    loop 2 i24 i2 i4 i3
    sti i24 p21 i22 8 0
    iadd i22 i22 i23
    endloop 2
    endif 1
    ```

26. **Array literals and concatenation** (LANGUAGE.md §6.9). (a) A fixed-size literal: a new home
    slot (rule 27), then the elements in source order (row by row, left to right), each stored
    right after its evaluation at its column-major place, element (i, j) of an r × c literal at
    byte `(i + j·r)·esize`: `stf V P - 0 off` (`sti`, `stb`). (b) A dynamic literal without
    concatenation (more than 256 scalars, or `str` or struct elements): `li R n` for one row of n
    elements (a vector), or `li R r` and `li C c` for r rows of c elements (a matrix), arrnew,
    data; then, when every element is an `f64`, `i64` or `bool` constant, a
    `dat dN elt n` record of the elements in column-major order, `la S dN`, `li B bytes`,
    `mcopy D S B`; otherwise the elements in source order, each stored at its column-major place
    (`st? V D - 0 off`; a `str` retained when borrowed; a struct element written in place: a
    `slit` writes its fields at the element's address `li O off`, `padd E D O`, any other struct
    value is copied there by rule 27). (c) A concatenation: the parts in source order (each a
    temporary or borrowed); the shapes: a row of scalars and vectors joins into a vector of the
    summed lengths, `iadd` in part order starting from the first part's length (a scalar part `li
    1`; no overflow is possible: each part has at most 2³¹ − 1 elements and a literal fewer than
    `SEA_LIM_NODES` parts), with no check of its own (a sum above 2³¹ − 1 is arrnew's
    `ARRAY_SIZE`); a row of matrices and scalars (1 × 1) checks each part after the
    first against the row's joined shape so far (Rr × Cr): `icmp ne S Rr Rk`, `chk S
    SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 Rr Cr Rk Ck`, then `iadd Cr Cr Ck`; the rows are stacked with each row
    after the first checked against the stack so far (Rs × Cs), a vector row counting as 1 × n:
    `icmp ne S Cs Ck`, `chk S SHAPE_MISMATCH site 4 Rs Cs Rk Ck`, then `iadd Rs Rs Rk`; arrnew of
    the result (or a home slot when every part is fixed, with static positions and no checks);
    data; each part copied in source order into its place, element (i, j) of a part at (r0 + i,
    c0 + j) of the result, by loop(Cp; J) around loop(Rp; I) (a scalar part one store; a `str`
    element retained); the temporaries released after the copies, in part order. (d) `[]`: arrnewz
    with the extent 0 (a vector) or 0 and 0 (a matrix); under a fixed-size type an 8-byte home
    slot without stores. Example (line 1 `let names = ["a", "bc"]`):

    ```
    li i1 2
    li i2 4
    li i3 1
    li i4 1
    rcall sea_arr_new 0:1 1 p5 4 i2 i3 i1 i4
    ldp p6 p5 - 0 40
    la p7 d1
    retain p7
    stp p7 p6 - 0 0
    la p8 d2
    retain p8
    stp p8 p6 - 0 8
    ```

    (`names` is `p5`; the data records are `str d1 a` and `str d2 bc`. A literal of 300 `f64`
    constants is `li` 300, arrnew, data, `la` of `dat d1 f64 300`, `li` 2400, `mcopy`.)

    From 4g (4g-1 for `str`, 4g-2 for structs and records) every literal reaches `sealower` as L9:
    the example above is L9 (b)'s `xblk` (`tmp R = ci 2`, the `anew` of a `str[]`, which is
    `sea_arr_new` by R21, `tmp D`, and per element `est 8 0 (cs …) (lv D) (ci k)`, the borrowed `la`
    retained by the initializing store); a struct element is written in place or copied by R19 at
    the element's address. From 4e a literal of `f64`, `i64` or `bool` elements reaches `sealower` as §3.5.9 L9 (its `str`
    and struct literals at 4g): the home slot of (a) and a fixed-size result of (c) are the `anew` of a
    fixed-size type (R1), the stores at `- 0 off` are `est`s with a constant index (R3), the `dat` is a
    `cdat` (R4); in (c) the joined lengths, extents and the offsets (r0, c0) are chains of new
    registers (`iadd`), a part's element (i, j) is read at `i + j·Rp` and stored at `(r0 + i) + (c0 +
    j)·R` (both in the innermost body), and with every part fixed-size the offsets are `li` of their
    static values; every site is the `arr`'s line.

27. **Structs and fixed-size arrays in memory.** (a) *Homes*: every struct or fixed-size array
    value lives in memory: a local's slot, a temporary slot of the node that computes it (a
    `slit`, a `call` with a struct result, a fixed-size element-wise result, a `fix`, a fixed
    literal, a copy), the caller's memory (a parameter: read-only), an array's buffer (an element)
    or a containing struct (a field). Its register is a `p` holding the home's address. A slot is
    `slot sK size 8`, size the type's size (§4.8, layout rule) rounded up to a multiple of 8, at
    least 8; the node's `sa P sK` comes where the node is evaluated, once per node (a loop
    re-evaluates the same slot). (b) A `bind` (or `tbind`) of a struct or fixed-size local: `sa`
    of the local's slot, then the value written into it: a `slit` stores its fields there, a
    `call` passes it as the hidden result address (§3.6.3), any other value is copied. (c)
    *copy(H ← S)* into a new home: `li N size`, `mcopy H S N`, and when S is borrowed, `ldp R H - 0
    off` and `retain R` for each reference field or element in ascending offset order (an owned
    source is moved: no retain, and it is not released). (d) *Assignment* to an existing home H
    (`asg set` to a `var` local or a `ref` parameter, an element store, a struct-typed field): the
    value into its own temporary home V (never H directly: the value may read H), or a borrowed
    value's address V; when V is borrowed, `retain` of its reference fields (`ldp R V - 0 off`,
    ascending); then H's old reference fields released (`ldp O H - 0 off`, `release O`,
    ascending); then `li N size`, `mcopy H V N` (identical regions are allowed, §3.6.4: `s = s`).
    (e) *Field read* `fld i` of a value at P: a scalar `ld? R P - 0 off`; a `str` or array field
    `ldp R P - 0 off` (borrowed); a struct or fixed-size field its address `li O off`, `padd R P
    O`. (f) *Field write* to a field of a `var` struct local or a `ref` parameter at P: a scalar
    `st? V P - 0 off`; a reference field `ldp O P - 0 off`, `stp V P - 0 off`, `release O` (V
    owned); a struct or fixed-size field by (d) with H = P + off. (g) A `slit` writes its values in
    their written order (§3.5.5: declaration order, `seq` temporaries keeping the source order),
    each stored at its field's offset right after it is evaluated. (h) A struct or fixed-size
    argument is its home's address (borrowed); a struct or fixed-size result is written by the
    callee into the hidden address it receives: `return e` writes a `slit` there directly and
    copies any other value by (c), before the releases of rule 16 (c). (i) `dyn`: arrnew with the
    static extents (`sea_arr_new_s` for structs), data, `li N bytes`, `mcopy D S N`, and the
    retains of (c) on the array's copy when S is borrowed. (j) `fix` of an array A: for a vector
    ext(A, 0), `li e n`, `icmp ne S r e`, `li V -1`, `chk S SHAPE_EXPECTED site 4 e V r V`; for a
    matrix both extents, `ior`, `chk S SHAPE_EXPECTED site 4 er ec r c`; then a home slot, data(A),
    `li N bytes`, `mcopy H D N`, the retains of the reference elements of H, and A released if a
    temporary. (k) An `ifx` of a struct or fixed-size type has a new temporary home slot of its
    own (`sa` before the condition); each arm writes its value into it by (c) (an owned arm value,
    such as a `slit` written in place or a call's hidden result, is moved: `mcopy` without
    retains, and its own home is not released; a borrowed one gets the retains), and the `ifx`'s
    value is owned: a temporary released by rule 15 (g) after its consumer, or moved into a
