static object (the string objects of LIR `str` records): `retain` and `release` leave it unchanged,
it is never freed, and it may live in read-only data; a dynamic object starts at count 1, and
`release` frees it at 0 (after releasing the objects it refers to: string elements, the reference
fields of struct elements, a handle's private references).

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_OBJ_RC` | 0 | u64: reference count |
| `SEA_OBJ_TAG` | 8 | u8: `SEA_TAG_*` |
| `SEA_OBJ_HDR` | 16 | bytes of the common header; a handle's private layout follows it |
| `SEA_RC_STATIC` | 0 | the count of a static object |
| `SEA_TAG_ARRAY` | 1 | dynamic array |
| `SEA_TAG_STR` | 2 | string |
| `SEA_TAG_FIGURE` | 3 | `Figure` handle |
| `SEA_TAG_AXES` | 4 | `Axes` handle |
| `SEA_TAG_LU` | 5 | `Lu` handle |
| `SEA_TAG_CHOL` | 6 | `Chol` handle |

**Dynamic array header**, 64 bytes (§4.1). Element (i, j) of an r × c matrix is element i + j·r of
the buffer, at `DATA + ESIZE·(i + j·r)`; a vector has `COLS` = 1. Unused header bytes are 0.

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_ARR_RC` | 0 | u64: reference count |
| `SEA_ARR_TAG` | 8 | u8: `SEA_TAG_ARRAY` |
| `SEA_ARR_EK` | 9 | u8: element kind `SEA_EK_*` |
| `SEA_ARR_RANK` | 10 | u8: 1 (vector) or 2 (matrix); bytes 11 … 15 are 0 |
| `SEA_ARR_ROWS` | 16 | u64: rows (a vector's length) |
| `SEA_ARR_COLS` | 24 | u64: cols; 1 for a vector |
| `SEA_ARR_CAP` | 32 | u64: capacity in elements, ≥ rows · cols |
| `SEA_ARR_DATA` | 40 | ptr: the buffer, `SEA_DATA_ALIGN`-aligned, column-major |
| `SEA_ARR_ESIZE` | 48 | u64: element size in bytes |
| `SEA_ARR_SLAY` | 56 | ptr: the struct layout descriptor for `SEA_EK_STRUCT`, else 0 |
| `SEA_ARR_SIZE` | 64 | header size |
| `SEA_DATA_ALIGN` | 64 | alignment of array buffers and of `dat` buffers |
| `SEA_EK_F64` | 1 | `f64` elements |
| `SEA_EK_I64` | 2 | `i64` elements |
| `SEA_EK_BOOL` | 3 | `bool` elements, one byte, 0 or 1 |
| `SEA_EK_STR` | 4 | `str` elements: string object pointers |
| `SEA_EK_STRUCT` | 5 | struct elements, inline (layout rule below) |
| `SEA_ESIZE_F64` | 8 | size of an `f64` |
| `SEA_ESIZE_I64` | 8 | size of an `i64` |
| `SEA_ESIZE_BOOL` | 1 | size of a `bool` |
| `SEA_ESIZE_PTR` | 8 | size of a `str`, dynamic array or handle value |

**Struct layout rule** (pass 3a's addressing, pass 4's descriptors and the runtime's copies agree
on it): fields in declaration order, each at the next offset that is a multiple of its alignment;
`f64`, `i64` and reference values (`str`, dynamic arrays, handles) have size 8 and alignment 8,
`bool` size 1 and alignment 1; a fixed-size array `T[n]` or `T[r,c]` is n or r·c elements of `T`
inline, column-major, with `T`'s alignment; a nested struct has its own size and alignment. A
struct's alignment is the largest of its fields' (1 if it has none) and its size is rounded up to
it. The same layout holds in stack slots and inside arrays.

**Struct layout descriptor**, read-only, emitted by pass 4 once per struct type that is the
element type of a dynamic array:

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_SL_SIZE` | 0 | u64: struct size in bytes (= the array's `SEA_ARR_ESIZE`) |
| `SEA_SL_NREF` | 8 | u64: number of reference fields, those of nested structs and fixed-size arrays included |
| `SEA_SL_REFS` | 16 | u64 × `SEA_SL_NREF`: their byte offsets in the struct, ascending |

**String object** (§4.1). The static string objects pass 4 emits for LIR `str` records have count
`SEA_RC_STATIC` and live in read-only data, 8-byte aligned.

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_STR_RC` | 0 | u64: reference count |
| `SEA_STR_TAG` | 8 | u8: `SEA_TAG_STR`; bytes 9 … 15 are 0 |
| `SEA_STR_LEN` | 16 | u64: length in bytes, 0 … `SEA_LIM_STR_BYTES` |
| `SEA_STR_BYTES` | 24 | the bytes, not NUL-terminated |

**Handles** (`Figure`, `Axes`, `Lu`, `Chol`): the common header (tag `SEA_TAG_FIGURE` …
`SEA_TAG_CHOL`), then a layout private to each runtime.

**Constant buffers** (LIR `dat` records): the n elements, contiguous, 8 bytes each for `i64` and
`f64` (the record's bit patterns) and 1 byte (0 or 1) for `bool`, in read-only data aligned to
`SEA_DATA_ALIGN`; no header.

**Pre-parsed formats** (LIR `fmt` records, LANGUAGE.md §11.1), read-only: a header and one piece
per `ftext`/`fconv` record, in order. A text piece points at its bytes (read-only, no NUL); a
conversion piece carries the letter, flags, width, precision and argument class of its `fconv`.

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_FMT_NPIECE` | 0 | u64: number of pieces |
| `SEA_FMT_NCONV` | 8 | u64: number of conversion pieces (= arguments) |
| `SEA_FMT_PIECES` | 16 | offset of the first piece |
| `SEA_FP_KIND` | 0 | u8: `SEA_FPK_*` |
| `SEA_FP_CONV` | 1 | u8: the ASCII conversion letter (`d i f F e E g G s`); 0 for text |
| `SEA_FP_FLAGS` | 2 | u8: `SEA_FF_*` bits; 0 for text |
| `SEA_FP_CLS` | 3 | u8: `SEA_CLS_*` of the argument; 0 for text |
| `SEA_FP_WIDTH` | 4 | i32: width, −1 if absent (and for text) |
| `SEA_FP_PREC` | 8 | i32: precision, −1 if absent (and for text); bytes 12 … 15 are 0 |
| `SEA_FP_TEXT` | 16 | ptr: the text bytes (text pieces), else 0 |
| `SEA_FP_TLEN` | 24 | u64: number of text bytes (text pieces), else 0 |
| `SEA_FP_SIZE` | 32 | piece size |
| `SEA_FPK_TEXT` | 0 | a text piece (`ftext`) |
| `SEA_FPK_CONV` | 1 | a conversion piece (`fconv`) |
| `SEA_FF_LEFT` | `0x01` | flag `-` (`fl` letter `l`) |
| `SEA_FF_PLUS` | `0x02` | flag `+` (`p`) |
| `SEA_FF_SPACE` | `0x04` | flag space (`s`) |
| `SEA_FF_ZERO` | `0x08` | flag `0` (`z`) |
| `SEA_FF_ALT` | `0x10` | flag `#` (`a`) |
| `SEA_CLS_I` | 0 | LIR class `i` (`i64`, `bool`) |
| `SEA_CLS_F` | 1 | LIR class `f` (`f64`) |
| `SEA_CLS_P` | 2 | LIR class `p` (`str`) |

**Argument slots.** `_sea_err`, and every entry point that takes a variable list of arguments
(formatting), receives them as consecutive 8-byte slots in argument order, which the caller
builds in its frame: an `i64` value, the bits of an `f64`, or an object pointer. A shape (`args`
letter `h`) takes two slots: the rows, then the cols of a matrix or `SEA_SHAPE_VEC` for a vector.

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_SLOT_SIZE` | 8 | bytes per slot |
| `SEA_SHAPE_VEC` | -1 | the second slot of a vector's shape |

**Error-site table** `_sea_sites`, read-only, emitted by pass 4: one record per distinct LIR site
`F:L` (§3.1), numbered from 0 in order of first occurrence in `sea.lir`; that number is the site
index passed to `_sea_err`, which prints `<file>:<line>: error: …` from the record.

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_SITE_FILE` | 0 | ptr: a static string object holding the `#file` path of `F` (§3.2) |
| `SEA_SITE_LINE` | 8 | u64: the line `L`, from 1 |
| `SEA_SITE_SIZE` | 16 | record size |
| `SEA_SITE_NONE` | -1 | the site index of an error with no location (all bits set); `_sea_err` then prints `error: <message>` without `<file>:<line>: ` |

**Kernel variants** (§4.4). The ids of the variants Sea's runtime can select; their names are
Baysick's `KV_NAME`s, which `SEA_KERNELS` and `_bsk_kern_use` take.

| Name | Value | Variant | Target |
|------|------:|---------|--------|
| `SEA_VAR_NEON` | 1 | `neon` | arm64-macos |
| `SEA_VAR_SSE2` | 2 | `sse2` | x86_64-linux |
| `SEA_VAR_AVX2` | 3 | `avx2` | x86_64-linux |

**Baysick version** (§4.3, §7.2): Baysick 0.6.0, whose `libbaysickrt.a` and `include/runtime.inc` the
runtime is built and checked against. The GEMM update entry `_bsk_kern_gemm_sub` and IEEE
propagation of §7.2 landed in Baysick 0.6.0 (Baysick commit `4c9b87a`, 2026-10-20) without a
version change, so 0.6.0 with that commit or later is the version `rt.inc` names.

| Name | Value | Meaning |
|------|------:|---------|
| `SEA_BAYSICK_MAJOR` | 0 | Baysick major version |
| `SEA_BAYSICK_MINOR` | 6 | Baysick minor version |
| `SEA_BAYSICK_PATCH` | 0 | Baysick patch version |

**Calling convention** (§3.6.3) on each target. Runtime entry points follow the platform ABI
exactly (AAPCS64 in its Darwin variant; System V AMD64), whose register assignments are those
of the table where the ABI has them; calls between Sea functions in `sea.s` use the whole table,
which extends the ABI's result registers (the `i`/`p` result registers beyond `x0`–`x1` and
`%rax %rdx`, the `f` result registers beyond `d0`–`d3` and `%xmm0`–`%xmm1`, and the area for
further results):

| LIR | arm64-macos | x86_64-linux |
|-----|-------------|--------------|
| `i` and `p` parameters, in order (hidden result addresses first, §3.6.3) | `x0`–`x7` | `%rdi %rsi %rdx %rcx %r8 %r9` |
| `f`, `x` and `y` parameters, in order, one register each (`x`, `y`: runtime vector forms only; `y` on x86_64 only) | `v0`–`v7` (`d0`–`d7` for `f`) | `%xmm0`–`%xmm7` (`%ymm0`–`%ymm7` for `y`) |
| further parameters | 8-byte stack slots in parameter order at `[sp]` at the call | 8-byte stack slots in parameter order at `0(%rsp)` at the call |
| `i` and `p` results, in order | `x0`–`x7` | `%rax %rdx %rcx %rsi %rdi %r8 %r9` |
| `f` results, in order | `d0`–`d7` | `%xmm0`–`%xmm7` |
| further results | written by the callee to an area of 8-byte slots whose address the caller passes as a hidden parameter after the hidden result addresses of §3.6.3: one slot per result that gets no register, in result order, whatever its class | same |
| callee-saved | `x19`–`x28`, `d8`–`d15` (low 64 bits); `x18` never used; frame record `x29`/`x30` in every non-leaf function | `%rbx %rbp %r12`–`%r15` |
| stack | 16-byte aligned at every call | 16-byte aligned at every call |

### 4.9 Code generation (pass 4)

Pass 4 (`seagen_a64`, `seagen_x64`) turns `sea.lir` into `sea.s` for the target of the `#target`
record, under the calling convention of §4.8 and the style rules of Baysick's runtime assembly
(frame record in every non-leaf function, `x18` never used, 16-byte aligned `sp`).

**Sites.** `_sea_sites` (§4.8) holds one record per distinct `F:L` in this order of first
occurrence in `sea.lir`: the `site` fields of the instructions, and the definition line of every
function, taken at its `func` record. Every function's line is a site, not only those of the
functions that check the stack limit (§4.6), because whether a function is checked depends on its
frame size, which only pass 4 knows, while pass 3b counts the sites (§2.7). A run-time check branches to an out-of-line
call of `_sea_err` with its code, the site index and its argument slots; an `rcall` of an entry
with site `S` passes the site index as its last argument (§4.8). That out-of-line call does not
make a function non-leaf (`_sea_err` never returns, so no frame record is needed for it); a
function is non-leaf when it contains a `call`, an `rcall` or (from sub-phase 4c) a `release`,
whose sequence calls `sea_free`. Until sub-phase 4c pass 4 rejects the vector, mask, `vfeat`,
`retain`, `release` and `mcopy` instructions and the `slay`/`soff` records with `BAD_RECORD`;
from 4c it accepts and emits `retain`, `release`, `mcopy`, `slay` and `soff` as "Phase-4 code"
below says, and the vector, mask and `vfeat` instructions stay `BAD_RECORD` until phase 7 (§8).

**What pass 4 validates.** Pass 4 checks its input as pass 3b does (§3.6.5, the whole list,
including `la` labels and `chk` argument counts), because it is the last pass before the
assembler and an unchecked record would become wrong machine code; any violation is
`BAD_RECORD`.

**The phase-1 allocator** (§8; from sub-phase 5b the allocator of §4.9.2 replaces it). Every virtual
register of a function has its own 8-byte slot in the frame; the frame holds the frame record,
the LIR `slot`s (§3.6.3) and the register slots, and its size is a multiple of 16. When the
largest alignment A of the function's `slot`s exceeds 16, the prologue rounds the stack pointer
down to a multiple of A after allocating the body (arm64 `mov x16, sp` / `and sp, x16, #-A`,
x86_64 `andq $-A, %rsp`), which moves it by up to A − 16 further bytes. **The checked frame
size** S of §4.6 covers every byte the prologue can move the stack pointer by, the worst-case
realignment included: S = 16 + B + R, where B is the body (every area below the frame record,
a multiple of 16) and R = A − 16 if A > 16, else 0. arm64 compares S (frame record 16 + B + R);
x86_64 compares S − 8 (`pushq %rbp` 8 + B + R; the other 8 bytes of the 16 are the return
address its caller's `call` already pushed). Both compare S with `SEA_STACK_LEAF_MAX` to decide
whether a leaf needs the check. Each
instruction loads its register operands from their slots into fixed scratch registers, computes
into a scratch register and stores the result to the destination's slot:

| Use | arm64-macos | x86_64-linux |
|-----|-------------|--------------|
| `i`/`p` operands, in operand order; result in the first | `x9`, `x10`, `x11` | `%rax`, `%rcx`, `%rdx` |
| `f` operands, in operand order; result in the first | `d16`, `d17`, `d18` | `%xmm8`, `%xmm9`, `%xmm10` |
| addresses of slots and data, the stack-limit check | `x16`, `x17` | `%r10`, `%r11` |

Calls load their arguments from the slots into the argument registers of §4.8 and store the
results back; no callee-saved register is used except the frame record (`x29`/`x30`;
`%rbp`), so none is saved. Structured LIR constructs become compares and branches to local labels
`L<function number>_<block>_<what>`. The phase-1 code is deliberately simple; §5.2 states what
phase 5 must reach.

**Phase-4 code** (sub-phase 4c; both targets, x86_64 forms in §4.9.1). The count of every object
is the u64 at offset `SEA_OBJ_RC` (= `SEA_ARR_RC` = `SEA_STR_RC` = 0, §4.8); a count of
`SEA_RC_STATIC` marks a static object, which neither sequence changes. The operand register of
`retain`/`release` is never null (§4.2), so neither tests for 0 as a pointer.

* `retain a` (a in `x9`):

  ```
      ldr     x10, [x9]            // the count
      cbz     x10, 1f              // static object: unchanged
      add     x10, x10, #1
      str     x10, [x9]
  1:
  ```

* `release a` (a in `x9`); the call is in line, so it is a call of the function (non-leaf, the
  §4.6 stack check, §4.9 above):

  ```
      ldr     x10, [x9]            // the count
      cbz     x10, 1f              // static object: unchanged
      subs    x10, x10, #1
      str     x10, [x9]
      b.ne    1f                   // still referenced
      mov     x0, x9               // count reached 0: free it and what it refers to
      bl      _sea_free
  1:
  ```

  The phase-1 allocator holds every virtual register in its slot, so nothing is live in a
  caller-saved register across the `bl`.
* `mcopy d s n` (d, s, n in `x9`, `x10`, `x11`; n ≥ 0, the regions never overlap, no alignment is
  assumed: unaligned 8-byte accesses are allowed on both targets), 8 bytes at a time and then
  single bytes, in increasing address order:

  ```
      cmp     x11, #8
      b.lo    2f
  1:  ldr     x16, [x10], #8
      str     x16, [x9], #8
      sub     x11, x11, #8
      cmp     x11, #8
      b.hs    1b
  2:  cbz     x11, 4f
  3:  ldrb    w16, [x10], #1
      strb    w16, [x9], #1
      subs    x11, x11, #1
      b.ne    3b
  4:
  ```

  `mcopy` is not a call: it does not make a function non-leaf.
* `slay` with its `soff` records is emitted in the data section with the other data records (in
  label order, §3.6.2), `.p2align 3`, its label `Ld<N>` (§4.9's data labels), then `.quad size`,
  `.quad n` and one `.quad off` per `soff` in order: exactly the `SEA_SL_*` layout of §4.8. A
  `la` of its label gives the descriptor address that `sea_arr_new_s` takes.
* The entries of phase 4 (§4.8, ids 9–22) are called by `rcall` like every entry: arguments in
  the §4.8 registers, the site index last for an `S` entry, results stored to their slots.
  `sea_str_f64`'s first argument is an `f` value (`d0`), its site the first integer argument
  (`x0`).

**Phase-4 validation** (pass 4 checks these as pass 3b does, §3.6.5; a violation is
`BAD_RECORD`): exactly the phase-4 additions of §3.6.5 ("Pass 3b from phase 4": the operand
classes of `retain`, `release` and `mcopy`, the `slay`/`soff` groups with offsets strictly
ascending multiples of 8 at most size − 8, and every `rcall` against the `entries` table).

#### 4.9.1 x86_64-linux code (`seagen_x64`)

`seagen_x64` (`passes/seagen_x64/`, built like every pass, §2.6.3, with the same modules and
`DATA` blocks as `seagen_a64`) is `seagen_a64` with the target changed: it reads `sea.lir` the
same way, validates the same things, lays out the same frame areas, numbers sites, constants,
cold blocks and labels the same way and emits the same data layouts (`rt.inc`, §4.8). Only what
this section says differs. As on arm64, the dump tests do not compare `sea.s`: the behaviour of
the program is what the tests check (§6.6), so the instruction sequences below are normative in
their results, and the named sequences are the ones to use.

**Syntax and naming.** GNU `as`, AT&T syntax (Baysick DESIGN.md §5.4.2: never
`.intel_syntax`), x86_64 ELF, `#` comments, 4-space indent, labels in column 0; first line `#
sea.s -- written by seagen_x64 from sea.lir (Sea DESIGN.md 4.8, 4.9)`. Symbols carry no leading
`_` (§4.8): the output defines `sea_main` (`.globl sea_main`, `.type sea_main, @function`) and
`sea_sites` (`.globl sea_sites`, `.type sea_sites, @object`) and refers to `sea_err`,
`sea_stack_limit` and the entry points by their ELF symbols (`sea_printf`, `sea_now`, `sea_log`, …). Every
arm64 local label `L…` is the assembler-local `.L…` (`.Lfn_<name>` for a function other than
`.main`, `.L<f>_ret`, `.L<f>_so`, `.L<f>_c<k>`, `.L<f>_e<k>`, `.L<f>_<b>_<what>`, `.Ld<N>` and
`.Ld<N>_t<k>` for data, `.Lsf<k>` for the site file strings); numeric labels `1:` … only inside
one instruction's sequence.

**Sections.** Code in `.text`, `.p2align 4` before each function; a function's cold blocks and
then its `f64` constants follow it in `.text` (`.p2align 3`, `.quad 0x<16 hex digits>`), as on
arm64. The data records and `sea_sites` go to `.section .data.rel.ro,"aw",@progbits` (they hold
absolute addresses), with `.quad`, `.long`, `.byte` and `.zero` (arm64's `.space`). The last line
is `.section .note.GNU-stack,"",@progbits` (a non-executable stack; without it GNU `ld` warns).

**Addressing and linking.** Data, constants and runtime variables are addressed RIP-relative
(`leaq .Ld1(%rip), %rax`, `movsd .L1_c3(%rip), %xmm8`, `movq sea_stack_limit(%rip), %r11`);
calls are direct (`call .Lfn_tri`, `call sea_err`, `call sea_printf`). The program is linked
non-PIE, exactly as Baysick's x86_64 programs (Baysick DESIGN.md §5.4.1): `as --64 -o prog.o
sea.s`, then `gcc -no-pie -o prog prog.o libsea.a libbaysickrt.a -lm` (Baysick's flags; Sea's
own code calls no libm function, `-lm` serves Baysick archive members), so the absolute addresses in `.data.rel.ro` are resolved at static link time. The driver does not run
these commands (x86_64-linux is a cross target, §2.2); the cross run does (§6.6.1).

**Frame.** A function is entered with `%rsp` ≡ 8 (mod 16). Its prologue is the stack check (when
§4.6 requires one), then `pushq %rbp`, `movq %rsp, %rbp`, `subq $F, %rsp`, where F is the size of
the arm64 frame's body (every area below the frame record, rounded up to 16), so `%rsp` ≡ 0
(mod 16) at every call; when the realignment of §4.9 applies, `andq $-A, %rsp` follows the
`subq` (the epilogue's `leave` undoes it). The areas lie from `%rsp` upwards exactly as on
arm64: outgoing stack arguments and the `sea_err` argument slots at offset 0, the results area
of calls, the LIR slots, 16 bytes per loop block, the saved address of the function's own
results area, the register slots. Every function has this `%rbp` frame (as every `seagen_a64` function has its frame
record); no other callee-saved register is used, so none is saved. The parameters are stored
from the §4.8 registers into their slots after the prologue; a parameter passed on the stack is
at `16+8k(%rbp)`. The epilogue is `leave`, `ret`. The scratch registers are those of the
phase-1 allocator table above; `%rdx` and `%rcx` double as the operands that x86 instructions
fix (`idivq`, shift counts in `%cl`).

**Stack check** (§4.6), before `pushq %rbp`, with N = S − 8 = 8 + F + R, every byte the
prologue can move `%rsp` by (S and R as in §4.9; F = B):

```
    movq sea_stack_limit(%rip), %r11
    movq %rsp, %r10
    subq %r11, %r10          # borrow (CF = 1): rsp already below the limit
    jb .L<f>_so
    cmpq $N, %r10            # N > 2^31 - 1: movabsq $N, %r11 / cmpq %r11, %r10
    jb .L<f>_so
```

and the cold block, reached with `%rsp` ≡ 8 (mod 16) and nothing allocated:

```
.L<f>_so:
    subq $8, %rsp            # realign for the call
    movl $15, %edi           # STACK_OVERFLOW (errors.inc)
    movq $<site index of the function's definition line>, %rsi
    movq %rsp, %rdx
    call sea_err
```

**Run-time error calls.** A check's cold block is `movl $<code>, %edi`, `movq $<site index>,
%rsi`, `movq %rsp, %rdx` (the argument slots at offset 0 of the frame, stored before the jump as
on arm64), `call sea_err`; `%rsp` ≡ 0 there. An `rcall` of an entry with site `S` passes the site
index as its last integer argument (§4.8).

**Instructions whose x86_64 form differs** (every LIR instruction keeps exactly its §3.6.4
meaning; operands are in the scratch registers in operand order, the result in the first):

| LIR | x86_64 |
|-----|--------|
| `li` | `movq $v, %rax` for −2³¹ ≤ v < 2³¹, else `movabsq $v, %rax` |
| `lf` | `movsd .L<f>_c<k>(%rip), %xmm8` (the function's constant, as arm64's `L<f>_c<k>`) |
| `la`, `sa` | `leaq .Ld<N>(%rip), %rax`; `leaq <offset>(%rsp), %rax` |
| `iaddc` `isubc` `inegc` | `addq %rcx, %rax` / `subq %rcx, %rax` / `negq %rax`, then `jo` to the `INT_OVERFLOW` cold block |
| `imulc` | `imulq %rcx, %rax`, then `jo` (OF is set exactly when the signed product does not fit) |
| `imulh` | `imulq %rcx` (one-operand form: `%rdx:%rax` = `%rax`·`%rcx`), then `movq %rdx, %rax` |
| `idivf` | `idivq` raises a divide error (`SIGFPE`) for a zero divisor and for −2⁶³ ÷ −1, so the checks come first: divisor 0 → `INT_DIV_ZERO`; divisor −1 and dividend −2⁶³ → `INT_OVERFLOW`; then `cqto`, `idivq %rcx` (quotient `%rax`, remainder `%rdx`) and the floored correction of arm64 (remainder ≠ 0 with a sign different from the divisor's: quotient − 1) |
| `imodf` | divisor 0 → `INT_DIV_ZERO`; divisor −1 → result 0 without `idivq` (the floored modulo by −1 is 0 for every dividend, −2⁶³ included, where `idivq` would fault and arm64's `sdiv` does not); otherwise `cqto`, `idivq %rcx`, and the floored correction (remainder ≠ 0 with a sign different from the divisor's: remainder + divisor) |
| `rcount` | the arm64 sequence with `divq` for its unsigned divisions (`xorl %edx, %edx` first; the zero-step check comes before) |
| `ishl` `ishr` `isar` | `shlq %cl, %rax` / `shrq %cl, %rax` / `sarq %cl, %rax` (the hardware masks the count to 6 bits, which changes nothing for the counts 0 … 63 the instruction allows) |
| `icmp`, `bnot` | `cmpq %rcx, %rax` (`testq %rax, %rax` for `bnot`), `set<cc> %al`, `movzbl %al, %eax`; cc `eq` `e`, `ne` `ne`, `lt` `l`, `le` `le`, `gt` `g`, `ge` `ge` (`bnot`: `e`) |
| `isel` `psel` | `testq %rax, %rax`, `movq %rdx, %rax`, `cmovneq %rcx, %rax` |
| `fsel` | `testq %rax, %rax`, `jne 1f`, `movapd %xmm9, %xmm8`, `1:` |
| `fcmp` | `ucomisd` (flags of D − S for `ucomisd S, D`; an unordered pair sets ZF, PF and CF): `eq` `ucomisd %xmm9, %xmm8`, `sete %al`, `setnp %cl`, `andb %cl, %al`; `ne` the same with `setne`, `setp`, `orb`; `gt` `ucomisd %xmm9, %xmm8`, `seta`; `ge` the same with `setae`; `lt` `ucomisd %xmm8, %xmm9`, `seta`; `le` the same with `setae`; then `movzbl %al, %eax`. With a NaN operand only `ne` gives 1 |
| `fnan` | `ucomisd %xmm8, %xmm8`, `setp %al`, `movzbl %al, %eax` |
| `fneg` `fabs` | flip / clear bit 63 through `%rax`: `movq %xmm8, %rax`, `btcq $63, %rax` / `btrq $63, %rax`, `movq %rax, %xmm8` (never `0 − x`, which gives +0 for −(+0)) |
| `fsqrt` | `sqrtsd %xmm8, %xmm8` |
| `fmin` `fmax` | not `minsd`/`maxsd`, which return their second (source) operand when either is NaN and when the operands are equal (±0 included); the result is arm64's: `fmin` gives b if b < a (an ordered comparison), else a, and then b if a is NaN; `fmax` the same with b > a |
| `ffloor` `fceil` `ftrunc` `fround` | SSE2 has no `roundsd`, so: if x is NaN or \|x\| ≥ 2⁵², the result is x (NaN, or already integral); otherwise t = `cvttsd2si` then `cvtsi2sdq` (exact for \|x\| < 2⁵²), and `ftrunc` gives t; `ffloor` t − 1.0 if t > x, else t; `fceil` t + 1.0 if t < x, else t; `fround` t + 1.0·sign(x) if \|x − t\| ≥ 0.5 (x − t is exact), else t; a zero result takes x's sign bit (`ftrunc(-0.5)`, `fceil(-0.5)`, `fround(-0.4)` and `ffloor(-0.0)` are −0.0), which gives exactly arm64's `frintz`/`frintm`/`frintp`/`frinta` results |
| `itof` | `cvtsi2sdq %rax, %xmm8` (round to nearest even: MXCSR is never changed) |
| `ftoi` | the checks come first, as on arm64: NaN, a non-integral x (the `ftrunc` above differs from x) and x < −2⁶³ or x ≥ 2⁶³ go to the `CONV_I64` cold block (x's bits in the argument slot); then `cvttsd2si %xmm8, %rax`. (`cvttsd2si` returns 0x8000000000000000, the "integer indefinite", for NaN and out-of-range inputs, so the conversion cannot be checked afterwards; −2⁶³ itself converts to that pattern correctly) |
| `ldi` `ldb` `ldf` `ldp`, `sti` `stb` `stf` `stp` | `movq`, `movzbl`, `movsd`, `movq`; `movq %rax`, `movb %al`, `movsd %xmm8`, `movq %rax`, on `off(base, idx, scale)` when scale is 1, 2, 4 or 8 and −2³¹ ≤ off < 2³¹; otherwise the address is computed into `%r10` first (`imulq`/`addq`, `movabsq` for a large offset), as arm64 computes it into `x16` |
| `chkb` | `cmpq %rcx, %rax`, `jae` to the `INDEX_OOB` cold block (unsigned, so idx < 0 fails too) |
| `chk` | `testq %rax, %rax`, `jne` to the cold block |
| branches | `jmp` and `j<cc>`: GNU `as` chooses the short or near form, and a near branch reaches any distance, so arm64's far form (and the mode-0 line count it needs) has no counterpart |
| `call`, `rcall` | arguments loaded into the §4.8 registers (stack arguments stored at `0(%rsp)`, `8(%rsp)`, …), `call`, results stored from `%rax %rdx %rcx %rsi %rdi %r8 %r9` and `%xmm0`–`%xmm7` (and the results area); no entry point is variadic, so generated code never sets `%al` |
| `ret` | the results into the §4.8 result registers (and the caller's results area), then the epilogue |

**Phase-4 code on x86_64** (sub-phase 4c; the meaning and the rules are those of §4.9's
"Phase-4 code"; operands in `%rax`, `%rcx`, `%rdx`, temporaries `%r10`, `%r11`):

| LIR | x86_64 |
|-----|--------|
| `retain` | `movq (%rax), %rcx`, `testq %rcx, %rcx`, `je 1f`, `incq %rcx`, `movq %rcx, (%rax)`, `1:` |
| `release` | `movq (%rax), %rcx`, `testq %rcx, %rcx`, `je 1f`, `decq %rcx`, `movq %rcx, (%rax)`, `jne 1f`, `movq %rax, %rdi`, `call sea_free`, `1:` (`%rsp` ≡ 0 mod 16 there, as at every call; the function is non-leaf) |
| `mcopy` | d, s, n in `%rax`, `%rcx`, `%rdx`: `cmpq $8, %rdx`, `jb 2f`, `1: movq (%rcx), %r10`, `movq %r10, (%rax)`, `addq $8, %rcx`, `addq $8, %rax`, `subq $8, %rdx`, `cmpq $8, %rdx`, `jae 1b`, `2: testq %rdx, %rdx`, `je 4f`, `3: movzbl (%rcx), %r10d`, `movb %r10b, (%rax)`, `incq %rcx`, `incq %rax`, `decq %rdx`, `jne 3b`, `4:` (never `rep movsb`, whose registers are the argument registers; the result is the same) |
| `slay`, `soff` | in `.section .data.rel.ro,"aw",@progbits` with the other data records: `.p2align 3`, `.Ld<N>:`, `.quad size`, `.quad n`, one `.quad off` per `soff` |

`sea_str_f64` takes x in `%xmm0` and the site in `%rdi`. The vector, mask and `vfeat`
instructions are `BAD_RECORD` until phase 7, as on arm64 (§4.9).

#### 4.9.2 The phase-5 allocator and code selection (both targets)

*(Agreed 2026-10-24: Decisions 59, 60 and lead decisions L-ac, L-ah, L-ai, L-an, L-aq, L-as of
§9.)* From sub-phase 5b both code generators allocate registers by the linear scan below, written
once in the shared module `passes/lib/ralloc.bas` (its interface in `passes/lib/API.md`; in the
`build.list` of `seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64`) and the same on both targets except for the register
tables. What §4.9 and §4.9.1 say stays valid except the phase-1 allocator and what this section
replaces: the register slots, the scratch-register table, the 16 bytes per loop block and the rule
that no callee-saved register is used. The sequences of §4.9 and §4.9.1 keep their meaning; how
their operands reach them, and which registers they may use besides, is given under "Templates"
below (L-an).

**Register tables** (Decision 60). Reserved as scratch and never allocated: arm64 `x15 x16 x17` and
`d29 d30 d31`; x86_64 `%rax %rcx %rdx %r11` and `%xmm14 %xmm15` (the operands and temporaries of the
staged templates below, the fixed registers of the one-operand `imulq`, of `idivq`, `divq` and
`cqto` and of a shift count in `%cl`, addresses, and the breaking of move cycles). The frame
registers (`x29 x30`; `%rbp`), the stack pointer and `x18` are never allocated. A register is taken
from the row of its class and of whether its interval crosses a call, first free in the order
written:

| Class, interval | arm64-macos | x86_64-linux |
|-----------------|-------------|--------------|
| `i`, `p`, crossing no call | `x9`–`x14`, `x8`, `x0`–`x7`, then `x19`–`x28` | `%rsi %rdi %r8 %r9 %r10`, then `%rbx %r12`–`%r15` |
| `i`, `p`, crossing a call | `x19`–`x28`, then `x9`–`x14`, `x8`, `x0`–`x7` | `%rbx %r12`–`%r15`, then `%rsi %rdi %r8 %r9 %r10` |
| `f`, crossing no call | `d16`–`d28`, `d0`–`d7`, then `d8`–`d15` | `%xmm0`–`%xmm13` |
| `f`, crossing a call | `d8`–`d15`, then `d16`–`d28`, `d0`–`d7` | `%xmm0`–`%xmm13` |

So 25 general and 29 floating-point registers are allocatable on arm64, 10 and 14 on x86_64. The
prologue's stack check and realignment (§4.6, §4.9) keep using `x16 x17` (`%r10 %r11`): no allocated
value is live before the parameters are moved.

**Positions and intervals.** The function's records are numbered 1, 2, … in order, block records
included; record k reads its operands at position 2k and writes its destinations at 2k + 1, and the
parameters are written at position 0. A register's interval runs from its first to its last
reference. Then, for each loop L (`loop`…`endloop`, `do`…`enddo`), a register r referenced inside
L has its interval extended to cover the whole of L (the opening record's position to the closing
record's) when r *may be live at L's top* (Decision 75, L-bg, L-bh), that is when some read of r
inside L is *uncovered in L*, or some read of r after L's closing record is *uncovered after L*.

* *Parts.* The parts are the function body, each loop's body, and each `if`/`ifz`'s first part and
  its `else` part; a part contains the parts nested in it. Each write has an *effective part*: the
  innermost part that contains it, except that a write standing in the `else` part of block B (in
  that part itself, not in a part nested in it) whose register's previous write, in record order,
  stood in B's first part with that part as its effective part has as effective part the part that
  contains B: both parts of B write the register, so every path through B does (L-bh). This is
  decided in the same walk; it makes `let t = if c { a } else { b }` (a register written in both
  parts and read after `endif`) a covered value.
* *Uncovered in L.* A read of r at record k inside L is covered in L when the latest write of r
  before k, in record order, lies inside L (after L's opening record, whose own write of `ind` is
  outside, L-az) and its effective part contains k; else it is uncovered in L.
* *Uncovered after L.* A read of r at record k after L's closing record (anywhere later in the
  function: in code after L, or in a later copy of a versioned or unswitched loop, which shares
  with L the registers live across the copies, L-bl) is covered after L when the latest write of r before k lies after L's closing record
  and its effective part contains k; else it is uncovered after L. A read in an enclosing loop M
  before L, reached around M's back edge, needs no test of its own: it is uncovered in M (its latest
  write is not inside M before it, or it would be covered), so r is extended over M, which contains
  L.

A covering write is passed on every path to k from L's top (or from L's end) within the same
iteration: an `exit` or `next` between them leaves its effective part, so such a path never reaches
k, and §3.6.4's property 2 (every register is written on every path before it is read), which holds
for `sea.lir1`, `sea.lir2` and `sea.lir` alike (L-bh), makes every read reached by some write. So r's
value at a covered read never comes from an earlier iteration, nor from before L's end. One
simplification keeps the rule decidable in one walk and is part of it (L-bf): a write inside a
nested loop never covers a read after that loop (its effective part has closed), since a `loop`
whose guard is false runs no iteration. A loop-carried value (read before it is written in the
iteration, as `dMax` or `ind`) and a value defined before L and read in it are extended; a
temporary written and read in the same part of one iteration (a value of an `if` part, the operands
of one statement; a sibling copy's temporaries have numbers of their own, L-bl) is not. The base
interval itself is never split: values that several copies of a loop share are only those written
before the copies or read after them (T6, T9, L-bl), and the values T7 and T8 put before a loop for
one copy's use are placed back into that copy's arm (T9, L-bm). T4's `isel R c S R` reads R:
when R holds a value from an earlier iteration that read is uncovered and R is extended, exactly as
the selection needs; when R was written earlier in the iteration in a part containing the `isel`,
the read is covered. Nested loops are handled by the same test for each loop of the nest. Every
rule below that speaks of an interval means this extended one; call crossing in particular ("The
scan") is decided on it, so a temporary whose interval no longer spans a call does not cross it. Each `loop` has a hidden register for its remaining count,
whose interval is the loop; and a hidden register for its step when the step register is written
inside the loop (otherwise the step register, or its immediate, serves). Hidden registers are
numbered after the LIR registers, in the order of their loops' opening records. A hidden register
that would be numbered above `SEA_LIM_LIR_REGS` is not created: that loop's count (and step) lives
in a spill slot of its own for the whole loop, read and written through the scratch registers as a
spilled interval is, so the register limit never makes pass 4 fail (L-aq, in the spirit of
Decision 72).

**Readings fixed during the build** (L-az). A loop with opening record o and closing record c covers
the positions 2o + 1 … 2c + 1, and the extension above makes an interval cover them; for deciding
whether a register is referenced inside or outside the loop, the opening record's references (its
reads at 2o and its write of `ind` at 2o + 1) count as outside and the closing record's as inside.
The closing sequence's references to `ind` and to a step register that is not hidden count at the
`endloop` record (reads at 2c, the write of `ind` at 2c + 1). With two hidden registers for one loop,
the count is numbered before the step. The loop-closing form is chosen by whether `ind` is
referenced after `endloop` (any reference in a later record). Spill slots are numbered in the order
of first use: a spilled interval's slot at its first reference, a save slot at the first call the
interval crosses, ties by register number; the slots of L-aq's loops come last, in the order of
their blocks. In the allocator's list of the intervals saved around a call record k (`ra_sv`,
`passes/lib/API.md`), the flag T (the interval crosses k) is not set for an interval that record k
itself writes, and such a result is listed with slot 0: it is neither saved nor reloaded. A
parallel move may name the same destination twice (a `call` or `ret` with one register for two
results): that is legal, `ra_pm` keeps the listed order in step 1, and the result listed last
is the one that remains, as LANGUAGE.md §7.3 requires.

**The interface change for Decision 75** (5c-2; `passes/lib/ralloc.bas` and its section of
`passes/lib/API.md`, owned by WP-RA2, §8). The reference walk gains one call, `ra_else D(), K, B`:
record K is the `else` of `if`/`ifz` block B, called where `ra_open` and `ra_close` are called in
the walk; the module then knows every part, since `ra_open` of an `if` opens its first part,
`ra_else` closes it and opens the `else` part, and `ra_close` closes the last part (`ra_open` and
`ra_close` of a loop open and close its body). The module keeps, for each register, the record and
effective part of its latest write and the outermost open loop over which the register must be
extended (applied when that loop closes), and for each block its parent; at a read uncovered after
some closed loops it extends r back over the outermost closed loop that contains r's first
reference and not the read (only such a loop needs it: a loop lying wholly between the first
reference and the read is inside the interval already). The old "first reference is a write at the
body's level" state is dropped. Cost: 85–160 lines in `ralloc` (counted in both code generators)
and 3–6 lines at each generator's walk (the `ra_else` call): **90–170 lines per code generator**;
no new array (the state fits the per-register columns and block rows of `D`, L-ac).

**The scan.** Intervals are placed in order of their start (ties: by register number). Before one is
placed, every active interval that ends below its start is expired and frees its register (so an
operand's last read at position 2k frees its register for a destination written at 2k + 1). An
interval *crosses* record k, a `call`, an `rcall` or a `release`, when it starts at or before 2k
and ends after 2k + 1: it holds a value from before the record that is read after it, along the
records or around a loop's back edge (a value of an outer loop that a call inside the loop
precedes is thus saved around that call). An interval *crosses a call* when it crosses any such
record. The register chosen is the *hint* if it is free, else the first free one of the interval's
row (except an *avoided* register, below). Hints: the destination of `mov D S` prefers S's register
when S's interval ends at that `mov`; on x86_64 the destination of a two-address instruction prefers
its first operand's register when that interval ends at the instruction, and for a commuting
operation (`iadd imul iand ior ixor fadd fmul`) its second operand's otherwise. On x86_64 the
destination of a two-address instruction `d = a op b` of any other operation (`isub isubc iaddc
imulc padd fsub fdiv`), with b a register operand other than a, *avoids* b's register (Decision 77):
when its hint is not free it takes the first free register of its row other than b's register, and
b's register only when no other register of the class is free. With d = b such an instruction needs
the scratch form of "x86_64 forms" below (one move more); since b's interval ends at the instruction
whenever its register is free there, the rule changes only which free register d takes. arm64 has
three-operand forms and no avoided register. When no register is free, the interval to spill is chosen
among the active intervals of the class and the new one: the one whose deepest reference has the
smallest loop depth; among those, the one that ends last; among those, the highest register number.
A spilled interval lives in its own 8-byte spill slot for its whole length (no splitting): each read
loads it into a scratch register, each write stores it from one (*Operands* below).

**Calls.** Around a `call` or an `rcall` k, and on the free path of a `release` k (after its
`b.ne`/`jne`, around the call of `sea_free`), every interval in a caller-saved register that crosses
k is stored to its spill slot (given at the first such store) before the call and loaded back after
it; the results, whose intervals start at 2k + 1, are not, and neither is a result of k whose
loop-extended interval starts before k (a value carried around a loop that the call redefines,
L-az). The order is: those stores, the argument
move, the call, the result move, those loads. The callee-saved registers the function allocates are
saved by the prologue after the frame record is set up and restored before the epilogue. The cold
call of `_sea_err` saves nothing: it never returns.

**Moves.** Parameters arrive in the §4.8 registers and are moved to their locations after the
prologue; the arguments of a `call` or `rcall`, its results, the values of a `ret`, the operands of
a staged template and the entry of a `loop` (`ind` ← start, its hidden count ← `last`, and its
hidden step, if it has one, ← step) are each one *parallel move*: every source is read before any
destination it overlaps is written. A source is a register, a spill slot or results-area slot, or an
immediate; a destination is a register, a spill slot or an outgoing stack-argument slot. It is
emitted in three steps (L-an):

1. every move to a memory destination, in the order of the destinations (spill slots by slot
   number, then the stack slots upwards): a register source stored directly; a memory or immediate
   source through the cycle scratch (`x17`; `%r11`; an `f` value moves as its bits through the same
   general register);
2. the register-to-register moves: repeatedly, the first (in destination order: the order of the
   §4.8 registers, or of the operands, or of the parameters) whose destination is no remaining
   move's source; when every remaining move is in a cycle, the first one's source is copied to the
   cycle scratch (`x17`, `d31`; `%r11`, `%xmm15`), which then stands for it;
3. every move from a memory or immediate source to a register destination, in destination order,
   loaded straight into the destination (`ldr`, `mov`/`movz`/`movk`; `movq`, `movsd`, `movabsq`),
   last, so that no register still to be read is overwritten.

The results of a `ret` beyond the result registers go to the caller's results area, whose address
the prologue saved in the frame (§4.9.2 Frame), in result order and before any register destination
of the `ret` is written (L-az): result j (from 0) at offset 8j of that area. arm64: `x16` is loaded
with the saved address, and the stores to `[x16, #8j]` are memory destinations of step 1 of the
`ret`'s parallel move, a register source stored directly, a spilled or immediate source through
`x17` (an offset above 32 760, which no record reaches, stops the compiler as an internal error).
x86_64: before the parallel move the saved address is loaded into `%r11` and each value is stored
through `%rax` (a register source directly), which is not yet a result register's value there. Both
come to the same: these stores read the results' locations before the register moves write any.

On x86_64 `%rdx` and `%rcx` are both argument registers and scratch registers, and the sources of
some moves are scratch or §4.8 registers (the results of a call, the results of a staged template);
that is safe because the three steps order every move by the rule above whatever its registers are,
and the cycle scratch register (`x17`, `d31`; `%r11`, `%xmm15`) is never a move's source or
destination outside step 2's cycle breaking, so it never holds a value a move still has to read.

**Frame** (replacing the phase-1 layout; from the stack pointer upwards): the outgoing stack
arguments and the `_sea_err` argument slots at offset 0; the results area of calls; the LIR slots;
the spill slots, 8 bytes each in order of first use; the saved callee-saved registers, 8 bytes each
in table order; the saved address of the function's own results area; then the frame record (arm64)
or the saved `%rbp`. The body B stays a multiple of 16, and S and the stack check of §4.6 and §4.9
are computed from it as before.

**Code selection** (both targets unless stated):

* *Operands.* An instruction uses its operands' registers directly. A spilled operand in operand
  position n (n = 1, 2, 3, the destination not counted) is loaded into scratch register n of its
  class (`x15 x16 x17`, `d29 d30 d31`; `%rax %rcx %rdx`, `%xmm14 %xmm15`; no direct instruction has
  three `f` operands), and a spilled destination is computed into scratch register 1 and stored.
  Loads and stores take their scratch registers by role instead (below). A `mov` between equal
  locations emits nothing.
* *Templates* (L-an). Every LIR instruction is *direct* or *staged*. **Direct** are `li lf la sa
  mov`, the wrapping integer and bit instructions, `iaddc isubc inegc imulc` (with their branch to
  the cold block), `imulh`, `ishl ishr isar`, `icmp fcmp bnot fnan`, `isel psel fsel`, `fadd fsub
  fmul fdiv fsqrt fneg fabs itof padd`, the loads and stores, `chkb chk`, `retain` and `release`:
  they use the allocated registers in place, as one machine instruction where the target has one,
  and otherwise as follows, each written so that a destination sharing a register with an operand
  is read correctly:
  * arm64 `imulc d a b`: `smulh x17, a, b`, `mul d, a, b`, `cmp x17, d, asr #63`, `b.ne` to the cold
    block (the high half first, so d may be a's or b's register). x86_64 `imulh d a b`: `movq a,
    %rax` (omitted when a is spilled: it is then in `%rax`), `imulq b` (b's register, `%rcx` when
    spilled), `movq %rdx, d`. x86_64 `ishl ishr isar d a b` with a register count: `movq b, %rcx`
    (omitted when b is spilled), then `movq a, d` (omitted when d = a) and `shlq`/`shrq`/`sarq %cl,
    d`; with an immediate count, the two-address form with `$v`.
  * Materialized comparisons: arm64 `cmp`/`fcmp` and `cset d, cc` (`fnan`: `fcmp a, a`, `cset d,
    vs`); x86_64 the comparison of §4.9.1 on the operands' registers, `set<cc> %al` (`fcmp` `eq`/`ne`
    with `setnp`/`setp %cl` and `andb`/`orb %cl, %al`), then `movzbl %al` into d.
  * x86_64 `isel`/`psel d c a b` after the flags of condition cc are set (fused below, or `testq c,
    c` with cc `ne`): when d = a, `cmov<¬cc> b, d`; otherwise `movq b, d` (omitted when d = b) and
    `cmov<cc> a, d`. `fsel`: when d = a, `j<cc> 1f`, `movapd b, d`, `1:`; otherwise `movapd b, d`
    (omitted when d = b), `j<¬cc> 1f`, `movapd a, d`, `1:`. `movq`, `movapd` and `leaq` leave the
    flags alone. arm64: `csel`/`fcsel d, a, b, cc`.
  * `retain a` and `release a`: §4.9's and §4.9.1's sequences with a's register (`x15`/`%rax` when
    spilled) for `x9`/`%rax` and the count in `x16` (`%rcx`); the free path's argument is `mov x0, a`
    (`movq a, %rdi`), with the saves of *Calls* around `bl _sea_free` (`call sea_free`).
  * Loads and stores: a spilled base is loaded into `x16` (`%rcx`), a spilled `idx` into `x17`
    (`%rdx`). When the address has no addressing form (arm64: `[base, idx, lsl #s]` with the scale
    1 or the access size and offset 0, or `[base, #off]` with an encodable offset; x86_64: `off(base, idx, scale)`
    with the scale 1, 2, 4 or 8 and −2³¹ ≤ off < 2³¹), it is formed in `x16` (`%r11`): arm64 `add
    x16, base, idx, lsl #s` for a power-of-two scale, else `mov x15, #z` (with `movk`) and `madd x16,
    idx, x15, base`, then the offset by `add x16, x16, #off` or through `x17` (`mov`/`movk`, `add
    x16, x16, x17`), where x16 stands for the base itself when there is no `idx`; x86_64 `imulq $z, idx, %r11` and `addq base, %r11` (without `idx`: `movq base,
    %r11`), then `addq $off, %r11` or `movabsq $off, %rcx` and `addq %rcx, %r11`. A spilled stored
    value is loaded after the address is formed, into `x15` or `d29` (`%rax` or `%xmm14`).

  **Staged** are the rest: `idivf imodf rcount ftoi fmin fmax ffloor fceil ftrunc fround mcopy`.
  Their operands are moved into the scratch registers in operand order by one parallel move, the
  sequence of §4.9 or §4.9.1 runs on them with its registers renamed (arm64 `x9 x10 x11` → `x15
  x16 x17` and `d16 d17 d18` → `d29 d30 d31`; x86_64 `%rax %rcx %rdx` unchanged, `%xmm8 %xmm9` →
  `%xmm14 %xmm15`, `%r10` → `%r11`), and its results are moved from the registers the sequence
  leaves them in (renamed) to their destinations. Where a sequence needs a register beyond these:
  arm64 `mcopy` moves its data through `d29` (`ldr d29, [x16], #8`, `str d29, [x15], #8`; `ldr b29,
  [x16], #1`, `str b29, [x15], #1`) instead of `x16`; x86_64 `ffloor`, `fceil` and `fround` keep t
  as an integer in `%rax` and change it there (`ffloor`: `decq %rax` when t > x; `fceil`: `incq
  %rax` when t < x; `fround`: |x − t| formed as `subsd %xmm14, %xmm15` (t − x, exact), then `movq
  %xmm15, %rcx`, `btrq $63, %rcx` (the bits of |x − t|), `movabsq $0x3FE0000000000000, %rdx` (the
  bits of 0.5), `cmpq %rdx, %rcx`, `jb 2f` (both are non-negative doubles, so their bits compare as
  integers), and when not below, `movq %xmm14, %rcx`, `sarq $63, %rcx`, `leaq 1(%rax,%rcx,2), %rax`,
  `2:`), then convert it again (`xorpd %xmm15, %xmm15`,
  `cvtsi2sdq %rax, %xmm15`) instead of adding or subtracting a 1.0 held in `%xmm10`: the same values,
  since |t| < 2⁵². No staged sequence needs anything else, and none is ever applied to allocated
  registers, so no early-clobber question arises.
* *Immediates.* An operand whose only definition is one `li` of a value v that the instruction can
  encode is written as an immediate: arm64 `add`/`sub`/`cmp`/`cmn` with a 12-bit value, optionally
  shifted by 12 (a negative v by the opposite instruction), the logical immediates, shift amounts
  0–63; x86_64 a sign-extended 32-bit immediate and shift amounts. The `li` is emitted only if some
  use needs the register. A comparison with the constant 0 is `testq a, a` on x86_64 (it sets the
  flags of every condition as `cmpq $0, a` does) and `cmp a, #0` on arm64.
* *Compare and branch fusion.* An `icmp`, `fcmp` or `bnot` whose result is read only by the next
  `if`/`ifz`, or by the condition of the next `isel`/`fsel`/`psel` with nothing between them whose
  emitted form sets the flags, sets the flags and is not materialized: `if B c` becomes one
  conditional branch to B's `else` or end on the inverse condition; `isel`/`psel` becomes `csel`
  (arm64) or the `cmov` form above (x86_64); `fsel` becomes `fcsel` (arm64) or the branch form above
  (x86_64). An `if`/`ifz` without `else` whose first part is exactly one `next B′` or `exit B′` is
  one conditional branch to that label. An `if`/`ifz` on a register (a condition not fused) is
  `cbz`/`cbnz` (arm64; an `icmp eq`/`ne` with the constant 0 read only by it becomes the same) and
  `testq c, c` with `je`/`jne` (x86_64). **Conditions** (L-as): `icmp` `eq ne lt le gt ge` are arm64
  `eq ne lt le gt ge`, x86_64 `e ne l le g ge`; `fcmp` `gt ge lt le` are arm64 `gt ge mi ls` after
  `fcmp a, b`, x86_64 `a ae` after `ucomisd b, a` and after `ucomisd a, b` for `lt le`; `fcmp eq ne`
  are arm64 `eq ne`. The inverse of each (arm64 `le lt pl hi ne eq`; x86_64 `be b be b`) holds when
  the operands are unordered, so a comparison with a NaN operand is false except `ne`, as LANGUAGE.md
  §6.8 requires. x86_64 `fcmp eq`/`ne` need ZF and PF: fused into an `if`, `eq` is `jp` and `jne` to
  the `else` (or end) and `ne` is `jp 1f`, `je` to the `else`, `1:`; as the one branch to `next
  B′`/`exit B′`, `eq` is `jp 1f`, `je` to the label, `1:` and `ne` is `jp` and `jne` to the label;
  they are never fused into a selection (the comparison is materialized and the selection tests it).
  A `chkb` whose index is an immediate compares the extent with it when 0 ≤ idx ≤ 4095 on arm64
  (`cmp ext, #idx`, `b.ls` to the cold block) and 0 ≤ idx < 2³¹ on x86_64 (`cmpq $idx, ext`, `jbe`);
  any other index, a negative one included, is in a register (`cmp idx, ext`, `b.hs`; `cmpq ext,
  idx`, `jae`), never turned into `cmn`: the comparison is unsigned.
* *Loop closing* (L-ai). The remaining count lives in the loop's hidden register, set by the entry
  move. When `ind` is not referenced after `endloop` (L-az), `endloop` is `add ind, ind, step` (an immediate when
  the step is a constant that the instruction encodes, "Immediates" above), `subs cnt, cnt, #1`, `b.hs` to the top (x86_64 `addq`, `subq $1`, `jae`),
  which runs last + 1 times for every last up to 2⁶⁴ − 1; otherwise `cbz cnt` to the exit, `sub cnt,
  cnt, #1`, the `add`, a `b` to the top (x86_64 `testq`, `je`, `decq`, `addq`, `jmp`). `next`
  branches to the closing sequence. For a loop's step, on both targets, a *constant* is a register
  whose only definition is an `li`, or a `mov` from a register whose only definition is an `li`
  (Decision 76, L-br's one level of `mov`: T3 leaves the lowering's `mov` of the step in that form);
  its value is the `li`'s. A step written as an immediate is no reference of the loop: the `loop`
  record's step operand is not reported to the allocator, its closing sequence reads no register
  for it, and the `mov` that defines it is still emitted, because the counted loop's `rcount` reads the step register before the loop.
* *x86_64 forms* (L-ah). For `d = a op b`: with d = a, `op b, d`; with d = b and a commuting operation
  (`iadd imul iand ior ixor fadd fmul`; never `fmin`/`fmax`), `op a, d`; with d = b otherwise, the
  result is computed in a scratch register and moved; else `movq`/`movapd a, d`, then `op b, d`. An
  `iadd` or `padd` with an immediate and d ≠ a is `leaq v(a), d` (it leaves the flags alone); an
  `i64` multiplication by an immediate is `imulq $v, a, d`, a checked one followed by `jo`. `itof` is
  `xorpd d, d` and then `cvtsi2sdq a, d`, so that the conversion does not depend on d's old value.
  `fabs` and `fneg` are `andpd` and `xorpd` with the function's 16-byte constants `.L<f>_abs` (two
  quads `0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`) and `.L<f>_neg` (two quads `0x8000000000000000`), placed after its
  `f64` constants with `.p2align 4`: the same bit operations as §4.9.1's, in one instruction.

The `-S` text of a given `sea.lir` is the same on every run (the allocation is a function of the
LIR alone), which the shape tests of §6.2 rely on.

### 4.10 Elementary functions

`log exp sin cos pow hypot` (LANGUAGE.md §10.4, Decision 6 in §9) are Sea's own, in
`runtime/<target>/rt_math.s` of each runtime. This section is their complete definition: every
operation, constant and table entry is given exactly, so that the two runtimes, the vector forms
of phase 7 and the compile-time evaluation of `pow` in constants (§4.10.5) compute **the same
bits for every input**. Whatever an implementation does differently from the text below (register
use, scheduling, branches turned into selects, which of two independent values it computes
first) must not change a single result bit.

**Rules every step obeys** (Decision 1, LANGUAGE.md §6.8):

* the only floating-point operations are IEEE binary64 `+ − × ÷` and `sqrt`, each correctly
  rounded to nearest, ties to even, plus the exact operations: sign flip and sign clear on the bit
  pattern, reinterpretation of a pattern, and conversion of an integer of at most 53 significant
  bits to `f64` (exact; `scvtf` / `cvtsi2sdq`). **No FMA** (SSE2 has none, and arm64 must not
  contract: every `×` followed by `+` below is two instructions), no x87, no long double, no
  approximate reciprocal, no flush-to-zero (FPCR and MXCSR are never changed; their exception
  flags may be set and are never read);
* integer operations are exact operations on 64-bit patterns: `+ − ×` modulo 2⁶⁴, the 128-bit
  unsigned product of two 64-bit values (arm64 `mul`/`umulh`, x86_64 `mulq`), `& | ^`, shifts by
  0 … 63 (`<<`, `>>` logical, `>>ₐ` arithmetic), unsigned and signed comparisons;
* results are within **1 ulp** of the correctly rounded value, and are **< 1 ulp** from the
  exact value everywhere (measured: §4.10.7), which also makes every exactly representable result
  exact (`exp(0)`, `log(1)`, `pow(2, 10)`, `pow(9, 0.5)`, `hypot(3, 4)`);
* special values follow C99 Annex F (F.9.1.6, F.9.3.1, F.9.3.7, F.9.4.3, F.9.4.4): ±0, ±∞,
  NaN and subnormals; **every NaN result is the pattern `#7FF8000000000000`** (Sea's `nan`),
  whatever the inputs' NaN payloads, so even the unobservable NaN bits (LANGUAGE.md §6.5) agree
  between the targets and with constant evaluation;
* the functions never fail, never trap, never write memory outside their own stack frame, read
  only their arguments and the tables, and call nothing outside `rt_math.s`.

#### 4.10.1 Entry points and ABI

The scalar entries are the `rt.inc` entries 3–8 of §4.8 (`SEA_ENT_LOG` … `SEA_ENT_HYPOT`;
symbols `_sea_log` … on `arm64-macos`, `sea_log` … on `x86_64-linux`). They follow the platform
ABI exactly, so they are also callable from C as `double sea_log(double)` and `double
sea_pow(double, double)` (the test harness of §4.10.6 does so):

| Entry | arm64-macos | x86_64-linux |
|-------|-------------|--------------|
| `sea_log` `sea_exp` `sea_sin` `sea_cos` | x in `d0`, result in `d0` | x in `%xmm0`, result in `%xmm0` |
| `sea_pow` `sea_hypot` | x in `d0`, y in `d1`, result in `d0` | x in `%xmm0`, y in `%xmm1`, result in `%xmm0` |
| may clobber | `x0`–`x17`, `v0`–`v7`, `v16`–`v31`, the upper 64 bits of `v8`–`v15`, NZCV, the FPSR flags | `%rax %rcx %rdx %rsi %rdi %r8`–`%r11`, `%xmm0`–`%xmm15`, the status flags, the MXCSR exception flags |
| preserves | `x19`–`x29`, `sp`, `d8`–`d15`, FPCR; never touches `x18` | `%rbx %rbp %r12`–`%r15`, `%rsp`, the MXCSR control bits, the x87 state; the direction flag stays clear |
| stack | at most 256 bytes below the incoming `sp`, so the call fits inside `SEA_STACK_MARGIN` (§4.6) | the same, below the return address |

The entries are leaf code in `rt_math.s`, which references no symbol of another runtime file, so
a program that links `libsea.a` pulls in only `rt_math.o` for them. They share internal helpers
(the logarithm and exponential cores below) under `_sea_`/`sea_` names that are not contract
(§4.5, "Internal runtime symbols").

**Vector forms** (phase 7, §5.1) compute, in each lane, exactly the scalar sequence of this
section: the branches of the scalar text become per-lane selects, table lookups become per-lane
loads, and the paths marked *rare* below (special inputs, `exp` with |x| ≥ 512, the Payne–Hanek
reduction of `sin`/`cos` for |x| ≥ 2²³, subnormal inputs) may be done by calling the scalar
entry for the lanes that need them (NEON and SSE2 have no 64 × 64-bit vector multiply). Their
entry points and register conventions are added to `rt.inc` and §4.8 by phase 7; their results
are bit-identical to the scalar entries for every input, which the tests of §4.10.6 check.

#### 4.10.2 Notation and shared primitives

`bits(x)` is the 64-bit pattern of `f64` x, `f64(u)` the `f64` with pattern u; `neg(x)` flips
and `abs(x)` clears bit 63; `itof(i)` converts a signed integer (every use is exact). `RN` is the
rounding of one operation; every `+ − × ÷` written below is one rounded operation, evaluated in
the order the parentheses give (without parentheses, left to right: `a + b + c` is `(a + b) +
c`). A hexadecimal number written `#…` is a 64-bit pattern; `2^k` is the exact power of two.

```
two_sum(a, b):      s = a + b;  bb = s - a;  e = (a - (s - bb)) + (b - bb);  return (s, e)
fast_two_sum(a, b): s = a + b;  e = b - (s - a);  return (s, e)
split(a):           g = 134217729.0 * a;  h = g - (g - a);  l = a - h;  return (h, l)
two_prod(a, b):     p = a * b;  (ah, al) = split(a);  (bh, bl) = split(b)
                    e = (((ah * bh - p) + ah * bl) + al * bh) + al * bl;  return (p, e)
```

`two_sum` gives s + e = a + b exactly for any finite a, b; `fast_two_sum` the same when a = 0 or
the exponent of a is at least that of b (each use below says why that holds); `two_prod` gives
p + e = a·b exactly when |a|, |b| < 2⁹⁹⁵ and no partial product underflows (each use is in that
range, or its error term is negligible where noted). `134217729.0` is 2²⁷ + 1 (`#41A0000002000000`).

The constants are given below as patterns; the column "definition" says what each one is, so
that the generator (§4.10.6) can recompute and check them. `RN₅₃(v)` is v rounded to the nearest
`f64`, `RNb(v)` to b significant bits, `RNgrid(v, e)` to the nearest multiple of 2⁻ᵉ, all ties to
even; v is the exact mathematical value.

#### 4.10.3 The tables: `include/math_tables.inc`

The tables are generated by `tools/math_tables.py` (§4.10.6), which computes every entry from
its definition with mpmath at 600 bits and rounds it as stated, and writes
`include/math_tables.inc`. The file is committed and is included by both runtimes'
`rt_math.s`; it is shared by Apple `as` and GNU `as` under the rules of §2.6 (Baysick DESIGN.md
§3.4: `//` comments only at the start of a line, no trailing comments, guarded by
`.ifndef SEA_MATH_TABLES_INC` / `.equiv SEA_MATH_TABLES_INC, 1` / `.endif`). It defines one
macro, `SEA_EMIT_MATH_TABLES`, which the including file invokes once in its read-only data
section (`__TEXT,__const` / `.section .rodata`); the macro emits `.p2align 6`, then the labels
and `.quad` lines below in this order, every value as `.quad 0x` and 16 upper-case hexadecimal
digits, one per line (a record of several words is several lines). Exact line shapes, which
`tools/gendata.bas` reads for the `mtab` block (§2.6.3): a label line is `sea_mt_<name>:` from
column 1 with nothing after it; a word line is four spaces, `.quad 0x` and the 16 digits. The labels are file-local
(`sea_mt_…`, never `.globl`); the macro defines no `.equiv` name other than the guard (the
counts below are fixed by this section, not by the contract tables of §2.6).

| Label | Records | Words per record | Record i |
|-------|--------:|-----------------:|----------|
| `sea_mt_const` | 1 | 32 | the constants of §4.10.4, in the order of the constant table there |
| `sea_mt_exp` | 128 | 2 | `EXP_TAIL[i]`, `EXP_SBITS[i]` |
| `sea_mt_log` | 128 | 3 | `LOG_INVC[i]`, `LOG_LOGC_HI[i]`, `LOG_LOGC_LO[i]` |
| `sea_mt_trig` | 52 | 4 | `TRIG_SH[j]`, `TRIG_SL[j]`, `TRIG_CH[j]`, `TRIG_CL[j]` |
| `sea_mt_tpi` | 20 | 1 | `TPI[w]` |

**`exp` table** (i = 0 … 127): T = 2^(i/128); `EXP_TAIL[i]` = `bits(RN₅₃((T − Tₕ)/Tₕ))` with Tₕ =
`RN₅₃(T)`; `EXP_SBITS[i]` = `bits(Tₕ) − (i << 45)` (mod 2⁶⁴). Spot values: record 0 = `#0`,
`#3FF0000000000000`; record 1 = `#3C9B3B4F1A88BF6E`, `#3FEFF63DA9FB3335`; record 127 =
`#3C5305C14160CC89`, `#3FEFF3C22B8F71F1`.

**`log` table** (i = 0 … 127). Block i is the set of patterns
[`LOG_OFF` + i·2⁴⁵, `LOG_OFF` + (i+1)·2⁴⁵) with `LOG_OFF` = `#3FE5F00000000000`, i.e. the values
z of that range; c is the arithmetic midpoint (a + b)/2 of the block's first value a and the
first value b after it. For the block that contains `#3FF0000000000000` (i = 80) `LOG_INVC` =
1.0 and both `LOGC` words are 0; otherwise `LOG_INVC[i]` = `RN26(1/c)` (26 significant bits),
and with L = −ln(`LOG_INVC[i]`) (exactly, from the rounded value), `LOG_LOGC_HI[i]` =
`RNgrid(L, 42)` and `LOG_LOGC_LO[i]` = `RN₅₃(L − LOG_LOGC_HI[i])`. Spot values: record 0 =
`#3FF745D178000000`, `#BFD7FAFA45D81000`, `#BD346C979BF72820`; record 79 = `#3FF0101010000000`,
`#BF70080549580000`, `#BD2166AECB31C67A`; record 81 = `#3FEFC07F00000000`, `#3F7FE02B6B100000`,
`#3D19E43F0DDA563A`; record 127 = `#3FE767DCE8000000`, `#3FD404307C26A000`,
`#3D3F925150499AC3`.

**`sin`/`cos` table** (j = 0 … 51): a = j/64; `TRIG_SH[j]` = `RN₅₃(sin a)`, `TRIG_SL[j]` =
`RN₅₃(sin a − TRIG_SH[j])`, `TRIG_CH[j]` = `RN₅₃(cos a)`, `TRIG_CL[j]` = `RN₅₃(cos a −
TRIG_CH[j])`. Spot values: record 0 = `#0`, `#0`, `#3FF0000000000000`, `#0`; record 1 =
`#3F8FFFAAAAEEEED5`, `#BC02AB639A9F0776`, `#3FEFFF000155549F`, `#3C828A28A03A5EF3`; record 51 =
`#3FE6E2B77C40BDE1`, `#BC70E729857FAD53`, `#3FE65DC1FDEB8CBA`, `#BC597C1B47337C77`.

**The 2/π table** (w = 0 … 19): the 1280-bit integer ⌊2/π · 2¹²¹⁶⌋, as 20 64-bit words, most
significant first; word 0 is zero, so bit g (counting from 0 at the most significant bit of word

argument (§4.10.4, `sin`/`cos`, step R2). The words, in order:
