  `movq`, `cmovlq`; `xorpd`, `cvtsi2sdq`, `divsd`, `movsd` (the store); `addq`, `subq`, `jae`. No frame
  access and no call in either. The dependency chain per step is the integer multiply, the
  multiply-high and the correction (an estimate of about 15 cycles, to be measured by §5.9).
* **W4 SOR**, the copy of the `j` loop for an interior column (unswitched on `i == 0` and `i == nx −
  1`, T9) inside the fast copy of the versioned `while` loop: every check proven (T1: `j ∈ 1 … ny −
  2` against the rows, `i` and `i ± 1` against the columns through the dominating comparisons), the
  column pointers of `fixed`, `src` and of `T`'s columns `i − 1`, `i`, `i + 1` (with `j ± 1` folded,
  T7) and `omega`, `0.25`, `dMax` in registers. arm64, **24 instructions** per point: `ldrb`, `cbnz`
  (the `fixed` test and its `continue`); six `ldr` (`T[j, i−1]`, `T[j, i+1]`, `T[j−1, i]`, `T[j+1,
  i]`, `src[j, i]`, `T[j, i]` once, T3); five `fadd`, two `fmul` (`× 0.25`, `× omega`), two `fsub`,
  `fabs`, `fcmp` and `fcsel` (`dMax`, T4), one `str`; `add`, `subs`, `b.hs`. x86_64, **27**: `movzbl`,
  `testq`, `jne`; six `movsd` loads, five `addsd`, two `mulsd`, two `subsd`, one `movapd`, `andpd`
  (`fabs`), `ucomisd`, `jbe`, `movapd` (`dMax`), one `movsd` store; `addq`, `subq`, `jae`. No frame
  access, no call, no cold branch. The loop stays latency-bound by the dependency on `T[j − 1, i]`
  stored by the previous iteration, as above.
* **Register pressure under Decisions 75 and L-bl, L-bm** (L-bo; derived from §5.8 and §4.9.2,
  checked by the shape tests). Each loop's values are counted in two groups: those referenced in
  the loop, which must fit the registers, and those live across it but not referenced in it, which
  may exceed them and are then the ones spilled, by §4.9.2's choice.
  * *W5, the fast copy*, both targets. Referenced: S (the promoted `s`, extended over the loop), J,
    the hidden count (the step 1 is an immediate of the closing `add`, Decision 76), U (the data address: an `ldp`, so T8 hoists it into the fast arm; L-bm places
    only pure instructions), and at most three temporaries at
    once (T with Q and N at `isar N`; R, A and L at the `icmp`). Constants: on x86_64 16807 and
    2147483647 are 32-bit immediates of `imulq`/`leaq`, 30 and 63 shift amounts and 0 the `testq`, so
    only M (#8000000100000003, for the one-operand `imulq`, whose `%rax`/`%rdx` are not allocated)
    takes a register: **8 of 10** general registers; on arm64 K1 (16807, for `smulh`/`mul`), M and C
    (2147483647, for `mul` and `add`) take registers: **10 of 25**. `f64`: F and two temporaries, 3.
    The slow copy's temporaries are numbered apart (L-bl) and do not overlap the fast loop. Live across
    the fast loop without a reference in it: `p1` (the address of `s`, read by the `sti` after the
    copies), the array `u` (read in the slow copy and returned) and the loop's count operand (read by
    the slow copy's `loop` record), and on arm64 nothing else that does not fit; on x86_64 8 + 3 = 11
    general values, so one is spilled, and the scan chooses `p1`: of the smallest deepest loop depth
    (0, with the count operand) it ends last (at the `sti` after the copies, the count at the slow
    copy's `loop` record); no value of the fast loop (depth 1) is a candidate before it. **The W5 counts 20 and 23 follow**; on
    x86_64 they depend on that spill choice.
  * *W4, the interior copy* (the last of T9's four copies), both targets. Referenced: J, the hidden
    count (the step 1, a `mov` of an `li` register, is an immediate of the closing `add`, Decision
    76, and takes no register), the seven pointers of the copy (`fixed`, `src`, `T`'s columns `i − 1` and `i + 1`, `T`'s
    column `i` at −8, 0 and +8, T7), all placed in its own arm (L-bm), and the `fixed` byte between
    its `ldb` and the `testq`/`cbnz`: **10 of 10** general registers on x86_64 at that point and 9
    elsewhere, 10 of 25 on arm64; `f64`: `omega`, `0.25`, `dMax` and at most four temporaries, **7 of
    14** (of 29 on arm64). The one x86_64 `movapd` besides `dMax`'s is the `fsub` of the update's
    change: its destination avoids the register of `T[j, i]`, whose interval ends there (Decision 77),
    so it is `movapd`, `subsd` and the `fabs` `andpd` in place. No other copy's value reaches it: the boundary pointers of `T[j, 1]` and
    `T[j, nx − 2]` are placed in the arms of the copies that read them, and the copies' temporaries
    are numbered apart. Live across it without a reference in it, on x86_64: `itSor`, `maxIt`, the
    `i` loop's count and non-empty flag (from its hoisted `rcount`), that loop's hidden count, its
    `ind` `i`, `nx − 1`, the `j` loops' count and flag, the header values loaded before the `while`
    loop (`T`'s rows and columns, the data pointers of `fixed`, `src` and `T`) and the arrays and
    values of `.main` read after the loop: at least 13 more, so at least 13 general values are
    spilled. Every one of them has its deepest reference at loop depth 2 or less (the `i` loop's
    body, the arms, the `while` body), except `T`'s column count: the boundary chains that L-bm
    places in the arms of copies 1 to 3 do not read it (they compute the pointers of columns 1 and
    `nx − 2` from the rows and the data pointer), but the two `chkb` of those columns do, and a
    `chkb` is checked, so neither T8 nor L-bm moves it: it stays inside copies 1 to 3 and reads the
    count at depth 3. That count is extended over the `while` loop and so ends after every value of
    the interior copy; the scan's choice (smallest deepest depth, then ends last) therefore spills
    them all before any value of the interior copy, and since that copy's referenced values never
    exceed 10 none of them is spilled. **The W4 counts 24 and 27 follow**, x86_64 at its limit (one
    more general value referenced in the copy would spill) and dependent on that spill choice; arm64
    has room. The shape tests check it as they check every target, by requiring no frame access in
    the measured loop on both targets (§6.2).
  * Without L-bl the copies would share their temporaries, whose base intervals would then run from
    the first copy to the last and be live in every copy (W5 x86_64 at least 13 general values in the
    fast loop, W4 at least 16 + 3 `f64` against 14); without L-bm the pointers of the boundary columns
    and the interior pointers shared by several copies would stand before the `while` loop or before
    the copies, and in copy 2 the scan would have to spill one that the interior copy reads (they all
    end at the interior copy's end, after copy 2's own values).

### 5.3 Small fixed-size values

`T[n]` and `T[r,c]` (≤ 256 elements) and structs are scalar-replaced by pass 3b when every
access uses constant indices after inlining and unrolling: each element becomes its own virtual
register (W3's `f64[4]` state; W2's `f64[4,4]` `ke`). Otherwise they live in the stack frame.
They never touch the heap. Fixed-size arithmetic (`x + h2 * k1`) is unrolled; pass 4 may pair
lanes into 2-wide vector operations when that does not change the operation sequence.

### 5.4 Allocation in hot loops

* Fused loops allocate nothing except their result.
* **Buffer reuse**: assigning a new array value to a variable whose current buffer has the same
  shape and a count of 1 writes into that buffer (`mid = 0.5 * (lo + hi)` in a loop allocates
  once). Pass 3a applies it whenever the old value is dead at the assignment.
* Temporaries that must be materialized inside a loop (barrier operands) get a buffer hoisted
  out of the loop and reused when the shape is loop-invariant.
* Remaining per-iteration allocations come from the small-block free lists or the large-block
  cache (§4.1): W2's `zeros(nDof, nDof)` per FSD iteration is a cache hit plus a 468 KB fill.

### 5.5 Estimated effect on the workloads (estimates, not measurements)

Planning estimates from instruction counts and kernel rates, to be replaced by the measurements
of §6.5. They show where the time should go, not a promise:

| Workload | MATLAB best compute (§1.2) | Where Sea's time should go |
|----------|--------------------:|----------------------------|
| W1 | 0.511 s | ≈ 260 k scalar `shaft_safety` evaluations with one `pow` each (only one branch of `kb` runs); 40 fused grid iterations; well under 0.1 s expected |
| W2 | 0.936 s | ≈ 400 dense factorizations of 241 × 241 (Cholesky ≈ 4.7 MFLOP each) and the 1441-RHS triangular solves; dominated by GEMM-rate updates; a few tenths of a second expected |
| W3 | 0.631 s | 480 k RK4 steps at a few tens of ns each, plus ≈ 0.96 M `sin` for the road (16001 × 60); around 0.1 s expected |
| W4 | 0.902 s | 31 M latency-bound SOR updates (≈ 20 cycles each by the add-chain latency) plus ≈ 1500 fused half sweeps; roughly 0.2–0.4 s expected |
| W5 | 0.764 s | 11 M LCG steps, 3 M `log` and 3 M `cos`, two 1 M-element sorts, 26 fused stack-ups over 7 M elements; roughly 0.1–0.3 s expected |

W4 and W5 are the workloads where Sea's margin over MATLAB is expected to be smallest, because
their dominant costs (a sequential dependency chain; memory traffic) are not things a compiler
can remove. Decision 1 in §9 states what the exactness rules cost on top.

### 5.6 What is not done

No automatic parallelism (single-threaded, like the kernels and the benchmark rules); no
reassociation or contraction for speed (LANGUAGE.md §6.8, Decision 1); no loop interchange or tiling of user
loops (the programmer's loop order is the operation order); no profile-guided or link-time
optimization beyond pass 2b's whole-program reachability.

### 5.7 Benchmark methodology

**Kernels** (`sea/bench/`): Baysick's methodology (`docs/BENCH.md`) unchanged — single-threaded
on both sides, a monotonic clock, untimed warm-up, ≥ 5 repetitions and ≥ 1 s per measurement,
the median reported with min and max, validation before timing, the vendor library (Accelerate /
OpenBLAS / the vendor libm) as one bar and the measured instruction-set peak as the other, machine,
load and variant recorded. Sea's own kernels (GEMV, LU, Cholesky, triangular solve, sort, vector
`log`/`exp`/`sin`/`cos`/`pow`) are measured this way, in Baysick's TSV format. The harness may be C
(built with `xcrun cc` / `gcc`), as Baysick's `bench/` is, because it is a measuring tool and
never part of Sea.

**Workloads versus MATLAB** (§6.5) cannot follow the kernel rules exactly, and the differences
are stated rather than hidden:

* **Threads.** The MATLAB baseline (`baseline_timings_matlab.json`, §1.2) ran with MATLAB's
  default thread count (`maxNumCompThreads` = 10), so its BLAS/LAPACK calls (W2's solves) may use
  several cores; Sea is single-threaded. The comparison is "Sea against MATLAB as users run it",
  which favours MATLAB. The single-threaded MATLAB run (`baseline_timings_matlab_1thread.json`)
  is reported alongside, not compared.
* **Repetitions.** The baseline is the best of 5 runs (first run included), still with visible
  variance (W2 compute 0.94–1.96 s). Sea is therefore compared with the **same rule: best of 5**
  consecutive runs (the first included). The median of those 5 runs is compared with MATLAB's
  five-run median, and the median and spread of 10 further Sea runs are reported next to them;
  neither is used for the pass/fail.
* **Same machine**: the comparison is valid only on the machine that produced the baseline,
  which must be recorded (§6.5).

### 5.8 Phase 5: the transformations of passes 3b and 3c

*(Agreed 2026-10-24: Decisions 58–75 and lead decisions L-ac–L-am, L-ao, L-ap, L-at, L-be of §9.)*
From sub-phase 5c-1 `seaopt` (pass 3b) transforms each function of `sea.lir1` by T1, T2, T3, T4 and
T10 below, in that order, and writes the result renumbered (§3.6.5; from 5c-2 as `sea.lir2`). From
sub-phase 5c-2 `sealopt` (pass 3c, Decision 74) transforms each function of `sea.lir2` by T5, T6,
T8, T7, T8 a second time, T9 and T10, in that order (L-ao: T7 needs the bases and the invariant index
terms that T8 moves out of the loop, and T8's second pass moves out what T7 adds; L-be: the
clean-up T10 runs at the end of each pass, so pass 3c starts from renumbered input with the dead
instructions of pass 3b removed), and writes `sea.lir` renumbered. It reads nothing but the function and the `entries`
table; its output does not depend on the `#target` record, so both targets get the same `sea.lir`
(Decision 58). Pass 4 then allocates registers and selects instructions (§4.9.2).

**What every transformation preserves.** A program's observable behaviour as LANGUAGE.md defines
it: the bytes it writes to standard output, standard error and files, the run-time error it reports
(message, line) or its normal end, its exit status, and the order of all of these; every class-E
value bit for bit (LANGUAGE.md §6.8: no `f64` operation is added, removed, reordered against its
operands or contracted, except the division of T2 that LANGUAGE.md §6.8 itself allows). In
particular no transformation changes which run-time error a program reports, or what it has
written before it. The one freedom used is L-ag: a run-time error ends the process and releases
nothing (§4.2, LANGUAGE.md §9.2), so a value that T5 keeps in a register need not be stored back on
a path that ends in a run-time error.

**Terms.**

* A *loop* is a `loop`…`endloop` or `do`…`enddo` block. The *guard* of a `loop` is the `if` block
  that directly encloses it in the patterns of rule 4 (`rcount C E lo hi st incl site`, `if B E`,
  `loop B+1 J lo C st`) and of rule 17's loop(N; K) (`li Z 0`, `icmp gt E N Z`, `if B E`, `li O 1`,
  `isub L N O`, `loop B+1 K Z L O`); a `do` has none. *Before L* means immediately before L's
  opening record, inside its guard. A `loop` runs its body at least once when it is entered (its
  guard has tested that), and so does a `do`.
* A *region* is a maximal sequence of consecutive instructions at one block level containing no
  block record (`loop endloop do enddo if ifz else endif`) and no `exit`, `next` or `ret`.
* *Failing* instructions are those with a `site` field (`iaddc isubc imulc inegc idivf imodf ftoi
  rcount chkb chk`, an `rcall` with a site) and `call`. *Effects* are `sti stb stf stp mcopy retain
  release call rcall`. *Pure* instructions are all others except the loads (`li lf la sa mov`, the
  wrapping integer, bit, comparison, selection and `f64` instructions, `imulh itof fnan padd`).
* *Invariant in L*: a register no instruction of L writes; a `loop` record writes its `ind` inside
  that loop (at the entry and at each closing), so an `ind` is never invariant in its own loop.
  **Scoping invariant:** every register that L reads, invariant in L or not, is written on every path
  from the function's entry to L's entry. This is §3.6.4 property 2 together with the lexical scoping
  of pass 3a's lowering: a local's register is written at its binding (rules 1 and 2), which lexically
  encloses every block that reads it, and a temporary is written before its use in the same
  statement; a register first written inside L and read only there needs no such path, and a register
  L reads before writing it in an iteration is written before L by the same rule. T5's pre-load and
  T6's count test, which run at L's entry whether or not the body reaches its own reads, rely on this:
  an invariant register therefore holds one defined value at L's entry.
* The *definitions* of a register are the instructions that write it (the `loop` record for its
  `ind`), and for a parameter its `func` record. A *symbol* is a register of class `i` that has exactly one definition, outside
  every loop (a parameter that is never written counts); an `ind` is never a symbol, its definition
  being inside its loop; a *constant* is a register whose only
  definition is one `li`.
* An *array register* is a `p` register every definition of which is the result of an `rcall` of
  `sea_arr_new`, `sea_arr_new_u`, `sea_arr_new_s`, `sea_sort`, `sea_argsort` or `sea_args`, the
  result of `rcall sea_arr_unique` of an array register, or a `mov` from an array register (entries
  named through the `entries` table, never by a written number). The definition is recursive
  through `sea_arr_unique` and `mov`, and the array registers are its *greatest* fixpoint: start
  from every `p` register each definition of which has one of these forms (taking the operand
  conditions as met) and repeatedly remove a register with a definition whose `sea_arr_unique`
  operand or `mov` source is not (or no longer) in the set, until nothing changes; so a cycle of
  `mov`s among candidates, as a loop-carried array gives, keeps all of them (L-bv). It is *shape-stable* when exactly
  one of its definitions is not of the form `mov A N` with N the result of `rcall sea_arr_unique …
  N 1 A` (the copy on write of rule 19 on A itself). For a shape-stable A whose other definition
  is `sea_arr_new`, `sea_arr_new_u` or `sea_arr_new_s` with symbol or constant operands R and C,
  rows(A) is R and cols(A) is C (both operands must be symbols or constants, else neither is
  defined, L-bb); for any other shape-stable A, and for a *dynamic-array parameter* A, rows(A) and
  cols(A) are the pseudo-symbols ⟨A, rows⟩ and ⟨A, cols⟩: the values of its header fields, which
  never change (§3.6.4, property 1). A dynamic-array parameter is a `p` parameter never written,
  never the base of a store and never an operand of `call` or `mcopy`, for which the function has
  both a `chkb` whose extent is the destination of an `ldi … A - 0 SEA_ARR_ROWS` (or `SEA_ARR_COLS`)
  and an `ldp D A - 0 SEA_ARR_DATA` whose D is the base of a load or store with an `idx`: rule 18's
  access to a dynamic array, which no struct, record, fixed-size array or string parameter gives
  (their extents are constants, or their bytes are inline). A pseudo-symbol stands only for those
  two header extent fields, read at `SEA_ARR_ROWS` and `SEA_ARR_COLS` (F2); a struct, record or
  fixed-size array parameter never gives one, so a field it holds at the same offset is an ordinary
  load with an unknown interval (L-ba).
* A *private base* is a `p` register that is a parameter never written, or whose every definition
  is an `sa` of one slot, and every use of which is as the base of a load or store without an
  `idx` (at any offset): never an argument, never a stored value, never an operand of `mov`,
  `padd`, `psel` or `mcopy`. A *private location* (P, off, size) is the 8 (or, for `ldb`/`stb`, 1)
  bytes at P + off. By §3.6.4 (properties 3 and 4) it is read and written in the function only by
  the loads and stores with base P (L-af).
* *Kinds* of memory access: `ldi`/`sti` (i64), `ldf`/`stf` (f64), `ldb`/`stb` (byte), `ldp`/`stp`
  (address). A load *may be changed* by an instruction X when: the load reads a header field
  (base an array register, offset `SEA_ARR_ROWS`, `SEA_ARR_COLS` or `SEA_ARR_DATA`): never; the
  load reads the count (`SEA_ARR_RC` of an array register): X is `retain`, `release`, `call` or
  `rcall`; the load reads a private location: X is a store with the same base whose bytes overlap
  it; any other load: X is a store of the same kind whose base is not a private base, an `mcopy`,
  a `call` or an `rcall`.

**Facts** (used by T1; L-ap). The walk carries a *state*: for each register of class `i` an
interval [lo, hi] whose bounds are each unknown, a constant k, or s + k with s a symbol or
pseudo-symbol, and for each symbol and pseudo-symbol s a constant lower bound L(s) and upper bound
U(s), each possibly unknown. Every constant in a fact lies in −2⁵² … 2⁵² (exact in a Baysick number,
§2.8); a bound that would leave that range becomes unknown. Bound s + k ≤ bound t + m holds when s =
t and k ≤ m, or s is a constant and t a symbol with s ≤ L(t) + m, or s a symbol and t a constant with
U(s) + k ≤ t, or s and t are two different symbols or pseudo-symbols with U(s) + k ≤ L(t) + m
(L-au), L and U taken from the current state; two bounds are *comparable* when one ≤ the other.
To *narrow* a bound by a candidate: an unknown bound becomes the candidate; a bound comparable with
the candidate becomes the tighter of the two (the smaller for an upper bound, the larger for a lower
one); a bound not comparable with it stays as it is. At the function's entry every interval and
every L, U is unknown, except L(⟨A, ·⟩) = 0 and U(⟨A, ·⟩) = `SEA_LIM_EXTENT` for each pseudo-symbol
(header fields of an array that exists wherever they are read). A symbol s defined by `li s v` is a
constant with the interval [v, v]; every other symbol s has the interval [s, s] wherever it is read
(a parameter from the entry on), whatever its definition computes; what that definition gives in
constants goes to L(s) and U(s) (F1). The walk visits the records in order once (no iteration to a
fixed point) and changes the state as follows:

* (F1) `li r v`: [v, v]. `mov r a`: a's interval. `iadd`/`iaddc` with a or b constant, and
  `isub`/`isubc r a b` with b constant: the other's bounds moved by ± the constant (an `isub r c b`
  whose only constant is the minuend c makes r unknown, L-av): after a checked one always (it did not
  fail, so the result is exact), after a wrapping `iadd`/`isub` only when T1's no-overflow condition
  below holds for it, else unknown. When r is a symbol, r keeps [r, r], and the bounds just computed,
  where they are constants, become L(r) and U(r).
* (F2) `ldi E A - 0 SEA_ARR_ROWS` (or `SEA_ARR_COLS`) with rows(A) (cols(A)) defined: E = [x, x],
  x being rows(A) (cols(A)); when E is a symbol (the load stands outside every loop), E keeps [E, E]
  and L(E), U(E) are narrowed by x's constant bounds instead (x itself when it is a constant, L(x)
  and U(x) when it is a symbol or pseudo-symbol; L-au). After the `rcall` of `sea_arr_new`, `sea_arr_new_u` or `sea_arr_new_s`
  that defines a shape-stable A whose rows(A) (cols(A)) is a symbol R: L(R) is narrowed by 0 and U(R)
  by `SEA_LIM_EXTENT` (the entry fails otherwise), in the state from that point on only.
* (F3) `loop B J S C T` with T a constant t > 0 in the pattern of rule 4 (S = lo, C the `rcount`'s
  d, T its st): J ∈ [lo.lo, hi.hi − 1 + incl], where lo.lo and hi.hi are the interval bounds of the
  `rcount`'s lo and hi registers at the `rcount`; with t < 0: J ∈ [hi.lo + 1 − incl, lo.hi]. In
  rule 17's pattern: K ∈ [0, N.hi − 1]. The guard's first part also records the non-emptiness on
  symbols: J's lower bound ≤ its upper bound gives, when one side is a constant c and the other s +
  k, a narrowing of L(s) by c − k or of U(s) by c − k. Like every change made inside a part, it is
  undone at the guard's `endif` by the join (F6).
* (F4) after `chkb I E d` (which passed): I.lo narrowed by 0 and I.hi by x − 1, x being E's upper
  bound. F4 changes neither a symbol's interval nor its L(s), U(s) (L-av).
* (F5) an `icmp cc C A B` followed, in the same region with A, B and C not written between, by `if
  B′ C` or `ifz B′ C`: in the part where the comparison holds, A and B are narrowed by it (`lt`: A.hi
  by B.hi − 1 and B.lo by A.lo + 1; `le`, `gt`, `ge` alike; `eq`: each by the other's bounds; `ne`:
  when B is a single bound b and A.lo = b, A.lo becomes b + 1, when A.hi = b, A.hi becomes b − 1); in
  the other part, by the negation. When A (or B) is a symbol s, whose interval stays [s, s], and the
  candidate bound for it is a constant, the narrowing is applied to L(s) (a lower bound) or U(s) (an
  upper bound) instead, in that part's state, so it ends at the `endif` like every other narrowing
  (`if k >= 0` gives L(k) ≥ 0 in its first part; a dominating `0 <= k < n` with a constant n thus
  proves `v[k]` for an extent at least n).
* (F6) Joins. At `if`/`ifz` both parts start from the state there (F5 then narrows each). After
  `endif`, the state is the join of the two parts' states at their ends: a part whose last record is
  `exit`, `next` or `ret` contributes nothing (the join is the other part's state), a missing `else`
  part contributes the state at the `if` with F5's negation, and when both parts end so, the state
  after `endif` is the one at the `if` (that code never runs). The join of two states: for each
  register, lo is the lower of the two lower bounds and hi the higher of the two upper bounds when
  they are comparable, else unknown; for each symbol, L(s) the smaller and U(s) the larger, unknown
  when either is unknown; the comparisons the join makes between bounds use these joined L and U
  (L-av). Records after an `exit`, `next` or `ret` in the same block never run. On
  entering a loop, the state just before its opening record is kept as its *entry state*, and every
  register written in the loop becomes unknown (then F3 sets J). After the loop's closing record, the
  state is its entry state with every register written in the loop unknown: the intervals and the L,
  U narrowed inside the loop are dropped, since the loop may be left by an `exit` from any point.
* Any other write of a register makes its interval unknown.

**T1. Checks and overflow.**

* A `chkb I E d` is deleted when I.lo ≥ 0 and I.hi ≤ x − 1, x being E's lower bound, before F4
  applies (Decision 61); with the comparison rule above, a symbol index k against a symbol extent E
  is proven when L(k) ≥ 0 and U(k) < L(E) in the current state (L-au), so `0 <= k < 8` over
  `zeros(8)` proves `v[k]` (F5 narrows L(k) and U(k); F2 gives L(E) = 8). A check that is not deleted stays exactly where it is: no check is ever
  moved, merged with another or reordered against any failing instruction or effect.
* An `iaddc`, `isubc` or `inegc` becomes `iadd`, `isub` or `ineg` (its `site` dropped) when the
  exact result's bounds, computed from the operands' intervals, lie in −2⁶³ … 2⁶³ − 1 (for a constant
  k added to s + c: the upper side holds when c + k ≤ 0 or U(s) + c + k ≤ 2⁶³ − 1, the lower side
  when c + k ≥ 0 or L(s) + c + k ≥ −2⁶³; this is also the no-overflow condition F1 asks of a wrapping
  `iadd`/`isub`; with two non-constant operands, each operand's bounds are first made constants
  through L and U, s + k giving L(s) + k and U(s) + k, unknown when L(s) or U(s) is, and the exact
  result of those constant bounds is tested, L-av); an `imulc` becomes `imul` when both operands have constant bounds whose products
  lie in −2⁵² … 2⁵².
* Nothing else changes (`idivf imodf ftoi rcount chk` and every `rcall` keep their checks; T2
  removes some divisions).

**T2. Division by constants** (Decision 65).

* `imodf d a b` and `idivf d a b` whose b is a constant c ≥ 1 (a negative or zero c leaves the
  instruction unchanged, with its zero-divisor and overflow checks): for c = 1, `li d 0` and `mov d
  a`; for c = 2ᵏ (k ≥ 1), `li m c−1`, `iand d a m` and `li m k`, `isar d a m` (exact for every a:
  the floored modulo and quotient by a positive power of two); otherwise the sequence

  ```
  li     M  <M>             the magic number below, as #hex
  imulh  H  a M
  iadd   H2 H a             only when M ≥ 2⁶³ (then H is H2)
  li     S  <s>             written also when s = 0 (then unread; T10 deletes it)
  isar   Q  H2 S            omitted when s = 0 (then Q is H2)
  li     K  63
  isar   N  a K
  isub   Q2 Q N             Q2 = the truncated quotient of a by c
  imul   P  Q2 b
  isub   R  a P             R = the truncated remainder, |R| < c
  iadd   A  R b             imodf; idivf: li O 1 / isub A Q2 O
  li     Z  0
  icmp   lt L R Z
  isel   d  L A R           imodf: R + c when R < 0; idivf: isel d L A Q2
  ```

  with every register new except a, b and d. The magic number is that of Hacker's Delight §10-1
  for 64-bit signed division: with nc = 2⁶³ − 1 − (2⁶³ mod c), p is the least integer ≥ 64 with 2ᵖ >
  nc · (c − 2ᵖ mod c), M = (2ᵖ + c − 2ᵖ mod c) / c (so M < 2⁶⁴) and s = p − 64. For c = 2147483647,
  M = #8000000100000003 and s = 30; for c = 10, M = #6666666666666667 and s = 2. Every
  instruction of the sequence is exact (no wrap occurs: |Q2 · c| ≤ |a|), so the result equals the
  floored `%` or `idiv` of LANGUAGE.md §6.6 for every a, −2⁶³ included, and the sequence cannot fail.
  The 128-bit arithmetic for M is a routine of `seaopt` on 16-bit limbs (L-am; it does not load
  `limb`, §2.7).
* `fdiv d a b` whose b's only definition is one `lf` of ±2ᵉ with −1022 ≤ e ≤ 1023 (a normal power of
  two: mantissa bits 0, exponent field 1 … 2046) becomes `lf R ±2⁻ᵉ` (a new register R, placed just
  before it; for e = 1023 the subnormal 2⁻¹⁰²³) and `fmul d a R`. LANGUAGE.md §6.8 allows exactly
  this: x · 2⁻ᵉ and x / 2ᵉ are the same correctly rounded value for every x, because 2⁻ᵉ is exact
  (L-al). No other `f64` division changes, and `%` on `f64` never does.

**T3. Value numbering in regions.** Two instructions are *equal* when every field but the
destination and the `site` is equal: the opcode, the condition code, the operand registers, the
immediates, slots, labels, the `idx`, scale and offset. T3 makes one forward pass over each region;
at each instruction in turn it applies the first of the first two rules below that holds and then,
when the instruction is (now) a `mov`, the third; the operands it compares are those already
rewritten by the copy propagations made earlier in the pass (so a chain of equal instructions
collapses in the one pass):

* an instruction that is pure, or one of `iaddc isubc imulc inegc`, and is equal to an earlier one of
  the region (the nearest earlier one that qualifies, L-av), with none of its operands and not the earlier one's destination D0 written between
  them, becomes `mov D D0`: the earlier one computed the same value, or failed;
* a load (with or without `idx`) of the same kind, base, `idx`, scale and offset as an earlier load
  or store of the region (the nearest earlier one that qualifies, L-av), with its base and `idx` not written between, no instruction between that
  may change it, and V not written between, becomes `mov D V` (V the earlier load's destination or
  the stored value);
* *copy propagation*: a `mov D S` (one of the region's own or one the two rules above have just made)
  where D has exactly one definition in the function (this one), every read of D lies later in the
  same region, and S is not written between the `mov` and the last of those reads: the reads of D
  read S, and the `mov` is deleted.

**T4. If-conversion.** `if B c` / `mov R S` / `endif B` becomes `isel`/`fsel`/`psel R c S R` (by R's
class); `ifz` swaps the last two operands; `if B c` / `mov R S1` / `else B` / `mov R S2` / `endif
B` becomes the selection of S1 and S2. Only these shapes (one `mov` per part, nothing else). A
form that reads its destination (`R c S R`, from an `if` or `ifz` without `else`) is created only
when R has a write on every path to the `if` record (a parameter, or a write earlier in record order
in a part that contains the `if`, the write's effective part as §4.9.2 defines it: this covers a
write earlier in the same iteration and a loop-carried value such as `dMax`, written before its
loop), or when R is read nowhere after `endif` (then T10 deletes the selection, L-bn); otherwise
the block is left as it is (L-bq). §3.6.4's property 2 for `sea.lir2` and `sea.lir`, and with it
L-bl's renaming and §4.9.2's liveness rule, rely on this rule.

**T5. Promotion of private locations.** For each loop L, outermost first, and each private location
ℓ = (P, off) read or written in L by `ldi`/`ldf`/`sti`/`stf` with base P, offset off and no `idx`,
where P is invariant in L (a parameter never written, or an `sa` register none of whose definitions
lies in L), L has no other access with base P whose bytes overlap ℓ, and ℓ was not promoted in a
loop enclosing L: a new register X of the access's class; `ldi`/`ldf X P - 0 off` before L; each load
of ℓ in L becomes `mov D X`, each store `st V P - 0 off` becomes `mov X V`; if ℓ is stored in L, the
store `st X P - 0 off` is placed immediately after L's closing record (where an `exit` naming L
also arrives), and immediately before every `exit` or `next` in L that names a loop enclosing L and
every `ret` in L. The locations promoted for one L are taken in the order of their first access in L
(ties: by offset): their pre-loads stand before L in that order, and at each place where post-stores
go, they stand in that order. Then: copy propagation (T3) of the `mov D X`; and *destination
rewriting* of each `mov X V`: when V has exactly one definition, earlier in the same region, X is
neither read nor written between that definition and the `mov`, every read of V lies in that
region, every read of V lies after that definition in record order (as copy propagation requires,
L-bv), and no instruction strictly between the `mov` and the last read of V in record order writes
X (L-bv), the definition writes X, the reads of V read X, and the `mov` is deleted. "Between" is by
record order inside the region; since a region holds no block record, `exit`, `next` or `ret`, all
those records run once each in that order whenever the region runs, and a read of V in a nested
part or loop, or anywhere outside the region, already fails "every read of V lies in that region"
(the rewriting is then not made). The last read of V may itself write X: it reads V before it writes
(as in L-bb's reading 2). When every read of V other than the `mov` lies before the `mov`, the new
condition holds trivially. (Without it, `s = a + b; let t = s; s = 0; w += t` over a promoted `ref s`
would read the 0 in `w += t`.) (W5's `ref s` in `lcg_fill` becomes one register for the loop,
loaded before it and stored once after it.)

**T6. Copy-on-write versioning** (Decision 62). A *cow* is rule 19's sequence on an array held in a
register A (`ldi C A - 0 SEA_ARR_RC`, a register holding the constant 1, `icmp ne S C O`, `if B
S`, `rcall sea_arr_unique site 1 N 1 A`, `mov A N`, `endif B`) or its memory form at a private
location (P, off) (the same after `ldp A P - 0 off`, with `stp N P - 0 off` before `mov A N`). The
*copy set* of an array A is A, the registers loaded in L from its location (memory form) and,
repeatedly, every register that a `mov` anywhere in the function copies from or into a member, and
every register that a `psel` writes when one of its selected operands is a member, together with both
selected operands of a `psel` that writes a member. For
each loop L that contains a cow and is not inside a loop already versioned, take the outermost such
L for which, for every array A (or location (P, off), with P invariant in L as in T5) cowed in L: A
is written in L only by its cows' `mov A N` (the location only by their `stp`), and every member of
A's copy set is used in L only as the base of loads and stores and as an operand of A's cows (so no
alias of A, whether made in L or before it, is retained, stored as a value, passed to a `call` or
`rcall` or returned in L). In the memory form the cow's leading load `ldp A P - 0 off`, or the
`mov A V` that T3 makes of it when it forwards an earlier `ldp V P - 0 off` of L (the load of a
bounds check, say), counts as part of the cow (L-bs): its use of V and its write of A are uses as an
operand of A's cows, so the condition can hold for a memory-form cow at all. The exactness argument
below is unchanged: the `mov` only copies one member of the copy set into another (V and A are both
members, since a `mov` copies between them), so it retains, stores, passes or returns nothing, and
when the location's count is 1 at L's entry the location is written in L only by the cows' `stp`, so
V, and A with it, is the array checked before L. Taking the cowed arrays in the order of their first
cow in L, L is then replaced, at its place, by

```
ldp    A1 P - 0 off                (memory form only)
ldi    C1 A1 - 0 SEA_ARR_RC        (these two for each cowed array in turn: A1, A2, …)
li     O  1
icmp   eq U1 C1 O                  (one for each cowed array in turn)
iand   V2 U1 U2                    (for a third array iand V3 V2 U3, …; none for one array)
if     B  V                        (V the last iand's destination; U1 for one array)
<L with every cow on those arrays deleted>      the fast copy
else   B
<L unchanged>                                   the slow copy
endif  B
```

A cow is deleted by removing its `ldi C`, its `icmp` and its `if`…`endif` block with everything in
it; the register holding 1 that it compared with is not part of the cow and stays (T10 removes it
when nothing reads it), and so does the `ldp` of the memory form (or T3's `mov A V` in its place,
L-bs), which also gives the stores their base. Exactness: when the counts are 1 at the entry of L, nothing in L can raise them (no member of a
copy set is retained, stored, passed or returned in L), so every deleted cow would have found a count
of 1 and called nothing; otherwise the original runs. *Registers of the copies* (L-bl): a register
is *local to* L when every reference to it lies in L's records from its opening record to its
closing record and L's opening record does not read it (it may write it: the `ind`); every other
register (written before L or read after it) keeps its number in both copies. The fast copy, first
in record order, keeps the numbers of L's local registers; in the slow copy each local register gets
a fresh number, the same throughout that copy, the fresh numbers taken one above another above the
highest number in use in the function, in the order of each register's first reference in the slow
copy. Renaming is exact: by §3.6.4's property 2 every read of a local register is preceded within
the same run of L by a write in L (the first entry to L carries no write of it), so no copy reads a
value the other wrote. No later rule of §5.8 depends on the numbers themselves, only on which
references share a register, and T10's renumbering by first appearance makes the written `sea.lir`
independent of the fresh numbers chosen. When a fresh number would exceed `SEA_LIM_LIR_REGS`, or the
copy would exceed another capacity limit of the function, L is not versioned (Decision 72). That
test does depend on the numbers: it is made on the numbers in use at that point, which still include
those freed by earlier deletions until T10 renumbers, so a copy may be refused that would fit after
renumbering; the output stays deterministic, since those numbers are a function of the input. Since the
fast copy's local registers are no longer read in the slow copy, T8 may move their definitions out
of the fast copy where it could not while the copies shared them ("D is not read outside L"). A slow
copy is never versioned again, and T9 does not unswitch inside it. (W4's `while` loop
is versioned once, on `T`; W5's `lcg_fill` loop on `u`.)

**T7. Strength reduction of addresses** (Decision 64). T7 runs after T8's first pass, so the header
loads and the invariant parts of the indices already stand before their loops (L-ao). For each loop
L, innermost first, whose `ind` J has a constant step st (for a loop's start and step only, a
*constant* is a register whose only definition is an `li`, or a `mov` from a register whose only
definition is an `li`: T3's copy propagation leaves the lowering's `mov` of the step in that form,
L-br; pass 4's loop closing reads a step the same way, Decision 76; the Terms' definition holds
everywhere else), and each load or store in L in record
order, those in loops nested in L included, whose base D is invariant in L, with `idx` X, scale z
and offset o. An access T7 has already reduced (for a loop nested in L) is not reduced again; an
access of a nested loop may be given an invariant-stride Q of L, whose `padd Q Q Δ` then stands at
the top of L's body, outside the nested loop:

* *unit stride*: when X is J, or is computed in L from J, constants and invariant registers by
  wrapping `iadd`/`isub` with J's coefficient 1 (X = J + c + σt: c a constant, t an invariant
  register with the sign σ = ±1, or absent), the access becomes `D′ J z 0`, where D′ = D + (σt · z
  + e) with e = c · z + o. The new pure instructions stand just before the access, in this order:
  when t is present, `li Z σz` and `imul T1 t Z` (both omitted when σz = 1: then T1 is t) and `padd
  D1 D T1`; when e ≠ 0, `li E e` and `padd D′ D1 E` (D1 being D when t is absent; D′ being D1 when e
  = 0). With t absent and e = 0, the access only takes J as its `idx`, and when X is J and o = 0
  nothing changes.
* *invariant stride*: when X = J · k + c + σt with k a constant ≠ 1 or an invariant register, the
  access becomes `Q - 0 o` with a new `p` register Q: before L, Q = D + ((start − st) · k + c + σt) ·
  z and Δ = st · k · z (start the `loop`'s operand, read before L as the `loop` reads it), and `padd
  Q Q Δ` as the first instruction of L's body (so `next` keeps it right). Accesses with equal D, k, c,
  σ, t and scale z share one Q and its Δ (both depend on z; the offsets o may differ, L-bv). The instructions before L stand after whatever T5, T6 and T8's
  first pass put there, each Q's (in the order of its first access) followed by its Δ's:
  * the term in start: when k is a constant and start a constant, it is folded into the constant
    term; when k is a constant, `li G kz` (the constant k · z) and `imul A start G`; when k is a
    register and start a constant, `li G f` with f = (start − st) · z and `imul A k G`; otherwise
    `li G st`, `isub A0 start G`, `imul A1 A0 k` and, when z ≠ 1, `li G2 z` and `imul A A1 G2`
    (A1 being A when z = 1);
  * the term in t, when present: `li Z σz` and `imul T1 t Z` (omitted when σz = 1);
  * the constant term e: (c − st · k) · z, plus start · k · z when it was folded, for a constant k;
    c · z for a register k;
  * Q: `padd Q1 D A` (when the term in start is not folded), `padd Q2 Q1 T1` (when t is present),
    `li E e` and `padd Q Q2 E` (when e ≠ 0), each operand being the previous one when a step is
    absent;
  * Δ: for a constant k, `li Δ v` with v = st · k · z; for a register k, `li G3 v` with v = st · z
    and `imul Δ k G3`.

Every constant T7 folds must lie in −2⁵² … 2⁵² (§2.8), else that access is not reduced. All of
these instructions wrap, as the address computation they replace does. The linear-index instructions
left unread are removed by T10. A chain that contains a checked instruction is not reduced.

**T8. Hoisting** (Decision 63). T8 runs twice, after T6 and after T7 (L-ao), each time from the
innermost loop outwards. An instruction I of loop L moves to before L when: I is pure, or is a load
without `idx` (L-aj) that no instruction of L may change; each operand of I is invariant in L or
written in L only by instructions already moved out of L; I is the only definition of its
destination D in L; every read of D in L lies after I and in I's block or a block nested in it; D is
not read outside L unless I is anticipated; and, for a load, one of: (a) I is anticipated; (b) its
base is an array register and its offset is `SEA_ARR_RC`, `SEA_ARR_ROWS`, `SEA_ARR_COLS` or
`SEA_ARR_DATA` (a header is always readable); (c) its base P is a private base and its bytes lie
inside the memory P reaches: 0 ≤ off and, for P an `sa` register, off + size ≤ the slot's size, for
P a parameter, off + size ≤ off′ + size′ for some load or store with base P at offset off′ in the
function (a `ref` parameter reaches an object as long as every access the function makes to it,
whether or not that access runs). I is *anticipated* when it lies at the top block level of L's body
and no record of L's body before it, at any depth, is a `ret`, an `exit` or `next` naming L or a
loop enclosing L, a `release` or a `call`: every iteration that begins then reaches I (an `exit` or
`next` of a loop nested in L does not skip it), and the first iteration always runs. A load is
hoisted by (a) only when its base is an *object pointer*: every definition of it is a parameter, the
result of a `call` or `rcall`, an `ldp`, an `sa`, or a `mov` from an object pointer (never a `padd`,
`psel` or `la`; and never an `ldp` of `SEA_ARR_DATA`, a *data pointer*, which addresses an element
buffer that may hold no element, so that no offset is known to lie inside it, L-bv). Such a pointer
is non-null and points to a live object wherever it is read (§4.2
"Null", §3.6.4 property 2, and no `release` lies before I in L), and the offset of a load lowered
from a field of its type lies inside that object; so the load, moved in front of a failing
instruction of L (a `chkb` that fails, say), reads valid memory, and its value is simply unused when
that instruction ends the program. The instructions moved before one opening record keep their
original order, after whatever already stands there (what T5, T6 and T7 placed, and in the second
pass everything the first pass moved); then, among all the instructions standing there (the first
pass's included when the second runs), an `li`/`lf` of a value an earlier one there already loads, or an
instruction or load equal (T3) to an earlier one there whose operands are not written between, has
its reads replaced by the earlier register when both destinations have exactly one definition in the
function (*constant commoning*), and is deleted.

**T9. Unswitching** (Decision 63). For each innermost loop L of the function as T8's second pass
leaves it (the copies T9 makes are not visited again), outside slow copies: the condition registers
of the `if`/`ifz` blocks in L that are invariant in L, in order of first use, the first two distinct
ones c₁, c₂ (no more): L is replaced by `if B c₁`, L[c₁ ≠ 0], `else B`, L[c₁ = 0], `endif B`, where
L[c₁ ≠ 0] is L with each `if` on c₁ replaced by its first part and each `ifz` on c₁ by its `else`
part (and L[c₁ = 0] the opposite); then the same for c₂ inside each copy that still contains an
`if`/`ifz` on c₂ after the first split (a copy without one is left whole, L-bt). So one loop becomes at most
four. Registers as in T6 (L-bl): at each split the first copy in record order (L[c ≠ 0]) keeps the
numbers of the local registers of the loop being split, and the second gets fresh ones, numbered as
in T6; the registers written before the loop or read after it keep their numbers in every copy. A
split that would exceed `SEA_LIM_LIR_REGS` or another capacity limit is not made (Decision 72). (W4's
`j` loop gets four copies on `i == 0` and `i == nx − 1`: c₁ is `i == 0` (its `if` comes first in
the body), and each of its two copies still holds the `if` on `i == nx − 1`, so both are split under
L-bt as before; the copy for an interior column has no branch but the `fixed` test.)

*Placement into the copies* (L-bm). T8 runs before T9 and cannot know the copies, so it may move out
of L an instruction whose value only one copy (or some of the copies) will read; T9 then places it
back. After the last split of L, let C₁ … Cₘ be L's copies in record order (m ≤ 4; a copy's records
run from its opening record to its closing record, so its `loop` record's reads are inside it). An
instruction I is *placeable* when: it is pure (no load: a load is never moved past the stores
between); it stands before C₁'s arm in record order, in a part that contains L's place; it has
exactly one definition in the function for each of its destinations; every read of each
destination lies in one of the copies or in another placeable instruction; and no operand of I that
is not a destination of a placeable instruction is written at a record between I and C₁'s arm, nor
in a loop that contains L's place but not I. The placeable set is the largest such set. For each
copy C in record order, the placeable instructions whose values C needs (those whose destinations C
reads, and repeatedly those whose destinations such instructions read) are placed just before C's
opening record, in C's own arm of T9's `if` (after whatever already stands there), in their
original order: the first copy that needs I receives I itself, each later copy that needs it a
duplicate whose destinations get fresh numbers (as in T6, in record order), and that copy's reads
of them, and those of the duplicates placed for it, are renamed. The placeable instructions are
then deleted from where they stood. A value placed this way is computed once per run of T9's `if`,
in the arm whose copy runs, and is live only over that arm, not over the enclosing loops. When the
duplicates would exceed a capacity limit of the function, nothing of L is placed (Decision 72). The
placement is part of T9, so T8's two passes and T7 are as written; T8's constant commoning has
already joined the equal constants of several loops, and a value read outside the copies (a
commoned constant, the condition of a T9 `if`, a header load) is not placeable. (In W4 the pointers
of `fixed`, `src` and of `T`'s columns `i − 1`, `i`, `i + 1` and the boundary columns 1 and `nx −
2`, which T7 creates and T8 moves out of the `j` loop, the `i` loop and the `while` loop's fast copy,
are each placed before the copies that read them, so the interior copy holds only its own seven.)

**T10. Clean-up.** Repeatedly until nothing changes: a pure instruction or load whose destination is
never read is deleted (a read by that instruction itself does not count, so an `isel`/`fsel`/`psel
R c S R` whose R nothing else reads is deleted, L-bn); `mov R R` is deleted; an `if`/`ifz` whose parts are empty is deleted with its
`else`; a `retain R` immediately followed by `release R` is deleted (the count is unchanged and
nothing is freed). Then the function is renumbered (§3.6.1, §3.6.4). T10 runs last in both
passes and deletes every selection whose result nothing else reads, the only instruction of
§5.8 that reads a register on a path where it may not have been written (T4's `R c S R` form when R
is dead after it), so §3.6.4's property 2 holds for `sea.lir2` and `sea.lir` (L-bn).

**Readings fixed during the build** (L-bb; normative, since the output is canonical):

1. In T3's first two rules, "written between" includes a write by the earlier instruction itself:
   an earlier instruction that writes one of its own operands (or the base or `idx` it reads) does
   not qualify (the interval between is open at the later instruction only).
2. In copy propagation, a write of S by the last instruction that reads D does not count as
   "written between" (it reads S before it writes it).
3. Records after an `exit`, `next` or `ret` at a part's top level, up to the part's end, never run;
   no transformation changes them (T10 does not delete them either). Their reads still count as
   reads for T3 and T10 (a register they read is not "never read"), the renumbering still renames
   the registers in them, and their record shapes stay as they are.
4. In F5, the candidate bounds for A and for B are both computed from the state before either is
   narrowed.
5. In F3, the guard's non-emptiness narrowing of L(s), U(s) is applied before the loop's entry state
   is kept (F6), so it holds inside the loop and after it, up to the guard's `endif`.
6. A constant (a register whose only definition is `li r v`) whose value lies outside −2⁵² … 2⁵² has
   an unknown interval.
7. T1's test for `inegc r a` uses a's extremes, symbolic bounds included: it becomes `ineg` when
   a.lo ≥ −2⁶³ + 1, a.lo = s + k counting through L(s) + k.
8. T3's second rule forwards an `stb` to a later `ldb` as written: the canonical lowering stores only
   `bool` values, 0 or 1, with `stb`, so the byte read back equals the stored register.
9. When T1's record of the changes to undo at the `endif`s and loop ends would exceed `seaopt`'s
   capacity, T1 makes no further change in that function (the deletions already made stand: each
   was proven where it stands), as Decision 72 does for the other transformations.
10. The rows(A) and cols(A) of an array register created with operands R and C are defined only
    when both R and C are symbols or constants (see Terms).

**The W5 loop after T1–T10** (`lcg_fill`, the fast copy; registers named, not numbered: S the
promoted `s`, J the `ind`, U the data address of `u`, K1, M, W, K63, C, F, Z0 the hoisted constants
16807, #8000000100000003, 30, 63, 2147483647, 2147483647.0 and 0):

```
loop   B J Start Last Step
imulc  T K1 S site              the one remaining check (s < 2³¹ is not provable)
imulh  H T M
iadd   H2 H T
isar   Q H2 W
isar   N T K63
isub   Q2 Q N
imul   P Q2 C
isub   R T P
iadd   A R C
icmp   lt L R Z0
isel   S L A R                  the new s, written straight into S (T5)
itof   X S
fdiv   Y X F
stf    Y U J 8 0
endloop B
```

before which stand, in the fast copy's arm, the hoisted `li`/`lf` constants and `ldp U u - 0 40`,
and after which the single `sti S p1 - 0 0`. Its exact text, with the whole function, is the
golden `opt5_lcg.lir` (§6.2).

### 5.9 Phase-5 micro-benchmarks

*(Decision 68.)* `sea/bench/micro/` holds two Sea programs and their C references;
`bench/micro.sh` builds and runs them on the Mac, and `bench/micro.sh --cross [-H host]` packs them
for the Linux host as `cross_pack.sh` packs tests. The methodology is Baysick's (BENCH.md; §5.7):
single thread, monotonic clock, untimed warm-up, at least 5 repetitions and 1 s per measurement,
the median with min and max, validation before timing, and the machine model, OS version, load
average and kernel variant recorded.

* `lcg.sea`: `lcg_fill` of `tests/accept/w5_stats.sea` verbatim, called once with 11 000 000
  steps from W5's seed 7 340 117, timed by `now()` around the call; it prints `lcg_final`, which
  must be 2145635252 (§8, row 1), and the seconds. Rate: ns per step.
* `sor.sea`: the scalar SOR of `tests/accept/w4_sor.sea` verbatim, timed around the `while` loop;
  it prints `it_sor` (832 ± 1, §6.3), `T_max` and the seconds, and the number of points updated per
  sweep (the non-`fixed` interior nodes, counted once before the loop, so the timed loop is W4's
  unchanged). Rate: ns per point update.
* `lcg_ref.c`, `sor_ref.c`: the same computations with the same operation order in C, built with
  `xcrun cc -O2 -ffp-contract=off` on the Mac and `gcc -O2 -ffp-contract=off` on the host, validated
  and timed the same way: the native bar, as Accelerate and OpenBLAS are for the kernels (§5.7);
  measuring tools, never part of Sea.
* Each Sea program is measured as compiled by the phase-5 compiler and by the phase-4 compiler (sea
  commit a6bfeb9, built in a scratch worktree that is not committed), so the record shows the change
  phase 5 made.
* The rows go to `bench/results/micro-<target>.tsv` (tab-separated, header `target cpu bench
  compiler reps median_s min_s max_s unit rate`, unit `ns/step` or `ns/point`), committed with
  sub-phase 5d, and 5d writes the measured table into this section with the machine it ran on.

**Measured in 5d** (2026-10-25; `sh bench/micro.sh` on the Mac and `sh bench/micro.sh --cross` on
the Linux host; rows in `bench/results/micro-arm64-macos.tsv` and `micro-x86_64-linux.tsv`). The
phase-5 compiler is the integrated 5d tree; the phase-4 compiler is sea commit a6bfeb9, extracted
with `git archive` into a scratch directory that is not committed and built there (the
"scratch worktree" above). Each binary was validated before it was timed (`lcg_final` 2145635252
and `u_last`; `it_sor` 832, `T_max` 160.76267159277148, 37 662 points per sweep), then measured
after one untimed warm-up with at least 5 repetitions and at least 1 s per measurement; the table
gives the median rate, with the median, min and max of one repetition's seconds. Both programs are
scalar loops that call no matrix kernel, so the kernel variant does not apply.

* Mac: Apple M2 Pro, macOS 26.6.2, `arm64-macos`, C built with `xcrun cc -O2 -ffp-contract=off`.
  The load average was 4.8 when the run started (other work was running; the machine was not
  idle), so these figures may be slower than an idle machine gives; the min and max show the spread.
* Linux host: Intel Core i7-4790 @ 3.60 GHz, Linux 7.1.8-arch1-3, `x86_64-linux`, C built with
  `gcc -O2 -ffp-contract=off`; load average 0.10 at the start.

| Target | Bench | Compiler | Reps | Median s | Min s | Max s | Rate |
|--------|-------|----------|-----:|---------:|------:|------:|-----:|
| `arm64-macos` | `lcg` | Sea phase 5 | 18 | 0.057961 | 0.056951 | 0.062560 | 5.269 ns/step |
| `arm64-macos` | `lcg` | Sea phase 4 | 9 | 0.116253 | 0.114389 | 0.130122 | 10.568 ns/step |
| `arm64-macos` | `lcg` | C `-O2` | 21 | 0.048605 | 0.047381 | 0.057863 | 4.419 ns/step |
| `arm64-macos` | `sor` | Sea phase 5 | 5 | 0.262436 | 0.262205 | 0.263430 | 8.375 ns/point |
| `arm64-macos` | `sor` | Sea phase 4 | 5 | 1.424302 | 1.422641 | 1.442721 | 45.454 ns/point |
| `arm64-macos` | `sor` | C `-O2` | 5 | 0.261219 | 0.260290 | 0.261398 | 8.336 ns/point |
| `x86_64-linux` | `lcg` | Sea phase 5 | 17 | 0.060619 | 0.060207 | 0.061800 | 5.511 ns/step |
| `x86_64-linux` | `lcg` | Sea phase 4 | 5 | 0.210053 | 0.208156 | 0.210601 | 19.096 ns/step |
| `x86_64-linux` | `lcg` | C `-O2` | 23 | 0.044823 | 0.044482 | 0.045586 | 4.075 ns/step |
| `x86_64-linux` | `sor` | Sea phase 5 | 5 | 0.245521 | 0.244351 | 0.247674 | 7.835 ns/point |

Ratios of the median rates: phase 4 / phase 5, `lcg` 2.01 (Mac) and 3.46 (host), `sor` 5.43 (Mac)
and 6.71 (host); phase 5 / C, `lcg` 1.19 (Mac) and 1.35 (host), `sor` 1.005 (Mac) and 1.006 (host).
So phase 5 made W4's scalar SOR loop 5–7 times faster and as fast as C on both machines (within
1 %), and W5's LCG step 2–3.5 times faster, 19 % (Mac) and 35 % (host) slower than C. These are
the two micro-benchmarks only, not the workloads (§6.5).

## 6. Testing and conformance

### 6.1 Principles (Baysick's, unchanged)

* **Expected outputs are derived from the specification, never from what the implementation
  prints.** If they disagree, the implementation is wrong unless the spec is changed on purpose.
* Every normative rule of LANGUAGE.md §3–§13 has at least one test; every error message has a test that
  produces it.
* Both targets must pass the same tests byte for byte (§6.6).
* No placeholder expected files: a test whose expected output cannot be derived by hand from the
  spec is not added until the spec says enough. (This is why v1 plot tests are structural,
  LANGUAGE.md §12.8.)

### 6.2 Test layout

```
sea/tests/
  programs/NAME.sea   + NAME.out (expected stdout)  [+ NAME.in (stdin), NAME.args (one argument
                      per line), NAME.err (expected stderr), NAME.status (expected exit status),
                      NAME.files/ (fixtures copied into the working directory),
                      NAME.expect/ (files that must exist afterwards, byte-exact)]
  errors/NAME.sea     + NAME.err (the expected compile-time or run-time diagnostic) + NAME.status
  passes/NAME.sea     + NAME.ast | NAME.res | NAME.hir1 | NAME.hir | NAME.hirl | NAME.lir1 |
                      NAME.lir (the --emit dumps of §3, built with --no-prelude, §3.8; pinned
                      like Baysick's tests/ir); every NAME.hir1 has a NAME.res (the input of
                      seacheck in stage.sh), and a NAME.res without NAME.hir1 is a program whose
                      sea.res holds an rerr (seaname hands an error on, §3.4.1); from 4e-0 every
                      NAME.lir1 beside a NAME.sea has a NAME.hirl (the input of sealower)
  passes/NAME.hirl    with neither NAME.sea nor NAME.hir, + NAME.lir1 (from 4e, with the records
                      82–87): a sealower test on hand-written sea.hirl (§3.5.9), for a record
                      sealoop does not write yet; stage.sh runs sealower on it and compares
                      with NAME.lir1
  plots/NAME.sea      + NAME.struct (the expected structure of each SVG it writes, LANGUAGE.md §12.8)
  math/               elementary-function identity tests (§4.10.6): <fn>.vec vectors written by
                      vectors/math_vectors.py from the model vectors/math_model.py, and the
                      C harness math_check.c that checks libsea.a against them (`make
                      test-math`, also in the cross run)
  link/               the link-map check of §4.3
  include_check.s, include_check_x86_64.s, include_asserts.inc
                      the contract-file checks of §2.6: Sea's .inc files assembled after
                      Baysick's include/limits.inc and include/runtime.inc, with the layout,
                      code-range and table-size assertions (`make check-includes`, Apple as;
                      `make -f Makefile.linux check-includes`, GNU as)
  cross_includes.sh   copies those files to the Linux host and runs the GNU as check there
                      (`make cross-includes`)
  check_contracts.sh  the drift check (`make check-contracts`, run first by `make
                      check-includes`; POSIX sh and awk): every SEA_* name and value and every
                      error, errno and entry record of the .inc files equals the tables of §2.6.1,
                      §2.6.2 and §4.8, and every record format of passes.txt equals the tables
                      of §3.2–§3.6 (§3.9), in both directions
  run.sh              Mac runner of programs/, errors/ and the passes/ dumps (it compiles with
                      the test's directory as working directory, so diagnostics name NAME.sea);
                      cross.sh, cross_pack.sh, cross_run.sh: the x86_64-linux cases on the
                      Linux host (§6.6.1, `make cross`, `make cross-pack`)
  NAME.status         the expected exit status: a decimal number and LF
  harness/            Baysick test programs of the shared modules (limb, f64emu, fltlit) that
                      read the committed vectors
  arith_check.sh      runs harness/ on vectors/ (exact arithmetic and float literals)
  lib_check.sh        checks passes/lib against the contract (e.g. the BAD_DATA copy, §2.6.2)
  driver_check.sh     the driver's options, messages and statuses (§2.2)
  passes/NAME.out     (optional, beside a dump test) the program's expected standard output when
                      built and run
  passes/NAME.lir     with neither NAME.sea nor NAME.lir1: a pass-4 test, LIR written by hand
                      (the input of seagen_a64, §3.6); + NAME.out (the expected standard output)
                      [+ NAME.err, NAME.status]. stage.sh runs seagen_a64 on it, assembles the
                      sea.s with `as`, links it with libsea.a and libbaysickrt.a as the driver
                      does, runs the program with standard input /dev/null and compares
                      standard output with NAME.out, standard error with NAME.err (else empty)
                      and the exit status with NAME.status (else 0)
  NAME.meta           (optional, beside a programs/ or errors/ test) `key=value` lines for the
                      runner: `stdout=epipe` connects standard output to a pipe whose reading
                      end is closed before the program starts (for `cannot write '<stdout>':
                      Broken pipe`, LANGUAGE.md §9.2); `stdout=closed` starts the program
                      with standard output closed (`>&-`, for `cannot write '<stdout>': Bad
                      file descriptor`); with either key NAME.out is not compared
  rt/arm64_macos/NAME.s, rt/x86_64_linux/NAME.s (§4.7.1) a runtime test: an assembly program, in
                      Baysick's assembly style, that calls runtime entry points through rt.inc
                      and is linked with libsea.a; + NAME.out [+ NAME.err, NAME.status], the
                      expected bytes derived from LANGUAGE.md and §4 (`make test-rt`)
  stage.sh            runs one pass on the committed golden output of the previous pass
                      (passes/NAME.ast → seaname → compare with NAME.res, NAME.res → seacheck →
                      compare with NAME.hir1, and so on; from 4e-0 the pairs NAME.hir → sealoop
                      → NAME.hirl and NAME.hirl → sealower → NAME.lir1 replace NAME.hir →
                      sealower → NAME.lir1), so each pass is tested on its own (`make test-stage`); a passes/NAME.lir with
                      neither NAME.sea nor NAME.lir1 is the input of a pass-4 test (above), a
                      passes/NAME.hirl with neither NAME.sea nor NAME.hir that of a sealower test
  protocol.sh         the pass-protocol tests (truncated inputs, missing #end, §2.2), for every
                      pass program (seaname on a truncated sea.ast, seacheck on a truncated
                      sea.res, …)
  check_data.sh       checks the generator (§2.6.3) on the contract files: every generated
                      line ≤ 255 bytes, every record present (`make check-data`)
  vectors/NAME.py     generators of exact test vectors (float-literal bits, printf digits),
                      run with `uv run`; their outputs are committed beside them, and the tests
                      read only the committed outputs (Python is never needed to run a test)
```

Test names carry the spec area: `lex_*`, `res_*` (`sea.res`, §3.4.1), `type_*`, `idx_*`, `op_*`, `stmt_*`, `fn_*`, `elem_*`,
`err_*`, `lib_*`, `fmt_*`, `json_*`, `plot_*`, `la_*`, `perf_*`.

* **Format tests** compare `printf` output for chosen values against the bytes the C99 rules give
  (the expected bytes are worked out from the exact binary values, including tie cases).
* **Literal-conversion tests** pin the bits of hard decimal-to-binary cases.
* **Folding tests** check that expressions near the limits of §2.8 (overflowing products,
  division by zero, `sqrt` of a negative constant, `inf`/`nan` operands) compile, are not
  folded, and give the IEEE results at run time.
* **Elementary-function tests** (`math/`) check the ≤ 1 ulp bound against reference values
  computed at high precision (the reference generator is a script run with `uv run --with
  mpmath`; Python is only ever run through `uv`), check that results which are exactly
  representable (`pow(2, 10)`, `exp(0)`, `log(1)`) are exact, and check that scalar and vector
  forms and both targets give identical bits.
* **Plot tests** (`plots/`): a `.struct` file lists, per SVG, the expected counts of plot areas,
  polylines, markers, bars, images and `<line>` contour segments, and the exact texts (titles,
  labels, legend entries, tick labels) — all derivable from LANGUAGE.md §12 by hand for tiny figures — and

  * **The heap check in every program run.** From 4c `tests/run.sh` and `cross_run.sh` run every
    program of `programs/`, `errors/` and `passes/` with `SEA_HEAP_CHECK=1` in the environment
    (§4.5). When the program exits with status 0, its standard error must end with the line
    `heap: 0 live objects` and LF, which the runner removes before it compares standard error
    with `NAME.err` (so no expected file mentions it); a missing line or any other count is a
    FAIL (`leak: <the line>`). With any other status the line must be absent (the runner
    compares standard error unchanged). A `NAME.meta` key `heap=off` runs that one program
    without the variable, and a key `env=SEA_HEAP_CHECK=<value>` (below) replaces the runner's
    value; in both cases the runner expects and removes the line only when the value is exactly
    `1` (the tests of the variable itself: `heap_env_unset` with `heap=off` and `heap_env_other`
    with `env=SEA_HEAP_CHECK=2`, each checking that nothing is written).
  * **`env=NAME=VALUE`** in a program case's `NAME.meta` (as in `rt/`, §6.6.1) sets one more
    environment variable for the run; only `SEA_HEAP_CHECK` is allowed in a program case.

    passes the same way (its pairs read the committed goldens; from 4h it skips the pair `hir1 →
    hir` when `NAME.hir1` is absent and the test has no `NAME.sea` or has a `NAME.prelude`

    `NAME.prelude` exists, so that a dump starting at `.hir` or `.hirl` is not a missing golden
    input). From 4h (Decision 57) allowed

    test without `--no-prelude` and compare the `#file` record of file 0 of its dumps as `#file
    std.sea` (the goldens are written so; the driver still writes the install path, §2.2).

  behaviour, so the first test is the whole corpus: every `programs/`, `errors/`, `passes/` and `rt/`
  case, the acceptance programs and `make cross` pass unchanged after each sub-phase. Expected outputs
  of the new tests are derived from LANGUAGE.md and, for dumps, from §5.8 by hand. New name prefixes:
  `opt_*` (programs whose output would change if a transformation were inexact), `opt5_*` (dumps of
  pass 3b), `ra5_*` (hand-written LIR for pass 4).
  * **`opt_*` programs** (T1 of 5c-1 and 5c-2, `tests/programs/opt_*`, `tests/errors/r_opt_*`):
    a loop that prints a line per iteration and then indexes out of bounds at a known iteration (the
    lines before, then the error with the exact index, dimension, extent and line); an overflow and
    an out-of-bounds index in the same iteration, in both orders; a check inside an `if` arm that never
    runs (no error), and inside an arm whose condition is loop-invariant and false (T8 and T9 must not
    move it); `j ± 1` over `1..n-1` and over `0..n` (the second fails at its last iteration); a range
    ending at `2^63 - 1` with `i + 1` in the body (`integer overflow` at the last iteration: T1 must
    keep that check); negative steps and `step 2`; facts that hold only inside a guard or a loop and
    must not be used after it (`a[n - 1]` after an empty `for i in 0..n` with `n = 0`, and an index
    narrowed by two `break` tests inside a `do` loop, used after the loop with a value the tests
    excluded: both report their errors); a `while` loop assigning an invariant value to a variable
    printed after it, run zero times (the old value is printed); a `ref` scalar updated in a loop,
    read by the caller afterwards, and the same with a run-time error part-way (the output before the
    error is what counts) and with a `continue` of an enclosing loop and a `return` inside the loop; a
    `ref` to an element (`f(ref v[3], v2)`) with both arrays printed afterwards; copy on write in
    loops: a loop storing into an array that another variable shares (the other one keeps its values),
    a loop whose stores are all skipped, a `ref` array parameter updated in a loop, a loop that stores
    into an array it also passes to a function (no versioning: the cow stays), and a loop that stores
    into an array after a copy made before the loop is passed to a function inside it; `%` and `idiv`
    by the constants 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 2147483647, 2^62 and 2^62 + 1 on −2⁶³, −2⁶³ + 1, −1, 0, 1,
    2⁶³ − 1 and multiples of the divisor ± 1; `% 0` and `idiv(x, 0)` with a constant 0
    and `idiv(x, -1)` with x = −2⁶³ (the errors unchanged, at their lines); a negative constant divisor;
    `f64` division by 4.0, 0.5, −2.0, 2^1023, 2^-1022 and 3.0 on values giving normal, subnormal,
    overflowing and signed-zero results, printed with `%.17g` (which round-trips) and as their
    `str()` text; an `if` with one `mov` per arm, as a value (T4); `f64` comparisons `==`, `!=`, `<`,
    `<=`, `>`, `>=` with a NaN operand in an `if`, as a selected value and as a loop exit (only `!=`
    holds); values live across calls inside loops (a value computed before a loop and read after a
    `printf` in it). Each has a hand-derived `.out` (and `.err`, `.status`); the cross runner runs
    them on the host.
