as ordinary calls (226, 242, 201, 255; named arguments by the phase rule until phase 6), and
`std.sea` uses LANGUAGE.md §10's parameter names, which those messages expose (§2.5, §2.6.2); L-u,
the callee's locals become `.i` locals of the caller, ordinary in every respect and numbered after
the `.l` locals, `.l`'s restrictions staying intact for `sealoop`'s own temporaries (§3.5.4,
§3.5.9 R28); L-v, `sealoop` drops the prelude functions and renumbers the rest densely, because
`sealower` requires dense `fid`s and no prelude function is a LIR function (§3.5.9 L18); L-w, the
order and ownership details of R26, R27, R29 and R30 (owned arguments released in the order R27 gives, after the `mov`s of a `tbind` and before the stores of a `tasg`,
an `iblk` without a destination yielding R1 … Rk, rule 2 (d)'s path for `tbind` and `tasg`, no
end-of-block releases after an `iret`), each the reading that makes an inline call behave as the
call it replaces (§3.5.9); L-x, a prelude function's result types are void, scalars, `str`,
dynamic arrays or tuples of those, rule 37's `mov` covering only register values, and `sealoop`
rejects others, which phase 6 specifies with LANGUAGE.md §8.6 (§2.5, §3.5.9); L-y, every prelude
error has its message: `bincount` with n < 0 or above 2³¹ − 1 and `linspace` with n above 2³¹ − 1
are `invalid array size n`, a too large `meshgrid` result is `out of memory`, all at the program's call line
(LANGUAGE.md §10.3, §10.7; §2.6.2); L-z, the close-out adds one test per after-phase-4 row that has
none (`@`, `format`, `solve`, `figure`), and no test names the four removed words, so none is
retired (§2.6.2, §6.2); L-aa, `w5_stats.sea` is Appendix D's text for what its four keys need,
followed by the `printf` JSON of §6.3 and nothing else on standard output (§6.2); L-ab, neither
`sealower` nor `sealoop` takes more than its spare array letters (`sealower` none, the `iblk` stack
living in its existing block tables; `sealoop` at most one, leaving at least 2) (§2.7, §8).
*For the user's information:* by LANGUAGE.md §10.3 rule 2, `linspace(0.0, 0.0, 4)` is `[0, -0, 0,
0]`; the reference `common.mlinspace` agrees, and a test pins it.

58. **Where the optimizations live.** Options: (a) **every LIR-to-LIR transformation in `seaopt`
    (T1–T10 of §5.8), target-independent; register allocation and instruction selection in pass 4**;
    (b) the loop transformations (T5–T9) in a new pass between `seaopt` and pass 4 (a new program,
    driver step and dump kind, the size of 4e-0's split); (c) check elimination in `sealower`, which
    knows shapes from the HIR (it has 527 lines left under its cap and phases 6–9 still to come).
    **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) keeps one program per concern and `seaopt`, the
    pass §2.7 sized for this work (2 444 lines), at 4 404–5 684; (b) only pays if `seaopt` cannot
    hold phase 7 too, which the gate after phase 5 measures (Decision 71); (c) spends `sealower`'s
    scarce margin. Affects §2.7, §3.6.5, §5.8, §8. *Revisited by Decision 74* (2026-10-24): after
    5c-1 `seaopt` measured 5 316 lines, so (b)'s condition is met and T5–T9 move to pass 3c.
59. **The allocator.** Options: (a) **one linear-scan allocator in a shared module
    `passes/lib/ralloc.bas`, built into both code generators with per-target register tables**; (b)
    the allocator in `seaopt`, its assignment carried to pass 4 in new `sea.lir` records (set `LF`),
    the code generators only mapping numbers to names; (c) a separate allocator written in each code
    generator; (d) a new pass `seareg` between `seaopt` and pass 4. **Decided: (a)** (the user,
    2026-10-24); (a) is written once, needs no contract change, and costs its 450–750 lines in each
    code generator (both stay ≤ 5 650); (b) also writes it once, but changes `passes.txt`, `seaval`
    and every LIR dump, and adds 600–900 lines to `seaopt`, which then cannot take phase 7 under the
    7 000-line cap; (c) doubles the work and the bugs; (d) adds a program and a dump kind for no
    gain over (a). Affects §2.7, §4.9.2, §8.
60. **Allocator policy.** Options: (a) **fixed scratch registers (arm64 `x15 x16 x17`, `d29 d30
    d31`; x86_64 `%rax %rcx %rdx %r11`, `%xmm14 %xmm15`), so 25/29 and 10/14 allocatable; values
    that cross a call kept in their registers and saved and reloaded around the call (callee-saved
    registers first on arm64); the spill victim chosen by the loop depth of its deepest use, then
    the farthest end; no interval splitting**; (b) the same, but x86_64's fixed operands handled by
    pre-coloured intervals instead of reserved registers (13 allocatable, about 150 more lines in
    the module and more cases to test); (c) values that cross a call only in callee-saved registers,
    otherwise spilled whole (simpler, but x86_64 has no callee-saved `xmm` register: W4's `omega`
    and `dMax`, which cross the slow copy's `sea_arr_unique` call, would live in memory in the hot
    loop). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) meets both §5.2 targets with registers to
    spare (W4's interior loop needs 9 general registers on x86_64), and saves cost only on the paths
    that call. Affects §4.9.2, §5.2.
61. **Bounds-check elimination, and the checks it cannot prove.** Options: (a) **a check is deleted
    only when §5.8's facts prove it (loop ranges from `rcount` and rule 17, creation extents of
    shape-stable arrays, the extents of unchanged parameters, dominating comparisons, checks already
    passed); every other check stays exactly where it is, as a compare and a branch to a cold block,
    never moved or merged; LANGUAGE.md §5.4's "hoists the others out of loops" becomes "keeps the
    others as a compare and a never-taken branch"**; (b) (a), plus loop versioning on a range test
    in front of a loop whose unproven checks are affine in its index (a check-free copy when the
    whole range fits, the original otherwise; exact, but up to twice the code and 200–300 more
    lines); (c) (a), plus hoisting an invariant check when it would run first in the first iteration
    (exact only under conditions that W4's boundary checks do not meet). **Decided: (a)** (the user,
    2026-10-24); (a) proves every check of W4 and W5 and keeps LANGUAGE.md's error order trivially;
    (b) helps loops over arrays whose extents are unrelated to the range, which no workload has in a
    hot loop; (c) adds subtle conditions for little. Affects §5.8, LANGUAGE.md §5.4 (one sentence,
    not a rule).
62. **Copy on write in loops.** Options: (a) **versioning (T6): a test of the counts in front of the
    outermost qualifying loop chooses a copy of the loop without the cows (counts 1) or the
    original; register and `ref`-parameter (memory) forms; one level, at most twice the loop's
    code**; (b) the cow hoisted in front of the loop (`sea_arr_unique` called before the loop even
    when no store would run: exact in values, but an `out of memory` can then come earlier, or where
    the program would not have copied, which LANGUAGE.md §9.2 would have to allow); (c) the cow kept
    in the loop (3 instructions per store, and the data address of the array cannot be hoisted, so
    W4's column pointers are reloaded each point: the W4 target is missed). **Decided: (a)** (the
    user, 2026-10-24); (a) is exact and makes the hot copy a plain store; it costs 200–320 lines and
    code size. Affects §4.2 (its copy-on-write paragraphs name the versioning), §5.8.
63. **What is hoisted, how memory is disambiguated, and unswitching.** Options: (a) **hoisting of
    pure instructions, of checked arithmetic once T1 has made it unchecked, of header loads (also
    from inside `if` arms, for array registers), of loads from private locations (unaliased `ref`
    parameters and private slots, L-af) and of anticipated loads; never of a failing instruction, an
    effect, or a load with an index (L-aj); memory disambiguated by the location classes of §5.8
    (header fields, private locations, then by access kind); promotion of private `i64`/`f64`
    locations to registers in loops (W5's `ref s`); value numbering within regions; if-conversion of
    one-`mov` arms; unswitching of innermost loops on at most two invariant conditions (T9)**; (b)
    (a) without unswitching (W4's two boundary tests stay as two well-predicted branches per point;
    arm64 26 instructions instead of 24, and on x86_64 the boundary arms' registers no longer fit
    the 10 allocatable ones, so the loop body gets spill loads); (c) (a) without promotion (W5's `s`
    is loaded and stored through memory each step: two memory operations and a store-to-load
    forwarding delay on the dependency chain). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); unswitching
    costs 100–180 lines and up to four copies of an innermost loop. Affects §5.2, §5.8.
64. **Strength reduction.** Options: (a) **both forms: unit stride (the index register with a
    hoisted base, constant offsets folded into the base) and invariant stride (a pointer advanced at
    the top of the body, so `next` stays right)**; (b) unit stride only now, invariant stride with
    phase 7's vectorization (W4 and W5 need only unit stride; W2's row access and any `A[i, j]` with
    `j` inner then keep a multiply per access until phase 7); (c) none: scaled addressing only, the
    linear index computed per access. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) meets §5.2's
    wording ("pointer increments of 8 and 8·ld") for 150–250 lines; (b) saves about 80 of them.
    Affects §5.2, §5.8.
65. **Division by constants.** Options: (a) **`%` and `idiv` on `i64` by a constant c ≥ 1: c = 1,
    powers of two (`iand`, `isar`), every other c by the signed multiply-high sequence of §5.8 with
    the floored correction (Hacker's Delight's magic numbers, computed by `seaopt` itself, L-am); a
    zero or negative constant unchanged; `f64` `/` by a normal power of two as a multiplication
    (L-al)**; (b) also negative constant divisors (by negation, the −2⁶³ and −1 cases kept checked;
    no workload divides by a negative constant); (c) powers of two only (W5's `% 2147483647` keeps
    its `sdiv`/`idivq`, hardware division on the dependency chain of every step). **Decided: (a)**
    (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) covers every workload use (`mod(16807*s, 2147483647)`, `mod(I + J,
    2)`, `mod(nPanel, 2)`); the sequence was checked against floored `%` and `idiv` on the edge
    dividends and 2 000 random ones for each of about 300 divisors (a scratch check while writing
    this; the `opt_*` tests of §6.2 make it permanent). Affects §5.8, LANGUAGE.md (none: §6.6 and
    §6.8 already allow it).
66. **How "meets the §5.2 shapes" is tested.** Options: (a) **two layers: hand-derived `opt5_*`
    `.lir` goldens of pass 3b (the W5 function and a small W4 loop among them), and `tests/shape.sh`
    on `-S` of the acceptance programs for both targets (instruction count bound, exact mnemonic
    counts, no frame access, no call, the number of cold branches), run on the Mac by `make test`**;
    (b) golden `-S` fragments for each target (brittle: any allocator or template change rewrites
    them, and they pin details §4.9.2 does not fix); (c) dynamic counts from performance counters or
    a simulator (not reproducible across machines, no simulator in the toolchain). **Decided: (a)**
    (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) tests the LIR exactly (it is specified exactly) and the machine code
    by its properties. Affects §6.2, §8.
67. **The corrected §5.2 targets.** Options: (a) **W5: 20 arm64 and 23 x86_64 instructions per step;
    W4: 24 arm64 and 27 x86_64 per interior point (§5.2 "Targets for phase 5"), derived from §5.8
    and §4.9.2; six `f64` loads per W4 point**; (b) keep "≈ 10" for W5 and add peepholes (arm64
    `msub`, shifted-operand `sub`, a Mersenne-specific remainder for 2³¹ − 1): about 16–18, still
    not 10, for more templates; (c) forward `T[j − 1, i]` from the previous iteration's store to
    reach five loads (needs a value carried across iterations through the `continue` path; not in
    phase 5's scope). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) states what the design produces;
    §5.5's time estimates do not change (they were made from latency, not counts). Affects §5.2,
    §6.2's shape files.
68. **The micro-benchmarks.** Options: (a) **`bench/micro/` with `lcg.sea` and `sor.sea` (the
    acceptance programs' loops verbatim, validated by `lcg_final` and `it_sor`), C references built
    `-O2 -ffp-contract=off`, `bench/micro.sh` on the Mac and the host, BENCH.md's methodology, each
    measured with the phase-4 and the phase-5 compiler; TSV committed under `bench/results/`, the
    table in §5.9**; (b) whole-program timings of `tests/accept/w4_sor.sea` and `w5_stats.sea` only
    (mixes in start-up, allocation and the other phases of W5); (c) numbers written into §5.9 only,
    no harness kept. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) isolates the two loops phase 5 is
    judged by and leaves a harness phase 10's `bench/` reuses. Affects §5.9, §8.
69. **Is `seaopt`'s output canonical?** Options: (a) **yes: §5.8 fixes the order, the conditions and
    the placement of every transformation, so `sea.lir` is derivable by hand and its dumps are
    golden tests, as for every other pass**; (b) only properties are specified (behaviour, and
    pattern checks on `.lir`), no goldens. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) follows the
    house rule that expected outputs come from the spec and catches a missed or misplaced
    transformation directly; it makes §5.8 longer and every golden slower to derive. Affects §5.8,
    §6.2.
70. **Sub-phases and gates.** Options: (a) **5a the specification; 5b pass 4's allocator and
    selection on both targets (no `seaopt` change, so the whole corpus checks it); 5c-1 `seaopt`'s
    analysis and local transformations, in parallel with 5b; 5c-2 the loop transformations; 5d the
    shape tests, the benchmarks and the size gate**; (b) one step after the specification; (c)
    `seaopt` first, the allocator last. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) proves the
    allocator against unchanged LIR before the LIR starts changing, and lets two teams work on
    disjoint files; (c) would leave the shapes unmeasurable until the end. Affects §8.
71. **`seaopt`'s size and phase 7.** Options: (a) **a gate after phase 5 records `seaopt`,
    `seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64` (§2.7); when `seaopt` + 2 000 exceeds 7 000, phase 7's
    vectorization is decided as a pass of its own at the gate after phase 6, with Decision 56's
    fusion seam**; (b) decide now that phase 7's vectorization is its own pass; (c) no gate until
    phase 7. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) decides with the measured size (the
    projection spans 4 404–5 684); (b) may create a pass that turns out unnecessary. Affects §2.7,
    §8. *Settled by Decision 74* (2026-10-24): phase 7's scalar replacement and vectorization go
    into pass 3c, `sealopt`, and the gate after phase 5 is revised (L-be, §2.7). *Revised by
    Decision 78* (2026-10-25): phase 7's scalar replacement and vectorization get a pass of their own
    after `sealopt`.
72. **Optimization against the capacity limits.** Options: (a) **a transformation whose result would
    exceed a LIR limit of the function is skipped, so optimization never causes `program too
    large`**; (b) the limit is reported as for any other pass. **Decided: (a)** (the user,
    2026-10-24); (a) keeps the compile errors a property of the program, not of the optimizer
    (versioning and unswitching can multiply a loop's size by up to eight). Affects §3.6.5, §5.8.
73. **A switch to turn the optimizations off.** Options: (a) **none: `seaopt` and the allocator
    always run; the corpus, whose expected outputs come from the spec, is the exactness test**; (b)
    a driver option (`-O0`) under which `seaopt` copies its input and pass 4 keeps the allocator,
    used by a differential test over the corpus and by the benchmarks (a change of §2.2's usage line
    and of `driver_check.sh`). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (b) adds a mode that must
    itself be tested; §5.9 gets its "before" numbers from the phase-4 compiler instead. Affects §2.2
    (only under (b)), §5.9, §6.2.
74. **Where the loop transformations live, after 5c-1** (taken at the gate arithmetic of §2.7,
    "Measured after 5b and 5c-1": `seaopt` 5 316 built lines, and T5–T9 at 770–1 270 would fail
    built + 3 000 ≤ 9 000). Options: (a) **a new pass 3c, `sealopt` (`sea.lir2` → `sea.lir`, LIR in
    and LIR out, after `seaopt` and before pass 4), holding T5, T6, T8, T7, T8, T9 and T10, with
    `seaopt`'s reader, validator, writer and T10 moved into a shared part `lirrw` that both passes
    load; `--emit lir` stays the final LIR and `--emit lir2` is new; phase 7's scalar replacement and
    vectorization go into `sealopt`**; (b) compact `seaopt` first, in a sub-phase like 4h-0 aiming
    at 700–1 000 lines, then add T5–T9 to it; (c) relax the gate for `seaopt`. This revisits
    Decision 58's option (b), which "only pays if `seaopt` cannot hold phase 7": that condition is
    now met. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); (a) gives the loop transformations and the
    vectorizer a pass sized for them (4 069–5 059 built after phase 5, 6 069–7 059 with phase 7, at
    the stress view 4 667–6 043 and 6 667–8 043, §2.7) and
    leaves `seaopt` with no further phase work; (b) costs a sub-phase and still leaves `seaopt` too
    full for phase 7; (c) gives up the stress margin the gates exist for. Affects §0, §2 (the pass
    table), §2.2, §2.6.3, §2.7, §2.10, §3.6.5, §5.8, §6.2, §8; lead decisions L-bc–L-be, L-bi–L-bk, L-bl, L-bm, L-bp.
    *Revised by Decision 78* (2026-10-25, at the gate after phase 5): phase 7's scalar replacement
    and vectorization get a pass of their own after `sealopt` instead of going into `sealopt`.
75. **Which intervals the allocator extends over a loop.** Options: (a) **only a register that may
    be live at the loop's top: read inside the loop, or after it, without a covering write earlier
    in the same iteration, or after the loop (§4.9.2, "Positions and intervals"), computed in `ralloc`'s
    reference walk with one new call, `ra_else`; landing with 5c-2, before 5d's shape targets**; (b)
    keep the first rule (every register first written inside an `if` part is extended over the
    loop) and measure again after 5c-2. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-24); under the first rule
    a temporary of an `if` part holds a register for the whole loop, which floods x86_64's 10
    general registers (W4's `j` loop about 60 % frame traffic after 5c-1, §5.2), while (a) extends
    the loop-carried values and the values defined before the loop and read in it, conservatively
    at nested loops, and costs about 90–170 lines per code generator; (b) would leave every loop with an `if` exposed to the same
    spills, which unswitching removes only for invariant conditions. Affects §0, §4.9.2, §5.2, §8;
    lead decisions L-bf, L-bg, L-bh, L-bl, L-bm, L-bo.
76. **Whether a loop's step that is a `mov` of an `li` register is a constant for pass 4** (found in
    5d by the shape tests: W4's interior `j` loop on x86_64 kept its step, `mov i342 i340` of `li
    i340 1`, in an 11th general register, spilled it and loaded it at every step, 29 instructions
    against §5.2's 27). Options: (a) **for §4.9.2's loop closing a step is a constant also when its
    only definition is a `mov` from a register whose only definition is an `li` (L-br's one level of
    `mov`), on both targets: the closing `add` takes the immediate and the step is no reference of
    the loop (`ra_open` gets no step register)**; (b) the same on x86_64 only; (c) a `sealopt` rule
    that rewrites the step operand of a `loop` record to the `li` register, which changes the `.lir`
    goldens. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-25); (a) is the reading T7 already uses (L-br), keeps
    §4.9.2 the same on both targets and frees a register in every lowered loop (arm64's text changes
    from a register step to `#1` with the same counts); (b) splits a both-target rule for no gain; (c)
    moves a code-generation question into the optimizer and changes goldens. Affects §0, §4.9.2,
    §5.2, §5.8 (T7's note), `passes/lib/API.md` (`ra_open`); L-br.
77. **Which register an x86_64 non-commuting two-address destination takes when its hint is not
    free** (found in 5d with Decision 76: W4's `fsub` of the update's change took the register of
    its dying second operand `T[j, i]`, so "x86_64 forms" computed it in `%xmm14` and moved it, one
    `movapd` more than §5.2's target). Options: (a) **on x86_64 the destination of `d = a op b` of a
    non-commuting operation, b a register operand other than a, takes, when its hint is not free,
    the first free register of its row other than b's, and b's only when no other is free; arm64
    unchanged; told to the allocator by a new call `ra_avoid`**; (b) a code-selection rule that
    computes such an instruction in place in b's register (impossible for `fsub`/`fdiv`/`isub`
    without changing the operation: a − b is not −(b − a) for equal operands, +0 against −0). **Decided:
    (a)** (the user, 2026-10-25); (a) costs nothing when another register is free and never spills
    more, since b's register is still taken when it is the only one; (b) would break LANGUAGE.md
    §6.8's exactness. Affects §0, §4.9.2 ("The scan"), §5.2, `passes/lib/API.md` (`ra_avoid`),
    `passes/lib/ralloc.bas`, `passes/seagen_x64/*`.
78. **Where phase 7's vectorizer lives, after the gate after phase 5** (taken at §2.7, "Measured
    after 5d": `sealopt` at 5 411 built lines passes the gate's three line conditions but has 0 free
    numeric array letters where the gate requires at least 2, its scratch tables having taken `S`
    and `V`, the 2 letters L-bp left it; and `sealopt` + phase 7's 2 000 is 7 411, above 7 000).
    Options: (a) **phase 7's vectorizer gets a pass of its own, a new pass 3d after `sealopt`,
    reading and writing the `sea.lir` format and sharing `seaopt`'s and `sealopt`'s reader,
    validator, writer and T10 through the shared main-program part `passes/lib/lirrw.bas` (L-bi),
    as `sealopt` does; `sealopt` stays as built**; (b) a compaction of `sealopt`'s tables with no
    change of behaviour, freeing 2 letters; (c) waive `sealopt`'s letter condition. **Decided: (a)**
    (the user, 2026-10-25); (a) takes the vectorizer's tables and lines out of `sealopt`, which
    addresses both the letter shortfall and the 7 411 > 7 000 projection, and leaves `sealopt` as
    built and tested; (b) costs a sub-phase and leaves `sealopt` + 2 000 = 7 411 > 7 000 for phase
    7; (c) the same, and gives up the headroom the letter condition keeps. Settled by phase 7's
    specification, not here: the pass's name, its input and output file names (and so which file
    is the final LIR that pass 4 reads and `--emit lir` dumps), its place in the driver's sequence
    and its `--emit` kind, its `SUB` prefix and line range, its budget at the gates (whether phase 7's scalar replacement,
    which Decision 74 put into `sealopt` together with the vectorization, stays there or joins the
    new pass was first left to it too, and is decided further below: it joins the new pass). No contract file changes with this decision
    (`include/*.inc`, `include/passes.txt`), and no code. Phase 7's specification starts from the
    room L-bp leaves a pass that loads `lirrw`: exactly 2 free numeric array letters (`S V`), the
    free columns of `R`, the scratch `W` between entries, and the unreserved string arrays and
    scalars. Affects §2 (the pass table), §2.7 (the gate after phase 5 re-applied, "Measured after
    5d"), §3.6 (the file table), §8 (rows 5d and 7), and the forward notes on Decisions 71 and 74
    and L-bp. *Decided further* (the user, 2026-10-25, after the gate was re-applied with (a): the
    gate as written still asked `sealopt` for 2 free letters, which it sets even for a pass with
    fixes only, and phase 7's scalar replacement had no home yet): options (a) **waive the letter
    condition for `sealopt`, and move phase 7's scalar replacement to the new pass 3d too, so
    `sealopt` receives fixes only**; (b) waive the condition, scalar replacement stays in
    `sealopt`; (c) keep the condition and compact `sealopt` to free 2 letters. **Decided: (a)**;
    `sealopt` then takes no new tables, so its letters guard nothing, and phase 7's LIR work
    (scalar replacement and vectorization) is specified and sized together in one pass; (b) would
    put new tables into a pass with 0 free letters; (c) costs a sub-phase for letters that only
    fixes would use. With it the gate after phase 5 passes all four programs (§2.7, "The gate after
    phase 5 with Decision 78's relief"), and phase 5 is complete (§8).
79. **What is an alpha, and what is GA.** Options: (a) an alpha release after phase 6 (W1 and W5
    end to end) plus release work (license, README, release notes, a version suffix, tags); (b)
    an alpha after phase 8; (c) **version-based: every Sea version 0.y.z is an alpha, and 1.0.0
    is GA, given when v1 is done (§1.2: all five workloads, phase 10); no git tag or release
    procedure is required**. **Decided: (c)** (the user, 2026-10-25); (c) needs no milestone or
    release step of its own, and the driver's `sea 0.1.0` (§2.2) already denotes an alpha; (a)
    and (b) add a release step and a version suffix to maintain. Affects §1.2 (one sentence); no
    row of §8, no contract file, no code.

80. **What phase 6's ports contain, given that figures are phase 9**
    (§2.11.8; W1 and W5 as MATLAB scripts and Appendix D draw figures, which need phase 9's plotting
    names, still reported by the phase rule). Options: (a) **the ports leave out every figure
    statement and the `--figures` option, and accept only `--export-reference`; phase 9 adds the
    figure code to the same files**; (b) the full text with the figure code, compiled only after a
    marker-stripping step in `tests/accept.sh`; (c) no ports in phase 6: smaller `printf`-and-JSON
    programs that reproduce the reference keys. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); it is what row 6's "without
    figures" says, keeps the ports ordinary Sea programs that the compiler builds as written, and the
    figures are additive in phase 9 (a new arm of the option loop and a block of plotting calls); (b)
    puts a preprocessor that Sea does not have into the test harness, and the stripped text is not
    the file that is compiled; (c) gives up the workload test that is phase 6's purpose. Affects
    §2.11.8, §6.3, §8 (rows 6, 6e).
81. **Where the checks of elemental functions and the §8.6 inlining
    class are made, and how the class reaches pass 3a** (§2.11.2, §2.11.3). Options: (a) **`seaname`
    makes one whole-program call pre-pass after resolving the bodies: effects (fixpoint), call-graph
    cycles, 228 and 232 through `rerr`, and the §8.6 class of every `fn` item on the source, written
    as `rfn`'s `el` 2 and carried by `seacheck` as the HIR `fn` kind `inl` (`enum fkind` gains `inl`;
    no record format changes)**; (b) all of it in `seacheck`, which holds the types; (c) `seacheck`
    reports 228/232, and `sealoop` recomputes the inlining class on `sea.hir`. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26);
    the class is defined on the source as written (call sites, statements, loops) and on names, which
    are `seaname`'s; the pre-pass is the first check at a `call` node, so moving 228 and 232 keeps the
    rule "Order across the two programs" (§2.6.2); `seaname` has the room (projection 5 611–5 921,
    §2.7) and `seacheck` does not (Decision 82); (b) adds 250–400 lines to the pass that is already
    over its cap at the upper end of its projection; (c) counts on rewritten HIR (defaults copied, pass
    2b's instances), where the counts of §8.6 differ from the source's, and puts a whole-program
    analysis into the pass with the most erratic estimates. Affects §2.11.2, §2.11.3, §3.4.1 and §3.5.4
    (contract change 2 of §2.11.1).
82. **Room in `seacheck` for phase 6** (§2.7, "Projected for phase 6":
    6 426 + 455–870 = 6 881–7 296, above 7 000 built lines at the upper end; its earlier increments
    landed inside their estimates; revised after the review found that `sealower`'s 4h-0 patterns
    do not carry over). The compaction available is smaller than first written: `seacheck` is in the
    `SUB`/`CALL` style (124 `SUB`s, 709 `CALL`s, 9 `GOSUB`s, no `DEF`), so C1, C4 and C6 (`GOSUB`
    fall-through and tail calls, multi-line `DEF` text helpers, one shared `GOSUB` child loop) have
    nothing to act on; C2 (merging consecutive `REM` lines, measured on its own code) saves at most
    219, C3 and C5 0–80: 150–300 in all, which leaves the projection after phase 6 at 6 581–7 146,
    so its upper end still above 7 000. Options: (a)
    **gate `seacheck` as Decision 50 gates `sealower`: its 7 000 condition is replaced by built +
    850 ≤ 9 000 and built + 1 275 ≤ 9 000 (passed at every end: 8 146 and 8 571), with at least 2
    free letters; no sub-step before 6b; the compaction (C2, C3, C5; 150–300) is the reserve that
    the measurement after 6c calls for if built + 120 + 1 275 > 9 000 there**; (b) the compaction
    first, as sub-step 6b-0 (150–300), and keep the 7 000 condition, accepting that the upper end
    still fails it and would need (a) or (c) at the gate; (c) split `seacheck` now: the library-call
    checks (overload tables and typing of §10's functions) into a new pass between 2a and 2b, a new
    intermediate format and driver step; (d) move the named-argument matching (224, 225, 226 of
    user and prelude functions) into `seaname`, which knows the signatures, saving 100–150 lines of
    `seacheck` but leaving `seacheck` to repeat the mapping to write `sea.hir1`. **Decided: (a)**
    (the user, 2026-10-26); `seacheck`'s remaining work after phase 6 is the smallest of the front end (850), so the
    7 000 condition, which exists to keep room for later phases, protects little here, while the
    9 000 conditions, which do, pass at every end; Decision 50 set the precedent for `sealower`
    after it had compacted; it costs no sub-phase and keeps the compaction in reserve; (b) spends a
    sub-phase for a saving that does not reach the condition it is for; (c) is the right shape only
    if phases 8–9 grow `seacheck` well past their 850, which the gate after phase 8 can still decide;
    (d) duplicates the matching across two programs. Affects §2.7, §8 (rows 6b-0, 6b), the gate
    after phase 6.
83. **What §8.6 inlining of the program's own functions covers in
    pass 3a** (L18 inlines the prelude, whose functions have scalar or array parameters and results
    and no `ref` parameter). Options: (a) **all of it: `ref` parameters (R31: the argument's address
    bound to a ref local, lowered exactly as a call's), aggregate results (R32: a caller-provided
    home, as a call's hidden result address), and `return` of a multiple-result call (`tret` → `tbind`
    of `.i` locals and `iret`), so every function §8.6 names is inlined**; (b) amend LANGUAGE.md §8.6
    so that a function with a `ref` parameter is not inlined; (c) exempt all three cases from §8.6.
    **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); §8.6 is normative, and W1's `make_params` (three call sites, but no loop,
    not recursive and about 15 statements, so class (c)) returns a struct, and W1's `shaft_safety`
    (elemental) returns a tuple; R31 and R32 reuse the lowering of calls and homes that phase 4
    tests, so the semantics of an inlined call are those of the call by construction; (b) and (c)
    change the language to fit the implementation and leave `make_params`'s struct result to a call,
    which the workload could live with but the rule does not allow. Affects §2.11.4 (L20), §2.11.5
    (R31, R32), §3.6.6.
84. **How an elemental call with array arguments is lowered** (§3.5.7
    step 3 writes `inst` and `emap`). Options: (a) **`sealoop` rewrite L19: arguments once, rule 22's
    broadcast extents, checks and loop nest, one `anew` per kept result (a result bound to `_` or
    `skip`, or under `eval`, is not allocated), an inlined per-element call, `est` of each kept
    result, L11's statement forms for k ≥ 2**; (b) as (a), but every result allocated; (c) pass 2b
    writes the loops in HIR as it does for `write_json`. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); rule 22 already owns
    broadcasting, its checks and its order, so an elemental application has the shapes, sites and
    error order of an elemental library call; skipping discarded results saves W1's grids work and
    memory and changes no output (an error in the body is still raised at the first failing
    element); (b) is simpler by about 40 lines but allocates arrays nobody reads, which the heap
    check would still pass; (c) duplicates rule 22's broadcasting in pass 2b, a second
    implementation of the shape rules that must agree with the first. Affects §2.11.4.
85. **The runtime interface of phase 6's output** (§2.11.6). Options:
    (a) **sixteen entries, ids 23–38: `FORMAT`, `PRINT`, `MAKE_DIR`, `FMOD`, and twelve JSON entries
    (open, close, object, array, end, key, four scalars, vector, matrix), all lowered by rule 39's
    table**; (b) one `sea_json` entry with an operation code as its first argument; (c) the emitter
    written as LIR by `sealower` around a small byte-writing entry. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); each entry
    has one fixed signature, so the entry table types its calls and rule 39 stays a table lookup
    (Decision 52); (b) needs a variadic argument class the entry table cannot describe; (c) moves the
    `%.17g` formatting and escaping into generated code on both targets and grows `sealower`, which
    has the least room. Affects §2.11.6, `rt.inc` (WP-CONTRACT), §4.8.
86. **How the ports are accepted** (§6.3). Options: (a) **a new
    `tests/accept.sh` for `sea/ports/`, beside `tests/accept4.sh`, which stays: `compare.py
    --candidate` and `compare_report.py` with the token maps on the Mac; on the Linux host byte
    identity of the report (minus the `Compute time` line) and of the JSON against the Mac's**; (b)
    merge both into one script with two modes; (c) run `compare.py` and `compare_report.py` on the
    host too. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); the phase-4 programs keep their own keys and the shape tests use
    them, and a separate script keeps phase 4's tests untouched; byte identity on the host is a
    stronger check than the comparators and needs no Python or NumPy there; (b) mixes two contracts
    in one file for no gain; (c) adds a NumPy dependency to the host for a check byte identity already
    implies. Affects §6.3, §8 (row 6e).
87. **How phase 6 is built** (§8). Options: (a) **the sub-phases 6a
    (specification), 6b (calls and output with WP-CONTRACT first, then WP-NAME, WP-CHECK, WP-LOOP,
    WP-LOWER and T2's re-derived goldens integrated together), 6c (elemental, then the measurement after 6c), 6d
    (`write_json`), 6e (ports, acceptance, gate), each with work packages that own disjoint files;
    6b-0 (the `seacheck` compaction) only as Decision 82 (a)'s reserve requires (the measurement
    after 6c)**; (b) one build
    after 6a with every package in parallel; (c) one sub-phase per pass. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); each
    sub-phase ends with a passing `make test` and `make cross` and removes its own phase-rule rows;
    6b's entries and fkind change come first so that 6c and 6d only use them; 6c is followed by the
    measurement of `sealoop` and `seacheck` before 6d adds to them; (b) puts five packages into the
    same passes at once, which the file-ownership rule forbids; (c) splits each feature across
    sub-phases, so no sub-phase tests a feature end to end. Affects §8.
88. **The gate after phase 6 and where phase 7's fusion goes**
    (§2.7: `sealoop` 6 319–6 839 after phase 6, and 7 819–8 339 with phase 7's fusion estimate of
    1 500, up to 9 089 under stress; its increments have missed their upper ends by up to 52 %).
    Options: (a) **write the gate's conditions now in Decision 71's form (each program ≤ 7 000 built
    lines after phase 6 except `sealower` and `seacheck`, Decisions 50 and 82, ≤ 9 000 with its
    remaining phases' estimates and with them × 1.5, 2 free numeric array letters except where
    waived); if `sealoop` fails the stress condition, the letter condition or both, and nothing
    else, phase 7's fusion gets a pass of its own ahead of `sealoop`, and that pass also takes L19:
    it reads `sea.hir`, where an elemental application is still an `emap`, and LANGUAGE.md §8.5
    requires elemental applications to fuse with the element-wise expression around them, so the
    pass treats an `emap` as a k-result element-wise operator, writes the fused broadcast nest with
    the per-element call, and leaves only that call to `sealoop`'s L20 (`sealoop` loses L19's
    180–350 lines in phase 7 and is gated with 1 000 of fixes); the measurement after 6c may bring
    this decision forward when `sealoop`'s measured 6b + 6c increment exceeds 1.5 times its estimate
    (a projection after 6d above 7 000 is relieved by a compaction instead, since the seam takes L19
    out of `sealoop` only in phase 7; wording clarified after the final review)**; (b) decide now that fusion is a new pass (with L19);
    (c) leave the question to phase 7's specification. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); `sealoop`'s
    projections have been the least reliable of all passes (4f 271 against 600–900, 4g-2 774
    against 315–510), so the decision is better taken on a measurement, and writing the condition
    and its consequence for L19 now means neither the gate nor the measurement needs a new question;
    (b) adds a pass and moves L19 before the numbers say it is needed; (c) leaves phase 6 closing
    without a rule for its largest risk, and phase 7 would then find L19 on the wrong side of the
    seam. Affects §2.7, §8 (rows 6c, 6e).
89. **What `make_dir` does when the directory or its parents exist or
    are missing** (LANGUAGE.md §10.10 said only that it creates a directory). Options: (a) **one
    level, as POSIX `mkdir(path, 0777)` under the umask; on any failure the errno is saved and the
    path is tested for a directory by `open(path, O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY)` (closed at once): a
    directory is not an error (so `/` and `.` succeed alike on macOS, where `mkdir("/")` gives
    `EISDIR`, and Linux, `EEXIST`); otherwise `cannot create directory '<path>': <saved errno
    text>` (an existing file `File exists`, a missing parent `No such file or directory`); no parent
    is created**; (b) create missing parents, as `mkdir -p`. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); the workloads
    create one output directory next to the program; the errors are the existing `CANNOT_MKDIR`
    message with the errno; testing with `open` rather than `stat` avoids the targets' different
    `struct stat` layouts and glibc's versioned `stat` symbols, and testing after any failure rather
    than only after `EEXIST` makes both targets agree; (b) needs a loop over path components with
    its own error rules (which component failed, races between them) that no workload needs.
    Affects LANGUAGE.md §10.10 (one sentence), §2.11.6 (`MAKE_DIR`).
90. **The existing dump tests that §8.6 inlining changes** (§6.2; the
    review found 21 lowering dump tests whose function §8.6 (b) or (c) covers, and about 70 `.res`
    and 51 `.hir1` goldens that `el` 2 and the kind `inl` may change). Options: (a) **re-derive every
    affected golden by hand from the rules; in the 12 tests whose subject is a call boundary (a
    §3.6.6 rule's verbatim example written inside a function, a `ref` parameter root, a
    multiple-result call bound by L12, calls inside a selection) make the function non-inlinable
    with a second call site at the end of `.main` and a `while false` loop with an empty body as its
    first statement, so the test keeps its subject; in the other 9 let the function be inlined and
    re-derive with L20's form; integrate T2's goldens with WP-NAME, WP-CHECK, WP-LOOP and WP-LOWER in
    one step (wording corrected after the final review)**; (b) a
    test-only driver option `--no-inline` (with `el` 0 and kind `fn` written) that the existing dump
    tests use through a `.meta` line, so their goldens stay as they are; (c) re-derive all of them
    with inlining, including the call-boundary tests. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); the tests keep testing
    what their `tests/CORPUS.md` row says, on the configuration users run; the work is mechanical
    (the class is decided on the source by §2.11.3's rules); (b) is the least work but adds a CLI
    option, a pass flag and a harness attribute to maintain, and tests a configuration no program
    is built with; (c) loses the coverage of call lowering that those 12 tests give (the verbatim
    examples of rules 15, 18, 23, 24, 29, 32 and 33 would no longer match their rule's text).
    Affects §3.6.6, §6.2, §8 (row 6b), L-ct.
91. **Where a parameter default's value is checked** (§2.11.2; the
    review found that the first text, which put every default check into `seaname`, needs what
    only `seacheck` has: the types of the default's expression (201 against the parameter's type)
    and the reporting of constant outcomes; `seaname` evaluates the `const` items into `rcn…`
    records, but `sea.res` carries no outcome for a default, and the errors of constants are
    `seacheck`'s, Decision 25; wording corrected after the final review, the decision unchanged). Options: (a) **`seaname` keeps
    the structural checks of the signature step (236, 227 at a `ref` parameter's default, the names
    resolved like a `const` value's); `seacheck` checks each default's value where it checks the
    `const` items (237, 201, 260, 261, a constant's outcome used as Decision 25 says), each error
    competing in source order as every other (§2.6.2)**; (b) all in `seaname`, which would then
    need the expression types and its own reporting of 201, 237, 260 and 261 (duplicating
    `seacheck`'s typing); (c) all in
    `seaname`, with defaults restricted to literals and constant names checked only for their
    type. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); the value check is the `const` check whose
    typing and reporting live in `seacheck` (which evaluates a default's `i64` operations itself,
    as for a `dim:` value), and
    the source-order rule already orders a default's error against a constant's (a default's error
    on line 50 loses to a constant's on line 1); it moves 40–80 lines from `seaname` to `seacheck`
    (counted in §2.7, and within Decision 82 (a)'s conditions); (b) duplicates the typing; (c)
    narrows LANGUAGE.md §8.1's "a constant default". Affects §2.11.2, §2.7, L-bx.
92. **An elemental function without results** (LANGUAGE.md §8.5
    required results "one result or a tuple" without saying whether none is allowed; L19 was
    written for k ≥ 1). Options: (a) **allowed: called with scalars it is an ordinary call
    statement; called with arrays it is applied at every element position for its errors only (it
    has no effects), with L19's k = 0 form (no result allocated, the inlined call as a statement)**;
    (b) forbidden: 253 at the `fn` item (the text `elemental function result must be f64, i64 or
    bool` then also covers "no result"). **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); it is the regular case of the rule
    (k results, k = 0), costs a few lines in L19, and makes an elemental validation routine
    (`check_ranges(x)` that calls `error` on a bad element) possible; (b) is simpler by those few
    lines but forbids a well-defined program for no semantic reason. Affects LANGUAGE.md §8.5 (one
    sentence), §2.11.2, §2.11.4 (L19).
93. **A named argument for a `ref` parameter** (Appendix A's `arg`
    does not let `name: ref x` parse, so a `ref` parameter cannot be given by name at all; the
    first text gave 254, `argument for ref parameter '%s' must be marked ref`, whose advice cannot
    be followed). Options: (a) **keep the grammar: a `ref` parameter is given positionally only,
    LANGUAGE.md §8.1 says so, and `name: x` for a `ref` parameter is 254 at x (the message names the
    parameter; the sentence in §8.1 explains it)**; (b) extend Appendix A so that `name: ref x`
    parses (pass 1, about 20–40 lines, and 115's start set), making named `ref` arguments legal;
    (c) report a named `ref` argument as 224 `unknown parameter`. **Decided: (a)** (the user, 2026-10-26); no workload
    passes a `ref` argument by name, the grammar has been fixed since phase 1 (`seaparse` has no
    other phase-6 change), and 254 at least names the parameter; (b) is a clean extension that can
    come later without breaking a program; (c) is wrong (the parameter exists). Affects LANGUAGE.md
    §8.1 (one sentence), §2.11.2, L-bw.

**Lead decisions of phase 5** (2026-10-24, within Decisions 58–73, each taken because one answer is
clearly right, reported to the user and agreed with the phase-5 text; each is written into its
normative section): L-ac,
`seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64` use all 26 numeric array letters, so the allocator adds none: its
per-register state widens the code generator's `D` and the module keeps small SUB-local arrays
(§2.7, §4.9.2); L-ad, `seaopt` keeps its facts in the six phase-5 columns of `R`, widened to
`R(99999,9)`, and takes one new letter, `W`, leaving `S` and `V` (§2.7); L-ae, §3.6.4 states the
four properties of `sea.lir1` that phase 5 relies on (headers never stored to, definite assignment,
`ref` memory reached only through the parameter, slots only through their `sa` registers); L-af,
`ref` parameters and private slots are unaliased within a function, which follows from LANGUAGE.md
§7.2 (no global variables) and §8.3 (no shared roots) with rule 31's copy on write (§5.8); L-ag, a
value kept in a register need not be stored back on a path that ends in a run-time error, because
the process ends and releases nothing (LANGUAGE.md §9.2, §4.2; §5.8); L-ah, the x86_64 forms of
§4.9.2 (two-address rules, `leaq` for an add of an immediate, `imulq $v`, `xorpd` before `cvtsi2sdq`,
`andpd`/`xorpd` for `fabs`/`fneg`); L-ai, the loop-closing sequences of §4.9.2; L-aj, only loads
without an index are hoisted, since an indexed load is valid only after its check (§5.8 T8);
L-ak, the `.lir` goldens a transformation changes (not `gen_arith`, a hand-written pass-4 test, L-bj) are re-derived from §5.8,
as L-i did for 4g-1 (§3.6.5); L-al, `f64` division by a normal power of two only (−1022 ≤ e ≤ 1023;
for e = 1023 the reciprocal is the exact subnormal 2⁻¹⁰²³), never `%` on `f64` (§5.8 T2); L-am,
`seaopt` computes the magic numbers with its own 128-by-64-bit division on 16-bit limbs instead of
loading `limb` (801 lines, of which it needs none) (§2.7, §5.8).

**Lead decisions of phase 5 after the review of its text** (2026-10-24; an independent review of
the agreed text found defects that the text could not leave open; none changes a user decision, and
each is written into its normative section): L-an, pass 4's templates (§4.9.2): every LIR
instruction is *direct* (allocated registers in place, with the multi-instruction forms written so
that a destination may share an operand's register: arm64 `imulc` computes the high half first, the
x86_64 `isel`/`psel`/`fsel` forms depend on whether d is a or b, `imulh` and variable shifts go
through `%rax`/`%rdx` and `%rcx`, addresses are formed in `x16` or `%r11`, `retain`/`release`
count in `x16` or `%rcx`) or *staged* (`idivf imodf rcount ftoi fmin fmax ffloor fceil ftrunc fround
mcopy`: §4.9's and §4.9.1's sequences on the scratch registers, renamed, with operands moved in and
results out; arm64 `mcopy`'s data through `d29`; x86_64 `ffloor`/`fceil`/`fround` adjusting t as an
integer instead of using `%xmm10`), and every parallel move is emitted in three steps (memory
destinations, then register moves with cycles broken through `x17`/`d31`, `%r11`/`%xmm15`, then
memory and immediate sources straight into their destinations); L-ao (split by L-be: T1–T4 and T10 in `seaopt`, the rest in `sealopt`), `seaopt` runs T8 before T7
and again after it (T1–T6, T8, T7, T8, T9, T10), because T7 needs invariant bases and index terms
that only T8 moves out of the loop (§5.8); L-ap, T1's facts are a state that the walk carries and
joins: the symbol bounds L, U and every narrowing hold only in the part or loop that made them (a
guard's facts end at its `endif`, a loop's at its closing record, which restores the loop's entry
state with what the loop writes unknown), a symbol other than a constant has the interval [s, s]
with what its definition computes in L(s), U(s), the bounds rows ≥ 0 hold from the `rcall` that
creates the array, a dominating comparison of a symbol with a constant narrows its L(s) or U(s) in
that part, and a narrowing between incomparable bounds keeps the old bound (§5.8); L-aq, a
loop whose hidden count register would be numbered above `SEA_LIM_LIR_REGS` keeps its count in a
spill slot, so pass 4 never fails on the register limit (§4.9.2, as Decision 72 does for `seaopt`);
L-ar, a shape test identifies its loop by its properties: the line passes when one of the named
function's innermost loops, found from `--emit lir`, meets all of them, so no block number is
derived by hand (§6.2); L-as, the condition codes of fused comparisons, whose inverses hold for
unordered operands on both targets, and x86_64 `fcmp eq`/`ne` as two branches (`jp` with `jne` or
`je`) and never fused into a selection (§4.9.2); L-at, an anticipated load is hoisted only through
an object pointer (a parameter, a `call`/`rcall` result, an `ldp`, an `sa`, or a `mov` of one), which
is non-null and points to a live object wherever it is read, so running it before a failing
instruction of the loop reads valid memory (§5.8 T8).

**Lead decisions of phase 5 during its build** (2026-10-24; questions the 5b and 5c-1 work
packages raised that implementers and golden writers must answer alike; none changes a user
decision, and each is written into its normative section): L-au, T1 compares two different symbols
through their bounds, s + k ≤ t + m when U(s) + k ≤ L(t) + m, and F2 gives a symbol extent its L, U
from rows(A) or cols(A), so `chkb k E` with symbols is proven when L(k) ≥ 0 and U(k) < L(E) (§5.8);
L-av, the readings of T1–T3 made normative because `seaopt`'s output is canonical (Decision 69): F4
changes neither a symbol's interval nor its L, U; T2 writes `li S s` also when s = 0, and T10 deletes
it; T3's first two rules use the nearest earlier qualifying instruction; `isub r c b` with only the
minuend constant makes r unknown; with two non-constant operands T1's overflow test uses the constant
bounds L and U give; the comparisons at a join use the joined L, U (§5.8); L-aw, `stage.sh` skips the
pair `sealower hirl lir1` when `NAME.hirl` is absent and `NAME.lir` exists, so the `opt5_*` tests are
`.sea`, `.lir1` and `.lir` only, `run.sh` still checking `--emit lir1` (§6.2); L-ax, `layout` takes
the lines 86 000 – 86 999 and `ralloc` 87 000 – 88 999, `ralloc` after `layout` in the canonical
order and in the build lists of `seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64` (§2.6.3); L-ay, after a `loop` ends
normally its `ind` holds start + last · step (§3.6.4); L-az, the allocator's readings of §4.9.2: a
loop covers 2o + 1 … 2c + 1 with the opening record's references outside and the closing record's
inside, the closing sequence's references at `endloop`, a call result whose extended interval starts
before its call neither saved nor reloaded around it, the closing form chosen by whether `ind` is
referenced after `endloop`, spill slots numbered by first use (ties by register, L-aq's last by
block), the hidden count numbered before the hidden step, and a `ret`'s results beyond the registers
stored to the caller's results area through its saved address before any register destination of
the `ret` is written (arm64 through `x16` in step 1 of the move, x86_64 through `%r11` and `%rax`
before the move); L-ba, a pseudo-symbol ⟨A, rows⟩ or ⟨A, cols⟩ comes only from a
dynamic-array parameter (one that rule 18 indexes: a `chkb` on its header extent and an indexed
access through its data address) and only for those two header fields; a struct, record or
fixed-size array parameter never gives one, since a field at the same offset would otherwise get the
bound `SEA_LIM_EXTENT` and lose an overflow check (§5.8 Terms); L-bb, the readings of `seaopt`'s
work package listed under "Readings fixed during the build" at the end of §5.8, normative because

targets as §4.9.2 lists them, which costs arm64 two moves around each (the operand into `d29`, the
result out of it) and is allowed as written; with Decisions 74 and 75: L-bc, pass 3c is named
`sealopt` (a loop optimizer, distinct from pass 3a's `sealoop`), its `SUB`s prefixed `lo_`, its own
files `passes/sealopt/*.bas` in lines 100 – 59 999, its `build.list` `lib io diag tables lirrw` and
`data errors exits consts entries records`, its output `sea.lir`, its input `sea.lir2` written by

`passes/lib/lirrw.bas` holds `seaopt`'s LIR reader, validator and writer and T10, moved out
unchanged and proved neutral (its form fixed by L-bi), in lines 69 000 – 81 999; the canonical order

and T10, `sealopt` runs T5, T6, T8, T7, T8, T9 and T10, both outputs canonical and golden (`.lir2`,

75's simplification, part of its rule: a write inside a nested loop never covers a read after that

creates a selection that reads its own destination only when that register has a write on every

step as L-bn, its golden changes re-derived by T2 (§5.8 T4, §8); during T2's 5c-2 golden
derivation: L-br, for a loop's start and step only, T7's "constant" is an `li` register or a `mov`
from one, since T3 leaves the lowering's step in that form and the Terms' strict definition would

`mov A V` that T3 makes of it by forwarding an earlier load, counts as part of the cow, without which
no memory-form cow could be versioned; the exactness argument holds, the `mov` copying one member of

of c₂ after the first split, so no identical copies are made; W4 still gets four copies (§5.8 T9);
and two notes: `opt5_promote_exit` covers only the exits Sea can write (an `exit` or `next` of an
enclosing loop from a nested one arises only through inlining), and Decision 72's skips are
covered by review, not by a golden (§6.2); during WP-LOPT's build: L-bu, the label rules "numbered
by first reference" and "every defined label is referenced" hold for `sea.lir1` only, since T10 may
delete `la` instructions while pass 3b keeps every label and data record; `sea.lir2` and `sea.lir`
keep every other label rule, `lirrw`'s reader applies the two only to `sea.lir1`, and `seaval`'s
`lir2` omits them as its `lir` already did; pass 4 already accepted such files (§3.6.2, §3.6.5,
§2.10); after independent reviews of the 5c-2 working tree: L-bv, (1) T5's destination rewriting
of `mov X V` also requires that no instruction strictly between the `mov` and the last read of V in
record order writes X (the last read may itself write X), since otherwise a read of V rewritten to
X sees a later store into the promoted location (`s = a + b; let t = s; s = 0; w += t` printed 0
for `w`); a region holds no block record, so a read of V in a nested part or loop is outside it and
blocks the rewriting; (2) T7's accesses share one Q and Δ only with equal D, k, c, σ, t and scale z,
since both depend on z; (3) a pass's own scratch tables (`seaopt`'s, `sealopt`'s `S()`, `V()` and
its columns of `R`) are bounded by their regions, and a transformation whose table would overflow
is not applied to that loop or function, extending Decision 72 from LIR limits to the pass's tables
so that no input can crash a pass or make tables overlap; (4) T8's object pointer excludes a data
pointer (an `ldp` of `SEA_ARR_DATA`): its buffer may hold no element, so no field offset is known to
lie inside it; no `.lir2` golden holds an index-free load through a data pointer, so no
optimization a golden shows is lost; (5) the array registers are the greatest fixpoint of their
recursive definition, so a loop-carried `mov` cycle of candidates stays in the set, as the code
computes; (6) `SEA_LIM_LIR_LABELS` is the user error `TOO_LARGE` only on `sea.lir1` input: in
`sea.lir2` or `sea.lir` a label number above it, defined or referenced, is a malformed record
(`BAD_RECORD`), and L-bd's "`sea.lir2` holds exactly what `sea.lir1` may hold" reads "except the
two `sea.lir1`-only label rules"; (7) `lirrw`'s API states that entry 69440 overwrites `I(n,0)`
and `R(r,2)` and that the reader's data-record scalars (`Z8` among them) are never written by the
pass, and the reserved scalars are 173 (149 numeric, 24 string) with `H5` and `V8`; (8) `ra_else`
requires B to be the innermost open block, of kind `if`/`ifz`, with its first part current, and
reports any other call through `dg_bug` before changing anything (so `ralloc` needs `diag`, which
both code generators load, and names itself `ralloc` in the message); (9) T5's destination rewriting
also requires that every read of V lies after V's definition in record order (the read at the
definition itself, which reads the old value, counts as before it), since a read before it sees a
value the definition does not produce and would be rewritten to read X before the new definition
writes it; and the bounds of the pass's tables are tested for the rows of `C` and `G` (the capacity
test of a transformation also requires that the rows it may add fit) and for the nesting stack of
`ANC` (a `loop` record counts against it too) (§3.6.2, §3.6.5, §5.8 Terms, T5, T7, T8, §2.6.3;
`passes/lib/API.md`).

**Readings fixed by the 5c-2 build** (where the specification was silent; recorded by the implementers
and kept by the lead, after L-bv; normative for the goldens).

*WP-LOPT* (`sealopt`):

* L-br counts one level of `mov` only: a start or step that is an `li` register, or a `mov` from one;
  a `mov` of a `mov` is not constant.
* T7's folded start term must lie within ±2⁵². T7 does not reduce when Q = D.
* A missing `ldi` means no copy-on-write (no cow is recognized without it).
* T5 skips dead records. Offsets outside ±2⁵² are unknown.
* L-bm renames with the final duplicate map (the one complete after the copier has finished).
* Decision 72 is applied with upper bounds and the pass's internal buffer limits: a transformation
  whose bound or buffer could be exceeded is not applied.
* L-bv fix (3), the T9 `PLACE` scratch table: when it overflows, the split is kept and only the
  placement is dropped; the output equals that of a `PLACE` that placed nothing, and is still correct.
* `V8` is a contract scalar (`passes/lib/API.md`), reserved by `lirrw`.

*WP-PIPE*: "the loop" of the `ra5_live` frame-access check is read as every innermost loop.

*WP-RA2*: a register read before any write counts as written at record 0.

**Lead decisions of phase 6** (written 2026-10-25 with the text of §2.11 and agreed by the user
together with Decisions 80–93 on 2026-10-26; each is a reading where
LANGUAGE.md or the earlier rules leave a choice, written into its normative section):

* **L-bw** A `ref` parameter with a default is 227 at the default expression (§2.6.2's `at` table
  says so for the `ref` position); a named argument for a `ref` parameter is 254 at its value
  (`name: ref x` does not parse, so a `ref` parameter is given positionally only, Decision 93).
  LANGUAGE.md §8.1 gains the sentence (§2.11.2).
* **L-bx** Per Decision 91: `seaname` makes a default's structural checks (236, 227, its names) in
  the signature step; `seacheck` checks its value with the `const` items, as the value of a `const`
  item annotated with the parameter's type (237, 201, 260, 261 at the nodes the `const` rules name,
  a named constant's outcome per Decision 25), in source order with every other error; a correct
  default is copied into each call that omits it with its own positions (§2.11.2).
* **L-by** A library function other than a prelude function accepts only its option names as named
  arguments; any other name is 224 at the `narg` (the promise of "Readings fixed by 4f") (§2.11.2).
* **L-bz** JSON layout: two-space indentation per depth, `"key": value`, `,` after every member or
  element but the last, `{}` and `[]` for empty containers, a matrix as an array of rows, a matrix
  with no element `[]`, one LF after the top value; escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, and every other
  byte below 0x20 as `\u00` with two lowercase hex digits; 0x7F and bytes 0x80–0xFF verbatim;
  `-0` written as `-0` (`%.17g`). LANGUAGE.md §11.4 gains the sentence (§2.11.6).
* **L-ca** A run-time error while a JSON file is open: `_sea_err` flushes and closes it, ignoring a
  failure of that flush, then reports the original error; an emitter's own failed flush or close is
  `CANNOT_WRITE` with the path and the errno. `JSON_OPEN` allocates the emitter's state (descriptor
  −1) before it opens the file, and `_sea_err` acts only when the descriptor is set (§2.11.6).
* **L-cb** `make_dir`'s details are Decision 89's: the path copied into a NUL-terminated buffer
  (freed on every exit; a NUL byte in the path is `EINVAL`), `mkdir(buf, 0777)` under the umask, on
  any failure the errno saved and the directory test by `open(buf, O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY)`, no
  `stat` (§2.11.6).
* **L-cc** A `format` result longer than `SEA_LIM_STR_BYTES`, like a failed allocation, is
  `out of memory` (no new error code); LANGUAGE.md §9.2's out-of-memory row names `format` (§2.11.6).
* **L-cd** `print` has its own entry `PRINT` writing into the standard-output buffer that `printf`
  uses, so the two interleave in program order and fail alike (§2.11.6).
* **L-ce** Pass 2b's step 4 writes `jvec (dyn e)` / `jmat (dyn e)` for a fixed-size value, so the
  emitter's entries take heap arrays only (§2.11.3).
* **L-cf** Inlined code of the program's own functions keeps its own positions (§3.6.4 "Sites");
  the `xblk`, its `tmp`s, the `iblk` and the `loc` records of the `.i` locals take the call's P
  (§2.11.4).
* **L-cg** After L19 and L20, `sealoop` drops the prelude, `elem` and `inl` functions and renumbers
  the rest densely (L-v extended); `sea.hirl` holds no `inst`, `emap` or kind `elem`/`inl`
  (§2.11.4).
* **L-ch** §8.6 (b) counts `call` nodes on the source over every function of the program's file,
  reachable from `.main` or not, including the function's own body; each call written counts once,
  however often it runs (inside a loop, or in an elemental function's body applied to an array);
  LANGUAGE.md §8.6 states it, since the guarantee is the programmer's to check (§2.11.3).
* **L-ci** §8.6 (c)'s statement count is one per Appendix A `statement`: an `if … else if … else`
  chain counts 1, a bare block statement counts 1, every other statement 1, and the statements
  inside every block (bodies, branches, arms, bare blocks) count; LANGUAGE.md §8.6 states it
  (§2.11.3).
* **L-cj** "Recursive" is membership in a cycle of the call graph of every `call` node of the
  stream (direct or mutual) (§2.11.3).
* **L-ck** An elemental application evaluates every argument once, in full, before any element;
  elements run in increasing linear (column-major) order, so an error in the body is raised at the
  first failing element with the callee's line (§2.11.4).
* **L-cl** `ind2sub` with an array `r` is a two-result elemental application of rule 36's scalar
  sequence by L19, every check at the call's site; L11 keeps the scalar case (§2.11.4).
* **L-cm** `FMOD`: b = ±0 returns a's bits; an infinite a or a NaN operand returns
  `#7FF8000000000000`; otherwise r = the C library's `fmod(a, b)` (exact by IEEE 754, the same bits
  on both C libraries), adjusted once by + b when r ≠ 0 and r and b differ in sign; not folded by any
  pass. The test vectors are computed with `math.fmod` and the adjustment, never Python's `%`, and
  committed as `tests/vectors/fmod6.vec` for the runtime tests (§2.11.6, §6.2).
* **L-cn** On the Linux host a port's standard output is compared with the Mac's byte for byte
  after removing, on both sides, the lines matching `^Compute time: .* s$`; its JSON byte for byte;
  the filter is a new case attribute `filter=compute-time` of `cross_pack.sh` and `cross_run.sh`,
  WP-ACCEPT's (§6.3).
* **L-co** The JSON emitter's container stack lives on the heap, grows as needed (no depth limit,
  `out of memory` if it cannot) and is freed by `JSON_CLOSE` (§2.11.6).
* **L-cp** Named arguments are evaluated in source order: when that differs from parameter order,
  pass 2a writes the `seq` of `.t` temporaries of "Evaluation order" (§3.5.5), which makes R11's
  `seq` case reachable (§2.11.2).
* **L-cq** 228 and 232 are reported by `seaname`'s call pre-pass through `rerr`, the first check at
  a `call` node, keeping "Order across the two programs" (§2.11.2).
* **L-cr** Rule 39 lowers only the nodes of its table; rules 8, 9, 14, 24, 34 and 35 stay as written,
  so no earlier golden changes (§2.11.5).
* **L-cs** The `entries` capacity of `sealower` (now 22) and of `seagen_a64` and `seagen_x64` (now
  29) becomes 64 (room for phases 8 and 9), two edited lines per pass; `seaopt` and `sealopt` keep
  399 (§2.11.1).
* **L-ct** A golden that §8.6 inlining changes is re-derived from the rules by T2, never copied
  from output, as Decision 90 says (the 21 lowering dump tests of §6.2 and the `.res`, `.hir1` and
  `.hir` goldens of `el` 2 and kind `inl`); `stack_gap` of `tests/accept/w5_stats.sea` becomes
  inlined, which changes no output (§3.6.6, §6.2).
* **L-cu** For `write_json`, `str` is a JSON scalar: a `str` value is a `jval`, a `str[]` or `str[,]`
  a `jvec` or `jmat` (fixed-size ones through `dyn`), although §4.5's classes count `str` as a
  reference type (§3.5.7 step 4 as amended).
* **L-cv** A matrix of structs or records with no element (r × 0 or 0 × c) is written `[]` by a
  guard in pass 2b's expansion, matching LANGUAGE.md §11.4 (§3.5.7 step 4 as amended).
* **L-cw** `seaname`'s call pre-pass is iterative (a worklist for the effects fixpoint, an explicit
  stack for the cycle search), so Baysick's limit of 1 024 active `CALL`s does not bound the call
  graph (§2.11.2).
* **L-cx** `tests/accept.sh` writes a port's standard output and standard error outside its run
  directory, which must then hold only `NAME.json` and the executable; a path that is a directory is
  tested with `write_json(".", …)`, since git keeps no empty directory (§6.2, §6.3).
* **L-cy** (6b, agreed 2026-10-28) In a call that reports `unknown parameter` (224), `missing
  argument` (226) is not reported, because the unknown name may be the missing parameter. Amends
  §2.11.2 ("Named arguments"); code: `passes/seacheck/sc9call.bas`.
* **L-cz** (6b, 2026-10-28) Inside an `iblk`, the "one statement" of §3.6.6 rule 12 is each statement
  of the inlined body (the callee's statements, L-w), and an `iret` is a statement just as a `ret`
  is; the rule's "statements inside an `xblk` belong to the statement that holds the `xblk`" applies
  to the `xblk`s of the body, not to the body itself. Amends R26 and §3.6.6 rule 12.
* **L-da** (6b, 2026-10-28) R32's home H is always a new home, allocated before `do B` after the
  `tmp`s of the inline `xblk`. Under a `bind` H is copied (moved) into the local; under a `tbind`,
  `tasg`, `tret` or `eval` H is copied into the home the parent provides, in R27's place of the

  of the same section.
* **L-dc** (6b, 2026-10-28) A reordered call whose bound values are all constants writes `seq … 0`,

* **L-df** (6b, 2026-10-28) Decision 90 with several inlinable functions in one test: each gets the

* **L-di** (6c, agreed 2026-10-28) `elemental function cannot be recursive` (232) stands at the
